t: Loneliness scores did not significantly correlate with any HRV measure in any group or across all participants.
SDNN did not significantly correlate with clinical symptom measures (ADOS scores in autism, Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale in schizophrenia).
IQ scores did not significantly correlate with SDNN in the autism and schizophrenia groups, either separately or pooled.
Better performance on the BACS cognitive composite was associated with higher SDNN, a relationship driven primarily by the schizophrenia group.
Better visual learning performance was associated with higher SDNN, with a stronger correlation in schizophrenia than autism.
Faster processing speed was associated with lower SDNN, in contrast to the direction of other cognitive correlations.

Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in TAB2 were identified in 11 individuals from 8 families with a novel multisystemic disorder featuring cardiovascular, facial, musculoskeletal, and cutaneous anomalies.
An additional affected subject carried a heterozygous 52 kb microdeletion spanning TAB2 exons 1 to 3.
Luciferase reporter assays showed that all tested TAB2 point variants reduced NF-κB-mediated transcriptional activation compared with wild-type TAB2.
Immunoblot analysis of patient fibroblasts showed reduced TAK1 phosphorylation compared with expected normal levels.
Osteoblast differentiation assays performed on patient fibroblasts showed impaired differentiation capacity.
Luciferase reporter assays showed that all identified point variants of TAB2 significantly reduced NF-κB-mediated transcriptional activation compared with wild-type protein.
Immunoblot analysis of patient-derived fibroblasts showed reduced TAK1 phosphorylation downstream of TAB2 variants.
Osteoblast differentiation assays in patient-derived fibroblasts demonstrated impaired differentiation associated with TAB2 loss-of-function variants.
RNA sequencing of patient fibroblasts revealed deregulation of multiple pleiotropic signaling pathways, including TGFβ, Ras-MAPK, and Wnt signaling networks.

The pleiotropic phenotype caused by TAB2 loss-of-function variants partly overlaps with the previously described 6q25.1 (TAB2) microdeletion syndrome, supporting recognition as a distinct 'cardio-facial-cutaneous-articular syndrome.'
Pathogenic variants identified in this cohort cluster within a restricted linker region of exon 4 of TAB2, distinct from the larger microdeletions previously reported.

The pleiotropic clinical manifestations observed in patients with TAB2 exon 4 variants partly overlap with those described in the 6q25.1 (TAB2) microdeletion syndrome, supporting a shared mechanism of TAB2 haploinsufficiency.

The authors propose that this newly delineated multisystem disorder be termed cardio-facial-cutaneous-articular syndrome, reflecting its characteristic cardiovascular, facial, cutaneous, and musculoskeletal features.
COP distance and sway area were significantly greater in children with cerebral palsy and developmental coordination disorder compared to typically developing children.

Typically developing children did not show significantly different postural control parameters compared to children with developmental coordination disorder, unlike the comparison with cerebral palsy.
Clinical severity scores correlated with COP distance and Root Mean Square distance across all diagnostic subgroups.
Age influenced postural control parameters only within the typically developing group, not in the DCD or CP groups.
Sex did not significantly affect postural control outcomes in any of the studied groups.
Child-rated anxiety scores (C-SCARED) showed a progressive dose-dependent reduction with increasing days of TEN treatment and an overall reduction with TEN compared to sham.
Parent-rated anxiety scores (P-SCARED) showed a dose-dependent decrease with more TEN treatment days and an overall reduction compared to sham.
The Parent-Rated Anxiety Scale (PRAS-ASD) decreased in most participants with a dose effect over treatment days, but the overall combined effect versus sham was not significant.
Total and sleep-anxiety subscale scores on the Children's Sleep Health Questionnaire decreased numerically one week after TEN treatment but did not reach statistical significance.
Performance on the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test (working memory/attention under stress) improved with more days of TEN and was better on TEN days than sham.
Performance on the symbol search task did not significantly change with TEN treatment and numerically worsened across days.
Working-memory performance on the n-back task improved with more TEN sessions and was better on TEN days than sham.
Salivary cortisol levels did not differ significantly between sham and TEN days, did not change with more TEN sessions, and did not change significantly across each experimental day.
At the group level, salivary alpha-amylase levels did not differ significantly between sham and TEN days and showed no consistent dose effect.
Heart rate variability was significantly higher (improved autonomic balance) during TEN stimulation and during the PASAT on TEN days compared to sham.
Phasic electrodermal activity during anxiety-provoking tasks decreased after the first TEN session but returned to baseline thereafter, with no significant group-level treatment effect.
Higher baseline IQ was associated with higher baseline anxiety scores on both the C-SCARED and P-SCARED, but not the PRAS.
Higher IQ was associated with better baseline PASAT performance but not with baseline NBT or SST performance.
Higher IQ was associated with higher baseline salivary alpha-amylase but not with its change or with cortisol.
Higher IQ was associated with more moderate (smaller) parent-rated improvement in anxiety on the P-SCARED and PRAS with TEN treatment.
Participants who responded well to TEN (responders) performed worse at baseline (sham day) on the symbol search task and PASAT than non-responders.

Participants defined as TEN responders (≥30% average C-SCARED improvement) showed a significantly greater decrease in anxiety than non-responders, with the difference increasing with more treatment days.

Salivary alpha-amylase decreased across treatment days and within sessions after TEN in responders, but progressively increased across days and showed inconsistent within-day change in non-responders.
TEN was well tolerated with no significant adverse events reported, and no participant reported discomfort from electrode placement or stimulation.

One female participant with a history of precocious puberty and periodic oligomenorrhea (off suppressive medication for 3 months) experienced a recurrence of oligomenorrhea after the trial; causal relationship to TEN is unknown.
Fecal/oral microbiome studies in ASD children consistently show decreased overall bacterial diversity together with an increased Bacteroidetes/Firmicutes ratio.
The Clostridium genus is the microbial taxon most frequently reported as overrepresented in the gut microbiota of individuals with ASD.
Gastrointestinal problems in children with ASD range from mild gastroesophageal reflux to severe symptoms, with chronic constipation being the most common complication.
Anxiety disorders (specific phobia, OCD, social anxiety disorder) are highly prevalent in individuals with ASD.
A person with ASD is reported to be four times more likely to experience a depressive disorder than a neurotypical individual.

Sleep disorders including insomnia, bedtime resistance, parasomnia, morning rise problems, daytime sleepiness, and sleep-disordered breathing are characteristic of individuals with ASD and impact social/academic functioning.
Individuals with ASD show four times more psychiatric and systemic comorbidities (anxiety, mood disorders, depressive disorders, sleep disorders, GI dysfunction) than those without ASD.

One recent open-label trial of microbiota transfer therapy (MTT) reported an 80% reduction in gastrointestinal symptoms in ASD, including significant improvement in constipation and abdominal pain, with prolonged duration of effect.

Intranasal oxytocin has shown only marginal benefits for social deficits in ASD and, due to rapid metabolism, poor brain penetration, and cross-activity at vasopressin receptors, continuous intranasal oxytocin alone cannot currently be recommended for treating social symptoms in high-functioning adults with ASD.
Plasma oxytocin levels are decreased in patients with dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome, and lower plasma oxytocin is also measured in children with recurrent abdominal pain.

ASD is associated with autonomic nervous system dysfunction, characterized by sympathetic over-activation driven by a background parasympathetic activity deficit, producing autonomic imbalance evidenced by faster/less variable heart rate, respiratory dysrhythmia, chronic sensory hyperexcitation, and increased tonic electrodermal activity.

ASD adults show distinct autonomic signatures in heart rate variability: lower high-frequency normalized spectral heart rate (HFnu) during wakefulness and a higher LF/HF ratio during REM sleep compared to children, regardless of clinical status.
Mice treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics that shift flora toward yeast dominance display behavioral abnormalities commonly associated with ASD.

Germ-free mice have lower myenteric nerve density and fewer neuronal cell bodies, along with an increased proportion of inhibitory nitroergic neurons in the small intestine, indicating gut microbiota is required for normal postnatal ENS development.

In mice, gut microbiota depletion during early adolescence reduces hypothalamic oxytocin and vasopressin levels under stress, and normalizing oxytocin levels reduces anxiety-like behavior and corrects cognitive deficits.

Transgenic mice with deletion of enteric glial cells develop fulminant jejunoileitis due to increased intestinal permeability, indicating enteric glial cells normally maintain gut barrier function via S-nitrosoglutathione-mediated upregulation of tight junction proteins.
The same increased Bacteroidetes/Firmicutes ratio observed in ASD gut microbiota has also been reported in depressive patients and in depressive-like rat models.

Unlike other psychiatric disorders with persistent dysbiosis (schizophrenia, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder), which show concurrent chronic low-grade systemic inflammation, ASD-associated dysbiosis is not accompanied by clear evidence of chronic low-grade systemic inflammation, despite likely neuroinflammation.

The authors' central hypothesis is that ASD-related autonomic imbalance (sympathetic over-activation, parasympathetic deficit) attenuates cholinergic stimulation of Paneth and goblet cell antimicrobial peptide/mucus and lectin secretion, decreasing bactericidal activity and thereby driving the persistent, heterogeneous dysbiosis and osmotic dysregulation seen in ASD.
Numerous studies of microbiota transfer therapy (MTT) for ASD-associated GI problems have shown some improvement, but typically of short duration.
Systematic reviews of dietary manipulations such as nutrient supplementation or gluten- and casein-free diets found little evidence of attenuating effects on ASD symptoms.
Adolescent males with Asperger syndrome showed a blunted cortisol awakening response compared to typically developing peers.

The majority of studies in prepubescent children with ASD found similar cortisol awakening response compared to typically developing children, suggesting CAR variation may emerge later in adolescence.
Lower diurnal salivary cortisol was associated with higher rates of repetitive behaviors in children with ASD aged 3-9 years, suggesting a possible self-soothing or down-regulated HPA function.

Youth with ASD showed a more shallow cortisol slope from morning to evening and higher evening cortisol values compared to typically developing peers, with elevated cortisol persisting across adolescence.
The most consistent finding across multiple studies is higher between-subject and within-subject basal cortisol variability in children and adolescents with ASD compared to controls.

Two studies reported a slower cortisol response to ACTH stimulation in ASD children, with lower plasma cortisol levels at 60 and 90 minutes post-infusion compared to controls, with no group differences by 120 minutes.

Children with ASD showed higher rates of non-suppression of cortisol in the dexamethasone suppression test compared to typically developing children, suggesting disturbed negative feedback of the HPA axis.

Studies using public speaking stress tasks such as the TSST-C predominantly demonstrated a blunted or relatively stable cortisol response in children and adolescents with ASD compared to typically developing controls, while peer interaction paradigms showed enhanced HPA responsivity in ASD.

In a large sample of early adolescents with ASD (n=138) compared to TD children (n=103), a blunted cortisol response and faster return to basal levels was demonstrated during the TSST-C, with age contributing to increased cortisol response to social evaluative threat during early adolescence.
High-functioning ASD children aged 7-15 years showed baseline sympathetic underactivity indexed by lower electrodermal activity than typically developing controls.

Several studies reported lower amplitude of respiratory sinus arrhythmia and/or faster heart rate at baseline or resting state in children and adolescents with ASD compared to controls, consistent with lower resting parasympathetic activity and higher sympathetic activity.

Higher baseline RSA amplitudes in ASD children were associated with better social behavior and receptive language abilities, and baseline RSA and RSA reactivity predicted restricted repetitive behavior severity.
Reduced tonic heart rate variability was found in children with ASD relative to typically developing children and was associated with atypical attentional responsivity to sensory stimulation.

Children with ASD (8-15 years) showed elevated heart rate at baseline and during a stress task with elevated but blunted phasic electrodermal activity compared to TD children, interpreted as a hyper-sympathetic state insufficiently attenuated by parasympathetic influences.
Adolescent males with ASD showed reduced sympathetic activation, indicated by a lower change in pre-ejection period, at the onset of a modified TSST compared to TD controls.

Lower afternoon salivary alpha-amylase levels significantly distinguished ASD children aged 20-72 months from age-matched children with Down syndrome and typically developing controls, with little diurnal variation observed in the ASD group.
Salivary alpha-amylase secretion levels were approximately 1.5-fold higher in preschool-aged ASD children with lower IQ.

In ASD children aged 10-13 years, an autonomic balance of increased parasympathetic combined with decreased sympathetic activity was associated with the lowest levels of depressive symptoms, whereas no single physiological system alone was associated with depressive symptoms.

Children with ASD show altered functional connectivity between the amygdala and prefrontal cortex, and reduced amygdala coupling with ventrolateral/ventromedial PFC during emotional face perception tasks, which may reflect early life stress or chronic stress influences and contribute to prolonged stress responses.

Multiple studies have demonstrated elevated plasma/serum pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12p40, IL-12, and interferon-γ, or decreased anti-inflammatory TGFβ1, in individuals with ASD.
Upregulation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway has been reported in children with ASD, suggesting a possible role of immune pathways in HPA axis dysfunction in ASD.

School-aged children with ASD had higher serum concentrations of high mobility group box 1 protein (HMGB1), an alarmin implicated in stress-induced innate immune sensitization and neuroinflammation, than typically developing controls.

Decreased glucocorticoid receptor mRNA levels and negative associations between cytokine mRNA and glucocorticoid receptor levels were reported in ASD subjects, suggesting a possible role of inflammation in altered glucocorticoid receptor function.

Adults with ASD showed higher anticipatory circulating cortisol and sustained stress reactivity to a social evaluative threat (TSST), whereas adolescents with ASD showed a more reactive cortisol response pattern with no anticipatory response, despite no baseline differences.

In the largest population-based study to date, a stressful event such as death of a first-degree relative, especially during the third trimester of pregnancy or the second postnatal year, increased the risk for ASD in the offspring.
One study found no association between prenatal maternal stress and ASD risk in the offspring, contrasting with other reports linking PMS to increased ASD risk.

21.4% of autistic adults reported a formal diagnosis of at least one central sensitivity syndrome (fibromyalgia, ME/CFS, IBS, restless legs syndrome, or TMJD), with 41 participants reporting more than one.

60% of autistic adults scored at or above the clinical cut-off of 40 on the CSI, indicating clinically significant central sensitisation symptoms, but only 31% of this high-scoring group had a formal CSS diagnosis.
Autistic adults with a diagnosed CSS scored significantly higher on the CSI than those without a CSS diagnosis.
Autistic adults with a diagnosed CSS reported significantly greater sensory sensitivity (lower SPQ scores) than those without a CSS diagnosis.
Autistic adults with a diagnosed CSS reported significantly more anxiety than those without a CSS diagnosis.
Autistic adults with a diagnosed CSS reported significantly more depressive symptoms than those without a CSS diagnosis.
Autistic adults with a diagnosed CSS reported significantly lower subjective wellbeing than those without a CSS diagnosis.
Autistic adults with a diagnosed CSS rated their physical health significantly lower than those without a CSS diagnosis.
Autistic traits (AQ-Short score) did not significantly differ between autistic adults with and without a diagnosed CSS after Bonferroni correction.

Confirmatory factor analysis supported a bifactor structure (one general factor plus four orthogonal factors) as the best-fitting model for the CSI in this autistic sample, supporting use of the CSI total score to assess central sensitisation in autistic adults.
Autistic women were significantly over-represented among those with a diagnosed central sensitivity syndrome compared to men.
Autistic women were significantly over-represented in the high-CSI group and scored significantly higher on the CSI overall than autistic men.
Autistic women reported significantly greater sensory sensitivity (lower SPQ scores) than autistic men.
There was no significant gender difference in depression scores between autistic men and women.

In hierarchical regression, sensory sensitivity and anxiety were strong significant predictors of CSI scores, and once they were entered, autistic traits (AQ) were no longer a significant predictor, with the full model explaining 50.9% of variance in CSI scores.

Path analysis indicated that the association between autistic traits and CSI (CSS symptom) scores was fully mediated by sensory sensitivity and anxiety, with autistic traits showing no significant direct effect on CSI scores.
CSI scores correlated positively with anxiety, female gender, and autistic traits, and negatively with sensory sensitivity (lower SPQ score = higher sensitivity).

The authors note that prior literature suggests autistic people (and people with ADHD) are over-represented in joint hypermobility/Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, mast cell activation syndrome, and dysautonomia, which frequently co-occur with or underlie CSS diagnoses.
16p11.2 deletions are strongly associated with autism and intellectual disability, while 16p11.2 duplications increase risk more strongly for psychotic disorders.
People with 16p11.2 deletions have higher BMI and lower head circumference, while those with duplications show the opposite phenotype.
A 16-year-old female with ASD, ADHD, learning difficulties, trichotillomania, self-injurious behavior, and depression was found by chromosomal microarray to carry a 16p11.2 duplication.
Longitudinal treatment including aripiprazole was associated with a decrease in the patient's anxiety and behavioral outbursts and a stable weight without additional gain.

Omega-3 fatty acids were recommended for the 16p11.2 duplication patient to reduce psychosis risk and to counteract antipsychotic-induced hypertriglyceridemia, based on evidence in other ultra-high-risk genetic conditions.

Cognitive-behavioral therapy was recommended as the treatment of choice given the patient's susceptibility to psychosis, based on its benefit in preventing transition to psychosis in high-risk individuals.

A maternally inherited 61 kb deletion spanning exon 1 of DLG2 transcript variant 9 was identified in a boy with mild intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, and language disorder who showed progressive cognitive decline from age 12.

DLG2 (PSD-93) anchors NMDA glutamate receptors and K+ channels at glutamatergic postsynaptic scaffolds, and its disruption is detrimental to hippocampal long-term potentiation; DLG2 mutant mice show deficits in associative learning and autism-like behaviors.
Rare disruptive DLG2 gene variants are associated with schizophrenia, intellectual disability, ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, and bipolar disorder.
Low-dose lithium treatment (serum level ~0.50 mEq/L) in the DLG2-deletion patient led to steady improvement in non-verbal IQ, reaching a maximum Leiter-R score of 94 after 8 months.
Cognitive improvement in the DLG2-deletion patient persisted more than one year after lithium was spontaneously discontinued, with non-verbal IQ of 84 compared to pre-treatment IQ/DQ under 65.
Selective visual attention, measured with the Bell test, steadily improved during lithium treatment in the DLG2-deletion patient.

Two anecdotal prior reports describe lithium reversing cognitive regression in patients with Phelan-McDermid syndrome due to SHANK3 haploinsufficiency, at slightly higher serum lithium levels (0.7-0.8 mEq/L) than used in the DLG2 case.

A 58-year-old female with spontaneous colon perforation, IBS, fibromyalgia, and Raynaud's phenomenon was found to carry a likely pathogenic COL3A1 variant (c.1961G>A; p.Gly654Glu) disrupting the collagen triple helix Gly-X-Y motif, causing vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Six affected individuals of both sexes across three generations of the family had colon perforation or surgical procedures due to imminent perforation risk, consistent with vascular EDS inheritance.
The proband with vascular EDS had comorbid fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and Raynaud's phenomenon since 18 years of age, in addition to colon perforation.
For COL3A1 pathogenic variants generally, major complications occur in 15% of patients prior to genetic testing, median survival is 50 years, and about 60% of patients are diagnosed before age 18.

Gastrointestinal perforations, usually involving the sigmoid colon, occur in about 15% of individuals with a COL3A1 pathogenic variant but seldom in those with null variants, consistent with this family's missense variant presentation.
Bowel rupture in COL3A1-related vascular EDS is rarely lethal (3%), with most deaths resulting from surgical complications such as hemorrhage or poor tissue healing rather than the rupture itself.
Routine colonoscopy was avoided for the vascular EDS proband and at-risk family members due to iatrogenic perforation risk; non-invasive gastrointestinal imaging surveillance was planned instead.
Two of the proband's adult daughters carried the same COL3A1 variant and displayed features of a connective tissue disorder including joint hyperflexibility and joint pain.

A strong association between the DD genotype of the ACE insertion/deletion polymorphism and the D allele was found in autistic patients, suggesting genetic diversity of the RAS may increase autism risk.
AVP concentrations in the CSF were found to be lower in children with autism, and AVP levels correlated with symptom severity.
Neonatal CSF AVP concentration was reported to predict a subsequent diagnosis of autism.
Oxytocin receptor (OTR) mRNA levels were lower in autistic patients, although no significant association was found for plasma/CSF oxytocin itself in this comparison.
V1aR mRNA levels were found to be lower in autistic patients.
In a Korean autistic population, significant associations were found between ASD and SNP RS1 and SNP RS3 in the 5′ flanking region of the V1aR (AVPR1A) gene.
A North American population study reported a significant link between autism and polymorphisms of the AVP V1a/V1b receptor genes, specifically SNPs rs35369693 and rs28632197.
Intranasal application of AVP for 4-5 weeks improved social abilities and reduced anxiety symptoms in children with ASD.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found that long-term intranasal application of oxytocin in individuals with ASD is well tolerated and safe.
A study of 314 autism-affected families suggested the OXTR gene region on chromosome 3p24-26 may increase susceptibility to autism spectrum disorder.
Multiple population-specific studies reported associations between OXTR SNPs and autism spectrum disorder susceptibility in Chinese, Caucasian, Japanese, European, and North American cohorts.
Two meta-analyses (of 8 and 10 studies) found significant associations between OXTR SNPs rs2254298, rs7632287, and rs2268491 and autism spectrum disorder.
Plasma oxytocin levels were found to be lower in children with autism spectrum disorder compared to controls.
Children with ASD had lower levels of the bioactive amidated form of oxytocin but higher levels of the OT precursor, suggesting altered peptide processing.
Intravenous oxytocin infusion was shown to ameliorate repetitive behavior in adults with ASD and Asperger's disorder.

In a clinical trial of 106 ASD patients, intranasal oxytocin reduced repetitive behavior and increased gaze fixation on socially relevant regions, but did not improve the primary outcome (ADOS social reciprocity subscale).
Randomized crossover trials in children with ASD found that intranasal oxytocin improved caregiver-rated social responsiveness.
Intranasal oxytocin enhanced learning in response to social targets and feedback in ASD, correlated with nucleus accumbens activation on fMRI.
Other studies failed to find beneficial effects of oxytocin treatment in autism spectrum disorder.
Human ACE2 binds the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and serves as the entry receptor mediating viral transmission into target cells, including brain cells.

Survivors of COVID-19 have been reported to manifest aggravated neuropsychiatric symptoms including cognitive/attention deficits (brain fog), new-onset anxiety, depression, psychosis, seizures, and suicidal behavior.
CSF vasopressin concentrations are lower in children with autism and correlate with symptom severity, and neonatal CSF AVP levels can predict a later autism diagnosis.
OTR and V1aR mRNA levels are lower in autistic patients, though no CSF oxytocin association was found.
In a Korean population, SNPs RS1 and RS3 in the 5′-flanking region of the V1aR gene were significantly associated with autism spectrum disorder.
In a North American population, V1bR SNPs rs35369693 and rs28632197 were significantly linked to autism spectrum disorder.
Intranasal AVP administered for 4-5 weeks improved social abilities and reduced anxiety symptoms in individuals with ASD.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found long-term intranasal oxytocin use in ASD to be well tolerated and safe.
A study of 314 autism-affected families suggested the p24-26 region of chromosome 3, expressing the OTR gene, may increase susceptibility to ASD.
Two meta-analyses (8 and 10 studies) reported significant associations between OTR SNPs rs2254298, rs7632287, and rs2268491 and ASD susceptibility.
Lower plasma oxytocin levels have been repeatedly observed in children with ASD.
Children with ASD show altered oxytocin peptide processing, with lower bioactive amidated OT and higher OT precursor levels.
OT infusion ameliorated repetitive behavior in adults with ASD and Asperger's disorder.
In a clinical trial of 106 ASD patients, intranasal oxytocin reduced repetitive behavior and increased gaze fixation on social regions but did not improve the primary ADOS social reciprocity outcome.
Randomized crossover trials in children with ASD found that intranasal oxytocin improved caregiver-rated social responsiveness.
Intranasal oxytocin enhanced learning in response to social targets and feedback, correlated with nucleus accumbens activation on fMRI.
Other studies failed to find beneficial effects of oxytocin treatment in ASD.
The DD genotype and D allele of the ACE insertion/deletion polymorphism were strongly associated with autism, suggesting RAS genetic diversity may increase autism risk.
Vasopressin-deficient Brattleboro rats and V1aR knockout mice exhibit schizophrenia-like symptoms with impaired social behavior.
In the MAM rat model of schizophrenia, AVP receptor concentrations were significantly lower in the prefrontal cortex and hypothalamus.
Post-mortem studies revealed lower AVP levels in the temporal cortex and reduced AVP mRNA expression in the PVN of schizophrenic patients.
Blood AVP levels in schizophrenia patients were variably elevated or unaltered, with a positive correlation between blood AVP and symptom severity found in female but not male patients.
Some schizophrenic patients with inappropriately high blood AVP levels manifest polydipsia, hypoosmolality, and hyponatremia, further potentiated by antipsychotic treatment.
Intranasal DDAVP (desmopressin) increased the effectiveness of risperidone in reducing negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
SNPs in the shared AVP/OT chromosomal region 20p13 (rs2740204, rs4813626, rs3011589) were significantly associated with schizophrenia.

Plasma oxytocin is lower in schizophrenia patients than healthy controls, and negatively correlates with symptom severity; the MAM model also shows reduced OT and OTR in prefrontal cortex and hypothalamus.
Intranasal oxytocin showed positive effects on social cognition in schizophrenia in some studies, but clinical trials and meta-analyses overall found no significant therapeutic effect.
CSF AVP concentrations were lower in children with autism and correlated with symptom severity.
Neonatal CSF AVP concentration was predictive of a subsequent autism diagnosis.

In a Korean cohort, V1aR receptor 5'-flanking SNPs RS1 and RS3 were significantly associated with autism spectrum disorder.
In a North American population, V1bR SNPs rs35369693 and rs28632197 were linked to autism spectrum disorder.

Multiple population-specific OXTR SNPs (Chinese, Caucasian, Japanese, European, North American cohorts) have been associated with ASD susceptibility.
Two meta-analyses (8 and 10 studies) confirmed associations between OXTR SNPs rs2254298, rs7632287, and rs2268491 and ASD.

Intranasal OT enhanced learning in response to social targets and feedback, correlating with nucleus accumbens activation on fMRI.

COVID-19 survivors show aggravated neuropsychiatric symptoms including cognitive/attention deficits (brain fog), new-onset anxiety, depression, psychosis, seizures, and suicidal behavior, potentially related to RAS dysregulation.
ACE2-mediated SARS-CoV-2 entry into carotid bodies has been hypothesized to contribute to silent hypoxemia in COVID-19.
Post-mortem studies found elevated AVP mRNA expression in the PVN/SON and a greater number of AVP and OT neurons in the PVN of patients with major depressive disorder.
Orally active V1bR antagonists reduced hyperemotionality and produced anxiolytic- and antidepressant-like effects in rodent models.
Oral V1bR antagonist TASP0390325 blocked the ACTH elevation induced by combined CRH and desmopressin administration.
The DD genotype and D allele of the ACE insertion/deletion polymorphism were strongly associated with autism, suggesting RAS genetic diversity may increase autism risk.

Two independent meta-analyses (encompassing 8 and 10 studies respectively) found associations between oxytocin receptor gene SNP polymorphisms (rs2254298, rs7632287, rs2268491) and autism spectrum disorder.
Children with ASD had lower levels of the bioactive amidated form of oxytocin and higher levels of the OT precursor, suggesting altered peptide processing in the brains of autistic children.

In a clinical trial of 106 patients with ASD, intranasally applied oxytocin reduced repetitive behavior and increased gaze fixation on socially relevant regions, but did not improve the primary outcome measure of social reciprocity (ADOS subscale).
Randomized crossover trials in children with ASD showed that intranasal oxytocin treatment improved caregiver-rated social responsiveness.
Intranasally applied oxytocin enhanced learning in response to social targets and feedback in ASD, an effect correlated with activation of the nucleus accumbens detected by functional MRI.
Some studies failed to find beneficial effects of oxytocin treatment in autism spectrum disorder.
A systematic review and meta-analysis of long-term intranasal oxytocin application in ASD found the treatment to be well tolerated and safe.
In a Korean population, gene polymorphism studies found a significant association between ASD and SNPs RS1 and RS3 in the 5' flanking regions of the vasopressin V1a receptor gene.
A study of 314 autism-affected families suggested that the chromosomal region p24-26 of chromosome 3, which expresses the OTR gene, may increase susceptibility to ASD.

OTR gene polymorphisms associated with ASD susceptibility differ by population: rs2254298 and rs53576 in a Chinese population, rs2254298 in Caucasian and Japanese populations, rs237887 in a European population, and rs2268493, rs1042778, and rs7632287 in a North American population.
Four to five weeks of intranasally applied vasopressin improved social abilities and reduced anxiety symptoms in patients, as reported by Parker et al.
Stimulation of V1b receptors in the hippocampus enhances social memory in mice.
Intranasally applied oxytocin did not influence the activity of brain regions affected by Alzheimer's disease in AD patients.
In Alzheimer's disease patients, plasma oxytocin concentration and OT signal value on MRI correlated with the volume of the right parahippocampal gyrus, an association not seen in controls.
Changes in methylation of the oxytocin gene were found in patients with Alzheimer's disease.
Intranasal application of the AVP derivative AVP-(4-8) markedly improved working memory and long-term memory in the APP/PS1 mouse model of Alzheimer's disease.
Joint hypermobility is highly prevalent among individuals with ASD, to the extent that some authors classify autism among hypermobility spectrum disorders.
Microglia, cells of mesodermal origin, comprise 10-15% of white matter and contribute to neurogenesis, axonal sprouting, brain wiring, and synaptic pruning during development.
ABIDE project neuroimaging data show short-range hyper-connectivity in parietal and subcortical fibers together with hypo-connectivity of cortico-cortical transcallosal fibers in ASD.
Immune-mediated inflammatory skin pathologies occur with a 5:1 frequency in ASD compared to the healthy population, predisposing to sensory and thermoregulatory alterations.
Slingsby et al. found children with ASD were more likely to have various dermatological alterations, particularly on the legs, knees, and forearms.

Yao et al. reported that activation of platelets and vascular endothelium, with altered platelet aggregation and oxidative-stress-related capillary dysfunction, may contribute to dermatological alterations in autism.
Immune-mediated skin inflammation in ASD is underpinned by increased nitric oxide levels and an altered CD4:CD8 lymphocyte ratio.
Eczema is one of the most commonly encountered atopic skin diseases in ASD, with a reported prevalence of up to 10.2%.
Sensory transmission delay was found in about 69% of cutaneous and subcutaneous alterations, correlating with altered tactile sensory processing in ASD.
Asthma and allergic rhinitis show a 5:1 prevalence in ASD compared to healthy subjects, with food-related cross-allergies and sensitivities affecting both manifestations.

A 2008 Egyptian study found that autism severity correlated with respiratory manifestations such as exhalation wheezing, chest constriction, and nocturnal breathing difficulty unresponsive to bronchodilators.
A 2009 Swedish study by Larsonn et al. found a greater prevalence of asthma in children with ASD aged 4-8 years.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, autistic children showed increased susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection and more severe forms of the disease.

A 2016 Japanese study found that ASD children with reduced resting vagal activity, measured by ECG parameters, showed alterations in self-regulation and greater behavioral dysregulation in response to unpredictable sensory stimuli.

A 2013 American study found that dysfunctions in cardiac autonomic control were directly related to attentional, emotional, and cognitive dysfunctions and consequent difficulties in social interactions, particularly relevant in children with ADHD or hyperactivity/inattention traits.

Sectorial retinal thickening and increased vascular density have been found in ASD subjects without a corresponding increase in blood flow, suggesting impaired autoregulation of blood flow relative to metabolic demand.
Full-field electroretinogram analysis in ASD subjects showed alterations in both cone and rod function, which are partially compensated at the post-receptoral level.
Gillberg et al. (1983) reported hearing loss in 13.3% of their autistic study population, attributed partly to recurrent otitis media.

Autosomal dominant mutations in the CDK8 gene are associated with intellectual developmental disorder featuring hypotonia and behavioral abnormalities, within conditions linking ASD and connective tissue alteration.
Autosomal recessive mutations in NTNG2 are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring behavioral abnormalities, absent speech, and hypotonia.
X-linked mutations in FMR1 are associated with Fragile X syndrome, a condition combining connective tissue and cognitive alterations linked to autism.
The UBE3A gene at the 15q11-q13 locus, implicated in Prader-Willi syndrome, is among thirty genes in this region associated with ASD prevalence and altered developmental trajectories.

Antigen exposure such as gluten at the intestinal epithelial barrier in ASD can increase zonulin and claudin synthesis, promoting greater intestinal permeability and immune reactivity with downstream cognitive and socio-linguistic effects.
Bacterial overgrowth in ASD is characterized by reduced Bifidobacteria and relative growth of Clostridia, detectable on stool analysis as a sign of tissue inflammation.

A 2016 Japanese study found that ASD children with reduced resting vagal activity, measured via precise electrocardiographic parameters, showed altered self-regulation and greater behavioral dysregulation in response to unpredictable visual-auditory stimuli.

A 2013 American study found that dysfunctions in cardiac autonomic control are directly related to attentional, emotional, and cognitive dysfunctions and consequent impairments in social interaction with peers, particularly in children with comorbid ADHD.

Autosomal dominant mutations in CDK8 are associated with intellectual developmental disorder featuring hypotonia and behavioral abnormalities, in the context of ASD-related joint hypermobility conditions.
Autosomal recessive mutations in NTNG2 are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring behavioral abnormalities, absent speech, and hypotonia.
An X-linked mutation in FMR1 causes Fragile X syndrome, which is associated with both autism and joint hypermobility.

The 15q11-q13 chromosomal region containing about thirty genes, including UBE3A, is frequently associated with ASD prevalence and with developmental, behavioral, and emotional trajectories, as well as with Prader-Willi syndrome.

Sectorial retinal thickening and increased vascular density, without a corresponding increase in blood flow, have been found in ASD subjects, indicating impaired self-regulation of retinal blood flow relative to metabolic demand.
Full-field electroretinogram analysis in ASD subjects showed alterations in both cone and rod responses, which were partially compensated at the post-receptoral level.
ASD subjects show asymmetry of saccades and difficulty with slow pursuit tracking of moving targets, suggesting impaired functional integrity of attention-related brain networks.

Gillberg et al. (1983) reported hearing loss in 13.3% of an autistic population, attributed largely to a higher prevalence of recurrent otitis media related to reduced immune efficiency and eardrum anatomy.
Latency anomalies in brainstem auditory evoked potential recordings have been found in children with ASD, attributed to altered myelin sheath maturation.
Cortical auditory evoked potentials show alterations at the level of cortical auditory integration in ASD subjects.
A study reported significant asymmetry between the two hemispheres in the reception and processing of auditory stimuli in ASD.
Neuroimaging studies report increased limbic system involvement, compared to controls, related to specific auditory stimulus avoidance/seeking behaviors typical of ASD.

Radiological data from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) project showed short-range hyper-connectivity in parietal and subcortical fibers alongside hypo-connectivity of cortico-cortical transcallosal fibers, plus volumetric and network anomalies, in ASD.
Immune-mediated inflammatory skin pathologies occur with a 5:1 frequency in ASD compared to the healthy population, predisposing to inflammation and altered sensory perception/thermoregulation.
Asthma and allergic rhinitis show a 5:1 prevalence in ASD compared to healthy subjects, with food-related cross-allergies and sensitivities contributing to both manifestations.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, increased susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection and more severe disease courses were observed in autistic children.

A 2008 Egyptian study found a correlation between autism severity and respiratory manifestations such as wheezing, chest constriction, and nocturnal breathing difficulty unresponsive to bronchodilators, plus symptoms following environmental allergen exposure.
A 2009 Swedish study by Larsson et al. found a greater prevalence of asthma in children with ASD aged 4-8 years.
Eczema is reported as one of the most frequently encountered atopic diseases in ASD, with a literature prevalence of up to 10.2%.
GABAergic and glutamatergic circuits are altered in ASD subjects, affecting the excitation-inhibition balance and potentially explaining hypersensitivity to environmental stimuli.

A clinical proposal associates chronic somatic fatigue and ligament laxity, detectable with body composition analysis tools, with psychopathological manifestations within pediatric hyperlaxity syndromes.

Whole genome sequencing identified a homozygous NTRK1 splice-site duplication (c.287+2dup), inherited from both parents, as the causal mutation for the patient's congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (CIPA).
The patient's Full Scale IQ score of 67, assessed by WPPSI-IV, indicated mild intellectual disability.
ADI-R and ADOS assessment scores for communication and social functioning exceeded the diagnostic threshold, supporting an ASD diagnosis.
PEP-3 evaluation of motor, communication, and behavioral domains indicated the patient had moderate developmental delay.

TEACCH-based intervention (one-to-one coaching, exercise, feeding, game and music classes, plus family training) improved the patient's language, motor, and social skills, and also reduced his self-mutilating behavior.
Besides the CIPA-causing NTRK1 mutation, the patient carried a MYBPC3 variant (c.2543C>T) that has previously been reported in four other patients with ASD.
Additional variants in OPLAH, KCNV2, ABCC8, PARN, and KARS1 were detected in the patient in addition to the NTRK1 mutation, but whether they contributed to the ASD phenotype is unknown.
A cited study of 23 CIPA patients found a negative correlation between intelligence quotient and age.
Approximately 40% of patients with ASD have developmental delays, and about 70% of those show some degree of intellectual disability, according to cited literature.
Many children with CIPA exhibit varying degrees of developmental retardation and severe ADHD symptoms, as noted in prior literature.

Children with ASD showed significantly greater postural sway than typically developing children across all four Biodex m-CTSIB testing conditions (eyes open/firm, eyes closed/firm, eyes open/foam, eyes closed/foam).

ASD children showed a disproportionately large increase in postural sway when vision was blocked compared with controls, suggesting heavy reliance on visual cues to maintain balance and a broader deficit in sensory integration rather than a single afferent pathway defect.

Within the ASD group, older children (10-14 years) showed lower (improved) postural sway scores than younger children (6-9 years) in the eyes open/firm surface and eyes open/foam surface conditions, suggesting some age-related improvement in postural stability.

Within the ASD group, children with an IQ score of 70-89 had higher (worse) postural sway scores across all testing conditions compared with ASD children with an IQ score of 90 or above, indicating lower IQ is associated with poorer postural stability.

Baseline RSA values in most children with ASD fall within the normal population range for age, indicating no autonomic dysfunction despite statistically significant group differences reported in several studies.

Kushki et al. found no significant differences between ASD and typically developing children in performance or autonomic reactivity across five cognitive/social tasks, despite reporting 'overall autonomic hyperarousal.'

Vaughan van Hecke et al. reported significantly lower baseline RSA in ASD children compared to controls, but these values fell within the normal population range, undermining claims of autonomic dysfunction.

Edmiston et al. found average baseline RSA in ASD adolescents (~6.9 ln(ms2)) statistically different from controls yet within the normal physiological range, concluding 'reduced physiological self-regulation,' a conclusion the reviewing authors reject.

Bal et al. reported significantly faster baseline heart rate and concluded 'lower overall vagal regulation' and 'hyperactive sympathetic activity' in ASD children, but the reviewed heart rate values remained within normal age-matched ranges.
Bricout et al. found that children with ASD showed no clinical signs of dysautonomia on head-up tilt testing and had baseline parasympathetic tone (RMSSD) not different from controls.

In a case series of six ASD patients with autonomic symptoms (postural lightheadedness, near syncope, GI dysmotility, early satiety), all exhibited postural tachycardia but none had orthostatic hypotension.

Guy et al. reported statistically lower RSA across cognitive and social tasks in ASD children (interpreted as vagal withdrawal supporting polyvagal theory), but absolute RSA values (6.29-6.61 ln(ms2)) remained within the normal range for typically developing children.

Muscatello et al. found ASD and typically developing youth did not differ in mean RSA or RSA responsivity during a social stress test (TSST-F) when controlling for age, despite the paper's title implying decreased parasympathetic response.

Toichi and Kamio found no differences between high-functioning adults with ASD and controls in heart rate, sympathetic activity, or resting parasympathetic activity, though individual variability in parasympathetic direction of change was noted.

A meta-analysis of HRV studies in ASD concluded that low HRV could be a potential biomarker but that it does not differentiate ASD from other psychiatric disorders, and comorbidities were not adequately accounted for.

Ferguson et al. found a significant correlation between lower gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., constipation) and lower parasympathetic tone in children with ASD, an association strengthened in those with co-occurring anxiety.

Nyström et al. concluded that infants at risk for autism have a hypersensitive pupillary light reflex suggestive of cholinergic autonomic disruption, though most infants' latency and constriction amplitudes fell within the normal control range.

Daluwatte et al. found children with ASD had significantly longer pupillary light reflex latency and reduced constriction amplitude compared to controls, suggested to reflect parasympathetic dysfunction, but this was not accompanied by differences in RMSSD.
In a cohort of 154 ASD children vs 116 controls, average heart rate was significantly higher in the ASD group, but this difference disappeared when only non-medicated ASD children were analyzed.

Mathewson et al. found that adults with ASD taking antipsychotic medication had significantly higher heart rate and lower RSA than both controls and unmedicated ASD adults, while baseline RSA and heart rate did not differ between controls and unmedicated ASD adults.
Thapa et al. confirmed that autistic children not on psychotropic medication showed no differences in heart rate, RMSSD, or high-frequency power compared to controls.

In a large study of anxious adults versus controls, lower RSA associated with anxiety survived adjustment for health and lifestyle factors but became non-significant after adjusting for antidepressant use, highlighting medication as a critical HRV confound relevant to interpreting ASD-HRV studies.
A self-report study in autistic adults found that anxiety and stress, but not autistic traits themselves, were correlated with self-reported autonomic nervous system-related physical health problems.

Vernetti et al. found comparable sympathetic (skin conductance) responses between ASD and control toddlers to anger, frustration, and joy stimuli, but a divergent response to fear stimuli (controls increased, ASD group decreased), with no baseline group differences or correlation with autism severity.

A prior systematic review by Benevides and Lane concluded that no clear differences in resting parasympathetic activity or task-related autonomic nervous system activity emerged across the ASD literature.
A case series of six ASD patients with symptoms of postural lightheadedness, near syncope, constipation, diarrhea, and early satiety all had postural tachycardia but no orthostatic hypotension.

A meta-analysis incorporating most of the reviewed studies concluded that HRV does not differentiate ASD from other psychiatric disorders and that co-morbidities not accounted for could affect the results.

A meta-analysis of 616 controls and 1,479 adults with anxiety found lower RSA in anxious subjects, but this association became non-significant after adjusting for antidepressant use, and a broader meta-analysis on anxiety and HRV found mixed results across studies.

Ferguson et al. found that lower baseline parasympathetic tone correlated with more severe gastrointestinal symptoms such as constipation in children with autism, particularly among those with co-occurring anxiety.

When ASD children were divided into those with known autonomic dysfunction (e.g., GI motility problems, syncope) and those without, heart rate and blood pressure were similar between asymptomatic ASD children and controls, but elevated in the symptomatic subgroup, suggesting comorbidity rather than autism itself drives higher heart rate.

In a study of 116 controls and 154 children with ASD, average heart rate was significantly higher in the ASD group (95.2 vs 90.1 bpm), but this difference disappeared when only the 82 non-medicated ASD children were compared to controls.

Mathewson et al. found that adults with ASD taking antipsychotic medication had significantly higher heart rate and lower RSA at baseline than both controls and ASD adults not on medication, while the unmedicated ASD group did not differ from controls.
Thapa et al. confirmed that no differences in heart rate, RMSSD, or high-frequency power were observed in autistic children not on psychotropic medication compared to controls.

Hirstein et al. hypothesized that amygdala damage causes chronic high sympathetic activity in autistic children, who use repetitive behaviors to self-regulate a malfunctioning autonomic nervous system, but the paper is noted to provide very little actual supporting data.

Nyström et al. concluded that infants at risk for autism have a hypersensitive pupillary light reflex, but the authors note that most infants had latency and constriction amplitudes within the normal control range.

Daluwatte et al. showed that children with ASD had significantly longer pupillary light reflex latency and reduced constriction amplitude compared to controls, though this was not accompanied by significant differences in RMSSD.

Fan et al. found that pupillary light reflex latency could discriminate ASD from control children/young adults, with lower constriction velocity in ASD significant only at specific light-adapted stimulus intensities, and no difference in reflex recovery velocity.

Panju found that ASD children with low anxiety levels did not differ from controls in baseline electrodermal activity or sympathetic responses to any stimulus, while children with high anxiety unexpectedly showed lower baseline electrodermal activity than controls.
Levine et al. showed that both ASD children and controls exhibited a similar increase in electrodermal (sympathetic) activity in response to the Trier Social Stress Test.

Vernetti et al. found that toddlers with ASD showed similar increases in sympathetic (skin conductance) activity to anger, frustration, and joy as controls, with no significant group difference in baseline sympathetic values, and concluded that toddlers with ASD should not be labeled as autonomically dysregulated or upregulated.
A self-report study in autistic adults found that anxiety and stress, but not autistic traits themselves, were correlated with self-reported autonomic nervous system-related physical health problems.

Bujnakova et al. reported an average baseline heart rate of 83 bpm in 7-15-year-old ASD children as evidence of tachycardia, but this value falls within the normal age- and gender-matched range and the authors acknowledged comorbid psychiatric symptoms may confound the finding.

Using the Poincaré plot, no sympathetic differences at rest or in response to a mental task were found in adolescents with ASD compared to controls, and parasympathetic activity decreased in most controls (18/20) but showed a more variable pattern in the ASD group (10/20 decrease, 3/20 no change, 7/20 increase).
Whole-exome sequencing identified a heterozygous de novo missense variant in SMAD4 (c.1498A>G, p.Ile500Val) as the pathogenic cause of Myhre syndrome in the patient.
Limited intellect and autism spectrum disorder-like behaviour have been reported in Myhre syndrome patients generally, which can impair normal social interaction.
The patient exhibited severe allergic reactions to insect bites and multiple allergies (vitamin K, pollen, mould) from 18 months of age, an atypical finding not previously reported in Myhre syndrome.

The patient developed recurrent bilateral circumferential choanal tumours causing severe nasal obstruction, dizziness and headaches, a predisposition to ENT tumours not previously reported in Myhre syndrome.
Audiometry revealed conductive hearing loss in the patient, consistent with previously reported recurrent ear infections leading to hearing loss in Myhre syndrome.
Ultrasound imaging revealed mild coarctation of the aorta without hemodynamically significant alterations.
The patient was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome based on haematuria, leukocyturia and proteinuria detected on routine urinalysis.

Suspected vasculitis was excluded because negative inflammatory markers, negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and negative anti-C1q serology did not support an autoimmune systemic inflammatory process despite the patient's ENT and renal manifestations.
The patient experienced chronic muscle and joint pain that was not associated with any neurological abnormalities.

The patient exhibited delayed dental eruption, with first teeth appearing at 18 months versus the normal range of 6-8 months, a particularity noted as atypical for Myhre syndrome, without other dental abnormalities.

The most common molecular defect in Myhre syndrome is a restricted spectrum of missense mutations at Ile500 (substitutions to threonine, valine or methionine) found in almost all patients, with no clear genotype-phenotype correlation established.
SMAD4-mediated TGF-β signalling is implicated in inducing and maintaining inflammatory responses and has been linked to allergic asthma and immunomodulation in prior literature.
The patient's father, who had multiple rectocolic micropolyps, tested negative for the SMAD4 mutation identified in the proband, supporting a de novo origin of the variant.

Myhre syndrome typically arises from a de novo SMAD4 pathogenic variant and confers a 50% recurrence risk to offspring of an affected individual, though fertility and reproduction have not been well studied in this condition.
The patient's severe menstrual abnormalities (dysmenorrhea and oligomenorrhea) were partially corrected with oestrogen and progesterone treatment.

Surgical removal of the bilateral choanal tumour under general anaesthesia produced an apparently favourable postoperative outcome, but follow-up showed early signs of recurrence, and recommended further investigation was not performed due to the patient's altered emotional status.

The patient's late diagnosis and lack of medical information led to generalized anxiety requiring psychological intervention, indicating significant psychological burden alongside chronic physical symptoms.

Loss of the full-length dystrophin isoform (Dp427) and its shorter isoforms, encoded by mutations in the DMD gene, disrupts development, differentiation, and consolidation of specific brain circuits including hippocampus, cerebellum, prefrontal cortex, and amygdala.

DMD-associated neurological disorders are primarily characterized by morpho-functional alterations of selective synaptic connections within affected brain areas, both in central and autonomic nervous systems.
The synaptic pathology seen in DMD is described as linking it to other severe neurological disorders such as schizophrenia, epilepsy, and autistic spectrum disorders.

Wild-type neonates emitted their first ultrasonic vocalization faster under cool (17°C) than ambient (25°C) exposure, whereas Magel2+/-p neonates showed no such shortening, indicating a blunted behavioral response to cooling.
The proportion of neonates responding to cooling (i.e., halving their call latency) was markedly reduced in Magel2+/-p compared to WT from P1 to P6.
The cool-induced call latency deficit in Magel2+/-p neonates was present and significant across postnatal ages P2, P3, and P6, but no genotype difference was seen under ambient temperature.

The number of USV calls was significantly reduced in Magel2+/-p under cool exposure but not under ambient temperature, ruling out a general motor/vocalization deficit; this deficit was independent of sex.
Dam separation and handling did not alter corticosterone levels in either WT or Magel2+/-p neonates of either sex, ruling out a stress-hormone explanation for the thermosensory deficit.

WT dams retrieved WT pups faster under cool than ambient conditions, but this cool-induced speedup was absent when retrieving Magel2+/-p pups, and dams were slower to retrieve Magel2+/-p pups than WT pups under cool conditions.

Under cool exposure, a significantly smaller proportion of Magel2+/-p pups were retrieved by dams within 30 seconds compared to WT pups, and over a third of Magel2+/-p pups were never retrieved, a failure not observed for WT.
Among unretrieved Magel2+/-p pups, there was no significant difference between males and females.
TRPM8 mRNA expression in dorsal root ganglia was not significantly different between Magel2+/-p and WT neonates, indicating peripheral cold thermoreceptor expression is not the site of the deficit.

Interscapular brown adipose tissue mass (normalized to body weight) was decreased in Magel2+/-p relative to WT at P2 but became increased relative to WT by P6, reflecting an abnormal developmental trajectory.
Cold exposure induced a similar significant reduction in BAT triglyceride content in both WT and Magel2+/-p pups, indicating normal lipolytic thermogenic response despite altered BAT mass.

UCP1 protein expression in BAT significantly increased after acute cold exposure in both WT and Magel2+/-p neonates at P2 and P6, demonstrating that UCP1-mediated non-shivering thermogenesis is fully functional in Magel2+/-p and is not the cause of the thermosensory behavioral deficit.
Loss of skin surface body temperature during a cool challenge was similar between WT and Magel2+/-p neonates, indicating intact autonomic thermoregulatory physiology despite the behavioral deficit.

Two-photon calcium imaging showed that Grueneberg ganglion neurons from both WT and Magel2+/-p neonates exhibited robust intracellular Ca2+ increases in response to cooling, indicating the peripheral cold-sensing organ is functionally intact in the mutant.

Chemogenetic (DREADD/CNO) inactivation of oxytocin neurons in wild-type neonates abolished the normal cool-induced decrease in call latency and reduced the cooling responsive rate to levels resembling Magel2+/-p neonates, implicating OT neuron activity as necessary for normal thermosensory reactivity.

Intranasal oxytocin (2 µg) administration rescued the cool thermosensory call behavior deficit in Magel2+/-p neonates, decreasing call latency and increasing the responsive rate to 77%, comparable to WT.

The selective oxytocin receptor agonist TGOT (0.2 µg intranasal) improved cool-induced call latency and increased the responsive rate of Magel2+/-p neonates to levels similar to WT, supporting a role for OT receptor activation in rescuing the deficit.

Intranasal vasopressin (AVP, 0.25 µg), which activates the oxytocin receptor with similar affinity to OT, also improved cool-induced call reactivity in Magel2+/-p neonates, similar to TGOT, though a minor contribution of AVP-specific receptors could not be excluded.

Cool exposure induced a significant reduction in brain phospho-Erk in WT neonates but not in Magel2+/-p neonates, and intranasal oxytocin restored the cool-induced P-Erk reduction in Magel2+/-p without affecting the WT response, implicating Erk signaling in the OT-mediated rescue mechanism.

Treating Magel2+/-p pups with TGOT improved maternal retrieval performance under cool exposure, reducing retrieval latency and increasing the proportion retrieved to over 70%, with no unretrieved pups, compared to poor performance with vehicle.

Plasma MCP-1 fell significantly in all EBV patients from baseline to 6 months.
At baseline, IM patients had higher levels of EBV VCA IgM antibodies than healthy controls, consistent with acute infection.

Plasma IP-10 levels correlated with supernatant IP-10 levels from Pam3Cys-stimulated (TLR1/2) PBMC cultures at baseline, linking in vivo and in vitro monocyte activation measures.
No significant correlation between plasma and in vitro IP-10 (or other monocyte/T-cell markers) was found at the 6-month follow-up or among healthy controls, unlike at baseline.

None of the monocyte-associated markers, in vitro or in vivo, discriminated between patients who developed chronic fatigue and those who did not, suggesting T-cell rather than monocyte activity is linked to fatigue development.

The exaggerated inhibitory response of immune cells to the beta-agonist isoproterenol in the chronic fatigue group at 6 months may reflect dysregulation of adrenergic receptors or their downstream signaling pathways, rather than the receptor downregulation typically seen in hyperadrenergic states.

Elevated CRP was already present at baseline in patients who went on to develop chronic fatigue at 6 months, suggesting low-grade inflammation is a risk factor for, rather than only a consequence of, chronic fatigue after EBV infection.

A 67-year-old woman developed CMV viremia and pericarditis (confirmed by cardiac MRI) approximately five weeks after receiving ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccination, following exclusion of other infectious and autoimmune causes.
Oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily) was associated with clinical improvement, normalization of liver enzymes, and a decline in CMV viremia from 415 IU/mL to <35 IU/mL at 54-day follow-up.

The authors hypothesize that CMV reactivation triggers a persistent inflammatory response in COVID-19 patients that may remain active long after SARS-CoV-2 clearance, potentially relevant to long COVID symptom persistence.
The authors propose that vaccine-induced stimulation of cellular immunity may precipitate CMV reactivation through a mechanism resembling immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
UK ONS data indicate that one in five COVID-19 patients report symptoms beyond 5 weeks, and 10% have symptoms persisting beyond 12 weeks.
Severity of acute illness, female gender, older age, presence of comorbidity, and minority ethnicity are reported risk factors that foster development of long COVID.
Evidence on whether COVID-19 vaccination reduces the risk of developing long COVID after infection is inconsistent, with some trials suggesting reduced risk and others no effect.

A meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies of hospitalized COVID-19 patients found approximately 20% prevalence of lung function abnormalities post-discharge, with diffusion impairment being the most common abnormality.

In a 390-patient subgroup of a large prospective cohort followed for a median of 6 months, no correlation was found between respiratory symptoms and lung function, exercise capacity, or chest CT imaging, despite DLCO reduced in 29-56% and 6-minute walk distance reduced in 24-29% of cases.
In a study of 134 patients, fatigue and/or dyspnea at 6 months was not explained by significant abnormalities in lung function tests or chest CT scans.

In a prospective cohort of 103 patients, 54% had persistent dyspnea at 3 months, though only 24% had reduced DLCO and most had normal lung volumes; CT showed ground-glass opacities in 25% and parenchymal bands in 19%.
Cortes-Telles et al. reported that patients with persistent dyspnea had reduced lung volume, lower DLCO, and increased exertional desaturation compared to those without persistent dyspnea.

Among 62 ICU patients with ARDS secondary to COVID-19 evaluated at 3 months, 82% had reduced DLCO and 70% had CT evidence of lung damage, with mechanical ventilation duration and age associated with severity of radiological alterations.

Among 76 patients evaluated 4 months after hospitalization, fibrotic-like CT abnormalities occurred in 20% of non-ventilated and 72% of mechanically ventilated patients, correlating with lung function decline, cough, and frailty but not dyspnea; illness severity, ventilation duration, admission LDH, and leukocyte telomere length were independent risk factors.

At 12 months after discharge, 24% of severe COVID-19 survivors who did not require mechanical ventilation had radiological abnormalities including interstitial thickening and reticular opacity, potential signs of evolving pulmonary fibrosis.

In 30 symptomatic patients with post-COVID interstitial lung disease, steroid treatment (0.5 mg/kg prednisolone tapered over 3 weeks) was associated with significant symptomatic, functional, and radiological improvement one month after discharge.
Autopsy studies on 39 COVID-19 patients identified virus in the heart tissue of 62.5% of patients, suggesting direct viral myocardial involvement.

High expression of ACE2 in COVID-19 patients leads to renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) overactivation, causing dysregulation of electrolyte and fluid homeostasis and increasing risk of thrombosis and hypertension.

BET inhibitors improved dysfunction in human cardiac organoids and prevented cardiac dysfunction and death in a mouse cytokine storm model, while also reducing ACE2 expression and SARS-CoV-2 infection of cardiomyocytes.

A Frankfurt University Hospital study found that 78% of COVID-19 survivors had cardiovascular alterations, with 60% still showing signs of persistent myocardial inflammation more than two months after diagnosis.
A study from Wuhan, China found that about 20% of COVID-19 patients had cardiovascular damage, and patients' conditions worsened when IL-6 levels were high.

Radin et al. showed that COVID-19 patients had prolonged relative tachycardia lasting on average 79 days after symptom onset, with 13.7% of patients not returning to resting heart rate baseline until after 133 days.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) has been reported as a complication in the post-COVID-19 phase.
Orthostatic intolerance without hemodynamic abnormalities has also been reported as a post-COVID-19 complication, distinct from POTS.

Post-COVID-19 neurological syndrome (PCNS) presents with heterogeneous symptoms including muscle pain, dizziness, headache, fatigue, anosmia, memory dysfunction, dysexecutive syndrome, ataxia, tetraparesis and sleep disorders.
An ongoing trial is testing daily lower-extremity electrical stimulation therapy as a feasible way to preserve muscle mass in ICU patients recovering from COVID-19.
Systemic inflammation in COVID-19 causes endothelial alterations and leukocyte migration across the blood-brain barrier, a proposed mechanism for post-COVID-19 neurological damage.
Direct SARS-CoV-2 damage to cerebral tissue may occur via transsynaptic transfer across infected neurons (e.g., olfactory nerve), potentially mediated by ACE2 receptor-spike protein interaction.
Histological examination of cerebral tissue from COVID-19 patients has demonstrated the presence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA and viral proteins in the brain.
About one third of COVID-19 patients develop depressive symptoms or clinically significant depression, most commonly within the first 12 weeks after infection.
In a study of 714 COVID-19 patients, nearly 97% developed symptoms compatible with post-traumatic stress disorder.

COVID-19-related systemic inflammation increases blood-brain barrier permeability, reducing circulating tryptophan and serotonin while increasing neurotoxic kynurenine-pathway metabolites, promoting neurotoxicity and reduced neurogenesis/synaptic plasticity.
The incidence of Takotsubo syndrome rose 4.5-fold during the COVID-19 pandemic, even among people without severe acute respiratory illness.
Chronic anxiety and/or depression are commonly reported comorbidities in patients with Takotsubo syndrome.
Interrupted and irregular sleep patterns, frequent in COVID-19 patients, can lead to impaired autonomic tone and endothelial vasomotor dysfunction with related symptoms.

Reported risk factors fostering the development of long COVID include severity of early COVID-19 (symptom load, level of hospital care, need for mechanical ventilation), female gender, older age, presence of comorbidity, and minority ethnicity.

COVID-19 vaccination reduces long COVID risk mainly by lowering the chance of infection, but among those who do get infected, trial evidence on whether vaccination further reduces long COVID risk is inconsistent.
Post-COVID-19 syndrome may be experienced more strongly by depressed patients, potentially reflecting shared underlying factors such as high neuroticism.
Memory problems following COVID-19 may indirectly increase cardiovascular risk, for example through missed medication doses.
Persistent myocardial inflammation and altered cardiac function may reduce lung perfusion, contributing to dyspnea in long COVID patients.
COVID-19-associated clot formation such as pulmonary emboli may lead some patients to develop chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension with dyspnea.
Post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis can progress to right heart failure.
Patients reporting respiratory-viral PASC symptoms at convalescence had significantly lower plasma cortisol levels compared to those without.
Patients reporting respiratory-viral PASC symptoms at convalescence had significantly lower plasma cortisone levels compared to those without.
Patients reporting neurological PASC symptoms exhibited elevated plasma protein signatures for negative regulation of the circadian sleep/wake cycle.
Plasma EBV viremia detected at initial diagnosis (T1) was specifically associated with fatigue and sputum PASC at convalescence.
Both EBV viremia and SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia measured at diagnosis (T1) were significantly associated with memory-related PASC at convalescence.
T1 SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia positivity was associated with increased mortality risk in COVID-19 patients.
Autoantibodies against IFN-α2 measured at T1 were uniquely associated with respiratory-viral PASC, independent of age, sex, and disease severity.
GI-related PASC and sputum production were associated with elevated levels of multiple anti-nuclear autoantibodies both at convalescence (T3) and as early as diagnosis (T1).
Anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike/RBD/nucleocapsid IgG titers were significantly anticorrelated with anti-IFN-α2 and anti-nuclear autoantibody levels at T3, validated in an independent cohort.
Atypical memory B cells (AtMs, IGHD-CD27-CD11c+FCRL5+) were expanded in COVID-19 patients, most pronounced in those with high autoantibody levels.
Atypical memory B cells from patients with high autoantibody levels showed upregulated CD79B expression, indicating enhanced BCR signaling.
Atypical memory B cells from patients with high autoantibody levels showed upregulated MX1 expression, implying enhanced interferon signaling.
Acute-stage (T2) plasma IL-6 levels were positively associated with autoantibody levels measured at T3 convalescence.
Acute-stage (T2) plasma C-reactive protein levels were positively associated with autoantibody levels measured at T3 convalescence.
Newly emerging cytotoxic CD8+ T cell clonotypes at convalescence (T3) were significantly enriched in patients reporting GI PASC.
Newly emerging cytotoxic CD4+ T cell clonotypes at convalescence (T3) were enriched in patients with GI PASC.

SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells showed opposite transcriptomic trajectories between GI PASC (undifferentiated at acute stage, cytotoxic at convalescence) and respiratory-viral PASC (opposite pattern).
Persistent cytotoxic CMV-specific CD8+ T cells at convalescence, marked by elevated GNLY, GZMB and PRF1, were positively associated with GI PASC, suggesting bystander T cell activation.
MDSCs, previously linked to immune paralysis and acute COVID-19 mortality, remained upregulated at convalescence in patients with sputum PASC.
A memory-like NK cell subtype at convalescence (T3) was positively associated with cough PASC.
Activated Treg levels measured during acute disease (T2) significantly and positively anticipated many different PASC categories.
Patients classified into the type-2-polarized immune endotype at convalescence had the highest hospitalization rate among four identified immune endotypes.
Patients in the naive immune endotype at convalescence reported fewer PASC symptoms (except anosmia/dysgeusia) compared to other immune endotypes.
The intermediate immune endotype, exhibiting both pro-inflammatory and type-2 signatures, was most strongly associated with high anti-IFN-α2 autoantibody levels and EBV viremia.
Plasma CTSL levels measured at diagnosis (T1) were predictive of patient mortality, with validation in an independent cohort (SJCI).
Pre-existing type 2 diabetes was significantly correlated with certain PASC categories after adjusting for age, sex, and disease severity.

T1-measured PASC-anticipating factors (autoantibodies, EBV viremia, SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia) showed multiple inter-relationships at diagnosis that sharply diminished by T2 and became virtually independent by T3 convalescence.
Female sex, COPD, and higher T1 red blood cell counts were associated with a greater likelihood of presenting more than three PASC symptoms.
Post-COVID healthcare workers showed significantly higher MFI general fatigue scores than a healthy reference sample.
The overall post-COVID sample's fatigue score was significantly lower than that of a validated chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) patient sample.

10.7% of the healthcare-worker sample (n=217) had clinically relevant fatigue scores (≥16 on MFI) comparable to those seen in CFS patients, and 95.6% of this subgroup attributed the symptoms to their COVID-19 infection.
Female sex was a significant predictor of greater post-COVID fatigue severity in multiple regression.
Smoking status was significantly associated with greater fatigue severity in the regression model.
Pre-existing psychiatric conditions significantly predicted greater post-COVID fatigue severity.
Pre-existing respiratory conditions significantly predicted greater post-COVID fatigue severity.
Better subjective health status before COVID-19 infection was associated with lower subsequent fatigue severity (i.e., worse pre-infection health predicted more severe fatigue).
A greater number of acute COVID-19 symptoms was the strongest predictor of subsequent fatigue severity.
Inpatient hospitalization during acute COVID-19 illness was significantly associated with greater subsequent fatigue severity.
Higher BMI correlated significantly with greater fatigue severity but did not add explanatory variance and was excluded from the final regression model.
Age and pre-existing cardiovascular, urogenital, skin, and hormonal/metabolic conditions were not significantly (or only marginally) associated with post-COVID fatigue severity.
Lower physical health-related quality of life (VR-12 physical component) was significantly associated with greater current fatigue severity.
Lower mental health-related quality of life (VR-12 mental component) was significantly associated with greater current fatigue severity.
Psychological distress (depression/anxiety) was strongly correlated with fatigue severity but did not add explanatory variance to the regression model.
Participants with clinically severe long/post-COVID fatigue had markedly higher rates of work incapacity since COVID-19 than those with milder or no long/post-COVID symptoms.
The severe-fatigue subgroup expressed a desire for rehabilitation far more often than the other subgroups and made greater use of outpatient follow-up and inpatient rehabilitation.
The severe-fatigue subgroup was disproportionately female and had a higher acute symptom burden, more frequent hospitalization, and lower quality of life than the other two long/post-COVID subgroups.
Peripheral neuropathy prevalence rises from 2.4% in the general population to 8% in those over 55, 12.1% in obese normoglycemic individuals, and 40.8% in obese individuals with diabetes.
Skin biopsy assessment of intraepidermal nerve fiber density (small unmyelinated C-fiber termini) has 90% sensitivity and 97% specificity for diagnosing small-fiber peripheral neuropathy.
