In a case-controlled study, patients with gluten neuropathy had lower physical functioning, energy, and overall health scores than matched controls.
In a study of 60 gluten neuropathy patients, strict adherence to a gluten-free diet was associated with a lower likelihood of neuropathic pain, reducing the odds by 88.7% on multivariate analysis.
Among MS patients, lifetime headache prevalence was 57.7%, with tension-type headache in 31.9% and migraine in 25.0%.
Migraine frequency among MS patients was roughly three-fold higher than the general population in both women and men.
In a large study of nearly 19,000 MS patients, migraine prevalence was more than double that of controls.
A meta-analysis found migraine prevalence among MS patients to be inconsistent across studies and to vary by geography, without a confirmed causal link between the two conditions.
Long COVID (long-haul COVID) is described as a postviral syndrome with a symptom constellation that is not necessarily the same as those experienced during acute infection.
COVID infection is associated with an increased rate of neuropathic pain, and the presence of neuropathic pain itself acts as a predictor of neurological complications.
During the COVID-associated cytokine storm, release of IL-1 and IL-6 increases nerve growth factor (NGF) production, contributing to peripheral sensitization and neuropathic pain.

NGF release increases localized sodium channel effects and induces COX-2 and prostaglandin production, promoting axonal transport changes and neuropeptide increases that drive peripheral sensitization.

TNF release causes axonal transport changes and increased bradykinin receptor expression and neuropeptide release, contributing to peripheral sensitization that combines with central sensitization in a feedback loop.
Acute COVID infection increases IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α, all of which stimulate nociceptors and have been linked to development of neurological symptoms.

Neuropilin-1 (NRP1), a transmembrane receptor, appears to enhance SARS-CoV-2 infectivity and is viewed as a host factor and potential therapeutic target, possibly facilitating viral entry into the brain via the olfactory epithelium.

SARS-CoV-2 spike protein is speculated to bind ACE-2 receptors to infect endothelial cells, with suspected downregulation of ACE-2 potentially contributing to pulmonary and circulatory complications in severe COVID.
COVID infection can cause endothelial dysfunction and a hypercoagulable state, disrupting the endothelium's normal antithrombotic, vasodilatory function.
Endothelitis with hyperproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines can cause the blood-brain barrier to rupture, allowing pro-inflammatory mediators and innate immune cells to enter the brain.
Chronic pain prevalence one year after ICU discharge has been estimated to range from 14% to 77%, a population that expanded greatly during the COVID pandemic.
Prolonged prone positioning during intensive care has been associated with neuropraxia and severe axonal damage to the ulnar nerve, brachial plexus, and forearm nerves.

COVID survivors with pre-existing neuropathic pain conditions may experience deterioration and exacerbation of that pain, and the healthcare system may see an increase in neuropathic pain in coming years.
Xiong et al. found that COVID-19 recovered patients reported significantly more long-term symptoms than a non-infected control group drawn from the general population.
Across studies, the reported frequency of post-COVID-19 condition ranged from 4.7% to 80% (based on 25 studies), occurring 3 to 24 weeks after acute infection or hospital discharge.

In a retrospective cohort of 236,379 electronic health records, Taquet et al. found an estimated 33% incidence of a neurological or psychiatric diagnosis within six months of a COVID-19 diagnosis, higher than in matched patients with influenza or other respiratory infections.

In an international online survey (56 countries) by Davis et al., 91% of respondents had recovery time exceeding 35 weeks, with fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction the most frequent symptoms after six months.

Post-COVID-19 condition risk is associated with a weak anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody response, illness severity, female sex, more than five symptoms in the first week of disease, older age, and presence of comorbidities.
Peghin et al. suggested that constantly elevated SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibody titers may be an independent risk factor for post-COVID-19 condition.

Seessle et al. reported that patients with at least one post-COVID-19 symptom at 12 months did not significantly differ in SARS-CoV-2 antibody levels from asymptomatic patients, although both physical and mental quality of life had significantly decreased.

Townsend et al. showed that persistent illness after the acute phase of COVID-19, affecting health perception, ability to return to work, and lasting fatigue, appeared unrelated to acute illness severity.
Post-COVID-19 condition develops at roughly a 2:1 ratio in women compared with men, a difference that becomes similar around age 60.

Shuwa et al. observed lasting alterations in the functional potential of CD8+ T cells from recovering COVID-19 patients up to six months after hospital discharge, suggesting a sustained change in cytokine potential contributing to ongoing inflammation, while B cell changes were largely restored during convalescence.

Glynne et al. reported that CD8+ effector memory T cells are diminished for up to 400 days following COVID-19 infection regardless of symptoms, while CD4+ and CD8+ central memory T cell PD-1 levels are augmented, more markedly in post-COVID-19 condition.
Seessle et al. observed that several neurocognitive symptoms in post-COVID-19 condition were associated with elevated antinuclear antibody titers, pointing to autoimmunity as a cofactor.
Post-COVID-19 condition has been related to a weaker initial inflammatory response, with lower baseline levels of C-reactive protein and ferritin.

Altered tryptophan absorption and metabolism have been suggested as key contributors to persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms, with numerous studies showing low levels of tryptophan and serotonin in SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals.

Patients with severe COVID-19 symptoms show more severe autonomic dysfunction, as indicated by heart rate variability analysis, compared with patients with mild symptoms, and amelioration of autonomic parameters correlates with improvements in immune, coagulation, and cardiac injury biomarkers.

Townsend et al. found no association between fatigue and autonomic dysfunction after COVID-19, but found a strong association between fatigue and increased anxiety in patients without pre-existing anxiety diagnoses.

Brain PET imaging showed hypometabolism in post-COVID-19 condition patients in the bilateral rectal/orbital gyrus, right temporal lobe (amygdala/hippocampus/thalamus), bilateral pons/medulla brainstem, and bilateral cerebellum, with cerebellar hypometabolism specifically associated with hyposmia/anosmia; these metabolic patterns distinguished patients from healthy subjects with high discriminative power.
Neutralizing antibody titers against SARS-CoV-2 are significantly lower at six-month follow-up compared with the acute phase.
ACE2 and TMPRSS2, the molecular complex used by SARS-CoV-2 for host cell entry, are expressed at higher levels in the thyroid gland than in the lungs.
Coperchini et al. showed in normal human thyroid primary cultures that interferon, and to a lesser extent TNF-alpha, regularly increased ACE2 mRNA levels.

Campi et al. found a temporary state of low TSH with normal T4 and low T3 in hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 patients, which was inversely associated with C-reactive protein, cortisol, and IL-6, and positively associated with normal thyroglobulin levels, likely due to cytokine-mediated effects on TSH secretion rather than destructive thyroiditis.
The THYRCOV study found that patients with acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and thyrotoxicosis had statistically significantly higher IL-6 levels.
Low free T3 levels are independently associated with increased mortality and disease severity in COVID-19 and may serve as a surrogate prognostic biomarker.

Gong et al. reported that patients with low TSH had significantly higher critical illness rates (74.07% vs. 37.40%, p = 0.001) and mortality rates (51.85% vs. 22.76%, p = 0.002) compared with a normal TSH group.

Asghar et al. found that among 54 COVID-19 patients, those with low TSH (<0.996 uIU/mL) had significantly lower survival than those with sufficient TSH (>0.996 uIU/mL), though the study was limited by small sample size.

Lui et al. found that spontaneous recovery of symptoms occurred more often among post-COVID-19 patients who were positive for anti-TPO antibodies at re-evaluation, suggesting a potential protective role of anti-TPO in post-COVID-19 condition.
Poma et al. detected SARS-CoV-2 in 9 of 25 (36%) examined thyroid specimens.
Thyroid autoimmunity, evaluated via anti-TPO antibodies, was more common in COVID-19 patients compared with pre-pandemic controls.
Small studies showed that AstraZeneca and Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccines were associated with overall improvements in post-COVID-19 condition symptoms.
Antonelli et al. found that the odds of having post-vaccination-infection symptoms lasting 28 days or more were approximately halved in individuals who had received two vaccine doses.
Post-COVID-19 condition in children presents similarly to adults, with symptoms including fatigue, dyspnea, myalgia, cognitive impairment, headache, palpitations, and chest pain.
COVID-19 survivors had a much higher incidence of new-onset (de novo) chronic pain than uninfected patients.
COVID-19 survivors had a much higher prevalence of new-onset headache compared with uninfected individuals.
Headache present at the onset of acute COVID-19 infection was associated with persistent long-term headache and fatigue up to seven months after hospital discharge.
More than a quarter of COVID-19 patients discharged from the hospital reported persistent joint pain.
In a small hospitalized cohort in China, 44% of COVID-19 patients had myalgia, and a third of those with myalgia had elevated creatine-kinase levels.
In a case series of 99 diagnosed COVID-19 patients, 11% reported myalgia and, among these, 13% had elevated creatine-kinase levels.

SARS-CoV-2 enters cells via spike-protein binding to ACE-2, which is densely expressed in musculoskeletal tissue, leading to speculation that the virus may directly damage skeletal muscle and contribute to myalgia.
Chronic neuropathic pain has been reported in up to 2.3% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, though the underlying mechanisms are not yet elucidated.
Stroke, myelitis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome are prevalent complications among COVID-19 patients and are associated with an elevated risk of neuropathic pain.
Over half of ICU patients who required mechanical ventilation report some form of functional impairment persisting for at least one year (post-intensive-care syndrome).
Among survivors of the 2002 SARS epidemic in Hong Kong, a quarter to nearly half suffered post-traumatic stress disorder and 15% had depression after infection.

Approximately 10% of patients who develop certain enteric (gastrointestinal) infections go on to develop irritable bowel syndrome, illustrating a general link between gastrointestinal infection and post-viral syndromes.
Although older age is a risk factor for acute COVID-19 infection severity, it does not appear to be a risk factor for developing long COVID-19.
Risk factors for prolonged (long COVID-19) symptoms appear to include the severity and duration of the acute COVID-19 infection and the patient's premorbid psychological status.
Initial concerns about the safety of ibuprofen use in COVID-19 patients were subsequently shown to be unfounded.
Opioids are effective for chronic pain but may suppress the immune system and mask infection symptoms, warranting cautious use during the pandemic.

Concurrent use of antidepressants or lithium with hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, or azithromycin during COVID-19 treatment may elevate the risk of QT-segment prolongation, with lithium considered contraindicated.
One intra-articular corticosteroid injection has been shown to increase the risk of contracting influenza, and by extension raises suggestive but unstudied concern regarding COVID-19.
Because corticosteroid injections suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, it has been suggested they be timed at least two weeks before or one week after an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine dose.
Perioperative COVID-19 infection increases postoperative morbidity and mortality, leading to recommendations to delay elective surgery for at least seven weeks after infection.
SARS-CoV-2 can persist on ultrasound equipment for up to nine days and remain in inert form for up to 96 hours, requiring careful disinfection between interventional pain patients.
Pooled prevalence of at least mild post-viral mental health problems was 46.3% in the acute stage, 35.5% at ongoing follow-up, and 38.8% at post-illness follow-up.
Pooled prevalence of moderate-to-severe post-viral mental health problems was 22.3% acute, 17.3% ongoing, and 18.8% post-illness.
Prevalence of both mild and moderate-to-severe mental health problems significantly decreased from the acute stage to the post-illness stage.
No significant difference in mental health problem prevalence was found between the acute and ongoing follow-up stages.
Pooled mild anxiety prevalence was 44.7% acute, 28.3% ongoing, and 33.5% post-illness across the included epidemics.
Pooled moderate-to-severe anxiety prevalence was 19.2% acute, 14.1% ongoing, and 12.1% post-illness.
Pooled mild depression prevalence was 45.3% acute, 30.8% ongoing, and 43.5% post-illness.
Pooled moderate-to-severe depression prevalence was 21.9% acute, 16.0% ongoing, and 18.2% post-illness.
Pooled mild post-traumatic stress prevalence was approximately 62.4% acute, 43.2% ongoing, and 38.6% post-illness, though based on very limited data.
Pooled moderate-to-severe post-traumatic stress prevalence was 25.3% acute, 20.9% ongoing, and 39.1% post-illness, based on limited data.
Pooled moderate general distress prevalence at the ongoing follow-up stage was 66.3%, though only estimable at this timepoint.

Meta-regression found no moderating effect of sex, age, education, history of a mental health condition, health-care worker status, hospitalization duration, ICU treatment, treatment type, response rate, or world region on overall post-viral mental health problem prevalence.
Studies using random/complete sampling methods reported lower mild mental health problem prevalence than studies using non-random sampling methods.

Meta-regression suggested a higher prevalence of moderate-to-severe mental health problems in H1N1 survivors compared to SARS-CoV-2 survivors, though based on very limited H1N1 data and interpreted cautiously.
Descriptively, predicted moderate-to-severe mental health problem prevalence estimates were somewhat lower for SARS-CoV-2 compared to other studied epidemics (SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, Ebolavirus).
All 80 blood-sampled Long COVID/PASC patients showed the presence of fibrin amyloid microclots in platelet poor plasma.
All 80 patients showed platelet hyperactivation, with an overall platelet and microclot severity score of 7±1.3 (moderate activation) in a subset of 30 patients.

High blood pressure was one of the most prevalent comorbidities among Long COVID/PASC registry participants and was linked in lattice analysis to a wide range of symptoms from digestive problems to shortness of breath.
High cholesterol (dyslipidaemia) was a prevalent comorbidity among Long COVID/PASC registry participants and was implicated as a risk factor via impaired endothelial function.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus was among the most prevalent comorbidities in the Long COVID/PASC registry cohort and was proposed as contributing to disease development.
Pre-existing autoimmune disease was identified as one of the most prevalent comorbidities among Long COVID/PASC registry participants.
A history of previous blood clots was identified as a prevalent comorbidity among Long COVID/PASC registry participants.
The Long COVID/PASC registry cohort was predominantly female (70%, n=593) compared to male (30%, n=252).
The most frequently reported Long COVID/PASC symptoms in the registry were fatigue, brain fog, loss of concentration, forgetfulness, shortness of breath, and joint and muscle pain.
Kidney problems, digestive problems, and low oxygen levels were reported less commonly among Long COVID/PASC registry participants compared to other symptoms.
A prior proteomic study by the same group identified dysregulation of the acute-phase inflammatory protein serum amyloid A in the circulation of Long COVID/PASC patients.

Alpha-2-antiplasmin, together with other proteins and antibodies, was found entrapped within fibrin amyloid microclots, causing it to go undetected in plasma-based biomarker assays despite being present.

In one Long COVID/PASC patient on self-administered aspirin (an anti-platelet agent) before blood collection, major microclots were still observed but platelets showed minimal hyperactivation, suggesting aspirin may reduce platelet activation without resolving microclotting.

Because fibrin amyloid microclots are insoluble and inert, they do not contribute to plasma viscosity, so thromboelastography (TEG) values can appear normal in Long COVID/PASC despite the presence of microclots.
Plasma IL-1β was persistently elevated in participants with ongoing PASC compared to those without PASC, confirmed in both discovery and validation cohorts.
Plasma IL-6 was persistently elevated in ongoing PASC and validated across two independent cohorts.
Plasma TNF was persistently elevated in ongoing PASC and validated across two independent cohorts.
Autoantibody positivity for RF, ANA, and aPL did not correlate with PASC status or sampling time point, and no new autoimmune diagnoses emerged.
67.8% of previously infected participants in the discovery cohort reported symptoms persisting beyond 4 weeks and were classified as having PASC.
Women showed a higher percentage of PASC than men among previously infected participants.
PASC incidence was independent of participant age.
Participants with more severe acute COVID-19 infection were more likely to report being affected by PASC.
The proportion of participants with ongoing PASC was similar regardless of whether they received post-infection SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, arguing against vaccination-driven resolution of PASC.
Plasma levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF were positively correlated with each other within PASC patients, suggesting they reflect a shared inflammatory process rather than distinct patient subsets.

There was no clear time-dependent decrease in IL-1β, IL-6, or TNF plasma levels with elapsed time after infection in participants with ongoing PASC, indicating a stable rather than resolving inflammatory state.
IL-12p70 and IFN-γ positively correlated with IL-6 but showed no association with PASC in either cohort.
IL-1β and TNF plasma levels were elevated in acute COVID-19 to concentrations exceeding those seen in bacterial pneumonia patients.
IL-6 was elevated in acute COVID-19 compared with uninfected individuals but less prominently than in bacterial pneumonia.

Single-cell transcriptomics of lung and BALF tissue showed that the IL-1β/IL-6/TNF cytokine triad was specifically expressed by the myeloid/macrophage compartment, especially pro-inflammatory macrophage subsets.

BALF-derived pro-inflammatory macrophages from COVID-19 patients showed especially high response scores for IL-1β and TNF, consistent with a chronic, self-sustaining activation loop, more marked than in bacterial pneumonia macrophages.
The proportion of peripheral CD14-expressing classical monocytes was elevated in COVID-19 patients in an integrated PBMC single-cell dataset.
Non-classical CD16-expressing monocytes were decreased in COVID-19 patients, but peripheral monocytes did not clearly recapitulate the IL-1β/IL-6/TNF signatures seen in BALF macrophages.
IL-1 receptor blockade with anakinra had no substantial effect on reducing mortality in critically ill COVID-19 patients, as reported in the cited literature.
IL-6-directed treatment combined with corticosteroids showed benefit in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, as demonstrated by the REMAP-CAP and RECOVERY trials.
TNF blockade might be beneficial in acute COVID-19 based on small observational case studies, and has a long history of use in rheumatic diseases with chronic TNF elevation.
Long-term metformin use was associated with a strikingly reduced risk of fatal COVID-19 courses, particularly in women with obesity or type 2 diabetes.
Metformin was shown to block NLRP3 inflammasome activation and inhibit IL-1β and IL-6 in alveolar macrophages, attenuating SARS-CoV-2-induced ARDS in a mouse model.
Fatigue and dyspnea were among the most prevalent PASC symptoms, with a considerable fraction of cases showing moderate to severe symptom load.

A subset of participants (approximately 27-40%) had ongoing PASC symptoms at blood sampling 8-10 months post-infection, with five individuals reporting persistent symptoms 16-24 months post-COVID-19, longer than durations reported elsewhere.
A cited external study monitoring 31 PASC patients over 8 months identified a set of interferons and IL-6 as classifiers of PASC with approximately 80% accuracy, supporting the role of IL-6 in PASC.

Most patients evaluated for cardiovascular symptoms after COVID-19 had a 'cardiovascular PASC syndrome' of palpitations, chest pain, and exertional fatigue/dyspnea without an identifiable cardiovascular diagnosis.
Three of 126 patients referred for cardiovascular PASC symptoms met criteria for POTS, with one confirmed by tilt table testing.
Severe acute COVID-19 illness was associated with significantly lower odds of developing cardiovascular PASC syndrome compared with mild acute illness.
Critical acute COVID-19 illness was associated with significantly lower odds of developing cardiovascular PASC syndrome compared with mild acute illness.
A subset of patients showed new left ventricular systolic dysfunction on echocardiogram, with no baseline scans for comparison.
Most patients who underwent Holter monitoring had non-exertional sinus tachycardia accompanied by symptoms.
New atrial fibrillation was identified via Holter monitoring in a small number of PASC cardiovascular clinic patients.

Most patients who underwent cardiac MRI showed evidence of myocardial involvement (late gadolinium enhancement and/or T2 inflammation) not classified as acute myocarditis given normal troponin and non-acute presentation.
A minority of patients who underwent stress testing had evidence of new myocardial ischemia.
A small subset of patients were newly diagnosed with nonischemic cardiomyopathy during PASC cardiovascular evaluation.

Two patients with ischemia and no obstructive coronary disease demonstrated endothelial dysfunction, developing coronary vasospasm on acetylcholine challenge, indicating a microvascular/endothelial mechanism for symptoms.
Among six patients who underwent stress PET/CT, only one case of coronary microvascular dysfunction was detected.

Patients undergoing cardiopulmonary exercise testing had low peak VO2 despite normal cardiac and pulmonary function in many cases, suggesting cardiometabolic impairment such as deconditioning or impaired oxygen extraction.
The majority of patients referred for cardiovascular PASC evaluation reported at least one of dyspnea, chest pain/pressure, or palpitations, with dyspnea being the most common symptom.

Many patients also reported 'brain fog' (memory problems, difficulty concentrating, sleep disturbance) and body aches, overlapping with symptoms of myalgic encephalomyelitis-chronic fatigue syndrome (ME-CFS).

The authors propose that bedrest deconditioning after acute COVID-19 leads to reduced plasma volume, decreased LV filling and stroke volume, and compensatory tachycardia, perpetuating a cycle of fatigue and reduced activity.

For patients with exercise intolerance, clinicians applied Levine protocol principles (originally developed for POTS), including structured recumbent exercise, hydration, salt loading, compression socks, and head-of-bed elevation.
Patients with vasospasm and endothelial dysfunction were treated with calcium channel blockers, nitrates, statins, and L-arginine.
Age, sex, and comorbidities were not significantly associated with cardiovascular PASC syndrome in this cohort.
The most prevalent symptoms reported after COVID-19 infection in this PASC cohort were fatigue, brain fog, headache, anxiety, and sleep issues.
Attention and executive function were frequently impaired among patients with persistent post-COVID symptoms.
The mean Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score among the PASC cohort was 26.0, within the generally normal cognitive range but noted alongside frequent attention/executive complaints.
Concentration and attention issues as well as memory issues were both significantly correlated with patients' complaint of brain fog.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom at baseline, occurring in 89.3% of participants after COVID-19 infection.
Headache was reported by 80.4% of participants at the baseline visit following COVID-19 infection.
Memory impairment was reported by 64.3% of participants at baseline and persisted in 68.8% of those affected at 6 months.
Decreased concentration was reported by 62.5% of participants at baseline and persisted in 61.5% of affected participants at 6 months.
80.4% of participants reported that their neurologic symptoms impacted quality of life at baseline, and quality of life remained reduced in 80% of those with 6-month data.
Complete resolution of neurologic symptoms was reported by 33.3% of participants at 6-month follow-up.

From baseline to 6 months, average symptom severity scores decreased most for fatigue (69.4%) and headache (64.3%), and least for memory impairment (38.6%), indicating differential rates of improvement across symptoms.

Five of 41 participants who completed neurologic exams at baseline had cranial nerve dysfunction, including facial sensation, hearing, extraocular movement, and facial weakness abnormalities, some of which were new findings in previously neurologically healthy patients.
Gait abnormalities were observed on exam in 10 of 35 participants (28.6%), most of whom had no prior neurologic disease.
Baseline MoCA average score was 26.0 (normal range 26-30), with participants most often missing points in delayed recall (70.5%), visuospatial/executive function (54.5%), and language (45.5%).

Average MoCA scores improved from 26.4 (SD 2.1) at baseline to 28.0 (SD 2.0) at 6 months, with 73.7% of participants showing improvement or no change, though authors caution this may reflect a practice effect.
Greater acute COVID-19 infection severity (mild/moderate/severe) was associated with a higher baseline Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (fatigue) score after adjustment for age.

In multivariable regression, age, gender, BMI, and duration of initial COVID-19 symptoms were not associated with IESR, MoCA, MFIS, or subjective memory/concentration outcomes in participants without prior neurologic disease.
Mean IESR (PTSD screening) scores decreased from 18.5 at baseline to 9.9 (SD 17.8) at 6 months, a 48.4% average decrease per participant.

PROMIS-29 scores worsened over 6 months in pain (+27.8%), pain intensity (+20.6%), and anxiety (+12.5%), while physical function, depression, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and social participation domains remained largely stable.

At 6 months, MFIS physical (-19.2%), cognitive (-22.3%), and total (-17.8%) subscores decreased, but the psychosocial fatigue subscore increased by 36.3%, indicating a dissociation between physical/cognitive fatigue improvement and worsening psychosocial fatigue.
Daytime sleepiness (ESS score) worsened from baseline to 6 months, with an average 29.9% increase per participant, contrasting with improvement in most other fatigue measures.

A novel neurologic phenotype of postacute COVID-19, termed PASC-TAC, characterized by tremor/ataxia and objective cognitive deficits, was identified in approximately 7% of participants with no prior neurologic history; imaging in these patients was unremarkable.
The cohort observed more women than men presenting with neuro-PASC symptoms, consistent with previously reported sex differences in long-COVID.
Only 8.9% of participants required hospitalization, and neuro-PASC commonly presented even in patients with mild or moderate acute COVID-19 infection rather than only severe disease.
Participants required decreasing levels of assistance to self-administer taVNS and physiology monitoring, achieving full independence by the fifth session.
Both sham and active taVNS groups maintained equally high session compliance during the 2-week blinded randomized phase.
During the open-label phase, compliance declined in both groups but more so in the group that had originally received sham stimulation.

The active taVNS group received on average more minutes of successful stimulation per session than the sham group during the blinded phase, with both groups' delivered stimulation time decreasing in the open-label phase.
Perceptual thresholds used to set taVNS current intensity did not differ significantly between the sham and active randomization groups.
No unanticipated adverse events occurred, though two participants experienced mild, transient skin irritation at the taVNS electrode site.
Neither the sham nor active taVNS group exhibited any bradycardic events during the first six monitored stimulation sessions.
The full battery of validated psychiatric, cognitive, and olfactory outcome measures showed no significant changes with taVNS treatment.
During the 2-week blinded phase, active taVNS reduced the proportion of reported Long COVID symptoms while sham stimulation showed no improvement.
After both groups had received the full 4-week active taVNS treatment course, initial sham and initial active groups converged to a similar proportion of reported Long COVID symptoms.
At follow-up, participants who received only 2 weeks of active taVNS (after initial sham) worsened, while those who received the full 4 weeks of active taVNS maintained improvement.

Individual trends showed the largest reductions in mental fatigue scores among participants who received the full 4-week course of active taVNS, compared to moderate improvement with only 2 weeks of sham followed by active taVNS.

The authors cite prior evidence that a different noninvasive cervical vagus nerve stimulation device produced mild anti-inflammatory effects in COVID-19 patients, supporting a possible anti-inflammatory mechanism for VNS in Long COVID.
Over one-third of the 60 post-COVID-19 participants (36.7%) scored below the clinical cutoff of 26 on the MoCA, screening positive for possible neurocognitive impairment.
Delayed Recall was the MoCA subcategory with the lowest performance, with only 10 of 60 participants achieving a perfect score.
Participants scoring below 26 on the total MoCA performed worse than those scoring at or above 26 on the Visuospatial, Attention, Language, and Delayed Recall subcategories.
Non-White participants were significantly more likely than White participants to screen positive for cognitive impairment on the MoCA.
Higher physical and mental fatigue on the Chalder Fatigue Scale correlated with lower total MoCA score.
Better instrumental activities of daily living functioning correlated with higher (better) MoCA total scores.
MoCA-defined impairment was not significantly associated with COVID-19 symptom severity (acute or current), time since illness, testing date, or number of medical comorbidities.
Participants with a prior self-reported psychiatric history were less likely to score below 26 on the MoCA than those without such history.
Participants with clinically significant depression on the PHQ-9 were more likely to score below 26 on the MoCA.
No significant associations were found between MoCA impairment and substance-use history, clinically significant anxiety, clinically significant PTSD, or psychotropic medication use.
Rates of MoCA impairment increased progressively across neuropsychological test performance groups: 16.7% in the Normal group, 35% in the Low group, and 68.8% in the Extremely Low group.
The MoCA had only moderate accuracy (63.3%) and low sensitivity (50.0%) for detecting any degree of poor neuropsychological test performance (Low or Extremely Low) versus normal performance.
The MoCA showed slightly better accuracy (73.3%) and sensitivity (68.8%) for distinguishing Extremely Low neuropsychological test performance from combined Normal/Low performance.
The MoCA's accuracy for detecting Extremely Low neuropsychological performance was significantly lower in non-White than White participants.
White participants scored significantly higher on the Test of Premorbid Functioning than non-White participants, though both means were in the High-Average to Average range.

In a logistic regression adjusting for age, COVID-19 symptom severity, comorbidities, psychiatric history, education, and gender, each one-unit increase in total MoCA score independently decreased the odds of Extremely Low neuropsychological test performance by 47%.
Female gender was independently associated with 79% lower odds of Extremely Low neuropsychological test performance compared to male gender.
Subjective memory complaints on the PAOF correlated significantly with total MoCA score.

Subjective complaints about cognitive/intellectual functioning on the PAOF correlated significantly with total MoCA score in the overall sample, but this correlation was not present in the subgroup with Normal/Low neuropsychological test performance.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had a significantly increased risk of incident heart failure in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to hospitalized controls.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had a significantly increased risk of incident pneumonia in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to hospitalized controls.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had a significantly increased risk of incident respiratory abnormalities in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to hospitalized controls.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had a significantly increased risk of incident cough in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to hospitalized controls.

Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had increased risk of delirium/dementia/amnesia and other cognitive disorders, as well as cognitive dysfunction or altered mental status, in the mid-stage post-acute period versus hospitalized controls.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had a greater risk of incident malaise and fatigue in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to hospitalized controls.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had an increased risk of angina pectoris during the late-stage post-acute period (90+ days) compared to hospitalized controls.

Non-hospitalized (outpatient) COVID-19 cases had a substantially increased risk of embolic and thrombotic disease (pulmonary embolism/infarction and venous embolism/thrombosis) in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to outpatient controls.
Outpatient COVID-19 cases had increased risk of atrial fibrillation/flutter and primary hypertension in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to outpatient controls.
Outpatient COVID-19 cases had an increased risk of new type 2 diabetes and vitamin D deficiency diagnoses in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to outpatient controls.
Outpatient COVID-19 cases had significantly increased risk of vascular dementia and other cognitive/dementia-spectrum diagnoses in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to outpatient controls.
Outpatient COVID-19 cases had increased risk of pneumonia and of malaise/fatigue in the mid-stage post-acute period compared to outpatient controls.

Outpatient COVID-19 cases showed a persistently increased risk (attenuated compared to mid-stage) for decubitus ulcers, type 2 diabetes, vitamin D deficiency, vascular dementia, and respiratory abnormalities into the late-stage post-acute period.
New-onset smell/taste disturbances and inflammatory or toxic neuropathy were uniquely elevated risks in the late-stage post-acute period among outpatient COVID-19 cases.
Hospitalized COVID-19 cases had a higher relative risk of dysphagia compared to outpatient COVID-19 cases, after normalizing for baseline inpatient/outpatient differences.

Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had a higher baseline (preexisting) prevalence of type 2 diabetes, gastroesophageal disease, obesity, chronic kidney disease, respiratory abnormalities, and heart failure compared to hospitalized controls, indicating worse preexisting health.
Outpatient COVID-19 cases had a higher baseline prevalence of gastroesophageal disease, obesity, and major depressive disorder compared to outpatient controls.

During the acute stage (within 29 days), hospitalized COVID-19 patients had higher cumulative incidence of viral pneumonia, respiratory abnormalities, pneumonia, malaise, fatigue, acute kidney injury, and hypovolemia compared to hospitalized controls.
None of the conditions found to be elevated in hospitalized COVID-19 cases during the mid-stage post-acute period remained significantly elevated into the late-stage period.

Unlike outpatients, hospitalized COVID-19 cases did not show a significant increased risk of pulmonary embolism or venous thromboembolism compared to hospitalized controls, possibly reflecting prophylactic anticoagulation use in inpatients.

Among hospitalized COVID-19 cases, the mid-stage post-acute incidence of cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions and symptomatic complaints declined across calendar quarters from 2020-Q1 to 2021-Q1, while metabolic condition incidence increased.

Among outpatient COVID-19 cases, the mid-stage post-acute incidence of cardiovascular, digestive, metabolic, and sensory organ conditions increased across calendar quarters, while other condition categories remained relatively constant.
In contrast to some prior literature, this study did not find significant changes over calendar time in gastrointestinal or dermatological post-acute sequelae of COVID-19.
Long-COVID-19 patients had significantly lower SDNN (standard deviation of NN intervals) than No-COVID-19 patients.
Long-COVID-19 patients had significantly lower SDANN than No-COVID-19 patients.
Long-COVID-19 patients had significantly lower SDNNi than No-COVID-19 patients.
Power spectral analysis showed significantly lower total power in Long-COVID-19 patients compared to No-COVID-19 patients.
The very-low-frequency (VLF) spectral component was significantly lower in Long-COVID-19 patients.

The high-frequency (HF) spectral component, reflecting vagal activity, was significantly lower in Long-COVID-19 patients and independently associated with Long-COVID-19 status on multivariable analysis.
The LF/HF ratio, a marker of sympatho-vagal balance, was significantly higher in Long-COVID-19 patients and independently associated with Long-COVID-19 status on multivariable analysis.
Minimum heart rate over 24-h monitoring was lower in No-COVID-19 patients than in Long-COVID-19 patients.
D-dimer levels were significantly higher in Long-COVID-19 patients and were independently associated with Long-COVID-19 status on multivariable regression.
NT-proBNP levels were significantly higher in Long-COVID-19 patients and independently associated with Long-COVID-19 status on multivariable regression, suggesting myocardial strain.
IL-6 levels were significantly higher in Long-COVID-19 patients compared to No-COVID-19 patients.
Echocardiography showed lower left ventricular ejection fraction in Long-COVID-19 patients compared to No-COVID-19 patients.

Using the Post-COVID-19 Functional Status Scale, the majority (56.7%) of Long-COVID-19 patients reported moderate/severe functional limitations, while 23.3% reported none/negligible and 20% slight limitations.

The authors propose that SARS-CoV-2 neurotropism and detection of the virus in the vagus nerve support a mechanism of persistent vagal fiber damage underlying parasympathetic impairment in Long-COVID-19.
Neurofilament light chain (NfL), a marker of axonal damage, was reported to increase with severity/course of COVID-19 disease, while GFAp decreased during the course of severe disease.
70% of the study patients (21/30) had Fatigue Severity Scale scores indicating clinically significant fatigue interfering with activities of daily living.
Approximately three-fourths of the cohort had clinically significant anxiety on the GAD-7 (mild n=12, moderate n=7, severe n=4).
Approximately half of the study population had PHQ-9 scores indicating clinically significant depression.
Among the 16 patients screened with the MOCA, 63% (10/16) scored below the cutoff of 26, suggesting cognitive impairment.
Patients with a pre-existing psychiatric history did not differ from those without one in reported severity of new anxiety, depression, or insomnia following COVID-19.
Patients with a past psychiatric history were significantly older than those without a past psychiatric history.
Severity of acute COVID-19 illness was not significantly associated with severity of depression symptoms.
Severity of acute COVID-19 illness was not significantly associated with severity of anxiety symptoms.
MOCA total score was not significantly correlated with PHQ-9 depression score.

Modafinil, often combined with an antidepressant, was the most commonly prescribed medication to target pervasive fatigue, with patients subjectively reporting improved fatigue and return to prior level of function.
Among patients offered antidepressant treatment, 80% were prescribed an SSRI while the remainder received an SNRI or NDRI for anxiety or depressive symptoms.
Insomnia (measured via the PHQ-9 sleep item) was noted in slightly less than three-fourths of individuals.
Substance abuse was reported in 7% (2/30) of patients, with one individual reporting increased use secondary to COVID-19 illness and the pandemic.
No individuals reported current suicidal ideation on the C-SSRS, though 13% (4/30) had a remote history of suicide attempt or ideation, all within the past-psychiatric-history subgroup.
Primary depressive disorder was the most common psychiatric diagnosis, occurring in 47% (14/30) of patients.
Primary anxiety disorder was diagnosed in 17% (5/30) of patients.
17% (5/30) of patients had adjustment disorder, and 15% (4/30) had no primary psychiatric diagnosis but presented exclusively with fatigue and cognitive complaints.
The majority of patients (80%) reported that psychiatric symptoms began simultaneously with the onset of COVID-19 illness, while 20% reported delayed onset a few months after diagnosis.

Among previously employed patients, three-fourths experienced significant interruption in their professional lives due to COVID-19 infection or its sequelae, with one-third of those unable to return to work at the time of most recent assessment.
Among 106 screened long-COVID patients, 38 (35.8%) had neuropathic or autonomic complaints or both.
Fatigue and headache were reported significantly more often in long-COVID patients who had autonomic and neuropathic complaints than in others.
The cutaneous silent period suppression index was significantly higher in long-COVID patients with autonomic/neuropathic complaints than in healthy controls.
Palmar and plantar sympathetic skin response did not differ between long-COVID patients and healthy controls.
Higher mTORONTO neuropathy scores were moderately correlated with lower palmar and plantar sympathetic skin response amplitudes.
Fatigue was the most common symptom reported by healthcare workers, affecting 25.5% of the cohort.
Headache was reported by 10.0% of healthcare workers.
Difficulty concentrating was reported by 7.9% of healthcare workers.
Exhaustion/burnout was reported by 7.1% of healthcare workers.
Insomnia was reported by 6.2% of healthcare workers.
Myalgia was reported by 6.7% of healthcare workers.
Arthralgia was reported by 6.3% of healthcare workers.
Irrespective of SARS-CoV-2 infection status, healthcare workers reported significantly higher rates of all measured symptoms than the general population.
SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthcare workers was associated with loss or change in smell.
SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthcare workers was associated with loss or change in taste.
SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthcare workers was associated with palpitations.
SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthcare workers was associated with dyspnea.
SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthcare workers was associated with difficulty concentrating.
SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthcare workers was associated with fatigue.
SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthcare workers was associated with headache.
Functional impairment was significantly more prevalent in healthcare workers compared to the general population.
Functional impairment showed a positive association with SARS-CoV-2 infection among healthcare workers.
The study title indicates an investigated association between Epstein-Barr virus reactivation and the development of fatigue in Long-COVID patients.
Sleep disturbances and clinically significant fatigue syndrome are commonly reported features of long COVID syndrome, with unknown pathophysiological correlations.
Multimodal individualized rehabilitation appeared suitable to help long COVID patients return to their premorbid level of functioning and substantially reduce insomnia complaints.

The authors propose that in long COVID, the ergoreflex—a cardiorespiratory reflex activated by exercise—is chronically overstimulated, producing heightened sympathetic, vasoconstrictor, and ventilatory drive that manifests as fatigue and breathlessness.

The authors propose that SARS-CoV-2 infection induces a hyperinflammatory and hypercatabolic state that reduces skeletal muscle mass and alters muscle function, potentially driving long COVID symptoms via enhanced ergoreflex activity.

The authors suggest exercise training may improve long COVID symptoms by preserving skeletal muscle mass and function and reducing ergoreflex activation, and call for tailored exercise interventions to be trialed.
Among 390 seropositive adults, 24.7% experienced at least one chronic COVID-19 symptom with a median persistence duration of 11 months.
Fatigue was the most common chronic COVID-19 symptom, reported by 11.3% of participants.
Change in sense of smell was reported as a chronic symptom by 9.5% of participants.
Change in taste was reported as a chronic symptom by 5.6% of participants.
Muscle or joint aches were reported as a chronic symptom by 5.4% of participants.
Weakness was reported as a chronic symptom by 4.6% of participants.
Females had a significantly higher proportion of persistent COVID-19 symptoms than males (31.5% vs. 18.6%).
Fatigue as a chronic symptom was significantly more common in females than males (15.8% vs. 7.3%).
Chronic fatigue as a persistent COVID-19 symptom was significantly more common in female participants than male participants.
Chronic headache as a persistent COVID-19 symptom was significantly more common in female participants than male participants.
Individuals who experienced six or more acute COVID-19 symptoms were more likely to develop chronic COVID-19 symptoms.
The latent symptom class characterized by chronic changes in smell and taste was associated with lower anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibody levels.
Persistent post-acute COVID-19 symptoms lasted a median of 11 months, ranging from 1 to 12 months.
Latent class analysis identified four distinct classes of chronic COVID-19 symptom patterns among participants.
Latent classes 2 and 3, characterized by multiple chronic symptoms, were associated with higher anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibody levels and more severe acute COVID-19 infection compared to class 1.
Among 102 long COVID patients with general fatigue, the most frequent accompanying symptoms were dysosmia, dysgeusia, headache, insomnia, dyspnea, and hair loss.
Kampo medicines accounted for 24.1% of the total 609 prescriptions given to patients with long COVID-related fatigue.
Hochuekkito was the most frequently prescribed Kampo medicine, accounting for 71.6% of Kampo prescriptions for long COVID fatigue patients.
The authors propose that general fatigue after infectious disease, including long COVID, reflects a 'qi deficiency' in Kampo medicine theory, justifying use of qi-compensating herbal treatments.
Among outpatients with mild COVID-19, 28.2% had long COVID-19, defined as symptoms persisting beyond 28 days.
42.28% of patients still had symptoms at 14 days after COVID-19 diagnosis.
16.3% of patients still had symptoms at 42 days (6 weeks) after diagnosis.
Musculoskeletal complaints were the most common symptom to persist beyond 28 days, affecting 12.7% of patients.
Upper respiratory tract symptoms persisted beyond 28 days in 7.6% of patients.
Fatigue persisted beyond 28 days in 6.8% of the total cohort, corresponding to 31.48% of the 54 patients who initially reported fatigue.
Arthralgia was the symptom most likely to persist beyond 28 days, with 64.7% of patients who had arthralgia still symptomatic.
Myalgia persisted beyond 28 days in 29.4% of the patients who initially reported myalgia.
Females had a significantly longer duration of symptoms than males (median 15 vs 10 days).
Significant fatigue (FSS ≥4) was more common in females than males (25.6% vs 6.5%).
Patients with long COVID-19 (>28 days) had a markedly higher mean FSS score than those without long COVID-19.
Patients with long COVID-19 had a significantly lower overall WHOQOL-BREF quality-of-life score than those without long COVID-19.
Males had a significantly higher overall WHOQOL-BREF score than females.
Overall quality of life was negatively correlated with the duration of COVID-19 symptoms.
Linear regression showed that each additional day of symptom duration was associated with a 0.3-point decrease in mean WHOQOL-BREF score.
Quality of life was negatively correlated with fatigue severity among patients reporting fatigue.
In multivariable logistic regression, female sex was associated with more than 3-fold higher odds of developing long COVID-19 compared to males.
Patients with BMI ≥23 kg/m2 were more likely to have persistent symptoms after adjustment for other variables.
Exercise intolerance was reported by 30.2% of patients and anxiety or low mood by 6.37%.
Among patients who were employed before COVID-19, 89.1% resumed work after a median of 13.5 days.
Patients with long COVID showed reduced global heart rate variability (RR interval, SDNN, SD2, and SD1/SD2) compared with COVID-free controls.
Long COVID patients demonstrated increased sympathetic modulation (LF and LF/HF) relative to COVID-free controls.
Long COVID patients showed decreased parasympathetic modulation (RMSSD, SD1, and HF) compared with COVID-free controls.
Sympathovagal balance (LF/HF ratio) was decreased in long COVID clinical groups relative to COVID-free controls.

Within the long COVID group, patients symptomatic for >3 and >6 months had higher HRV, while those symptomatic for ≤3 months showed reduced parasympathetic modulation and increased sympathetic modulation influence.
Hospitalized long COVID patients showed a reduction in sympathovagal balance compared with non-hospitalized long COVID patients.
No significant differences in approximate entropy (ApEn) or sample entropy (SampEn) were observed between long COVID clinical groups and COVID-free controls.
Patients with long COVID commonly reported persistent dyspnoea, fatigue, muscle weakness, and chest pain, and were predominantly women.
The authors propose that HRV measurements may be useful not only for monitoring COVID-19 patients but also for early identification of long COVID patients at risk of clinical deterioration.
In a Wuhan cohort of over 1700 patients surveyed 6 months after COVID-19, 63% reported fatigue/muscle weakness, though these symptoms were not further differentiated.
In an app-based survey of 4182 patients assessing 14 symptoms, fewer than 5% reported postinfectious myalgia, with fatigue and headache being much more common.
A Dutch study reported that more than 53% of hospitalized and 71% of non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients complained of persistent muscle pain.
A German (Cologne) study of non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients found only about 3% reported muscle pain 6 months after infection, notably lower than other cohorts.

Myalgia is also very common in the general (non-COVID) population, occurring in up to 10% of people, and biopsy in myalgia patients with otherwise normal neurological exam is pathological in only 2% of cases.

Multiple case reports and case series suggest autonomic dysfunction, particularly excessive tachycardia with orthostasis, occurs in some long-COVID patients and is classified as postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS).

A study found that sinus tachycardia in long-COVID patients (without other POTS features) was associated with reduced heart rate variability, leading the authors to postulate reduced parasympathetic activity as the cause.
An Italian study found orthostatic hypotension in 13.8% of all long-COVID patients, while none of the patients studied had POTS.
Several retrospective case series from the early pandemic phase suggested increased rates of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) in regions heavily affected by COVID-19, such as Spain and Italy.
A study from England found a slightly lower incidence of GBS during the first 2020 COVID-19 wave compared to previous years (2016-2019), contradicting the increased-rate findings from other regions.

A Swedish study of over 100 patients found that those who developed ICU-acquired weakness (ICUAW) after COVID-19 had a more severe disease course, longer ICU stay, and higher serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels, a biomarker for axonal degeneration.

A small study comparing COVID-19 ICU patients to those with other pneumogenic sepsis found COVID-19 patients had lower muscle strength but recovered faster than the comparison group, though the study was limited by small sample size and lack of electrophysiological confirmation of ICUAW.

In the Wuhan cohort, patients who had severe COVID-19 (requiring oxygen or mechanical ventilation) were significantly more likely to have myalgia, showing a dose-response ('biological gradient') relationship with an odds ratio of 2.69.
Muscle cells express the ACE2 receptor, the primary receptor for SARS-CoV-2 tissue invasion, providing a theoretical basis for direct viral muscle injury underlying long-COVID myalgia.
Early pandemic reports described nonspecific muscle damage/rhabdomyolysis with muscle fiber necrosis in COVID-19 patients, without evidence of inflammatory infiltrates in muscle or vessels.
Autopsy studies detected SARS-CoV-2 RNA in various organs, including muscle, without observing specific pathological changes.

Functional autoantibodies against G-protein coupled adrenergic and cholinergic receptors (GPCR-fAABs), discussed as pathogenetically relevant in POTS, have also been detected in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome, although final assessment (e.g., via passive antibody transfer in animal models) is still lacking.

ACE2, the functional cell-entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2, is highly expressed in vascular endothelium; increased angiotensin II (a vasoconstrictor) could theoretically induce local hypoperfusion and hypoxia, potentially underlying orthostatic intolerance in POTS or myalgia.
A small Canadian study during the 2003 SARS-CoV(1) pandemic described postinfectious myalgia, though only in a very small sample of 22 patients.
A Singapore case series found that 7 of 14 patients infected during the 2003 SARS-CoV(1) pandemic developed POTS after recovery, supporting a postviral link between coronavirus infection and POTS.
In the study by Fernández-de-Las-Peñas et al., men and women were equally affected by myalgia after COVID-19, unlike the overall sex disparity reported for long-COVID broadly.
CLOCK gene expression appears decreased in individuals with autism spectrum disorder compared to typically developing individuals.
PER1, a circadian clock gene active in brain areas controlling sleep-wake transition, was suggested to be mutated in ASD subjects.
A Japanese study found genetic variants at the CLOCK gene locus, such as rs3762836, exclusively in ASD patients who also had sleep disorders.

In a case-control sequencing study of 18 canonical CLOCK genes and CLOCK-controlled genes, function-altering mutations of circadian-relevant genes were more frequent in ASD subjects (n=28) than controls (n=23).
CACNA1C, a calcium channel gene with circadian expression supporting circadian entrainment, was found among genes overlapping ASD and sleep-problem gene sets.
In lymphoblastoid cell lines, AANAT (an enzyme converting serotonin to melatonin) was among 15 circadian-rhythm-regulating genes differentially expressed in the higher-severity ASD phenotypic group.
A systematic review of 35 studies concluded that melatonin or melatonin metabolite levels are below average in individuals with ASD compared with controls.

A large cross-sectional study found hyperserotonemia and a deficit in melatonin production, along with increased platelet N-acetylserotonin, in ASD individuals versus controls, with first-degree relatives showing intermediate levels.
Mothers of ASD children excreted significantly lower urinary 6-sulphatoxy-melatonin than control mothers.
Two ASMT single-nucleotide polymorphisms (rs4446909 and rs5989681) were more frequent in ASD individuals and were associated with decreased ASMT enzymatic activity and lower plasma melatonin levels.

Rare variants in melatonin receptor genes MTNR1A and MTNR1B altered receptor functional properties, with a significant association detected between ASD and two variants specifically in affected males.
Pineal gland volume was reduced in ASD samples, and this reduction was related to primary insomnia, parasomnias, and problems waking in the morning.
Blood platelet analysis of post-mortem samples found reduced AANAT and ASMT enzyme levels (melatonin synthesis enzymes) in ASD individuals compared with controls, correlating with insomnia.
Urinary corticosteroid excretion levels were higher in ASD children (low, medium, and high functioning) than in typically developing controls, suggesting altered HPA axis function.
A quarter of ASD children showed an attenuated evening decline in salivary cortisol compared with typically developing peers, while morning levels did not differ.

Among ASD children, those with more severe repetitive behaviors showed lower diurnal salivary cortisol than those with less severe repetitive behaviors, suggesting a link between HPA regulation and repetitive behavior severity.
ASD individuals across age ranges showed higher evening cortisol levels and a blunted diurnal cortisol slope than controls, with evening cortisol increasing through development.

ASD adults showed a greater reduction in evening cortisol concentrations than controls, with poorer sleep efficiency and increased wake duration correlating with cortisol levels near habitual sleep onset.
ASD children showed lower diurnal salivary alpha-amylase secretion than typically developing children in a four-group comparison including ADHD and specific learning disorder groups.

A study comparing prepubertal ASD males and controls found no significant difference in cortisol awakening response between groups, contrasting with other studies reporting altered cortisol rhythms in ASD.

ASD children showed more low-frequency and less high-frequency heart rate variability than controls, alongside elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid, indicating reduced cardio-vagal activity and increased sympathetic activity.
ASD adults showed significantly higher resting heart rate, lower RMSSD, and lower high-frequency HRV than controls, suggesting reduced parasympathetic activity.
ASD children showed a larger tonic pupil size and lower afternoon salivary alpha-amylase levels than age-matched controls, hypothesized to reflect norepinephrine over-production.

During overnight polysomnography, ASD children had higher heart rate during NREM stages N2/N3 and REM sleep, with lower high-frequency HRV (vagal modulation) during N3 and REM sleep, suggesting sympathetic dominance during sleep.
In an open trial, melatonin administered before bedtime was effective in improving sleep quality and reducing family stress in 47 of 51 children with neurodevelopmental disabilities including ASD.
A dose-escalation open-label trial found melatonin (1-3 mg) improved sleep latency and was well tolerated and safe in 24 medication-free children with ASD.

A placebo-controlled trial of pediatric prolonged-release melatonin (PedPRM) demonstrated efficacy and safety versus placebo for long-term (up to 52 weeks) treatment of insomnia in children with ASD, with improved caregiver quality of life.
Three months of agomelatine treatment significantly increased night total sleep time and improved sleep stability and phase correction in ASD subjects with sleep problems.
Gabapentin administered before bedtime was effective in improving sleep in 18 of 23 ASD children studied.

Urinary corticosteroid excretion levels were higher in children with low, medium, and high functioning ASD than in typically developing controls, with an altered cortisol excretion pattern specifically in low-functioning ASD.
Evening salivary cortisol showed an attenuated decline in a quarter of ASD children compared with typically developing peers, with no difference in morning levels.

In ASD children with more severe repetitive behaviors, diurnal salivary cortisol was lower than in those with less severe repetitive behaviors, suggesting repetitive behaviors may relate to glucocorticoid downregulation.

In high-functioning ASD girls, more than half showed inverse cortisol awakening response and over 14% showed inverted diurnal fluctuation compared with typical population models, with CAR status linked to depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation.

Evening cortisol levels were higher and diurnal slope blunted in ASD individuals compared with controls, with the elevation increasing from childhood to adolescence and potentially linked to impaired sleep quality.
ASD adults showed greater reduction in evening cortisol compared with controls, and poor sleep efficiency plus increased wake duration correlated with cortisol measured before habitual sleep onset.
ASD children showed lower diurnal salivary alpha-amylase secretion compared with typically developing children, while ADHD children showed significantly higher evening sAA than controls.
Two studies found no significant difference between ASD and control groups in cortisol awakening response or salivary alpha-amylase, though one noted differences in variability of levels.
ASD children showed more low-frequency HRV and less high-frequency HRV than controls, along with higher urinary VMA, indicating reduced cardio-vagal activity and increased sympathetic activity.
ASD adults had significantly higher resting heart rate and lower RMSSD and high-frequency HRV than controls, suggesting lower parasympathetic activity.
ASD children showed larger tonic pupil size and lower afternoon salivary alpha-amylase with little diurnal variation compared with controls, hypothesized to reflect norepinephrine over-production.
During sleep, high-functioning ASD children showed higher high-frequency HRV and RMSSD than controls, with a smaller decrease in heart rate during deep sleep despite higher parasympathetic tone.

ASD children had higher heart rate during N2, N3 and REM sleep and lower high-frequency HRV during N3 and REM sleep than controls, with higher LF/HF ratio during REM, suggesting sympathetic dominance during sleep.

Propranolol, a beta-blocker, was proposed as a therapeutic option for dysautonomias and emotional behaviors in ASD, reportedly improving verbal problem solving, social skills, conversation reciprocity, anxiety, and autonomic deregulation.
Melatonin administered before bedtime to children with neurodevelopmental disabilities improved sleep quality and reduced family stress in 47 of 51 children.
A 14-week open-label dose escalation study of melatonin (1-3 mg) in ASD children showed improved sleep latency with good tolerability and safety.

A placebo-controlled trial found pediatric-appropriate prolonged-release melatonin (PedPRM) effective and safe for up to 52 weeks of treatment of insomnia in ASD children, also improving caregiver quality of life.

A meta-synthesis of 38 studies found melatonin supplementation to be the most successful intervention for sleep initiation and maintenance in ASD, while behavioral intervention/education was most effective for night wakings and self-settling.
