Self-reported physical activity of daily living, assessed by the IPAQ, did not differ between people with epilepsy and controls.
People with epilepsy had a lower maximum heart rate during exhaustive exercise testing compared with matched healthy controls.
Heart rate reserve during exercise was lower in people with epilepsy than in healthy controls.
The chronotropic index was lower in people with epilepsy compared with matched healthy controls.
The ratio of low- to high-frequency heart rate variability changes (LF/HF ratio) was lower in people with epilepsy than in healthy controls, suggesting altered sympathovagal balance.

In two patients with idiopathic genetic epilepsy, generalized interictal epileptiform discharges were seen on EEG only after exercise, not before, though the post-exercise EEG recording was three times longer and no exercise-induced seizures were reported.
The authors suggest that, besides epileptogenesis itself, anti-seizure medications may also contribute to the observed autonomic differences between people with epilepsy and controls.

In two patients with idiopathic genetic epilepsy, generalized interictal epileptiform discharges were seen on EEG only after exercise and not before, though the post-exercise recording was three times longer than the pre-exercise one and no exercise-induced seizures were reported.
The authors suggest that, in addition to epileptogenesis itself, anti-seizure medications may also contribute to the observed autonomic nervous system differences in people with epilepsy.
People with epilepsy are reported to have an increased risk of sudden cardiac death, which is believed to be mediated in part by imbalances within the autonomic nervous system.

Prior evidence on autonomic dysfunction in epilepsy is noted to be derived mostly from patients with medically refractory seizures, whereas this study recruited a community-based sample with mostly seizure-free patients.
A 47-year-old woman developed left postganglionic Horner syndrome two weeks after an episode of Epstein-Barr virus-related glandular fever.
Apraclonidine 0.5% and phenylephrine 1% eye drop pharmacologic testing confirmed left Horner syndrome with a probable postganglionic lesion location.
Doppler ultrasound performed a week after the initial MRA revealed bilateral findings compatible with internal carotid artery dissection, despite the acute MRA not showing dissection.

Enlarged lymphoid tissue within the carotid sheath, seen on MRA as irregular narrowing of the left internal carotid artery, is proposed as a possible mechanism of sympathetic nerve disruption causing postganglionic Horner syndrome.
The authors hypothesize that plasma oxytocin is reduced in long-COVID due to acute and post-viral damage to the hypothalamus and oxytocinergic neurones.
The authors propose that SARS-CoV-2 may infect oxytocinergic neurones, contributing to hypothalamic dysfunction underlying long-COVID.
The authors propose intranasal oxytocin as the most clinically appropriate route to restore oxytocinergic function and potentially alleviate long-COVID symptoms.
A meta-analysis found a 3-month fatigue prevalence of 0.32 among 25,268 COVID-19 patients regardless of disease severity.
Fatigue frequency 2-3 months post-infection was over 50% in hospitalized versus 10% in ambulatory COVID-19 patients in a study of 9362 patients.
Female sex, higher BMI, comorbid asthma, older age, and more than 5 acute-phase symptoms including fatigue predict development of Post-COVID syndrome with an odds ratio of 3.53.
In a Swiss cohort of 431 COVID-19 patients, 40% required renewed healthcare contact 6-8 months post-infection, 18% received new diagnoses, 44% had to reduce work hours, and 12% reported income loss.
Post-COVID patients showed increased use of anxiolytics, sedatives, opioids, and antidepressants.
In the acute phase, 98% of COVID-19 patients reported fatigue and 91% reported headache.
3-month incidence of any psychiatric first diagnosis was 5.8%, with anxiety disorders at 4.2% and sleep disorders at 1.9% following COVID-19.
6-month incidence of psychiatric disorders post-COVID included 17.4% anxiety, 13.7% depression, 1.4% psychosis, 6.6% addiction disorders, and 5.4% insomnia.
In the US study of 73,435 patients, 6 months after COVID-19 there was elevated hazard ratio for fatigue (1.8), insomnia (1.3), post-traumatic stress disorder (1.3), and anxiety disorders (1.2).
A systematic review of 250,351 mostly hospitalized COVID-19 patients found fatigue in 38% and anxiety disorders in 30% at 6 months.
A meta-analysis of SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 infections found comparable 6-month prevalences of 30-40% for depression and anxiety regardless of virus type.
In a prospective cohort of 128 COVID-19 patients, female sex and comorbid anxiety or depression were identified as predictors for the development of fatigue.
In MERS-CoV survivors, depression (PHQ-9 score) at both 12 and 18 months mediated the relationship between fatigue severity at 12 months and post-traumatic stress symptoms at 18 months.
Patients with mild COVID-19 who had anxiety or depression showed lower psychological resilience according to the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale.
During the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection, a cytokine storm leads to excessive release of IL-2, IL-7, G-CSF, IP-10, MCP-1, MIP-1α, and TNF-α.

Molecular mimicry is discussed as a mechanism whereby human coronavirus-specific T cells cross-react with myelin in multiple sclerosis patients, potentially relevant to autoimmune processes in Post-COVID syndrome.
An FDG-PET study of 14 patients with COVID-19-associated fatigue found no changes in cerebral glucose metabolism.

The UK Biobank COVID-19 Re-Imaging Study found significant gray matter loss in the left parahippocampal gyrus, left lateral orbitofrontal cortex, and left insula (extending into anterior cingulate cortex, supramarginal gyrus, and temporal pole) in SARS-CoV-2 positive individuals compared to non-infected controls, along with increased diffusion indices in olfactory-connected regions.

FDG-PET studies in Post-COVID syndrome 3-4 months after acute infection showed hypometabolism in the orbitofrontal cortex, medial temporal lobe (hippocampus, amygdala), thalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum.

Neuropathological studies of COVID-19 show microglial activation with formation of microglial nodules and astrocytes primarily in white matter of brainstem and cerebellum, along with CD8+ and CD4+ T-cell infiltration and blood-brain barrier dysfunction, a pattern reported to be distinct from other inflammatory CNS diseases.
Methylphenidate and modafinil have been trialed for fatigue treatment, with methylphenidate found to be more effective.
Paroxetine had positive effects on tumor-associated fatigue, whereas fluoxetine did not.
Bupropion, a noradrenaline-dopamine reuptake inhibitor, can be used for tumor-associated fatigue, and aripiprazole also appears effective.

Meta-analyses of cognitive behavioral therapy for tumor-associated and post-viral fatigue found predominantly positive effects versus waitlist and other interventions, with greater effectiveness in patients with comorbid anxiety or depression, though long-term effects on post-viral fatigue were not demonstrated at 1 year.
40% of manifest Post-COVID syndrome patients reported symptom reduction following COVID-19 vaccination.

An international cohort study of 3762 patients with confirmed or suspected COVID-19 found that in over 91% convalescence exceeded 35 weeks, with symptom peaks occurring at 2 weeks for courses under 90 days versus 2 months for longer courses.
In the Swiss cohort at 6-8 months, 74.2% reported feeling healthy again, but fatigue persisted in 54.7% of initially included subjects.

Post-COVID patients who had severe acute illness reported fewer persistent deficits, whereas patients with mild acute illness showed significantly higher scores for depression, anxiety, and stress-related symptoms, though objective cognitive deficits were similarly present across both subgroups.

A French population-based cohort study of 26,823 volunteers found that perceived persistent psychiatric symptoms after COVID-19 were not significantly associated with serologically confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom among chronic Lyme disease (CLD) focus-group participants, described by 13 of 15 participants.
Cognitive problems such as confusion, reduced attention span, and memory loss were reported by 8 of 15 CLD focus-group participants.
Muscle and joint pain (myalgia and arthralgia) were reported by 7 of 15 CLD participants.
Impaired motor coordination, including falling and difficulty walking, was reported by 5 of 15 CLD participants.
Visual and/or auditory impairments (e.g., foggy vision, hearing loss) were reported by 5 of 15 CLD participants.
Sensations of abnormal body temperature, including feverishness, coldness, and flu-like feelings, were reported by 5 of 15 CLD participants.
Many participants described their CLD-related symptoms as invisible to others, either inherently unnoticeable or actively concealed to avoid perceived ridicule.
Participants described an unpredictable, fluctuating illness course with alternating periods of feeling better and worse, and noted that CLD manifests very differently from person to person.
Symptoms had far-reaching consequences on participants' ability to work, attend school, maintain a social life, or leave the house, evoking sadness, grief, and anger.

Most participants reported negative experiences with general practitioners and other physicians, citing perceived lack of knowledge about Lyme disease, insufficient investigation, and rapid attribution of unexplained symptoms to psychological causes.

Several participants had been referred to psychologists, either when doctors could not identify an organic cause or alongside somatic work-up, and reactions to this were mixed, particularly negative when referral seemed to reflect an inability to diagnose.

Participants used complementary/alternative medicine practices (e.g., strict diets) partly to regain a sense of control after disappointment with conventional medical care, describing perceived psychological benefit regardless of objective efficacy.

Interactions with peers and other CLD patients were highly variable: some participants reported strong emotional support, while others found learning about other patients' severe experiences distressing or frightening.

Participants frequently used impersonal generic 'you' to describe their own experiences, a linguistic device that creates common ground and validates shared experience, occurring in 12.7% of all speaking turns.

Over 85% of interactive speaking turns among participants in the first four focus groups contained explicit or implicit agreement with another speaker, reflecting collaborative construction of common ground about CLD.

The authors hypothesize that CLD patients collectively construct and expand the meaning of the CLD classification through mutual validation, potentially reinforcing a disabling illness narrative via a 'looping effect'.
The paper cites that post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (persistent symptoms after treatment of confirmed Lyme disease) occurs in approximately 5-10% of treated patients.
The paper proposes that persistent inflammation and autoimmunity following acute SARS-CoV-2 infection play a critical role in the development of post-COVID syndrome.

An autoimmune phenomenon is proposed as a major mechanism underlying most causative theories of post-COVID syndrome, and latent autoimmunity in PCS may lead to an increase in autoimmune diseases in coming years.
Most participants described severe, unrelenting fatigue in long COVID that was qualitatively different from ordinary tiredness.
Post-exertional malaise was commonly reported and triggered by a wide range of physical and cognitive activities.
Participants reported variable breathing difficulties ranging from mild to debilitating, with differing impact on daily functioning.
Long COVID symptom presentation was frequently described as unpredictable, relapsing and remitting, though some participants instead experienced persistent or gradually improving symptoms.
Participants described marked reductions in functional capacity that disrupted their ability to care for their home, family, and themselves.
Most participants had stopped working or greatly reduced work hours to manage long COVID symptoms, with concerns over lost income and job security.
Fear of symptom exacerbation led many participants to reduce or avoid physical activity, reflecting diminished trust in their own bodies following post-exertional malaise experiences.
The majority of participants reported feeling ignored or dismissed by primary healthcare providers when seeking help for long COVID symptoms.
Participants described trying pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments for long COVID symptoms, which offered only minor relief for some and none for others.
The authors note, in discussion, that long COVID may progress to ME/CFS in some patients, drawing an analogy to post-infectious ME/CFS following illnesses such as mononucleosis.
Participants' mourning of their pre-illness identity and inability to participate in prior roles and leisure activities paralleled experiences previously reported in fibromyalgia and ME/CFS.
The majority of participants had been managing long COVID symptoms for more than 10 months at the time of the survey.
A higher proportion of participants with Long COVID or severe Long COVID (>5 symptoms) had EBV nuclear antigen (NA) IgG levels above the assay quantitation limit compared to those without Long COVID.

In unadjusted analysis, CMV seropositive participants trended toward lower rates of Long COVID or Long COVID with >5 symptoms compared to those without Long COVID, but this was not statistically significant.
Participants with detectable EBV EA-D IgG (a marker of recent EBV reactivation) had higher adjusted odds of experiencing fatigue approximately four months after COVID-19 diagnosis.
In the subgroup restricted to HIV-negative participants, EBV EA-D IgG positivity remained significantly and positively associated with fatigue.
In the subgroup excluding hospitalized participants, the association between EBV EA-D IgG and fatigue strengthened, confirming this association is not solely due to acute COVID-19 severity.
Participants with high EBV NA IgG levels (>600 U/mL) had higher adjusted odds of experiencing neurocognitive Long COVID symptoms, with non-significant trends for severe LC and fatigue.
Pre-existing autoimmune disease (mainly thyroiditis) was independently associated with higher odds of fatigue in Long COVID.
Hospitalization during acute COVID-19 infection was independently associated with higher odds of severe Long COVID (>5 symptoms), fatigue, gastrointestinal, and cardiopulmonary symptom clusters.
Female sex was independently correlated with gastrointestinal and neurocognitive Long COVID symptoms.
After covariate adjustment, CMV seropositivity was significantly associated with lower odds of neurocognitive Long COVID, with non-significant trends toward lower odds of overall LC and severe LC.

Pre-existing HIV infection was associated with higher odds of Long COVID symptom clusters overall, with a statistically significant association for neurocognitive symptoms and a near-significant association for gastrointestinal symptoms.
Circulating EBV DNA was rarely detectable in convalescent plasma months after acute COVID-19; only one of fifty tested participants had detectable (sub-quantifiable) EBV DNA.
In the HIV-negative subgroup, CMV seropositivity remained significantly negatively associated with neurocognitive Long COVID, replicating the full-cohort finding.
Participants with measurable EBV EA-D IgG had significantly higher plasma neurofilament light chain (NFL) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) levels than those without.
Participants with EBV VCA IgG levels above the assay quantitation limit had significantly higher plasma TNFα, IL-10, and MCP-1 levels than those without.

Despite having lower odds of neurocognitive Long COVID, CMV seropositive participants had significantly higher plasma neurofilament light chain, IL-6, IP-10, and TNFα levels than CMV seronegative participants.

Adjusting for CMV serostatus strengthened the previously reported associations between systemic inflammatory markers (e.g., IL-6, TNFα) and Long COVID, suggesting inflammation sources unrelated to CMV are more likely to drive Long COVID risk.
EBV VCA IgG positivity, high-titer VCA IgG, and VCA IgM results were not significantly associated with Long COVID across any analyses and were excluded from final regression models.

The overall number of Long COVID symptoms was roughly similar across symptom-cluster groups (median 8 to 9.5), but was significantly higher in those with gastrointestinal symptoms compared to those with neurocognitive symptoms.
Nearly 40% of patients who experience smell loss during SARS-CoV-2 infection may go on to develop qualitative olfactory dysfunction, most commonly parosmia.
The incidence of parosmia following COVID-19 correlates negatively with age, suggesting younger patients are more likely to be affected.
The presence of parosmia predicts persistence of quantitative olfactory dysfunction (i.e., ongoing smell loss).
Onset of parosmia can occur months after initial COVID-19 infection, and symptoms may persist for well over 7 months.
Patients affected by parosmia report increased anxiety and decreased quality of life.
Structured olfactory training with essential oils is identified as the preferred treatment for parosmia following COVID-19.
Parosmia predicts recovery of aspects of quantitative smell loss when patients undergo olfactory training.
There is limited evidence suggesting that nasal corticosteroids may accelerate recovery of olfactory function following COVID-19.
Symptoms of qualitative olfactory dysfunction may persist for years, carrying a psychosocial burden that patients should be prepared to cope with.
Long COVID participants showed marked differences in specific circulating myeloid and lymphocyte cell populations compared to matched controls.
Participants with Long COVID exhibited elevated humoral (antibody) responses directed against SARS-CoV-2 relative to matched controls.
Long COVID participants showed unexpectedly increased antibody responses against non-SARS-CoV-2 viral pathogens, particularly Epstein-Barr virus.
Cortisol levels were uniformly lower among Long COVID participants relative to matched control groups.
In machine learning models integrating immune phenotyping data, decreased cortisol was identified as the single most significant predictor distinguishing Long COVID from controls.
Approximately 50% of patients show at least one PASC symptom up to 12 months after COVID-19 infection, though exact prevalence remains undetermined.
The specific pathophysiology of PASC has not yet been clarified, resulting in the absence of definite diagnostic criteria for the condition.
Despite extensive ongoing research, there are currently no clear diagnostic methodologies or treatments for PASC.
VWF was found at significantly increased levels within digested fibrin amyloid microclots from long COVID high-responder patients compared to healthy controls.
Platelet factor 4 (PF4/CXCL4) was found significantly increased in microclots of long COVID patients compared to controls, consistent with platelet activation-driven release.
Alpha-2-antiplasmin was only marginally increased in this larger cohort, in contrast to a significant increase seen previously in a smaller cohort.
Plasma kallikrein (KLKB1) was found decreased in long COVID microclots, which may impair plasminogen activation and downstream fibrinolysis.
Galectin-3-binding protein was found increased in the microclots of long COVID patients, consistent with viral-infection induced inflammation.
Thrombospondin-1, an adhesive glycoprotein released from platelet alpha-granules, was found increased in long COVID microclots.
Alpha-1-acid glycoprotein-2 was found elevated in long COVID microclots and is known to modulate the immune system during the acute-phase reaction.
ITIH1 was found elevated in the long COVID population, consistent with a prior report of higher abundance in a COVID-19 survivor group.
ITIH2 was found elevated in the long COVID population and has been previously associated with demyelinating diseases.
Lactotransferrin (lactoferrin) was found decreased in long COVID microclots, possibly indicating suppression of host antiviral immune response.
LPLC1, a LPS-binding protein important in innate immunity, was found decreased in long COVID microclots.
Adiponectin, an anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic adipokine, was found reduced in the long COVID population.
Alpha-1-acid glycoprotein 1, an acute-phase transport protein, was found reduced in the long COVID cohort, potentially indicating dysregulated inflammatory response.
Apolipoprotein C-II, a component of VLDL and chylomicrons, was found increased in the long COVID cohort's microclots, reflecting dysregulated lipid metabolism.
Apolipoprotein A-II, a major HDL component, was found reduced in the long COVID cohort's microclots.
Serum IL-6 levels were significantly different (higher) between high responder long COVID patients and healthy controls.
Serum ferritin concentrations showed no significant difference between long COVID patients and healthy controls.
Immunoglobulin kappa chain V-III region POM, identified as rheumatoid factor, was found present/elevated in long COVID microclots and may act as an autoantibody.
Immunoglobulin kappa chain V-III region CLL, another rheumatoid-factor-like antibody, was found elevated in the long COVID cohort.
Three specific immunoglobulin fragments were found only in long COVID high-responder samples and absent in controls, occurring in 27%, 24% and 22% of samples respectively.
Long COVID plasma showed a moderate to severe fibrinaloid microclot load (stage 2-4) by Thioflavin T fluorescence microscopy, versus minimal load (stage 1) in healthy controls.
Platelets in long COVID patients showed mild-to-severe activation (CD62P/PAC-1 positive) and clumping compared to minimally activated platelets in healthy controls.
Hypertension and hyperlipidaemia comorbidities did not correlate with VWF, plasma kallikrein, or PF4 levels and did not differentiate long COVID from control groups.
The most prevalent self-reported long COVID symptoms in this cohort were constant fatigue and cognitive impairment ('brain fog'), with anxiety also commonly reported.
The authors hypothesize that hyperactivated platelets in long COVID may shed stored serotonin, leading to serotonin depletion that could contribute to anxiety and depressed mood.
A 5-day course of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir led to resolution of PASC symptoms and conversion to a negative antigen test within 3 weeks of treatment completion.
PASC symptoms and antigen positivity recurred 4 weeks after completion of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, suggestive of viral reactivation/rebound.
Stopping tocilizumab for 10 days led to worsening of PASC symptoms and new-onset cognitive impairment (brain fog).
Resuming tocilizumab led to resolution of fatigue and brain fog and decreased headache severity within 3 weeks.

The patient's T cell responses against Nucleocapsid (a non-vaccine antigen) were enhanced after receiving the Moderna booster vaccine, indicating ongoing viral antigen exposure rather than vaccine-induced immunity alone.

Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment led to retention of Spike-specific but loss of Nucleocapsid-specific T cell responses, while halting tocilizumab was associated with elevated responses to both antigens, and resuming tocilizumab decreased responses to both.

The patient never mounted a detectable antibody response against Nucleocapsid, despite persistent T cell responses to it, while anti-Spike RBD antibody titers followed kinetics similar to T cell responses.

Antiviral CD4+ Tfh cell activation was highest after the vaccine booster (post-infection) and after stopping tocilizumab, and lowest after nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment and resumption of tocilizumab.

Total CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, TEM subsets, and cytotoxic CD8+ TEMRA cells showed maximal SARS-CoV-2-specific activation (to Spike, Nucleocapsid, Orf1ab, Orf7) at post-booster and post-tocilizumab-withdrawal visits, with minimal activation after antiviral treatment and tocilizumab resumption.

Autoreactive T cell responses to the rheumatoid arthritis-associated cartilage autoantigen YKL-40 oscillated in parallel with SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses, peaking post-booster and post-tocilizumab-withdrawal and dropping after antiviral treatment and tocilizumab resumption.

The patient tested intermittently positive for SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal antigen for at least 14 weeks post-infection despite negative RT-PCR results from 14 days post-infection onward and no known re-exposure, indicating prolonged antigen persistence.
Cited literature reports elevated serum IL-6 in the majority of PASC patients compared with asymptomatic convalescent controls assessed 8 months post-infection.
A cited cohort study found increased plasma IL-6 levels at 5 months post-infection in PASC patients with severe or moderate symptoms accompanied by cognitive impairment.
The authors' own prior research found that Neuro-PASC patients have increased CD8+ T cell production of IL-6 upon SARS-CoV-2 antigen stimulation compared with healthy COVID convalescents.
Cited literature reports significant positive correlations between susceptibility to PASC and pre-existing autoimmune disease diagnoses, consistent with this patient's comorbid rheumatoid arthritis.
There was a dose-dependent relationship between COVID-19 severity and the number of concomitant long-lasting symptoms, with more severe cases reporting more symptoms.
Fatigue was the most common long-lasting PASC symptom among severe/life-threatening C-19 cases, occurring in 61.3% of them.
Post-exertional malaise occurred in 49.6% of severe/life-threatening C-19 cases, making it the second most common PASC symptom.
Insomnia symptoms (difficulty falling or staying asleep) occurred in 47.4% of severe/life-threatening C-19 cases and were consistently among the most common PASC symptoms across all severity levels.
Excessive daytime sleepiness occurred in 35.8% of severe/life-threatening C-19 cases and was among the most common PASC symptoms across severity groups.
Brain fog/cognitive dysfunction occurred in 46.7% of severe/life-threatening C-19 cases.
Shortness of breath occurred in 46.7% of severe/life-threatening C-19 cases and was emphasised among severe cases relative to moderate cases, likely reflecting more severe pulmonary pathology.

Joint/muscle pain occurred in 40.4% of severe/life-threatening C-19 cases, but long-lasting joint/muscle pain was actually more common among non-C-19 controls (14.9%) than among asymptomatic C-19 cases (6.7%).
Long-lasting loss of smell/taste was far more common among asymptomatic C-19 cases (9.1%) than among non-C-19 controls (1.4%), though less common than in more severe cases (17.2%-20.1%).
All 21 assessed PASC symptoms differed significantly in prevalence between non-C-19 controls and C-19 cases.
Severe/life-threatening C-19 cases reported significantly more depression developed after the infection compared with milder C-19 cases.
Severe/life-threatening C-19 cases were less vaccinated against C-19 than milder cases, while non-C-19 controls had the highest vaccination level.
Severe/life-threatening C-19 cases had higher BMI and more obesity than non-C-19 controls and milder C-19 cases.
Severe/life-threatening C-19 was more common among men than among women compared with non-C-19 controls and milder severity C-19 cases.
Participants reported a mean of 21 symptoms each (range 1-93) among a total of 101 distinct symptoms captured, indicating a heavy symptom burden in PASC.

The most prevalent PASC symptoms reported were fatigue, headache, shortness of breath, difficulty concentrating, inability to exercise, cough, change in sense of taste, diarrhoea, and muscle or body aches.
Nearly all respondents (98.0%) reported that at least one of their symptoms remained unresolved at the time of the survey.
97.8% of respondents reported that at least one of their symptoms was intermittent, temporarily remitting and later relapsing.

PASC symptoms appear to progress in a temporal sequence, with flu-like symptoms (fatigue, fever/chills, headache, exercise intolerance, sore throat, cough, congestion) occurring early, followed by neurological, gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal symptoms, and later by microvascular, integumentary, gynaecological and endocrine symptoms.

The authors suggest, citing prior literature, that the evolving pattern of PASC symptoms may reflect endothelial dysfunction, immune-mediated inflammation, oxidative stress and hormonal imbalance, though no causal relationship has been established.

The symptoms perceived to most impair ability to work included fatigue, personality change, 'brain pressure,' insomnia, exercise intolerance, difficulty concentrating, memory problems, confusion, shortness of breath, and the relapsing/remitting nature of symptoms.
Women were substantially over-represented among PASC respondents (85.7% female), consistent with other reports suggesting PASC occurs more frequently in women.
Most participants (89.3%) were never hospitalised for COVID-19, indicating PASC occurs and causes substantial impact independent of acute COVID-19 severity.
Symptom duration among PASC survivors ranged widely, from about 2 weeks after onset to over 100 days, with changing/evolving symptoms being a prominent long-lasting feature.
On average, the time from initial COVID-19 diagnosis to survey completion (reflecting persistence of symptoms) was 20.88 days, with participants averaging 21 reported symptoms.
Estimates suggest that 30% to 75% of people recovering from COVID-19 may experience Long COVID symptoms.
A UK Office of National Statistics survey of over 8,000 non-hospitalized COVID-19-positive respondents found 21% symptomatic at 5 weeks post-infection and 9.9% symptomatic at 12 weeks.
A Canadian study of hospitalized COVID-19 patients using patient-reported outcome measures found over 50% had reduced quality of life 3 months post-infection.
Patients who went on to develop PASC had higher levels of TNF-α during early recovery from acute COVID-19.
Patients who went on to develop PASC had higher levels of the chemokine IP-10 (CXCL10) during early recovery from acute COVID-19.
Elevated blood urea, D-dimer, and C-reactive protein levels have been linked to long-term pulmonary, cardiac, and hepatic abnormalities months after acute COVID-19.
Low lymphocyte levels have been linked to long-term pulmonary, heart, and liver abnormalities after acute COVID-19.

A study following Long COVID patients found highly activated innate immune cells and elevated serum proinflammatory cytokines up to 8 months post-infection, suggesting dysregulated inflammation contributes to PASC.
The SARS-CoV-2 S1 spike protein has been found to persist in nonclassical proinflammatory monocytes, suggesting viral antigen persistence may drive ongoing inflammation in Long COVID.

Persistent COVID-19 symptoms were more strongly associated with experiencing more than 5 acute-phase symptoms (hoarseness of voice, fatigue, headache, dyspnea, and myalgia) than with acute disease severity.
Age, sex, and comorbidities such as diabetes, hyperglycemia, obesity, cardiovascular disease, asthma, and renal disease have been associated with increased risk of developing PASC.
ICU admission or need for ventilation during acute COVID-19 has been correlated with subsequent PASC development, although mild/moderate cases can also develop long-term symptoms.

In SARS-CoV-2-infected Syrian hamsters, CXCL10 remained elevated in the lung through day 15 post-infection (after viral clearance), suggesting a persistent inflammatory signature relevant to PASC-like lung pathology.
IFN-β was significantly downregulated in the nasal turbinate and lung of SARS-CoV-2-infected Syrian hamsters, with the strongest inhibition at day 2 post-infection.
IFN-γ was upregulated in the lungs of SARS-CoV-2-infected Syrian hamsters, resolving by day 15 post-infection.

SARS-CoV-2 infection in Syrian hamsters increased cardiac expression of TNF-α, IL-6, IL-4, IL-5, IL-2, and IL-10, accompanied by histopathological evidence of eosinophilic myocarditis and microthrombi.

Hamsters infected with SARS-CoV-2 developed ventricular wall thickening, increased ventricular mass/body mass ratio, interstitial coronary fibrosis, and elevated serum cardiac troponin I, cholesterol, and LDL between days 7-14 post-infection, resembling human cardiovascular complications of COVID-19.

SARS-CoV-2-infected Syrian hamsters developed progressive bone loss in the femur and tibia with induction of osteoclastogenesis, driven by respiratory-derived IL-1β and TNF-α rather than direct bone infection, with no restoration of bone density by 60 days post-infection.

At 31 days post-infection, SARS-CoV-2-recovered hamsters (unlike influenza-recovered hamsters, which returned to baseline) still showed a robust type I interferon response and microglial activation in the olfactory bulb despite absence of infectious virus or viral RNA.

SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed significant differences from controls in a marble burying test (a proxy for repetitive/compulsive-like behavior) at 26 days post-infection, despite olfactory food-finding deficits resolving by day 15.
A UK survey of non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients found 21% remained symptomatic at 5 weeks post-infection and 9.9% remained symptomatic at 12 weeks.
A Canadian cohort study using patient-reported outcome measures found that over half of hospitalized COVID-19 patients had reduced quality of life 3 months after acute infection.
Patients who later developed PASC had higher levels of TNF-alpha and IP-10 during early recovery from acute COVID-19 compared to those who did not develop PASC.
Elevated blood urea, high D-dimer, elevated C-reactive protein, and low lymphocyte counts have been linked to long-term pulmonary, cardiac, and liver abnormalities months after acute COVID-19.

In obesity, adipocyte-derived inflammatory adipokines (IL-8, PAI-1, MCP-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-18) and serum amyloid-A are hypothesized to amplify macrophage-driven chronic inflammation contributing to PASC risk.
SARS-CoV-2 S1 protein was found to persist in nonclassical proinflammatory monocytes, supporting a viral persistence mechanism for PASC.
Long COVID patients showed highly activated innate immune cells and elevated proinflammatory cytokine expression in serum up to 8 months post-infection.
K18-hACE2 mice exhibit lethargy during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, suggesting reduced activity in this model could be tracked as a surrogate for post-acute fatigue in PASC.

In the MISTRG6 humanized mouse model, SARS-CoV-2 infection led to sustained viral RNA, persistent weight loss, lung fibrosis, aberrant inflammatory macrophage responses, and persistent interferon-stimulated gene signatures 28 days post-infection.
In rhesus and cynomolgus macaques, serum IL-6 levels remained sustained at 5 to 6 weeks post-infection in some animals, corresponding to ongoing lung pathology.

Adult rhesus macaques exhibited higher serum IL-6 and a profibrotic transcriptomic signature in the respiratory tract compared to infant macaques, potentially explaining age-related differences in disease severity.
In African green monkeys, disease severity following SARS-CoV-2 infection correlates with increased age.
In ferrets, males showed a delayed type I interferon response that was exacerbated by age and was associated with prolonged SARS-CoV-2 replication in the upper respiratory tract.
Ferrets become lethargic during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, a phenotype hypothesized to persist into chronic post-viral fatigue and to disproportionately affect ferrets by sex.
A Phase II trial of RSLV-132, an RNase-Fc fusion protein that digests extracellular RNA to prevent interferon/TLR activation, is underway in Long COVID patients.
In an uncontrolled, non-randomized study of 22 Long COVID patients, sodium pyruvate nasal spray was associated with improvements in headaches, coughing/sneezing, and breathing difficulties.

A clinical trial is evaluating nicotinamide riboside (Niagen), a NAD+ precursor supplement, for improving neuropsychological complications of Long COVID including cognitive function, depression, anxiety, and physical symptoms.

In a marble burying test conducted at 26 days post-infection, SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed significant differences from controls, suggesting persistent disruption of repetitive/compulsive-like behavior.

SARS-CoV-2 infection led to decreased thalamic activity in hamsters at 3 days post-infection (versus increased activity with influenza), hypothesized to contribute to PASC-associated cognitive deficits.
IL2RG knockout hamsters appear susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 neuroinvasion, while data from wild-type hamsters regarding neuroinvasion remain inconclusive.
Syrian hamsters exhibited progressive bone loss in the femur and tibia into the post-acute phase, with no restoration of bone density by 60 days post-infection.
89% of survey respondents reported that they had not returned to their pre-COVID-19 level of health at the time of the survey.
More than two thirds of PASC patients continued to experience fatigue, post-exertional malaise, palpitations, chest pain, stomach upset/nausea, memory problems, muscle pain and joint pain.

Thams et al. developed a protocol combining transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) with concurrent cognitive training for post-COVID-19 patients, but results have not yet been published.
In a comparative cognitive task study, only the 'No COVID' control group was able to complete a Test of 2D mental rotation, indicating a reasoning deficit in the Long COVID patient group.
Virtual reality (VR) gaming rehabilitation was perceived as a positive and motivating treatment after Long COVID, with reported benefits for stress reduction and cognitive functioning.

Inflammation may cause neuronal injury through cytotoxic and chemotactic mediator release, activating surrounding microglial cells and intensifying microglia-mediated neuroinflammation, contributing to neuronal loss and neurodegeneration.
Peripheral activation of the trigemino-vascular system through an inflammatory cytokine storm is implicated in the development of headache in Long COVID.
Long COVID patients showed a deficit in reasoning compared to healthy participants, as only the non-COVID group could complete a specific 2D mental rotation cognitive task.
The COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale (C19-YRS) was developed as a 22-item patient-reported outcome measure to evaluate the long-term impact of COVID-19 and the effect of rehabilitation.
The Symptom Burden Questionnaire for Long COVID (SBQ-LC) was validated as a novel outcome measure comprising 16 symptom-domain scales plus an interference scale assessing everyday-life impact.
The Post-COVID-19 Functional Status Scale (PCFS) was proposed by Klok et al. to measure the full spectrum of functional outcomes following COVID-19.

Sabel et al. hypothesized that transorbital alternating current stimulation (tACS) might reduce Long COVID visual and cognitive symptoms linked to neurovascular dysregulation, though substantial evidence is lacking.
Thams et al. developed a protocol combining transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) with concurrent cognitive training for post-COVID-19 patients, but results had not yet been published.
Virtual reality (VR) gaming was perceived as a positive and motivating rehabilitation treatment after Long COVID, with reported benefits for stress reduction and cognitive functioning.
Rehabilitation programs based on endurance and balance training yielded improvements in cognition among Long COVID patients.
Tele-rehabilitation enables home-based exercises tailored to Long COVID patients' cognitive deficit areas, and tele-therapy/tele-counseling can address emotional and mood disturbances.
The GAD-7 is a widely used anxiety screening tool with a cut-off score of 10, standardized in a sample of Colombian general practitioners during the COVID-19 pandemic.
A bivariate meta-analysis of 18 validation studies identified PHQ-9 cut-off scores between 8 and 11 as optimal for detecting major depressive disorder.

Compagno et al. reported that a multidisciplinary rehabilitation (MDR) program combining physical training and psychological treatment was safe and feasible and could reduce residual symptoms while promoting physical and psychological recovery in Long COVID patients.
Greater respiratory sinus arrhythmia reactivity (parasympathetic withdrawal) predicted higher concurrent observed emotion dysregulation in children with ASD, independent of ASD symptom severity.
Baseline RSA (resting parasympathetic activity) was not significantly related to observed emotion dysregulation in children with ASD.
Higher ASD symptom levels were significantly correlated with greater observed emotion dysregulation in children with ASD.
Child IQ was not significantly related to observed emotion dysregulation in children with ASD.
The right-to-left shunt through the secundum ASD worsened from grade 3 in the recumbent position to grade 4 in the upright (Fowler's) position on contrast echocardiography.
A home pulse oximeter recording showed SpO2 dropping from 87% to 81% when the patient changed from a recumbent to a sitting position, which raised suspicion of platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome.
Aortic tortuosity resulting from thoracic vertebral compression fractures acted as a functional element that displaced the heart and facilitated right-to-left shunting through the ASD.
PFO and ASD, common anatomical substrates for POS, are present in approximately 25% and 0.16% of the adult population respectively.
Percutaneous transcatheter closure of the ASD resulted in resolution of the SpO2 drop in the upright position and dramatic symptomatic improvement.

4D flow MRI demonstrated that blood from the IVC, but not the SVC, preferentially passed through the ASD into the left atrium, explaining the greater bubble transit seen with lower-limb versus upper-limb contrast injection.

Right heart catheterization showed left atrial pressure exceeding right atrial pressure, consistent with the mechanism enabling right-to-left shunting despite a predominantly left-to-right shunt on Qp/Qs.
As main effects, neither baseline RSA (RSA-B) nor RSA reactivity (RSA-R) were significantly associated with sleep problems or sleep duration in children with ASD after controlling for age.
The interaction between baseline RSA (RSA-B) and RSA reactivity (RSA-R) significantly predicted sleep problems (but not sleep duration) in children with ASD, controlling for age.
Among children with high RSA reactivity, lower baseline RSA (indicating lower vagal tone) was associated with significantly more parent-reported sleep problems.
In the context of low RSA reactivity, baseline RSA was not significantly associated with sleep problems.
The combination of high baseline RSA and high RSA reactivity appeared protective, being associated with fewer sleep problems and suggesting a possible resilience phenotype in children with ASD.
Older children in the ASD sample had significantly fewer parent-reported sleep problems.
Child age was significantly positively related to (age-adjusted) baseline RSA in the ASD sample.
IQ, gender, and ASD symptom severity (ADOS score) were not significantly related to sleep problems, sleep duration, or RSA indices in this sample.
Sleep problems—including insomnia, poor sleep efficiency, parasomnias, and disrupted sleep-wake cycles—are reported as ubiquitous in autism spectrum disorder, with estimated prevalence of 50%-80%.

Approximately 30% of lumbar intervertebral foramina showed either an increase or decrease in foraminal area and foraminal height of more than 5% when patients with adult spinal deformity moved from supine to standing position.
Foraminal area decreased specifically in the lower lumbar spine when patients stood upright compared to supine positioning.
The concave side of the spinal curvature had a significantly higher rate of decreased foraminal area and foraminal height than the convex side.
ROC curve analysis identified narrowing of the intervertebral disc wedge (cutoff >0.05°) as a risk factor for decreased lumbar foraminal area and height when standing.

Chronic stress-induced alterations in cellular homeostasis are proposed to trigger a 'mitochondrial allostatic load' characterized by functional and structural mitochondrial changes leading to oxidative stress, inflammation, mtDNA damage and apoptosis.

Mitochondrial functional aberrations in the nucleus accumbens of highly anxious mice were found to mediate low social competitiveness, and enhancing mitochondrial function could reverse the sociability deficits.

A specific mitochondrial DNA mutation previously linked to autism spectrum disorder was shown to produce autistic endophenotypes in mice by altering the respiration chain and increasing reactive oxygen species production.
Mitochondria act as integrators of stress by sensing and transducing stressors such as glucocorticoids and catecholamines into cellular adaptation mechanisms as part of allostasis.

Parents of autistic individuals showed a significantly later-shifted primary peak in their task-evoked pupillary response to emotional faces compared with parent controls, as revealed by growth curve analysis (negative cubic term).
There was no significant main effect of group on mean pupillary response between ASD parents and parent controls.
Macro-level peak pupillary response and latency to peak pupillary response did not differ significantly between ASD parents and parent controls.
IQ was a significant positive predictor of mean pupillary response across both ASD parent and parent control groups, with higher IQ associated with larger pupillary responses.

A significant three-way interaction between the cubic (timing) growth curve term, diagnostic group, and IQ was observed, indicating that the relationship between IQ and pupillary response timing differed by group.
In ASD parents, longer latency to peak pupillary response was correlated with greater pragmatic language difficulties, though this did not survive Bonferroni correction.

In ASD parents, a larger peak pupillary response was associated with poorer performance on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes social cognition test, an association significantly different from that in parent controls.
In parent controls, macro-level pupillary response variables were not significantly correlated with pragmatic language or social cognition.
In exploratory parent-child dyads, parent peak pupillary response was correlated with their autistic child's peak pupillary response, with a high probability that this correlation exceeded chance.

There were no significant group differences in proportion of fixation duration to facial areas of interest between ASD parents and parent controls, indicating visual attention patterns did not differ.
Parents of autistic individuals did not differ from parent controls on total Broad Autism Phenotype Questionnaire score.
taVNS increases endogenous release of the hypothalamic neuropeptide oxytocin and biases visual attention toward salient facial features important for emotion recognition.
Invasive VNS increased plasma oxytocin concentrations in rats immediately after stimulation, supporting a vagal-oxytocin mechanism relevant to social cognition.
Clinical trials in children with ASD have reported improvements in social symptoms following taVNS treatment.
taVNS improved interoception, evidenced by increased cardiac interoceptive accuracy in a heartbeat discrimination task, a process considered fundamental to emotional processing.
taVNS modulated attention to direct gaze, a salient social cue, in a Rapid Serial Visual Presentation task, suggesting enhanced perception of gaze direction and joint attention.
Massage that increases vagal activity has been reported to improve social responses and parent-child relationships in children with ASD.

taVNS reduced gastric action potential frequency but increased action potential amplitude, and raised gastrin levels 3 hours after stimulation, suggesting a role in regulating GI dysfunction relevant to ASD.
taVNS reduced gastric activity frequency without acutely altering resting energy expenditure, while high frequency taVNS increased gastric motility in another study.
taVNS has been shown in healthy populations to improve novel orthography acquisition and speech category learning, suggesting potential as an adjunct to language training for children with ASD.
taVNS enhanced response control including backward inhibition and response inhibition, and increased adaptation to conflict in a Simon task, in healthy participants.

taVNS improved response selection during sequential action, automatic motor inhibition, self-control in delay discounting, cognitive flexibility, general adaptive control, and sustained attention in healthy populations, suggesting therapeutic potential for ADHD-related inattention/impulsivity.

After one month of taVNS treatment, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores were significantly reduced compared to a control group in adult MDD patients, associated with increased default mode network functional connectivity.
taVNS compared to sham stimulation decreased BOLD signals in limbic brain areas and improved subjective well-being ratings.
taVNS decreased attention to sad stimuli in adolescents with MDD during emotion recognition tasks, and reduced the ability to recognize sadness in dynamic bodily expressions in healthy subjects.

Active taVNS improved use of cognitive reappraisal strategies to down-regulate responses to negative emotional pictures, improved cognitive flexibility/divergent thinking, and facilitated reward-seeking behavior via increased invigoration.

Active taVNS reduced attentional engagement to threat and negative thought intrusions in high trait worrying adults, and facilitated extinction of declarative fear and explicit fear extinction learning compared to sham stimulation.

Extinction training combined with taVNS resulted in rapid anxiolytic effects and inhibition of the fear-potentiated startle response, and enhanced associative/recollection-based memory relevant to extinction memory retention.

Four weeks of taVNS treatment improved chronic insomnia symptoms by decreasing Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and Flinders Fatigue Scale scores, and increasing reduced dorsolateral prefrontal cortex neuroexcitability, with the excitability change predicting treatment efficacy.

A systematic review of 1322 participants across 51 studies found the most common taVNS side effects were local skin irritation, headache, and nasopharyngitis, usually mild and temporary, with no correlation between stimulation frequency/pulse width and occurrence of side effects.

taVNS has been used to treat oral feeding dysfunction in premature newborns (≤33 weeks) and pediatric nephrotic syndrome in young patients (4-17 years) without observing stimulation-related adverse events.

fMRI evidence showed that stimulation of the cymba concha induced the strongest activation of the nucleus tractus solitarius, the main recipient of afferent vagal projections in the brainstem, compared to the ear canal, inner tragus, and earlobe.

Right-ear taVNS stimulation showed greater beneficial effects on heart rate variability modulation compared to left ear stimulation, and a systematic review concluded right-ear stimulation does not increase risk of aversive effects.
A study systematically varying taVNS parameters in 20 healthy individuals found that a combination of 0.5 ms pulse width and 10 Hz frequency induced the greatest effects on heart rate.

Several studies failed to observe increased noradrenergic activity in active taVNS compared to sham stimulation, raising questions about biomarker reliability and possibly reflecting suboptimal stimulation parameters or insufficient afferent-only fiber activation.
Hyperacusis, a loudness intolerance disorder, is reported to be comorbid with autism spectrum disorder.
Hyperacusis is described as comorbid with fibromyalgia among more than twenty non-auditory medical disorders.
Hyperacusis is described as comorbid with migraine among more than twenty non-auditory medical disorders.

Neural models propose that hyperacusis may arise from enhanced central gain, whereby signals from a damaged cochlea are progressively amplified as they ascend through the auditory pathway and non-auditory brain regions involved in emotion, memory and stress.
The previously reported ~4:1 male-to-female sex bias in ASD diagnosis is now understood to be largely due to affected females being better able to mask/camouflage their symptoms than males.

ASD currently affects around 1 in 68 children worldwide, a 35-fold increase since the earliest epidemiologic studies conducted in the late 1960s-1970s, though this increase may partly reflect diagnostic/administrative biases.
Autistic children show early increases in brain volume and cortical thickness during infancy and toddlerhood, followed by accelerated decline into adolescence and beyond.
Regional brain overgrowth in ASD is concentrated in frontal and temporal cortices and the amygdala, sometimes followed by degeneration.
Young autistic males show a significant excess of neuron number in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, likely arising from prenatal dysregulation of cortical layer formation.
Conception during winter months is associated with a 6% increased risk of ASD compared with summer conception.
Autism spectrum disorder is significantly associated with increased subsequent incidence of inflammatory bowel disease.
Unlike many psychiatric diseases, there is a lack of evidence for systemic low-grade inflammation in individuals with ASD.
Rapid early increases in bilateral amygdala size in ASD correlate positively with the severity of social interaction and communication deficits at age 5.
Youths with ASD show greater amygdala spine density than age-matched typically developing controls, a difference that decreases with age, unlike in typical development.
Young ASD subjects show an initial overabundance of amygdala neurons followed by reduction across all nuclei in adulthood, contrasting with the maturation pattern in typical development.

ASD cortical overgrowth involves a 7% increase in overall cerebrum size, with 5% and 10% increases in total gray and white matter respectively, beginning before age two and followed by arrested growth by end of childhood.
ASD subjects show greater spine densities on pyramidal cells in superficial and deep cortical layers of frontal, temporal, and parietal regions compared with age-matched controls.

ASD brains show excessive short- to medium-distance axons with increased branching beneath the anterior cingulate cortex, along with decreased myelin thickness in the orbitofrontal cortex, consistent with prefrontal overconnectivity.
High cortical spine densities, associated with decreased brain weight, are most commonly found in ASD subjects with lower levels of cognitive function.
ASD individuals lack the decline in cortical surface area between ages 9 and 20 that is consistently observed in typical development.

ASD shows a slower rate of cortical thinning from childhood through adolescence followed by faster thinning in late adolescence, contrasting with typical development, where thinning occurs during teen years/early puberty.

Reelin and its signal transducer Dab1 show reduced protein and mRNA levels in the frontal and cerebellar cortex of autistic brains compared to controls, with a non-significant reduction in parietal areas.
mRNA for the reelin receptor VLDLR is significantly elevated in superior frontal and cerebellar areas of autistic brains compared to controls.
The S-allele of the serotonin transporter gene SLC6A4 is considered particularly important for conferring susceptibility to ASD.
CPEB4, which governs mRNA polyA-tail dynamics, binds to the transcripts of most high-confidence ASD-risk genes.
Cortical minicolumns in ASD brains are spaced farther apart with lower cell density than in typical development, with a 6-10% difference in minicolumn width observed across all cortical regions.
By late childhood, spine density drops by 50% in typically developing brains but only about 16% in ASD brains, reflecting reduced synaptic pruning and impaired signal-to-noise discrimination.

ASD-affected individuals show autonomic nervous system dysfunction, with sympathetic over-activation on a background of parasympathetic activity deficits, which is hypothesized to drive dysregulation of the gut-brain axis and intestinal homeostasis.

In a mouse model, moderate maternal immune activation increases circulating tryptophan and its placental conversion to serotonin, increasing fetal serotonin exposure and restricting serotonergic axonal outgrowth during forebrain development.

In a rabbit model of intrauterine inflammation, placental IDO is markedly upregulated alongside intense microglial activation, increased fetal brain kynurenic and quinolinic acid, and a drop in the serotonin precursor 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.
Maternal infection and/or increased fetal serotonin supply during pregnancy is associated with a higher risk of autism but does not by itself account for overt ASD pathogenesis.

Unlike schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, which show excessive pruning, gray matter loss, and links to low-grade systemic inflammation, there is no conclusive evidence for systemic inflammation in ASD.
Reduced functional connectivity is observed in the right posterior inferior temporal gyrus, fusiform gyrus, and bilateral inferior occipital cortex in ASD, regions implicated in facial recognition.

Post-mortem studies show dendritic spine density in the temporal lobe is higher in individuals with ASD than in typically developing controls, with substantial age-related variability within the ASD group.

Across the NPD cohort, higher PASS Total autonomic symptom scores were significantly associated with higher SRS Total scores (greater ASD trait severity), controlling for age and sex.

PASS Circulation, Thermoregulation, Sleeping Patterns, and Breathing subscale scores were significantly related to SRS Total autism trait scores, though not to Social Awareness and Social Motivation SRS subscales.
PASS Urinary/Gastrointestinal Systems subscale scores were significantly related to SRS Restricted/Repetitive Behaviors and Social Awareness subscale scores, but not other SRS subscales.

In an early Wuhan cohort of 214 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 36% exhibited neurological symptoms including loss of taste/smell, headache, dizziness, muscular weakness, cerebrovascular problems, and reduced awareness, rising to 45% among the severe-disease subgroup.
About one-fifth of COVID-19 patients in one study showed changes in consciousness (encephalopathy) persisting more than 24 hours, often following extubation and sometimes lasting weeks to months.
A UK-wide surveillance study found that one-quarter of COVID-19 patients showed some degree of neurocognitive impairment.

Zhang et al concluded that three-quarters of COVID-19 patients report fatigue, making it the most common CNS-related symptom, consistent with reports of persistent post-infection exhaustion and dyspnea described as post-COVID/long-COVID syndrome.
A meta-analysis found that a significant percentage of patients experience fatigue and/or cognitive impairment after resolution of acute COVID-19 symptoms.
A meta-analysis of 43 community-based studies found that anxiety prevalence during the COVID-19 pandemic was three times higher than pre-pandemic levels.
A meta-analysis of 29 studies found that anxiety and depressive symptoms among children and adolescents doubled compared to pre-pandemic periods.
COVID-19 survivors showed a high rate of emerging mental health sequelae, with 55% scoring positive for at least one psychiatric condition, with elevated risk of PTSD, severe depression, and anxiety.
A survey conducted one month after the epidemic in Wuhan found a 7% prevalence of post-traumatic stress disorder among 285 patients.
A meta-analysis of psychiatric presentations in severe COVID-19 found that steroid-use-related psychosis occurred in 0.7% of patients.

Mania or hypomania has been reported to emerge after COVID-19 infection even in previously healthy individuals, with risk increased by psychosocial stress, elevated inflammatory biomarkers, and prior bipolar disorder history.
A meta-analysis of 54 studies found that rates of suicidal thoughts, suicide attempts, and self-harm were elevated during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 44 publications (54 231 individuals, 13 countries) found a global pooled sleep-difficulty prevalence of 35.7%, with COVID-19 patients most affected (74.8%), followed by healthcare workers (36.0%) and the general population (32.3%).

Both viral infection and psychological stressors activate immune inflammatory pathways and nitro-oxidative stress, raising proinflammatory cytokines and reducing antioxidant defenses, which the authors link to depression, chronic fatigue, psychosomatic symptoms, anxiety/PTSD, suicidal ideation, psychosis, and neurocognitive deficits.
A Saudi survey reported that isolation during COVID-19 quarantine significantly increased psychological distress (OR 2.12, 95% CI 1.10-4.08, P=.03) but was not associated with sleep quality.
In the same Saudi survey, quarantine isolation was not significantly associated with sleep quality, despite raising psychological distress.
Immunohistochemistry demonstrated ACE2 receptor expression in adrenal cortex cells, identifying a plausible site of direct SARS-CoV-2 viral entry.
TMPRSS2, a protease required for SARS-CoV-2 entry, was also shown to be expressed in adrenal cortex cells by immunohistochemistry.
In severe COVID-19 infection, hypocortisolemia was reported in roughly one-fifth of patients, attributed to ACTH antibody-mediated hypophysitis or adrenalitis.

A single-center retrospective transversal study found that hypocortisolemia was statistically significantly more frequent in patients with moderate-to-severe COVID-19 than in those with mild disease (oxygen saturation >94% with no comorbidities).

In a prospective observational study of 70 adults assessed three months after COVID-19 infection, basal cortisol and post-Synacthen stimulation test results were normal, suggesting recovery of adrenal function.
Some authors proposed persistent adrenal axis involvement in long COVID syndrome, associated with asthenia, fatigue, and cognitive impairment lasting weeks to months after infection.
Systemic corticosteroid administration reduces all-cause mortality in hospitalized COVID-19 patients and probably decreases the need for mechanical ventilation.
Glucocorticoid use was correlated with a reduced rate of progression from mild to severe COVID-19 disease.

A post-mortem study of 28 patients who died of COVID-19 found adrenal lesions in 46% of cases, including necrosis with ischemia, cortical lipid degeneration, focal adrenalitis, and necrosis with hemorrhage.
A separate post-mortem case series identified adrenal infarcts, vascular thrombi, acute fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles and gland capsule, and sub-endothelial vacuolization in COVID-19 decedents.

A retrospective study of 219 COVID-19 patients undergoing chest CT found incidental adrenal lesions suggestive of infarction in 23% of subjects, with bilateral lesions in 88% of these cases, though only 8% had confirmed biochemical adrenal insufficiency; the finding correlated with a longer hospital stay.

A UK post-mortem study of 9 COVID-19/SARS decedents found adrenal microinfarction in 33% and thrombotic events (mostly pulmonary) in 89%, alongside diffuse alveolar damage, lymphocyte depletion, and hemophagocytosis.

COVID-19 infection was reported to induce positive anti-phospholipid antibodies, proposed as a key contributor to thrombosis-related adrenal hemorrhage, though the level of statistical evidence remains low.

COVID-19-associated stress involves a procoagulant coagulation profile with increased D-dimers, fibrinogen, and factor VIII, alongside reduced anticoagulant protein S, activated protein C, and factor XII.
In females with COVID-19 pneumonia, total and calculated free testosterone rose alongside cortisol and inflammation markers, reflecting more intense adrenal cortex activity.

Adrenal infarction may occur even in less severe COVID-19 cases, and accompanies cytokine storm-related generalized inflammation in critically ill patients, estimated at 1-5% of COVID-19 cases depending on the study.

Adenoviral vector-based COVID-19 vaccination has been mechanistically linked to vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia, which can cause acute complications including bleeding (e.g., adrenal hemorrhage) or thrombosis (e.g., acute renal failure).

A case is described of a 50-year-old male with bilateral adrenal hemorrhage incidentally detected on CT during COVID-19 pneumonia, complicated by deep vein thrombosis and fatal massive pulmonary embolism; he had a pre-existing adrenal tumor, a combination exceptionally reported in COVID-19-positive adrenal hemorrhage.

A 66-year-old female with prior antiphospholipid syndrome developed COVID-19-associated adrenal hemorrhage with adrenal insufficiency followed by renal vein thrombosis, illustrating the proposed 'two-hit' pathogenic model.

Infection with an Omicron variant is associated with about half the risk of developing long Covid compared to infection with earlier SARS-CoV-2 strains.
A cited study found that the increased risk of seizures, psychosis, dementia, and epilepsy following COVID-19 persists for at least two years.

Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia-like illness are noted to sometimes develop after infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus, and after SARS and MERS caused by related β-coronaviruses.
A study demonstrated persistence of SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA and viral antigens in the gut mucosa of patients with long Covid, supporting viral persistence as a contributing mechanism.
Reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus during or after acute COVID-19 is suggested to be an early event that increases the risk of developing long Covid.
Production of anti-nuclear antibodies was found to correlate with the development of long Covid features.
Autoantibodies neutralizing interferon-alpha were found to correlate with the development of long Covid features.
Virus-specific or bystander-activated T lymphocytes are suggested to contribute to the pathology of long Covid.
Vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 may reduce symptoms in some long Covid patients, but the beneficial effect is described as limited.
When acute COVID-19 occurs despite vaccination (breakthrough infection), the risk of developing long Covid is only moderately reduced.
Observation of viral rebounds after a 5-day course of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir raises concerns about the effect of this antiviral treatment on long Covid.
Approximately 80% of individuals remain with long-term sequelae after the acute phase of COVID-19.
About 63% of individuals with COVID-19 sequelae report difficulty with daily tasks, self-care, mobility, and social/occupational functioning.
In 458 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients, fatigue measured by the Chalder Fatigue Scale was present in ~46% and persisted about four months after diagnosis.
In a Wuhan hospital cohort of 1733 discharged COVID-19 patients, fatigue was present in ~63% of the sample and persisted approximately six months.
23% of 1692 COVID-19 infected patients showed reduced exercise capacity on the 6-minute walk test.
Among 58 asymptomatic COVID-19 patients, 16 (27.6%) had fatigue in the days following hospitalization.

In a multinational sample of 3762 patients, persistent fatigue, post-exertional malaise, cognitive dysfunction, sensorimotor changes, headache, sleep disturbance, and muscle/joint pain remained at seven months post-onset.

Fatigue and cognitive dysfunction (brain fog, memory problems, attention issues, sleep disturbances) are more common at six months or more than at less than six months post-COVID, with anxiety/depression frequency also increasing over time.
Fatigue after MERS persisted in ~48% of patients at 12 months and ~32% at 18 months, and after SARS in ~40% of patients at 3.5 years, informing expectations for COVID-19.
Impairment of intracortical GABAergic circuits in the primary motor cortex (M1) was found in post-COVID-19 patients with persistent fatigue and cognitive dysfunction.
IL-6-induced hyperinflammation was proposed to reduce functional GABA receptor density, causing an imbalance between synaptic inhibition and excitation, a candidate mechanism for post-COVID fatigue.

A meta-analysis found a higher proportion of fatigue and cognitive impairment in females (46% fatigue, 56% CG) than males (30% fatigue, 35% CG), though the difference was not statistically significant.
No significant difference in fatigue/cognitive impairment proportions was found between hospitalized vs non-hospitalized patients, or between <6 months vs >6 months persistence groups.
Compared to males, females had an odds ratio of 1.43 for fatigue at 12 months post-COVID-19.
A meta-analysis of COVID-19 survivors found greater self-reported fatigue in women after hospital admission, with an OR of 1.78.
A significantly lower number of IL-2-producing T cells was observed in women with post-COVID-19 fatigue.
A significantly lower number of IFN-γ-producing T cells was observed in women with post-COVID-19 fatigue.
IL-6 levels were higher (though within normal range) in COVID-19 patients with fatigue, and were higher in women than men with post-viral fatigue.
A 23.1% prevalence of PTSD was found within 3 months after COVID-19, similar to PTSD rates seen after other infectious disease pandemics (23.0%).
Chronic pain commonly co-occurs with long-term fatigue and depressed mood in COVID-19 patients.
The mean FACIT fatigue score was 16.8 (SD 13.2) among 1036 subjects at seven months after COVID-19 hospitalization.
Fatigue persisted up to 163 days after COVID-19 hospitalization; 47.6% of assessed patients had moderate fatigue by Brief Fatigue Inventory.
71 of 124 (57%) patients had relevant fatigue at hospital discharge post-COVID-19 by Fatigue Severity Scale.
138 of 246 (56.1%) former ICU patients had abnormal fatigue by Checklist Individual Strength up to one year after COVID-19.
Fatigue was present in 120 of 150 (80%) subjects assessed with the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire.

38.4% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients with persistent fatigue showed cognitive impairment on the d2-R attention test.
16.2% of 767 COVID-19 patients with mild to very severe disease showed cognitive impairment (MoCA <23) up to six months after infection.
Up to 80% of 87 patients in COVID-19 rehabilitation had cognitive dysfunction by MoCA.
Using the FACIT-Fatigue scale, 1036 patients had a mean fatigue score of 16.8 (SD 13.2) at seven months after COVID-19 hospitalization.
Using the Brief Fatigue Inventory, fatigue persisted up to 163 days after COVID-19 in most assessed patients, with nearly half showing moderate fatigue.
Using a Visual Analog Scale, hospitalized COVID-19 patients reported a mean physical fatigue score of 8/10 and mental fatigue score of 7/10.
Using the Fatigue Severity Scale, over half of evaluated patients had clinically relevant fatigue at hospital discharge.
During a walk test scored on the modified BORG scale, hospitalized COVID-19 patients reported low mean perceived fatigue.
Using the Checklist Individual Strength, over half of former ICU patients had abnormal fatigue up to one year after COVID-19.
The Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory showed hospitalized COVID-19 patients had persistent fatigue with the highest scores in the reduced motivation and mental fatigue domains.
The Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire found fatigue present in the large majority of a hospitalized COVID-19 sample.
The Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire mean total score indicated a high post-viral fatigue burden in post-COVID-19 patients.
Fatigue measured by the Pulmonary Functional Status and Dyspnea Questionnaire was positively associated with functional status impairment among COVID-19 participants.
Using the d2 test of attention (d2-R), over a third of hospitalized COVID-19 patients with persistent fatigue showed cognitive impairment.
Using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, about one in six patients with mild to very severe COVID-19 showed cognitive impairment up to six months later.
In a rehabilitation cohort assessed by MoCA, the large majority of patients with COVID-19 sequelae had cognitive dysfunction.
Using MoCA, nearly a quarter of patients with COVID-19 sequelae showed cognitive dysfunction.
Mini Mental State Examination scores in a sample of patients with COVID-19 sequelae were within a broadly normal range on average.
Using the Rey Auditory-Verbal Learning Test, up to two-thirds of patients showed cognitive impairment four months after COVID-19.
Using the Number Span Forward test, a high prevalence of cognitive impairment was detected in patients up to six months after COVID-19.
On the six-minute walk test, a subset of COVID-19 patients had below-normal walking distance one year after infection.
On the Incremental Shuttle Walk Test, patients with COVID-19 sequelae referred for rehabilitation walked an average distance of 300 meters.
Using the Short Physical Performance Battery, about a fifth of patients had impaired lower-limb physical performance four months after hospital discharge for COVID-19.
Maximum Voluntary Isometric Contraction testing showed high rates of quadriceps and biceps muscle weakness in COVID-19 patients without pre-existing disability.
Hand grip strength testing showed lower values in female COVID-19 patients than males, and lower still in females with a history of severe disease compared to non-severe cases.
Electromyography showed changes compatible with myopathy in over half of patients with persistent post-COVID-19 fatigue.

In a case series of 10 hospitalized people with Parkinson's disease (PwP) with SARS-CoV-2 infection, motor and non-motor symptoms worsened (anxiety, fatigue, orthostatic hypotension, cognitive impairment, psychosis), requiring therapy adjustment in half of cases.

A community-based case-control study of 12 non-hospitalized PwP with SARS-CoV-2 infection versus 36 PwP without infection found worsened motor symptoms (increased daily OFF-time) and non-motor symptoms (urinary problems, fatigue), with therapy adjustment in a third of cases.
A telephone survey of 8 PwP with SARS-CoV-2 infection found worsening of motor symptoms with therapy adjustment in a quarter of cases.
A case report of 2 PwP with deep brain stimulation (DBS) who had SARS-CoV-2 infection showed worsening of motor symptoms and cognitive impairment.

A telephone survey/cross-sectional study of 15 PwP with SARS-CoV-2 infection versus 553 PwP without infection found higher rates of hallucinations (23% vs 0%), motor fluctuations (61% vs 36%), dementia (16% vs 7%), and behavioral problems (34% vs 15%).

A case-control study of 7 PwP with SARS-CoV-2 infection versus 733 PwP without infection found no subjective worsening of symptoms during the lockdown period and no described difference between infected and uninfected PwP.

In a large case-control study, PwP with SARS-CoV-2 infection (n=51) reported worsening of motor (63%) and non-motor (75%) symptoms, compared with PwP without infection (n=7158) who reported worsening of motor (43%) and non-motor (52%) symptoms.

In a retrospective analysis of 675 PwP, 26 developed acute akinesia, with infection identified as the precipitating factor in 17 of these; levodopa serum levels were within normal range, arguing against malabsorption as the cause.

Cytokines released during infection reduce the expression of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which is involved in transporting cytosolic dopamine into vesicles, providing a candidate mechanism for infection-related dopaminergic dysfunction.

In non-human primates, chronic exposure to interferon-alpha decreases presynaptic dopamine D2 receptor expression in the striatum, suggesting a mechanism by which infection-related inflammation could impair dopaminergic signaling.
A meta-analysis and systematic review found that SARS-CoV-2 infection, particularly more severe infections, consistently increased serum cortisol levels.

A meta-analysis of 37 published articles reported fatigue (16-64%), dyspnea (15-61%), cough (2-59%), arthralgia (8-55%), and thoracic pain (5-62%) as the most prevalent persistent symptoms 4 weeks after severe (hospitalized) SARS-CoV-2 infection, with lower persistence in milder cases; risk factors for long-COVID included female sex, older age, comorbidities, and acute severity.

A case report described a 73-year-old male with Parkinson's disease who developed severe and persistent oropharyngeal dysphagia after a severe COVID-19 infection, with no dysphagia reported prior to COVID-19.

A multicentre international case series of 27 PwP found that 23 (85%) developed prolonged post-COVID-19 symptoms, most commonly worsening of motor symptoms (52%), increased levodopa daily dose requirements (48%), fatigue (41%), cognitive disturbances such as brain fog (22%), and sleep disturbances (22%); severe acute infection was not a prerequisite for persistent symptoms.
Among 20 reported cases of new-onset parkinsonism following COVID-19, genetic testing was performed in three patients, with one testing positive for a heterozygous GBA mutation.
Among the same three genetically tested patients with post-COVID-19 parkinsonism, one tested positive for a heterozygous LRRK2 mutation.

Among 7 patients with post-COVID-19 parkinsonism who underwent dopaminergic uptake imaging (DaTscan or F-FDOPA PET), all showed decreased dopamine uptake in one or both putamina, resembling typical Parkinson's disease.
In a large cohort of 129,008 SARS-CoV-2 positive patients of all ages, 138 cases of encephalitis were confirmed, an incidence of 0.215%.

Among five post-COVID-19 parkinsonism cases treated with immunomodulatory/immunosuppressive therapy (corticosteroids, IVIg, convalescent plasma), three achieved full resolution of symptoms and one had a good response with persistent parkinsonism and cognitive decline at 9-month follow-up.

Among 11 patients treated with dopaminergic therapy for post-COVID-19 parkinsonism, one had full recovery, six had significant improvement, and one had moderate improvement, suggesting an underlying, sometimes reversible, dopaminergic pathway impairment.

Increased proinflammatory cytokines and a high titre of anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies were detected in the cerebrospinal fluid of one post-COVID-19 parkinsonism/encephalopathy patient, a rare but previously described phenomenon.
Objectively measured processing speed, executive function, and memory did not differ between chronically fatigued, non-fatigued, and healthy control adolescents six months after EBV infection.
