Chronically fatigued adolescents reported significantly more subjective cognitive problems than both non-fatigued adolescents and healthy controls six months after EBV infection.
Within the chronically fatigued group, the subgroup diagnosed with CFS rated their cognitive symptoms even more severely than the broader chronic fatigue group.
Adolescents diagnosed with CFS did not differ from other groups on objective cognitive performance tests despite reporting the highest subjective symptom burden.
The proportion of CD4+ T cells positive for perforin was higher in hospitalized COVID-19 patients than in healthy controls.
The proportion of CD8+ T cells positive for perforin was higher in COVID-19 patients than in healthy controls.
In patients, the proportion of CD4+ T cells expressing perforin correlated positively with the proportion expressing granzyme B.
In patients, the proportion of CD8+ T cells expressing perforin correlated positively with the proportion expressing granzyme B.
Perforin expression and CD107A (degranulation marker) expression were not correlated in CD4+ T cells.
Perforin-positive CD8+ T cells were inversely correlated with CD107A-positive CD8+ T cells, suggesting perforin consumption during degranulation.
Perforin-positive CD4+ T cell percentages were similar between ICU and non-ICU COVID-19 patients.
Perforin-positive CD8+ T cell percentages were similar between ICU and non-ICU COVID-19 patients.
Perforin expression in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was not correlated with C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation severity.
Perforin expression in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was not correlated with lactate dehydrogenase, a marker of tissue damage.
Perforin expression in T4 and T8 cells was not correlated with peripheral lymphocyte or monocyte counts.
Perforin expression in T4 and T8 cells showed no link to plasma levels of 15 cytokine/chemokine biomarkers of COVID-19 severity (including TNF-alpha, IL-6, IFN-alpha, IFN-gamma, IP-10).
Perforin-positive CD4+ T cell percentages did not differ between ICU patients who survived and those who died.
Perforin-positive CD8+ T cell percentages did not differ between ICU patients who survived and those who died.
Acute-phase CD4+ T cell perforin expression did not differ between patients who later developed long COVID and those who did not.
Patients with lower acute-phase CD8+ T cell perforin expression were more likely to develop long COVID (persistent symptoms) one year later.

Among 23 followed patients, 13 developed long COVID, most commonly presenting fatigue, sleep disorders and cognitive dysfunction (54%), shortness of breath (31%), anxiety and tachycardia/palpitations (15% each), and depression (8%).
A higher proportion of post-COVID-19 condition patients (58%, 7/12) had detectable circulating HERV-W ENV protein compared to acute COVID-19 patients (41%, 9/22).
HERV-W ENV signal-to-noise levels were similar between post-COVID-19 condition and acute COVID-19 patients but both were significantly elevated compared to healthy control groups.
Two of seventeen pre-pandemic chronic fatigue syndrome patients were strongly positive for HERV-W ENV antigenemia.

CFS and post-COVID-19 condition patients showed largely overlapping symptom burden, differing significantly only in total FIQ score, MFI general fatigue, and SF-36 general health and mental health domains, with CFS patients reporting more pain/worse mental health and post-COVID-19 patients reporting worse fatigue/general health.
Pandemic healthy blood donors (sampled after vaccination campaigns began) showed significantly elevated anti-spike IgG and IgE compared to pre-pandemic controls, consistent with vaccination.
The majority of acute COVID-19 patients showed markedly increased total IgG, IgA, IgE and IgM against SARS-CoV-2 antigens compared to control groups.
A substantial subgroup of post-COVID-19 condition patients maintained elevated anti-spike IgG and IgA months to years after infection, not attributable to recent vaccination.

A large proportion of post-COVID-19 condition patients had detectable IgE against SARS-CoV-2 antigens, with anti-spike IgE significantly higher than in acute COVID-19 patients, and both anti-spike and anti-nucleocapsid IgE significantly elevated versus pre-pandemic controls.
Only three post-COVID-19 condition patients showed increased anti-nucleocapsid IgM, consistent with a post-acute infection stage lacking active IgM response.
In acute COVID-19, IgG correlated moderately with IgA but not with IgE, while IgA correlated weakly with IgE.
In post-COVID-19 condition, IgG, IgA and IgE levels were strongly inter-correlated, unlike the weaker correlation pattern observed in acute COVID-19.
In acute COVID-19, patients positive for HERV-W ENV antigenemia had significantly higher anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG, IgM and IgE levels than HERV-W-negative patients.
In post-COVID-19 condition patients, no significant difference in anti-SARS-CoV-2 immunoglobulin levels was found according to HERV-W ENV positivity, though this may reflect the small sample size.
No specific correlation was found between HERV-W ENV antigenemia levels and anti-SARS-CoV-2 immunoglobulin levels overall, despite group-level differences by positivity status.
Higher anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG, IgA and especially IgE levels correlated with worse physical functioning scores in post-COVID-19 condition patients, indicating association with greater disability.
The authors propose that HERV-W ENV, a known TLR4 agonist with immunopathogenic and neurotoxic effects, may be a pathogenic contributor to post-COVID-19 condition rather than merely a biomarker.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported PASC symptom, occurring in 84.8% of surveyed patients.
Dyspnea was reported by 54.5% of PASC patients surveyed.
Cognitive dysfunction was reported by 53% of PASC patients surveyed.
Myalgias were reported by 37.1% of PASC patients surveyed.
Lightheadedness or vertigo was reported by 36.4% of PASC patients surveyed.
Chest pain was reported by 34.8% of PASC patients surveyed.
Palpitations were reported by 34.8% of PASC patients surveyed.
Headaches were reported by 34.1% of PASC patients surveyed.
Arthralgias were reported by 31.8% of patients as a post-acute sequela of COVID-19.
Unrefreshing sleep was reported by 31.1% of patients as a post-acute sequela of COVID-19.
The paper notes accumulating evidence that PASC prevalence is higher among women, White/Caucasian individuals, and middle-aged individuals.

PASC patients with reduced exercise capacity showed lower peak VO2max (<85% predicted), an earlier aerobic threshold, and earlier CPET termination compared with patients with normal exercise capacity, despite normal pulmonary function, suggesting significant deconditioning.

POTS, characterised by orthostatic intolerance and an exaggerated heart-rate rise on standing, has been described as occurring in some PASC patients, though the relationship between PASC and POTS is not well understood.

A 6-week rehabilitation program combining aerobic exercise, strength training, and education improved walking capacity and symptoms of fatigue, cognition, and respiratory function in post-COVID-19 patients.
Eight weeks of combined aerobic and resistance training improved cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness in Long COVID Syndrome patients assessed 3 months after hospital discharge.

A multidisciplinary program of endurance training (60-80% VO2peak) and resistance training (30-50% 1-RM), three 90-minute sessions weekly, significantly decreased residual COVID-19 symptoms and improved muscular strength, cardiopulmonary parameters, mental health, depression, and anxiety.
A home-based telerehabilitation program of aerobic and strength exercise benefited persistent fatigue and improved VO2max, maximal aerobic power, and walking distance in post-COVID-19 patients.

Pulmonary rehabilitation via respiratory muscle training, with or without endurance training, increased exercise capacity, reduced dyspnea, and improved QoL in post-COVID-19 patients with lung impairment and comorbidities, without adverse events.

A 6-week personalised pulmonary rehabilitation program combining endurance, strength, and inspiratory muscle training (3x/week, 3-4h sessions) improved exercise capacity, functional status, dyspnea, fatigue, and quality of life in PASC outpatients.
Maximal exercise capacity is independently and inversely associated with the likelihood of hospitalisation due to COVID-19.
Physical inactivity is associated with a higher risk for severe COVID-19 outcomes.
Moderate-intensity exercise positively affects immune function and inflammation, whereas intensive exercise may increase inflammation risk and exacerbate viral infections such as COVID-19.
Initial data reported that 15% of competitive athletes showed myocarditis and 39% showed pericarditis following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Subsequent studies and registries documented a much lower prevalence of myocarditis (0.7-1.4%) among athletes post-COVID-19 than initial reports.
A large U.S. registry of college athletes found that 1.2% were symptomatic beyond 21 days after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
In a smaller U.K. cohort, 14% of young elite athletes experienced symptoms beyond 28 days after infection, and 27% were unable to return to full sports participation at 1 month.
Case series of athletes with PASC, POTS, and exercise/orthostatic intolerance showed CPET was useful for diagnosis and graded exercise training was beneficial for treatment.

For patients with tachycardia, exercise/orthostatic intolerance, and deconditioning, recumbent or semi-recumbent exercise (e.g., rowing, swimming, cycling) is recommended over upright exercise, with gradual transition to upright exercise as orthostatic intolerance resolves.
Deconditioning pathophysiology in PASC patients may be related to direct viral effects on muscle tissue combined with prolonged rest.

Active M1 HD-tDCS combined with a rehabilitation program produced significantly greater reduction in total fatigue (MFIS score) than sham stimulation plus rehabilitation after five weeks in PASC patients.
Active HD-tDCS significantly reduced the cognitive fatigue subscale of the MFIS compared to sham.
Active HD-tDCS significantly reduced the psychosocial fatigue subscale of the MFIS compared to sham.
Active HD-tDCS did not significantly differ from sham in reducing the physical fatigue subscale of the MFIS.
Active HD-tDCS significantly reduced anxiety symptoms (HAM-A) compared to sham.
Active HD-tDCS significantly improved quality of life (WHOQOL-bref) compared to sham.
Active HD-tDCS did not significantly reduce pain (McGill Pain Questionnaire) compared to sham.
A significantly greater proportion of patients receiving active HD-tDCS achieved clinically meaningful fatigue improvement (≥5-point MFIS reduction) than those receiving sham.

Higher baseline anxiety severity was associated with reduced improvement in fatigue (MFIS change) in a multiple regression model, whereas age, sleep difficulty, and depression were not significant predictors.
Skin redness was significantly more frequent as an adverse event in the active HD-tDCS group than in the sham group, though no serious adverse events occurred in either group.

The authors propose that tDCS benefits for fatigue arise via neuroplastic after-effects and top-down modulation along the ascending midbrain-thalamic-cingulate pathway through descending motor cortex fibers, possibly also modulating inflammatory processes.
Among 442 community-dwelling COVID-19-positive adults surveyed a median of ~12 months post-infection, 77% reported experiencing PASC symptoms.
43% of participants reported current cardiac-related PASC symptoms and 27% reported newly diagnosed cardiovascular risk factors or cardiovascular disease.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported general PASC symptom, affecting 42.3% of participants, followed by inability to exercise in 17.7%.
Among cardiac-related symptoms, heart palpitations (14.5%), tachycardia (12.9%), and feeling faint (10.9%) were the most commonly reported.
Other commonly reported PASC symptoms included shortness of breath, joint and muscle pain, difficulty concentrating, headaches, sleep difficulty, anxiety, and depression.
Roughly 30% of participants reported severe fatigue and 28% moderate fatigue on the FACIT Fatigue Scale.
Participants reporting PASC symptoms had significantly lower (worse) FACIT fatigue scores than those without PASC symptoms.
After adjustment for age, sex, race, education, income, and pre-existing conditions, PASC patients had nearly seven-fold higher prevalence of severe fatigue than those without PASC symptoms.
Participants with cardiac PASC symptoms had over four-fold higher adjusted prevalence of severe fatigue compared to those without.
Participants with new cardiovascular disease diagnoses had over two-fold higher adjusted prevalence of severe fatigue compared to those without.
Participants with PASC symptoms were more likely to report fair or poor quality of life compared to those without PASC symptoms.
Participants with PASC symptoms had significantly worse mental health functioning scores than those without.
Persons who reported PASC symptoms were more likely to be older, female, have pre-existing conditions, and have been hospitalized for COVID-19 than those without PASC symptoms.
Qualitative interviews revealed that some participants experienced dismissal of their PASC symptoms by care teams and social networks, including symptoms being labeled as psychosomatic.
In qualitative interviews, persistent chest pain, resting heart palpitations, and tachycardia were commonly described cardiac PASC symptoms with varying character across participants.
Most interviewees reported neurological symptoms, describing 'brain fog,' confusion, and amnesia that impacted daily functioning; interviewers also observed participant confusion during interviews.

The authors cite a prior study finding that persistent dyspnea after acute COVID-19 could not be explained by pulmonary, cardiac, or ventilatory limitations on cardiopulmonary exercise testing, suggesting the mechanism of exercise intolerance in PASC remains unclear.
Participants reported that brain fog and fatigue impaired their ability to complete household chores, personal care tasks, and leisure activities, often requiring frequent rest periods.
Participants described a diurnal pattern in which brain fog and fatigue were milder in the morning and worsened as the day progressed.
Participants described a relapsing-remitting symptom course with unpredictable good and bad days, complicating illness management.
Many participants perceived a synergistic relationship between brain fog and fatigue, in which increasing fatigue worsened cognitive symptoms and vice versa.
Nine of fifteen (60.0%) participants reported that PASC symptoms affected their ability or comfort with driving, attributed to brain fog, fatigue, and/or anxiety.
Six of fifteen (40.0%) participants reported current unemployment as a direct result of PASC symptoms.
Brain fog was described as having the greatest impact on the work/employment domain, with participants struggling with previously easily managed tasks, multitasking, and focus.
Most participants reported difficulty with multitasking and focus at work, perceiving themselves as less efficient and productive than before their infection.
Participants experienced perceived and explicit stigma related to the legitimacy of PASC symptoms, exacerbated by broader misinformation and conspiracy narratives.
Participants described feelings of isolation outside the household, driven both by symptom-related limitations and by perceived discomfort or disbelief from others.
Participants with children at home reported difficulty being fully present as parents due to low energy and cognitive symptoms.
During acute infection, 40.0% of participants were hospitalized and 13.3% required ICU admission.
The average time from COVID-19 diagnosis to study participation (i.e., persistent symptom duration) was 11 months, ranging from 6 to 19 months.
Of 15 participants, 14 (93.3%) had a confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis, with the remaining case strongly suspected clinically due to limited early-pandemic testing access.
Unemployment resulting from PASC created financial strain that burdened partners and families, complicating access to ongoing healthcare.

The authors note that persistent debilitating neurocognitive impairment and fatigue in PASC resemble symptoms described in fibromyalgia ('fibro fog'), cancer-related cognitive impairment, traumatic brain injury, ME/CFS, mast cell disorders, autoimmune disorders, and postural tachycardia syndrome.
60% of COVID-19 survivors were physically inactive (<150 min/week of moderate-to-vigorous activity) 6-11 months after hospitalization.
The prevalence of physical inactivity in this COVID-19 survivor cohort (60%) exceeded the ~47% inactivity rate reported for a similarly aged general Brazilian population.
Patients with one or more persistent PASC symptoms had significantly greater odds of being physically inactive than those without any persistent symptoms, after adjusting for confounders.
Patients reporting 5 or more persistent PASC symptoms showed substantially greater odds of physical inactivity compared to those with no persistent symptoms.
Severe muscle/joint pain as a persistent COVID-19 symptom was associated with significantly greater odds of physical inactivity.
Persistent fatigue was strongly associated with greater odds of physical inactivity, remaining significant even after Bonferroni correction.
Persistent dyspnea was the strongest symptom predictor of physical inactivity, remaining significant after Bonferroni correction.
Persistent insomnia was associated with significantly greater odds of physical inactivity, though it did not survive Bonferroni correction.
Post-traumatic stress symptoms were associated with significantly greater odds of physical inactivity, unlike depression or anxiety.
Memory impairment, depression, anxiety, taste loss, and smell loss did not show a statistically significant association with physical inactivity in adjusted models.
Female cancer patients were significantly more likely than males to develop persistent post-acute COVID-19 symptoms (PASC).
Hypertension was significantly more common in cancer patients who did not develop PASC than in those who did.
Cancer patients with PASC were significantly less likely to have relapsed or refractory malignancy than those without PASC.
Cancer patients who did not develop PASC were more likely to have had severe acute COVID-19 at diagnosis than those who developed PASC.
Cancer patients without PASC had significantly higher mortality beyond 30 days after COVID-19 diagnosis than those with PASC.
60% of cancer patients followed longitudinally after COVID-19 diagnosis developed PASC/long COVID over a median follow-up of 7 months (up to 14 months).
Among PASC patients, the most commonly reported persistent symptoms were fatigue, sleep disturbance, myalgias, gastrointestinal symptoms, headache, altered smell/taste, dyspnea, and cough.
Among PASC patients, 31% were re-admitted to the hospital during follow-up for any cause, but only 8.5% of all PASC patients had a COVID-19-related re-admission.
Rates of delay in cancer treatment after COVID-19 were similar between PASC and non-PASC cancer patients.

Markers of acute COVID-19 severity and management—neutropenia, lymphocytopenia, lower respiratory tract infection, hypoxia, oxygen requirement, inflammatory biomarkers, COVID-related hospital admission, multiorgan failure, and medical management—did not differ significantly between PASC and non-PASC cancer patients.

The authors hypothesize that the ACE2-spike protein interaction driving acute COVID-19 severity may play a lesser role in long COVID compared to ongoing residual inflammatory processes, and postulate a different mechanism (unrelated to ACE2 expression) underlying the female predominance of PASC.

COVID-19 survivors show up to a 2,000% increase in risk of cardiovascular, pulmonary, metabolic, and neurological conditions within 1 to 6 months after infection, based on a study of 5 million patients.
Post-COVID Guillain-Barré syndrome (PCGBS), a form of dysautonomia, is described as the most common neurological post-COVID disorder, observed in 15% of patients.

Approximately 13% of acute and long-COVID patients develop PCGBS, a dysautonomia characterized by microinflammation localized to autonomic (not motor) nerve fibers, driving chronic sympathetic activation, arrhythmogenesis, orthostatic hypotension, altered peristalsis, and cognitive decline.

COVID-19 survivors had a significantly higher risk of developing cardiovascular diseases—including cerebrovascular disease, dysrhythmias, cardiac inflammatory disease, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, thromboembolic disorders, and non-ischemic cardiomyopathy—up to 12 months post-infection compared with contemporary and historical uninfected control cohorts, independent of pre-existing cardiovascular morbidity.

Vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of developing myocarditis and pericarditis, supporting a direct viral role in COVID-19 cardiovascular sequelae rather than pre-existing comorbidities.
Current evidence indicates that up to 50% of COVID-19 patients may develop a post-acute syndrome following the original SARS-CoV-2 infection.
One study found that 87% of patients continued to exhibit at least one COVID-19 symptom more than 2 months after initial infection.
In a study of patients with inflammatory bowel disease, 70% showed persistent SARS-CoV-2 RNA and viral proteins in gut tissue more than 6 months after mild acute COVID-19.

A pilot study validated HRV analysis using short ECG recordings and AI-based processing as a predictor of inflammatory and autonomic status in post-COVID patients, suggesting utility for diagnosing long-COVID dysautonomia and predicting cardiovascular dysfunction.

A pilot cardiovascular rehabilitation program (CRP) in Japan involving 50 patients aged 65-74 achieved 90% adherence and produced significant reductions in anxiety along with improved autonomy and quality of life.

A case study of a patient with confirmed PCGBS reported dramatic improvements in dyspnea, fatigue, muscular strength, autonomy, and functional state following a personalized cardiovascular rehabilitation program.
Approximately 30% of COVID-19 cases exhibit neurological dysfunction, including demyelination, encephalitis, encephalopathies, hallucinations, and behavioral alterations.
The underlying mechanisms of pediatric multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C) and adult long-COVID appear similar, involving systemic inflammation, cytokine storm, and oxidative stress.

HRV analysis is proposed as a more suitable diagnostic tool than the COMPASS-31 survey for post-COVID dysautonomia because it yields a quantitative, non-invasive, recall-independent score with established clinical validation.
Cardiovascular sequelae of COVID-19 are related to development of dysautonomia, which is thought to arise from chronic systemic inflammation increasing sympathetic nerve activity.
In a cohort of 70 patients with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), 73% were found to have some form of cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction on formal testing.
Initial orthostatic hypotension on active standing test was the most common autonomic abnormality, present in 61% of the PASC cohort.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) was diagnosed in 30% of the PASC cohort.
Inappropriate sinus tachycardia was uncommon in the PASC cohort, found in only 1.4% of patients, though the study protocol lacked prolonged ECG monitoring needed for accurate detection.
POTS occurred significantly more often in female PASC patients (36%) than in male PASC patients (7%).

Overall prevalence of cardiovascular dysautonomia was similar between hospitalized and nonhospitalized PASC patients, suggesting acute disease severity is not a risk factor for later autonomic dysfunction.

Patients were evaluated at a median of 399 days after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, and the persistence of cardiovascular dysautonomia at this time point suggests these hemodynamic abnormalities are unlikely to resolve quickly after infection in many patients.
A meta-analysis found the global pooled prevalence of long COVID to be 43%, with the highest regional prevalence in Asia (51%), followed by Europe (44%) and the USA (31%).

In a UK cohort of over 480,000 adults, female sex, ethnic minority status, socioeconomic deprivation, smoking, obesity, and comorbidities including COPD, anxiety, depression, migraine, multiple sclerosis, and fibromyalgia were associated with developing long COVID.
Downregulation of respiratory and myocardial ACE2 pathways has been proposed to result in lung edema, myocardial inflammation, and acute lung injury in COVID-19/long COVID.
Upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines is postulated to drive systemic inflammatory response and multi-organ involvement, particularly cardiovascular compromise, in long COVID.
A large study by Su et al. found that antibodies targeting type I interferons could be implicated in the pathogenesis of long COVID.
A cohort of 215 individuals showed a unique immunoglobulin signature that, along with age, asthma, and pre-morbid illness, predicted the risk of developing PASC.
Pretorius et al. suggested that persistent circulating microclots resistant to fibrinolytic therapy may explain the lingering symptoms of long COVID.
Raised troponins indicating myocardial injury are well documented in patients hospitalized with acute COVID-19 and are associated with poor prognosis.

In a study of 346 participants followed for four weeks to four months post-COVID-19, those with persistent symptoms showed diffuse myocardial edema on cardiac MRI, suggesting ongoing cardiac inflammation explains symptoms like chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, and dizziness.
Mandal et al. reported high rates of persistently elevated D-dimer and C-reactive protein for up to eight weeks in patients with breathlessness and cough after COVID-19.

A UK social-media questionnaire cross-sectional study found cardiorespiratory symptoms made up 88.8% of self-reported symptoms, while multisystem involvement was associated with more severe disability and functional impairment.
Puntmann et al. found that 73% of patients with mild COVID-19 reported new cardiac symptoms, dyspnea being most common (62%) and syncope in 3%, with 3% having disabling symptoms.
Puntmann et al. found that post-COVID patients had higher diastolic blood pressure readings compared to healthy controls.
A study among medical professionals found no significant difference in cardiac manifestations between COVID-19-affected cases and healthy controls at six months.
Radin et al. demonstrated both tachycardia and bradycardia associated with dyspnea in wearable device users up to two to three months after COVID-19 infection.

24-hour Holter monitoring studies in symptomatic post-COVID patients showed an increased incidence of ventricular arrhythmias including premature ventricular contractions and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia.
Follow-up echocardiography showed that most abnormalities (right ventricular dysfunction, myocarditis, pericarditis, cardiomyopathy) eventually improve, though ventricular remodeling can occur.
A large proportion of patients remain with diastolic dysfunction on follow-up echocardiography after COVID-19.

A subgroup of patients with elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin, NT-proBNP) during acute infection had persistently elevated biomarkers at five months, associated with altered ventricular function on echocardiography.
Early cardiac MRI studies showed around 60% of patients with ongoing myocardial inflammation at 71 days post-recovery from COVID-19.
More recent CMR studies found very little evidence for persistent or prolonged myocardial inflammation, even in symptomatic long COVID patients, contradicting earlier reports.
Baum et al. postulated that a small subgroup of long COVID patients with severe functional impairment may have significant cardiac dysfunction.
Mancini et al. showed cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) helped categorize dysfunctional breathing, hypocapnia, and chronic fatigue syndrome in patients with unexplained dyspnea in PASC.

Autonomic dysfunction, presenting as postural dizziness, hypotension, and syncope, is an increasingly recognized manifestation of PASC, diagnosable via tilt table testing or a 10-minute standing test for POTS.
A study from Israel found that two doses of COVID-19 vaccination were associated with a lower risk of developing long COVID symptoms.
A large UK study found that post-acute symptoms were more frequent among unvaccinated infected individuals compared to vaccinated ones.
ECG depolarization/repolarization abnormalities were less common post-COVID than during acute infection, but sinus arrhythmia and persistent sinus tachycardia were still reported in several studies.
Radin et al. found both tachycardia and bradycardia associated with dyspnea in wearable-device users up to two to three months after COVID-19 infection.

24-hour Holter monitoring studies in symptomatic post-COVID patients showed an increased incidence of arrhythmias, including premature ventricular contractions and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia.

On echocardiographic follow-up, most abnormalities such as right ventricular dysfunction, myocarditis, pericarditis, and cardiomyopathy improved over time, though ventricular remodeling occurred and a large proportion of patients retained diastolic dysfunction.

A subgroup of patients with elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin-I, troponin-T, NT-proBNP) during acute COVID-19 had persistently elevated levels at five months, associated with altered ventricular function on echocardiography.
Early CMR studies found around 60% of patients had ongoing myocardial inflammation at 71 days post-recovery from COVID-19.
More recent CMR studies found very little evidence of persistent or prolonged myocardial inflammation, even among symptomatic long COVID patients, contradicting earlier reports of high prevalence.
Baum et al. postulated that a small subgroup of patients with severe functional impairment may have significant underlying cardiac dysfunction.
Delayed, catastrophic pulmonary emboli have been reported as a complication after acute COVID-19.
CT angiography has been shown to be useful for detecting delayed arterial thromboemboli and microangiopathic disease in long COVID patients.
Mancini et al. showed that cardiopulmonary exercise testing helped categorize dysfunctional breathing, hypocapnia, and chronic fatigue syndrome in patients with unexplained dyspnea post-COVID.
Tilt table testing or the 10-minute standing test can be valuable for diagnosing postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) in long COVID patients with autonomic dysfunction.
A study from Israel found that receiving two doses of COVID-19 vaccine was associated with a lower risk of long COVID symptoms.
A large UK study found that post-acute symptoms were more frequent in unvaccinated individuals infected with COVID-19 compared to vaccinated ones.
Perlis et al., studying over 16,000 patients, reported that completing vaccination prior to acute infection was associated with a reduced risk of developing long COVID.
There have been reports of vaccine-induced myocarditis, though the overall risk-benefit ratio remains favorable toward vaccination.
At initial COVID-19 diagnosis, the most commonly reported symptoms were fatigue, shortness of breath, exercise intolerance, and palpitations/heart racing.
At 3-months postinfection, the most reported symptoms were fatigue, 'brain fog'/memory or cognitive impairment, exercise intolerance, and shortness of breath.
At the time of the survey, the most concerning symptoms reported by patients were fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath, and cough.
Comparing initial infection to 3-months postinfection, symptom burden shifted significantly within-subjects, with more participants reporting fewer symptoms over time than reporting more.
Women reported a higher prevalence of most symptoms than men, particularly fatigue and cough, although fewer men answered this open-ended item.
Rates of hospital or ICU admission for acute COVID-19 did not significantly differ between men and women.
Rates of outpatient/home management for acute COVID-19 did not significantly differ between men and women.
Approximately 23% of PASC clinic patients had significantly reduced global physical health (≥1.5 SD below general population norms) on the PROMIS GH-10.
Approximately 16% of PASC clinic patients had significantly reduced global mental health on the PROMIS GH-10.
Approximately 18% of PASC clinic patients had significant difficulty with cognitive function on the PROMIS CA-4a.
The odds of reporting reduced physical health, mental health, or cognitive function on PROMIS measures did not differ by sex or by initial level of acute care (outpatient vs inpatient).
Patients with significantly reduced mental health scores reported roughly double the number of neurological symptoms compared to those without reduced mental health.
Patients with reduced mental health reported substantially more total symptoms overall than those without reduced mental health.

Acute-phase symptoms were not associated with reduced PROMIS scores, but higher symptom burden at 3 months postinfection was associated with the lowest PROMIS physical, mental, and cognitive scores across most body systems.
New or worsened mental health symptoms including anxiety, depression, and sleeping difficulties were reported by about 30% of patients within 3 months of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Higher initial COVID-19 symptom burden was positively correlated with the number of subspecialty referrals made after infection.
Higher initial COVID-19 symptom burden was positively correlated with the number of subspecialty referrals completed after infection.

Right-sided ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block (SGB) with bupivacaine and dexamethasone produced immediate improvement in fatigue and malaise the day after injection in a patient with long COVID.
A repeat contralateral SGB performed 12 days after the first injection produced further improvement in shortness of breath and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Long COVID dysautonomia may be driven by hyperinflammation-induced sympathetic overdrive resulting from dysregulated bidirectional communication between the autonomic nervous system and the inflammatory system.
SGB is proposed to treat dysautonomia by increasing cerebral and regional blood flow, thereby resetting autonomic nervous system function.
Prior literature reports SGB has reduced or eliminated anosmia in select groups of long COVID patients.
Partial Horner's syndrome (ptosis and chemosis of the right eye, unilateral facial flushing) developed post-procedure, serving as clinical confirmation of adequate stellate ganglion blockade.

Injectate volume for SGB is not standardized; one cited study found 4ml produced successful Horner's syndrome in 100% of patients, while another found 2ml produced spread below C7-T1 in 100% of patients.
Dexamethasone was added to the local anesthetic injectate to prolong the effect of the stellate ganglion block, as previously reported.
Among patients receiving SGB for long COVID reported to date, all experienced further symptom improvement after the contralateral block was administered.
Up to 30% of individuals infected with COVID-19 go on to develop long COVID with symptoms that can persist indefinitely.
Ten sessions of Rebalance® neuro-meditation significantly reduced physical fatigue scores in long COVID patients compared with baseline, while no change occurred in the control or healthy groups.
Mental fatigue scores decreased significantly in the intervention group after neuro-meditation, with no change in control or healthy groups.
Anxiety scores decreased significantly following neuro-meditation in the intervention group only.
Depression scores were significantly reduced in the intervention group following neuro-meditation.
Muscle and joint pain ratings decreased significantly with neuro-meditation in the intervention group.
Headache severity decreased significantly in the intervention group after the neuro-meditation program.
Total mood disturbance score improved substantially in the intervention group, with the POMS profile shifting closer to that of healthy controls.
Sleep quality scores improved significantly in the intervention group after the neuro-meditation program.
Response times on the choice response time task decreased significantly only in the intervention group, with improvements persisting and increasing one week after the last session.
Incongruent-trial response times on the pattern comparison task improved most in the intervention group, with the largest reduction observed one week after the intervention ended.
Response times on incongruent Simon task trials decreased significantly only in the intervention group one week after the program ended, indicating improved selective inhibitory control.
Working memory performance on the Corsi block-tapping task improved significantly in the intervention group only, following the neuro-meditation program.
At baseline, long COVID patients showed slower response times and impaired performance across all five cognitive tasks compared with healthy participants.
Cognitive dysfunction is reported as a symptom in approximately 70% of long COVID patients according to cited literature, consistent with the study's baseline findings.
The authors suggest that ~80% of the study's long COVID patients experienced 'brain fog' post-infection, which may have altered strategy on the easiest pattern-recognition trials.
Female long COVID patients are reported to be at greater risk of long COVID and to experience greater fatigue, pain, anxiety, and depression than male patients, per cited literature.
The authors cite evidence that cognitive impairment in long COVID may relate to loss of gray matter, particularly in the left hemisphere, which could produce functional cognitive deficits.
Long COVID control-group patients showed greater deviation from the tracked target on a fine-motor/visuospatial coordination task compared with healthy controls.
Long COVID patients showed significantly higher dyspnea scores than healthy controls, with a main effect of group and of time but no significant group-by-time interaction.

Long COVID patients (both G-Con and G-Int) showed lower vigor scores than healthy controls, though there was no significant time-by-group interaction indicating no clear treatment effect on this subscale.

At baseline, all long COVID patients reported clinically significant anxiety/depression, elevated fatigue, impaired sleep quality, and moderate muscle/joint pain and headaches, while healthy participants reported none of these symptoms.

The authors cite prior work showing the Rebalance® neuro-meditation program improves sympathetic control, autonomic regulation, blood pressure, resting heart rate, and heart rate variability, proposed as a mechanism for the observed cognitive and mood benefits.
Overall, 36.5% of COVID-19 survivors developed some form of neuropsychiatric post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC).
Fatigue was the most frequent neuropsychiatric sequela, documented in 24.6% of the whole study population.
Insomnia was the second most common neuropsychiatric PASC symptom, present in 16.4% of participants.
Major depressive disorder meeting DSM-5 criteria was diagnosed in 15.3% of participants, mostly mild severity.
Anxiety disorders meeting DSM-5 criteria (generalized anxiety disorder or panic disorder) were present in 14.4% of participants.
Mild cognitive impairment on MoCA testing (scores 19-25) was identified in 10.2% of participants.
Olfactory and gustatory disturbances (anosmia/hyposmia, cacosmia, ageusia/hypogeusia) persisted post-COVID in 13.9%, 7.1%, and 10.4% of participants, respectively.
Neuropathic pain, assessed by the DN4 questionnaire (cut-off ≥4/10), was found in 13% of participants.
Dizziness, tinnitus, and headache persisted post-COVID in 14.1%, 8.1%, and 6.9% of participants, respectively.
Female sex was significantly associated with a higher frequency of neuropsychiatric PASC compared to males.
In logistic regression, male sex decreased the odds of developing neuropsychiatric PASC.
Moderate COVID-19 infection increased the odds of developing neuropsychiatric PASC approximately two-fold.
Severe COVID-19 infection increased the odds of developing neuropsychiatric PASC nearly four-fold.
Non-vaccination before COVID-19 infection increased the odds of developing neuropsychiatric PASC by 1.67 times.
Fully vaccinated subjects before COVID-19 infection had a significantly lower frequency of moderate and severe COVID-19 infection than non-vaccinated subjects.
Full vaccination before infection was associated with lesser severity of post-COVID-19 fatigue, ageusia/hypogeusia, dizziness, tinnitus, and insomnia compared to non-vaccinated subjects.
There was no statistically significant difference in protective effect against neuropsychiatric PASC among RNA, viral vector, and inactivated COVID-19 vaccines.
Female sex was independently associated with increased odds of developing Long COVID compared to males, after adjustment for age, race, HPI, and monoclonal antibody administration.
Hospitalization for acute COVID-19 infection was independently associated with markedly increased odds of developing Long COVID.
Poorer self-rated health prior to COVID-19 infection was independently associated with increased risk of developing Long COVID.
Patients with Long COVID did not differ significantly from those without Long COVID in age, race, or Healthy Places Index (a community-level socioeconomic health resource score).
Univariate analysis found patients with Long COVID were more than twice as likely to have received intravenous monoclonal antibody treatment during acute COVID-19 infection.
Among Long COVID patients, those previously hospitalized for acute COVID-19 reported a significantly greater number of discrete symptoms than those never hospitalized.
Female sex was positively associated with greater Long COVID symptom burden (number of discrete symptoms) in multivariate analysis.
Poorer self-appraised health prior to COVID-19 infection was negatively associated with number of Long COVID symptoms (i.e., worse pre-COVID health predicted more symptoms).
Previously hospitalized Long COVID patients were more likely to screen positive for clinically relevant depression than non-hospitalized patients.
Previously hospitalized Long COVID patients showed a non-significant trend toward higher rates of anxiety compared to non-hospitalized patients.

Exploratory factor analysis of 16 Long COVID symptoms identified a five-factor solution (gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, neurocognitive, airway, and cardiopulmonary clusters) explaining 57% of cumulative variance in symptom presentation.
Younger age was associated with higher gastrointestinal symptom cluster scores among Long COVID patients.
Older age was associated with higher musculoskeletal symptom cluster scores among Long COVID patients.
Patients identifying as Other or Mixed race had higher musculoskeletal symptom cluster scores compared to White patients.
Higher neurocognitive symptom cluster scores showed a non-significant trend toward association with prior COVID-19 hospitalization.
Higher neurocognitive symptom cluster scores were associated with substantially greater odds of screening positive for depression, independent of other risk factors and symptom clusters.
Higher neurocognitive symptom cluster scores were associated with greater odds of screening positive for anxiety.
Older age was associated with lower odds of reporting anxiety among Long COVID patients.
Women trended toward lower odds of reporting depressive symptoms than men, though this was not statistically significant at the study's threshold.
Nearly half of survey respondents who previously tested positive for COVID-19 reported ongoing symptoms attributed to Long COVID.
Weakness/tiredness, sleep disturbances, and difficulty thinking/concentrating (brain fog) were the most commonly reported Long COVID symptoms among affected patients.
Loss of taste/smell (anosmia/ageusia) did not load substantially onto any of the five identified Long COVID symptom clusters.
Chronic fatigue and affective symptoms occurring in both acute and long COVID are proposed to be attributable to activation of immune-inflammatory pathways.
Long-COVID was more likely to develop in patients who reported more than five symptoms (fatigue, headache, dyspnea, hoarse voice, myalgia) during the first week of acute infection.
Sudre et al. reported that 13.3% of COVID-19 patients had symptoms lasting more than 28 days, 4.5% more than eight weeks, and 2.3% more than twelve weeks.
Nalbandian et al. reported that up to 55% of COVID-19 patients may develop persisting symptoms after acute infection.

Giszas et al. found that although 70.7% of participants reported persistent post-COVID symptoms, only about one-third of those reported significantly reduced quality of life, leading to a proposed distinction between Long-COVID 'disease' and 'condition'.
The likelihood and severity of Long-COVID symptoms were not associated with the initial severity of acute COVID-19 infection.

In hospitalized COVID-19 patients assessed shortly after acute infection, PET imaging showed frontoparietal hypometabolism together with increased brainstem and cerebellar activity, and this pattern correlated with the severity of cognitive impairment.
At a six-month follow-up, frontoparietal hypometabolism in COVID-19 patients had partially reversed but remained significantly reduced compared to healthy controls.

In Dressing et al., 67% of Long-COVID patients reported subjective fatigue above the critical cutoff for cognitive fatigue, yet objective cognitive testing showed only mild impairment and PET scans showed no significant differences from healthy controls.
Repetitive at-home transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) produced a mild-to-moderate reduction in mental fatigue in a subset of people with Long-COVID.

A case report showed that 20 sessions of repetitive frontal tDCS in one Long-COVID patient produced a clinically meaningful 50-point reduction in subjective trait fatigue, along with reduced anxiety and improved cognitive performance.

In two Long-COVID patients receiving 15 at-home frontal tDCS sessions, one patient showed significant fatigue improvement while the other remained stable, but both returned to work and resumed most prior activities.

In healthy subjects, 40-Hz gamma-tACS applied over the visual cortex during a vigilance task counteracted the time-on-task increase in reaction time, though effects on subjective fatigue could not be determined because subjective ratings were not collected.

In people with Alzheimer's disease, one-hour daily 40-Hz gamma-tACS sessions over two to four weeks significantly increased cerebral blood flow in the temporal lobes and improved cognitive performance.

Fluge et al. proposed that in ME/CFS, an initial inflammatory response leads to release of B-cells and antibodies that affect the vascular system, impair neurovascular control, and cause impaired blood flow autoregulation and tissue hypoxia.
Reactive oxygen species released after an immune response are implicated in triggering a vasoconstrictor response followed by decreased regional cerebral blood flow in ME/CFS pathophysiology.
Reduced cerebral blood flow has been reported across studies of MS-related fatigue, chronic fatigue syndrome, and Long-COVID-related cognitive fatigue (LCOF).

tDCS effects on cerebral blood flow are dose- and polarity-dependent: anodal tDCS increases CBF with larger increases at higher intensities, while cathodal tDCS decreases CBF, with high interindividual variability and cumulative effects across repetitive sessions.
Persistent inflammation together with simultaneous immune suppression has been consistently reported in people with Long-COVID and also in chronic fatigue syndrome.
47.35% of respondents reported at least one persistent symptom lasting at least 3 months after COVID-19 infection, and 21.87% reported more than 3 such symptoms.
The most frequently reported symptoms lasting more than 3 months after COVID-19 infection were fatigue, lack of energy and breathing difficulties.
Among respondents with long COVID, 71.76% experienced symptoms of a neuropsychiatric nature.
Obesity was significantly associated with an increased likelihood of developing long COVID.
Pre-existing respiratory disease was significantly associated with an increased likelihood of developing long COVID.
Pre-existing blood or immune disorders were significantly associated with an increased likelihood of developing long COVID.
Engaging in more than 3 hours of physical activity per week was associated with approximately half the risk of developing long COVID.
Overall health-related quality of life, as measured by the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire, was reduced in personnel with long COVID compared to those without.
Among the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions, only the self-care dimension was not significantly affected by the presence of long COVID.
The most frequently reported symptoms persisting for more than three months after COVID-19 infection were fatigue, lack of energy, and breathing difficulties.
The prevalence of long COVID observed among Belgian Defence personnel was similar to figures reported in the general Belgian population.
Long COVID-19 patients had higher mean heart rate compared to controls.
Control patients had higher SDNN-24 and SDANNi values than long COVID-19 case patients.
Low-frequency (LF) HRV component was elevated in long COVID-19 patients compared to controls, reflecting increased sympathetic activity.
High-frequency (HF) HRV component, a marker of parasympathetic activity, was higher in controls than in long COVID-19 patients.
SDNN-24 and SDANNi were strongly positively correlated across the study population.
rMSSD and pNN50 were strongly positively correlated across the study population.
Pulmonary involvement on chest CT was significantly greater with increasing COVID-19 severity, with mean impairment of 4.3%, 14.2%, and 25.8% in mild, moderate, and severe cases respectively.
BNP levels differed significantly across COVID-19 severity categories in the case group.
D-dimer levels differed significantly across COVID-19 severity categories in the case group.
CRP levels differed significantly across COVID-19 severity categories and are proposed as a prognostic inflammatory marker in the case group.
A cited external study found that a 50% rise in CRP was followed by a 40% drop in heart rate variability in long COVID-19 patients.
The case group (long COVID-19 patients) had lower overall HRV than controls, consistent with increased systemic inflammation.

The authors propose that COVID-19-induced cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-alpha increase catecholaminergic tone, which may alter cardiomyocyte ion channel expression, prolong ventricular action potentials, and predispose to arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation.
The study concludes that long COVID-19 is associated with a predominance of parasympathetic activity in autonomic heart rhythm control.
56.1% of participants had one or more Long COVID sequelae at a median of 357 days after COVID-19 onset.
The prevalence of one or more sequelae was similar between Mild (52.9%) and Severe (57.5%) acute COVID-19 groups, suggesting Long COVID risk is largely independent of initial disease severity.
Persistent fatigue was the most prevalent sequela, reported by 20% of participants at the time of the survey.
Dyspnea, alopecia, concentration problems, memory problems, sleeplessness, joint pain, and headache each persisted in ≥10% of participants at the time of the survey.
During the acute phase, fatigue occurred in ≥60% of participants, cough/dyspnea/lack of appetite in >50%, and sore throat/concentration problems in ~40%.

Among participants reporting each symptom, severity scores of 3-4 (likely to affect QOL) occurred in sputum production (21%), fatigue (10.4%), dyspnea (16.2%), anosmia (12.0%), alopecia (17.1%), concentration problems (15.5%), memory problems (16.7%), joint pain (26.6%), red eyes (16.6%), and diarrhea (12.5%).
Univariable ordinal logistic regression showed strong associations (OR ≥4) between acute COVID-19 severity and persistent sputum production, chest pain, dyspnea, sore throat, and diarrhea.
Older age was strongly associated (OR ≥4) with persistent cough as a Long COVID sequela.
Underlying hypertension was strongly associated (OR ≥4) with persistent sore throat as a Long COVID sequela.
Underlying dyslipidemia was strongly associated (OR ≥4) with persistent red eyes as a Long COVID sequela.
No association was found between acute COVID-19 severity and persistent fatigue, dysgeusia, anosmia, alopecia, or sleeplessness.

Fatigue, alopecia, concentration problems, memory problems, sleeplessness, dizziness, joint pain, red eyes, headache, and diarrhea tended to persist in more than 50% of affected participants for at least 1 year.
Diarrhea persisted only among participants with severe acute COVID-19, unlike other symptoms whose persistence patterns were similar regardless of severity.

In the Severe group, persistent cough, sputum production, fatigue, dyspnea, lack of appetite, red eyes, and diarrhea affected quality of life, indicating that more severe acute COVID-19 is associated with a greater diversity of QOL-impairing sequelae.

Across 102 included studies, the most consistently reported neurological symptoms in long COVID were cognitive difficulties, headaches, pain, dizziness, fatigue, sleep-related symptoms, and ageusia/anosmia.
Three of the 102 reviewed studies described temporal inconsistency of neurological symptoms, a positive clinical feature suggestive of functional neurological disorder.
Only one of the reviewed studies specifically hypothesized that some individuals with long COVID might be experiencing a functional disorder.
Eight of the reviewed studies described a chronic-fatigue-syndrome-like response occurring in association with long COVID.

Only 13 of the 102 reviewed studies specifically focused on long COVID following mild acute infection, limiting the ability to disentangle functional symptoms from confounders related to severe illness.
Sympathetic skin responses were unrecordable from the lower limbs in 58% of long-COVID patients and from the upper limbs in 25%, indicating a distal small-fiber/autonomic sympathetic dysfunction.
SSR latencies recorded from the feet were significantly longer in long-COVID patients compared with healthy volunteers, consistent with sympathetic small-fiber impairment.
SSR latencies recorded from the upper limbs did not differ significantly between long-COVID patients and healthy controls.

Quantitative multi-motor unit analysis (MMUA) of deltoid and tibialis anterior muscles showed no significant differences in MUP duration, amplitude, area, or polyphasia between long-COVID patients and healthy controls, arguing against a myopathic process.
Repetitive nerve stimulation showed only a mild decrement of CMAP amplitude that remained within the normal range, excluding a neuromuscular transmission disorder.
Serum creatine kinase levels were within normal limits in all long-COVID patients, arguing against significant muscle fiber damage.
Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG were unremarkable in all long-COVID patients, with no spontaneous denervation activity and a normal interference pattern on voluntary contraction.
A subset of long-COVID patients with autonomic involvement who were treated with steroids (prednisone, starting dose 25 mg/day) reported subjective improvement of both sensory and muscle symptoms.
A six-week multidisciplinary rehabilitation program significantly reduced abdominal fatty tissue mass in patients with long COVID-19.
Waist circumference significantly decreased after the rehabilitation program.
Cell hydration significantly decreased after the rehabilitation program.
Skeletal muscle mass significantly increased after the rehabilitation program.
Phase angle, a marker of cellular health, significantly increased after the rehabilitation program.
Peak oxygen consumption did not significantly change after the rehabilitation program in the subset of patients who underwent cardiopulmonary exercise testing.
Percentage of predicted peak VO2 showed a slight, non-significant increase after rehabilitation.
The ventilatory efficiency slope (VE/VCO2) showed a small, non-significant decrease after rehabilitation.
Percentage of predicted anaerobic threshold was unchanged after rehabilitation.
Perceived dyspnea, measured by the Modified Borg Scale, significantly improved from moderate to slight after rehabilitation.
Dyspnea assessed by the mMRC scale significantly improved after rehabilitation.
Fatigue impact, measured by the MFIS, decreased after the rehabilitation program.
Walking distance on the 6MWT significantly increased after rehabilitation.
Chair stand repetitions significantly increased after rehabilitation.
Overall physical performance (SPPB) significantly increased after rehabilitation.
Exercise intolerance was the most frequently reported long COVID-19 symptom, occurring in 73.2% of patients after the acute phase of COVID-19.
Sleep disturbances were the second most commonly reported long COVID-19 symptom, occurring in 46.9% of patients.
Fatigue was the third most commonly reported long COVID-19 symptom, occurring in 39.2% of patients.
A cited cross-sectional survey from Israel found that receiving at least two doses of COVID-19 vaccine was associated with reduced risk of developing long COVID-19 symptoms.
A cited UK nested case-control study using smartphone app data found that double vaccination against COVID-19 was associated with a decreased risk of developing long COVID-19.

A cited Italian study of 50 long COVID-19 patients with reduced exercise capacity found that an 8-week aerobic and resistance exercise training program significantly increased VO2peak and predicted VO2, and decreased VE/VCO2 slope.
A previously healthy 51-year-old woman developed a dissociative (functional) movement disorder—including limb jerks, weakness, and ataxic gait—two weeks after recovering from moderate COVID-19.
Case 1 was treated with quetiapine and clonazepam, resulting in slight improvement in night sleep and frequency of psychogenic seizures.

A 60-year-old woman with pre-existing stress-related motor/fatigue episodes experienced significant worsening of functional motor symptoms and new dissociative motor disorder with comorbid moderate depression after COVID-19 infection and bereavement.
Initial treatment of case 2 with amitriptyline and diazepam produced short-term improvement in mood, sleep, tremor, and independent walking, but symptoms later relapsed.
Following relapse, case 2 was treated with quetiapine and fluoxetine, leading to improved mood and activity, though fatigue and weakness persisted.
A 53-year-old woman with a childhood history of trauma and prior stress-induced motor episodes developed dissociative motor disorder with akinetic seizures after moderate COVID-19 infection.
Case 3 was treated with duloxetine and benzodiazepines, resulting in improved condition and reduced myoclonus at discharge.

A systematic literature search (Dec 2019-Feb 2022) found only three case reports and one cohort study describing functional movement disorders after COVID-19, suggesting FMDs are rarely reported relative to other post-COVID neurological sequelae.
A retrospective cohort study by Xiong et al. reported two patients with functional tic/tremor following COVID-19.

The authors argue that depression and functional movement disorder likely coexist as separate COVID-19-related conditions in case 2, rather than depression causing the functional motor disorder, since FMD symptoms only slightly improved despite good depression treatment response.
All 79 non-hospitalized long COVID patients completed the 30s-STS test remotely via telehealth with no serious adverse events, aside from two participants reporting mild dizziness.
60.8% of long COVID patients performed below sex- and age-specific reference values on the 30s-STS test, with mean performance of 11.5 ± 3.2 repetitions.
Long COVID patients with low 30s-STS performance had significantly greater dyspnea-related activity limitation (higher LCADL scores) than those with normal performance.
Long COVID patients with low 30s-STS performance had significantly higher fatigue (FAS) scores than those with normal performance.
Participants with lower 30s-STS performance had significantly worse health-related quality of life on the EQ-5D-5L index score.
Participants with lower 30s-STS performance had significantly lower self-reported general health status on the EQ-5D visual analogue scale.
Long COVID patients with low 30s-STS performance had significantly more severe pain/discomfort than those with normal performance.
Long COVID patients with low 30s-STS performance had significantly more severe functional status impairment (higher PCFS grades) than those with normal performance.
There were no significant differences in age or time since infection between long COVID patients with low versus normal 30s-STS performance.
A low but significant positive correlation was found between fatigue reported on the FAS and post-exertional lower limb fatigue rated on the modified Borg scale after the 30s-STS.
A high and significant positive correlation was found between the LCADL dyspnea-related activity limitation score and post-exertional dyspnea rated on the modified Borg scale after the 30s-STS.
Overall, 72.2% of the non-hospitalized long COVID sample reported moderate to extreme pain, alongside high levels of dyspnea and fatigue at baseline.
Long COVID patients performed fewer repetitions on the 30s-STS (median 11.5) than a previously reported telehealth oncology cohort (median 13.5), despite being on average 18 years younger.
TMS treatment (semi-piTBS to left DLPFC plus low-frequency rTMS to right LOFC) significantly reduced depressive symptom severity as measured by MADRS from baseline to after 20 sessions.
Self-reported depressive symptoms measured by PHQ-9 significantly improved after the TMS treatment course.
PS score, a measure of chronic-fatigue-related functional impairment, significantly improved after TMS treatment but subjective clinical improvement in fatigue was reported as only minor.
Cognitive function (brain fog), assessed with PDQ-D-5, significantly improved after the TMS treatment course, with no patients showing deterioration.
Exploratory subgroup analysis found a significant sex difference in MADRS improvement rate, with male patients showing greater improvement in depressive symptoms than female patients.
No significant correlation was found between patient age and treatment efficacy of TMS for any outcome measure.
No significant association was found between COVID-19 severity (as indexed by history/number of hospitalizations) and treatment response to TMS.
No significant association was found between the number of COVID-19 vaccinations received and treatment response to TMS.

TMS treatment was generally safe and tolerable, with only 4 of 23 patients reporting scalp pain at the stimulation site and no other significant adverse events, including no worsening of fatigue or cognitive function.

Patients with high acute muscle mass loss during hospitalization did not fully recover vastus lateralis cross-sectional area by 6 months post-discharge, unlike the low muscle loss group which fully recovered.
High muscle loss patients showed a greater decrease in handgrip strength at hospital discharge than the low muscle loss group, though this difference resolved by 6 months.
Patients with high acute muscle mass loss had a significantly higher prevalence of fatigue 6 months after hospital discharge than those with low muscle loss.
Patients with high acute muscle mass loss had a significantly higher prevalence of myalgia 6 months after hospital discharge than those with low muscle loss.
Chest pain prevalence trended higher in the high muscle loss group but did not reach statistical significance.
Hospital readmission rates at 2 and 6 months after discharge did not significantly differ between high and low muscle loss groups.
No significant between-group differences were observed in self-perceived health status items at 2 or 6 months after discharge.
Patients with high acute muscle mass loss incurred substantially greater hospital admission and total COVID-19-related health care costs than those with low muscle loss at 2 months post-discharge.

Patients with high acute muscle mass loss continued to incur significantly greater hospital admission and total COVID-19-related health care costs than those with low muscle loss at 6 months post-discharge.
In an adjusted linear regression model, the magnitude of muscle mass loss was an independent, significant predictor of total COVID-19-related health care costs at 2 months after discharge.
In an adjusted linear regression model, the magnitude of muscle mass loss remained an independent, significant predictor of total COVID-19-related health care costs at 6 months after discharge.

COVID-19 hospitalized patients showed a nearly two-fold greater magnitude of acute muscle mass loss (~10% over ~10 days) compared to previously reported losses (5%-7%) from other catabolic conditions like disuse/bed rest over 5-14 days.
Fatigue showed the largest improvement of all outcome measures after pneumological rehabilitation, with an effect size of 1.30.
Anxiety showed the smallest but still significant improvement among all outcome measures after rehabilitation, with an effect size of 0.76.
Breathlessness on exertion, one of the corona symptoms, improved significantly by the end of rehabilitation.
Lack of strength, another corona symptom, improved significantly by the end of rehabilitation.

Rehabilitants most often named improving health (92%), improving performance (92%), and improving respiratory muscle strength (78%) as their rehabilitation goals, with 60-70% of participants achieving these goals.
Only 32% of rehabilitants reported achieving restoration of their ability to work by the end of rehabilitation, a significantly lower rate than for other goals.
Only 17% of rehabilitants reported achieving a better ability to concentrate, the lowest goal-achievement rate among reported outcomes.
76% of participants rated their rehabilitation success as good to excellent at the end of the program based on a single self-report question.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported psychiatric/neuropsychiatric symptom in long-COVID syndrome, with prevalence estimates ranging from about 93.2-82.3% down to 11.5% across included studies.
Cognitive impairment/dysfunction was commonly reported in long-COVID patients, with prevalence estimates ranging from 61.4% to 23.5% across studies.
Depressive and anxiety symptoms were commonly reported in long-COVID patients, with prevalence ranging from 23.5% to 9.5% across studies.

COVID-19 is characterized by a cytokine release syndrome with elevated serum interleukin-6 and other inflammatory cytokines that correlate dose-dependently with respiratory failure and adverse outcomes, and this immuno-inflammatory dysregulation is thought to contribute to acute and post-acute psychiatric and cognitive symptoms.

SARS survivors, a comparable coronavirus illness, showed that at least 30% reported significant reduction in mental health one year after infection, suggesting long-COVID psychiatric symptoms may follow a similar course.

SARS-CoV-2 enters host cells via binding of the viral S1 spike protein subunit to the ACE2 receptor, with proposed neuroinvasion via retrograde axonal transport from olfactory neurons or breach of the blood-brain barrier, potentially explaining cognitive impairment in long-COVID.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and Internet-based CBT have been suggested as cost-effective interventions for managing psychiatric conditions associated with long-COVID while adhering to public health guidelines.

Anosmia, a common COVID-19 symptom, has previously been associated with the onset of dementia and neurodegeneration, raising concern about a possible link between COVID-19 infection and later dementia risk.
Long COVID is reported to occur in 30-50% of patients who had COVID-19.

In a cohort of 1884 children with COVID-19 followed for 90 days, about 10% of those admitted and 5% of those discharged from the emergency department developed Long COVID, with weakness, cough, and dyspnea as the most frequent symptoms.

An epidemiological study of 47,780 people found that a COVID-19 diagnosis was associated with a 3-fold increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events within 4 months, compared with non-hospitalized controls.
A survey found fatigue, headache, loss of smell, shortness of breath, cough, chest pain, diarrhea, and delirium as the most commonly reported symptoms 28 days after acute COVID-19.

Oxidative stress and inflammatory pathways triggered by SARS-CoV-2 are proposed to cause ryanodine receptor (RYR) calcium leakage, dysregulating intracellular calcium and activating calcium-dependent enzymes that drive massive hyperphosphorylation of tau protein.
COVID-19 is associated with a 3.8-fold increase in oxidative stress marked by elevated glutathione disulfide (GSSG)/glutathione (GSH) expression in the brain cortex.
Circulating kynurenine levels, a marker of inflammation, are increased and linked to increased PKA and CaMKII binding activity in COVID-19-related tau pathology.

Full activation of the inflammatory/oxidative pathway in COVID-19 leads to elevated TGF-β production, which in turn increases NOX2 activity and decreases calstabin 2, promoting pathological calcium leakage into the endoplasmic reticulum.
Calstabin 2 levels are decreased as part of the TGF-β-driven pathway that leads to pathological calcium leakage in COVID-19-related tau pathology.
The NLRP3 inflammasome, activated during SARS-CoV-2 infection, influences tau protein phosphorylation and is proposed to play a crucial role in COVID-19-related tauopathy.

COVID-19 patients show elevated levels of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-7, IL-10, IL-13, IL-17, G-CSF, GM-CSF, M-CSF, and IP-10, reflecting dysregulated immune pathways.
Oxidative stress in neurons leads to elevated phosphorylation of tau at Thr231 (p231T) and its mislocalization within the neuron.
An in vitro brain organoid model infected with SARS-CoV-2 showed massive phosphorylation of tau protein (pTau231) accompanied by neuronal cell death.

Massive tau hyperphosphorylation is linked to small-fiber (Aδ and C-fiber) and major-fiber peripheral neuropathy featuring tactile allodynia, impaired thermoregulation, slowed motor nerve conduction, and decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber density.
Post-COVID-19 neuropathy prevalence estimates vary widely, between about 11.7 per 100,000 and 13.3 per 10,000, and are considered likely underestimates.
A literature review cited in the paper reports that complications following COVID-19 occur in 20-25% of patients, representing a significant healthcare expense.
Dysautonomia, the malfunction of the autonomic nervous system controlling involuntary bodily functions, is listed as one of the neurological manifestations of Long COVID.
Studies are evaluating the long-term gastrointestinal consequences of COVID-19, including post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome, as part of the Long COVID clinical spectrum.

Long COVID risk is described as greater in women, older individuals, those who are obese or overweight, and those hospitalized for COVID-19, with susceptibility also increasing with number of acute-phase symptoms (particularly dyspnea).
Fatigue was the most commonly reported physical symptom of long COVID, occurring in 92.6% of 162,282 participants across 55 studies.
Shortness of breath was the second most commonly reported physical symptom of long COVID, reported by 81.8% of participants.
In two of the included cohort studies, muscle and joint pain (rather than fatigue or breathlessness) were reported as the most common long COVID symptom.
The majority of cohort studies (45 of 57) reported that more than half of long COVID sufferers were female, with an average of 56.1% female participants across studies.
The mean age of long COVID patients across studies was 43.5 years, with a median of 47 years, and the most commonly documented age group was 35-45 years, corresponding to peak working-age adults.
Long COVID participants had, on average, an overweight BMI of 27.13, suggesting overweight status may be associated with long COVID risk.
Among studies reporting smoking status, an average of 23.7% of long COVID participants were active smokers.

A case report described a 42-year-old woman who developed postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) three months after mild acute COVID-19 infection, presenting with fatigue, chest pain, muscle aches, and postural light-headedness.
A case report described a 53-year-old man who developed ANCA vasculitis one month after mild acute COVID-19 infection, presenting with fatigue, generalised muscle pain, and loss of appetite.

The review notes that overlapping symptoms of fatigue, pain, and shortness of breath seen in long COVID are also present in ME/CFS and POTS, both known post-infectious disease syndromes, suggesting a shared post-infectious mechanism.

Case reports/case series in the review described a variety of distinct post-COVID syndromes, including multi-system inflammatory sequelae, Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves' disease, subacute thyroiditis, POTS, pulmonary fungal infection, Kawasaki-like syndrome, neuropathic pain, and ANCA vasculitis.

Long COVID physical symptoms reported across cohort studies span neurological (fatigue, back pain, dizziness, sleep disturbances, headache, weakness), respiratory (SOB, cough), musculoskeletal (muscle and joint pain), and cardiac (orthostatic intolerance, palpitations) systems.
Mean motor unit potential duration was decreased in at least one muscle in 52% of Long COVID patients, consistent with myopathic changes.
Increased jitter on single fiber EMG was found in the tibialis anterior muscle in 17% of Long COVID patients.
Increased jitter on single fiber EMG was found in the extensor digitorum communis muscle in 25% of Long COVID patients.
Lower quality of life scores correlated with higher jitter values in Long COVID patients.
Quality of life scores did not correlate with quantitative EMG (qEMG) measures in Long COVID patients.
Muscle biopsies from Long COVID patients showed damage to terminal nerves and motor endplates with abundant basal lamina material.
At the motor endplate, axons were present but vesicle-containing nerve terminals were absent in Long COVID muscle biopsies.
The post-synaptic cleft appeared atrophic in areas, with short clefts and coarse crests, in Long COVID muscle biopsies.
A large Wuhan cohort found that 56% of discharged COVID-19 patients had persistently abnormal diffusion capacity at 6 months, worsening with initial illness severity.

Among 102 critically ill COVID-19 patients reassessed 6 weeks post-discharge, 15% had obstructive abnormalities, 19% restrictive abnormalities, and 27% reduced exercise capacity on 6-minute walk test.
A Swedish cohort found ICU-discharged COVID-19 survivors had higher rates of polyneuropathy or myopathy than other ICU patients.
A UK post-hospitalization study reported common psychological symptoms of PTSD, memory loss, and concentration difficulties, with greater severity among ICU-admitted patients.

In a large Chinese cohort at 6 months post-discharge, fatigue/muscle weakness, sleep difficulties, dyspnea, and anxiety/depression were common; at 12-month follow-up, dyspnea and anxiety prevalence increased while fatigue decreased.
A US retrospective study found most hospitalized COVID-19 survivors were unable to independently perform all activities of daily living one month post-discharge.
The first pediatric long COVID study found that more than half of children aged 6-16 had at least one symptom lasting over 4 months, with 43% impaired in daily activities.
A Swiss pediatric cohort found only a small proportion of children and adolescents had long COVID symptoms lasting over 3 months, most commonly tiredness and poor concentration.
A Swedish cohort found recovery time from long COVID correlated with acute infection severity, with mild cases recovering within 2 weeks and severe cases taking 2-3 months.
An Italian study found older ICU-admitted patients (50+ years) were more likely to experience residual symptoms than younger patients (18-35 years).

A UK cohort showed higher rates of respiratory disease, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease diagnoses, along with elevated readmission and death rates, among long COVID patients compared to matched non-COVID controls.
A UK community-based case-control study of 1.2 million people found double COVID-19 vaccination reduced the risk of developing long COVID by half.
A Dutch study of healthcare workers found T cell and IgG responses against SARS-CoV-2 were detectable one year after infection in mRNA-vaccinated individuals.
A UK case-control study of over 4000 participants found two vaccine doses reduced the prevalence and severity of long COVID symptoms compared to no vaccination.

A TriNetX electronic health record study of over 81 million U.S. patients found one and especially two vaccine doses were associated with lower risk of multiple post-COVID complications including respiratory failure, ICU admission, and thromboembolism.
In a French study of 910 patients with existing long COVID, vaccination reduced symptom severity, improved quality of life, and doubled the remission rate.
A 2021 prospective cohort study found female sex was independently associated with increased risk of developing long COVID syndrome.
Some studies report higher rehospitalization rates for male patients within one month, while other studies find no sex difference, illustrating conflicting sex-disparity data in long COVID outcomes.
A UK study found female sex was associated with greater likelihood of fatigue and depression as long COVID symptoms, without adjustment for prior mental illness history.
Lower baseline SARS-CoV-2 IgG levels, along with anosmia and diarrhea during acute infection, were associated with higher risk of developing long-term symptoms.
In a large cohort, female sex was associated with increased odds of any persistent symptom category after COVID-19, with the strongest association for dermatological symptoms.
Pre-existing asthma was associated with post-COVID neurological and mood/behavioral symptoms, while pre-existing chronic pulmonary disease was associated with chronic fatigue.

A cohort of 2198 participants found a 16.1% prevalence of long COVID symptoms at 12 weeks, with duration predicted by younger age, female gender, rural residence, prior functional limitation, and smoking.

A large survey found ongoing long COVID symptoms (breathing problems, fatigue, muscle weakness, sleep disturbance, cognitive problems, mood changes, cough) were common but did not appear related to acute illness severity or pre-existing conditions.
