A UK asthma survey found respondents with long COVID reported worse breathing, increased inhaler use, and worse asthma management than those without long COVID.

A multivariate analysis identified female gender, pre-existing lung disease, and ER visit as predictors of higher risk of chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) after COVID-19, and identified predictors of MRC dyspnea and exercise tolerance scores.
A study found oxygen saturation, D-dimer, and serum ferritin levels were significantly correlated with presence and severity of dyspnea in post-COVID patients.
A survey study reported common long COVID symptoms of general fatigue and weakness, mood changes, insomnia, loss of smell/taste, cough, dyspnea, and GI symptoms with varying severity.

A systematic review found Black and Hispanic populations experience disproportionately higher rates of SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19-related mortality, which may extend to long COVID outcomes though data are lacking.

Risk factors for COVID-19 rehospitalization included male sex, age over 65, discharge to skilled nursing/home health services, and comorbidities such as COPD, heart failure, diabetes with complications, chronic kidney disease, and BMI ≥30.
A lower baseline level of SARS-CoV-2 IgG, together with anosmia and diarrhea during acute COVID-19, was associated with a higher risk of developing long-term symptoms.
In a cohort of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, female sex was associated with increased odds of any persistent symptom category, with the strongest association for dermatological symptoms.

Asthma was associated with increased odds of neurological symptoms and mood/behavioral changes, while chronic pulmonary disease was associated with increased odds of chronic fatigue, among long COVID patients.

Among 2198 participants, the prevalence of long COVID symptoms at 12 weeks was 16.1%, with the most common symptoms being fatigue, pain, dyspnea, cough, anosmia, appetite loss, headache, and chest pain, lasting an overall duration of 21.8±5.2 weeks.
Structural equation modeling predicted that longer duration of long COVID symptoms was related to younger age, female gender, rural residence, prior functional limitation, and smoking.

In another cohort, the most frequently reported ongoing symptoms were breathing problems, fatigue, muscle weakness/joint stiffness, sleep disturbances, mental ability problems, mood changes, and cough, and these did not appear related to the severity of acute illness or presence of pre-existing conditions.

Among individuals reporting COVID-19 with asthma, those with long COVID were more likely than those without long COVID to report worsened breathing, increased inhaler use, and worse asthma management.

In a large cohort of 47,780 individuals discharged after acute COVID-19 and followed for a mean of 140 days, nearly a third were readmitted and more than 1 in 10 died, at rates four and eight times greater respectively than a matched control group, with significantly elevated rates of respiratory disease, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

Rate ratios for respiratory disease after COVID-19 discharge were higher in individuals under 70 years old versus those 70 and older, and higher in non-white ethnic groups compared with white individuals.

In a small cohort, most participants who had COVID-19 experienced symptoms post-recovery and mild depression, with 41.4% reporting the highest mental-health impact of the pandemic, while 74.3% reported no anxiety on the Corona Anxiety Scale.

Female gender, pre-existing lung disease, headache at presentation, ICU admission, critical COVID-19, and post-discharge ER visit predicted higher MRC dyspnea scores, while female gender, older age (>67 years), arterial hypertension, and ER visit were associated with lower exercise tolerance (MET) scores at follow-up.

Female gender, pre-existing lung disease, and ER visit were associated with a higher risk of chronic fatigue syndrome, while age, dyslipidemia, hypertension, pre-existing lung disease, and duration of symptoms were negatively associated with WHO-5 well-being scores.

In another cohort, 34% of patients reported respiratory symptoms after 2 months, and lower oxygen saturation, elevated D-dimer, and elevated serum ferritin were significantly correlated with the presence and severity of dyspnea; smoking history and COPD were also significantly associated.

In another survey, general fatigue and weakness were each reported by 73% of respondents, alongside moderate mood changes and insomnia, marked loss of smell and taste, mild cough, moderate dyspnea and appetite loss, and mild gastrointestinal symptoms.
Individuals with the comorbidity asthma had marginally higher odds of self-reporting COVID-19 symptoms.
Male individuals had significantly lower odds of self-reporting COVID-19 symptoms compared to females.
Increased BMI and the comorbidity hypertension were not significantly associated with self-reported COVID-19 symptoms.

In univariate analysis, female individuals were 1.7 times more likely to report PLC symptoms than males, but this association was not significant after multivariable adjustment for age, BMI, and COVID-19 symptoms.
COVID-19-associated anxiety was an independent risk factor for developing post/long-COVID symptoms.
Strong COVID-19-associated hyposmia was an independent risk factor for developing post/long-COVID symptoms.
COVID-19-associated fatigue was an independent risk factor for developing post/long-COVID symptoms.
COVID-19-associated heart palpitations were an independent risk factor for developing post/long-COVID symptoms.
Heavy COVID-19-associated headache symptoms were an independent risk factor for developing post/long-COVID symptoms.
COVID-19-associated memory loss was associated with increased odds of developing post/long-COVID symptoms.
Individuals who experienced strong loss-of-taste symptoms during COVID-19 were less likely to develop post/long-COVID symptoms.
COVID-19 fatigue strongly predicted subsequent PLC fatigue.
COVID-19 heart palpitations were associated with increased odds of developing PLC fatigue.
COVID-19 anxiety was associated with increased odds of developing PLC fatigue.
COVID-19 fatigue was strongly associated with developing PLC dyspnoea.
COVID-19 heart palpitation symptoms were associated with increased odds of developing PLC dyspnoea.
COVID-19 fatigue was a strong predictor of low resilience during the PLC period.
COVID-19 muscle pain doubled the likelihood of reporting PLC hyposmia.
COVID-19 hyposmia tripled the likelihood of reporting PLC hyposmia.
COVID-19 heart palpitations were significantly associated with PLC heart palpitations.
COVID-19 muscle pain was a strong predictor of PLC heart palpitations.
Fatigue was the most prevalent self-reported PLC symptom, affecting over half of individuals with PLC, followed by dyspnoea, decreased strength, decreased sense of smell, and memory loss.
Among a larger follow-up sample of self-reported COVID-19 cases collected through July 2022, 13% reported PLC symptoms.

The authors propose that postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS), linked to autonomic nervous system malfunction, may underlie the heart-palpitation-related associations with PLC dyspnoea and fatigue observed in this study.
Individuals reporting COVID-19 within the last 12 weeks had markedly higher odds of loss of smell compared to those with no COVID-19.
Loss of taste was strongly associated with recent COVID-19 (within 12 weeks) relative to no COVID-19.
Fever was significantly associated with COVID-19 in the last 12 weeks.
Cough was significantly associated with COVID-19 in the last 12 weeks.
Shortness of breath was significantly associated with COVID-19 in the last 12 weeks.
About one-fifth of individuals with no reported COVID-19 nonetheless reported headaches, illustrating substantial baseline symptom burden in the COVID-19-free population.
Fatigue was reported by roughly one-fifth of individuals with no COVID-19, indicating high baseline prevalence unrelated to COVID-19.
Among people with COVID-19 more than 12 weeks ago and no functional limitation, loss of smell remained elevated relative to those with no COVID-19, though less than in the acute group.
Among people with COVID-19 more than 12 weeks ago and no functional limitation, loss of taste remained elevated relative to no COVID-19.
In the long COVID group with functional limitation at 12 weeks, loss of taste showed the largest elevation relative to no COVID-19.
In the long COVID group with functional limitation at 12 weeks, loss of smell was strongly elevated relative to no COVID-19.
Fatigue was strongly elevated in the long COVID group with functional limitation compared to those with no COVID-19.
Shortness of breath was strongly elevated in the long COVID group with functional limitation.
Muscle pain or aches were significantly elevated in the long COVID group with functional limitation.
Chest tightness was significantly elevated in the long COVID group with functional limitation.
Memory loss was significantly elevated in the long COVID group with functional limitation.
Difficulty concentrating was elevated in the long COVID group with functional limitation, though with a wide confidence interval.

Latent class analysis of core symptoms supported only two symptom patterns (a low-symptom 'well' pattern and a high-symptom-burden pattern) in every COVID-19 group and study, with no evidence for further subtyping.
The high-symptom-burden latent class ('symptom pattern 2') was more common among females than males across nearly all studies and COVID-19 groups, including the long COVID group.
Prevalence of the high-symptom-burden pattern was strongly associated with longer duration of functional limitation, being greatest among those unable to function as normal for 12 weeks or more.
The prevalence of runny nose and sneezing did not differ meaningfully between those with and without COVID-19, or by time since COVID-19, suggesting these symptoms are not COVID-19-specific.
In age-heterogeneous studies, the high-symptom-burden pattern was more common at younger ages in the no-COVID-19 group, and to a lesser extent in the long COVID group.

In the secondary analysis using the maximal symptom set, chills and heaviness in arms or legs were additionally identified as excess symptoms in acute COVID-19, while heaviness in arms or legs was additionally identified for long COVID.
Nearly half of older adults reported new or worsened fatigue (asthenia) 6 months after COVID-19 hospital discharge.
Over a third of older adults reported new or worsened joint or muscle pain post-COVID-19.
About a third of older adults reported new or worsened shortness of breath during daily activity post-COVID-19.
About 15% of older adults reported new mental health problems post-COVID-19.
About 72% of older COVID-19 survivors reported long-lasting clinical complications 6 months after discharge.
Severe fatigue (FSS ≥4) was present in 16.5% of older adults and low physical activity in 86.77%.
Higher fatigue severity was the strongest independent predictor of lower physical component score (PCS) of HRQoL in multiple regression.
Lower physical activity levels independently predicted lower physical component score of HRQoL.
Higher educational level was independently associated with better physical component score of HRQoL, the only demographic variable significantly related to PCS.
New or worsened pain post-COVID-19 independently predicted lower physical component score of HRQoL.
Worsened difficulty with activities of daily living independently predicted lower physical component score of HRQoL.
Cognitive-communication problems (36% prevalence) were the strongest independent predictor of lower mental component score (MCS) of HRQoL.
Longer hospital stay was independently associated with lower mental component score of HRQoL.

Worsened shortness of breath during daily activity was negatively associated with initial CT-scan disease severity and positively associated with changes in mobility, self-care, and activities of daily living.
Fatigue severity correlated with worsened shortness of breath, pain, changes in self-care/mobility/daily activities, lower physical activity, and worsened economic status.
Physical and mental HRQoL scores were not significantly associated with sex, admission SpO2, number of comorbidities, post-COVID functional status, or initial chest CT severity grade.
Overall HRQoL was poor in older COVID-19 survivors 6 months post-discharge, particularly in the mental health domain, compared to Iranian population norms.

In typically developing children, affective tactile stimulation elicited a combined sympathetic response (pupil dilation and skin conductance elevation) together with a parasympathetic response (heart rate deceleration/RR interval increase).

In TD children, the latency of maximum pupil dilation was longer following hand (CT low-density) stimulation than arm (CT high-density) stimulation, though overall dilation magnitude did not differ by site.

In TD children, pupil dilation AUC and maximum amplitude did not differ between CT high-density (forearm) and CT low-density (palm) stimulation sites, not supporting a CT-fiber-specific autonomic signature.
In TD children, skin conductance response parameters (AUC, amplitude, latency) did not differ between forearm and palm stimulation sites.
In TD children, heart rate deceleration (RR interval increase) during touch did not differ significantly between forearm and palm stimulation sites.
Children with ASD showed no significant pupil dilation during tactile stimulation, in contrast to typically developing children who showed a clear dilation response.

Children with ASD showed significantly less heart rate deceleration (smaller RR interval increase) during affective tactile stimulation than TD children, reflecting reduced parasympathetic engagement.
Skin conductance response magnitude did not significantly differ between ASD and TD children overall, though a non-significant trend toward a location-by-group interaction was observed.
Baseline (resting, inter-trial) pupil diameter was smaller in children with ASD than in age-matched TD children.
Baseline RR interval was shorter (i.e., resting heart rate was faster) in children with ASD compared with age-matched TD children.
Baseline skin conductance did not significantly differ between ASD and TD children.

No significant correlations were found between any of the three autonomic parameters (pupil, SCR, RR interval) and the four Short Sensory Profile 2 subscale scores (seeking, avoiding, sensitivity, registration) in either TD or ASD children.
In children with ASD, greater autism symptom severity (higher CARS score) was associated with less heart rate deceleration (lower RR interval variation) during affective touch.
In children with ASD, higher ADOS-2 severity scores were associated with a longer latency of maximum pupil dilation response to touch.

In TD children, lower baseline pupil diameter and lower baseline RR interval predicted larger stimulus-evoked responses, but this baseline-response coupling was absent when comparing across ASD and TD groups, suggesting reduced reactivity in ASD is not simply explained by altered resting autonomic tone.

Nearly half of the ASD children (17 of 37) who consented to the study could not complete the tactile/autonomic recording protocol, and those excluded showed overall more severe autism, more developmental delay, and more atypical sensory scores than those successfully tested.
ASD and TD groups differed significantly in verbal IQ, non-verbal IQ, and SSP2 sensory profile scores, but not in age.

A previously cited study suggested that individuals with ASD may have a lower peripheral density of C-tactile (CT) low-threshold mechanoreceptor fibers than typically developing individuals, offered as a candidate (unconfirmed) explanation for atypical affective touch responses.

In typical fetal mouse development, the absolute cross-correlation coefficient (CC1) between maternal and fetal RR intervals was significantly higher at later embryonic days (ED17.5 and ED18.5) than at earlier stages.

Low-frequency coherence (CLF) between maternal and fetal RR intervals was significantly lower at ED13.5 compared to ED15.5, ED17.5, and ED18.5, indicating increasing frequency-domain coupling with fetal age.

High-frequency coherence (CHF) between maternal and fetal RR intervals increased with fetal age, being significantly higher at ED18.5 than ED15.5 and ED13.5, and higher at ED17.5 and ED15.5 than ED13.5.
Unlike CC1, the signed cross-correlation coefficient (CC2) showed no significant differences across any of the developmental stages studied.

At embryonic day 15.5, valproic-acid-exposed (ASD model) fetuses showed significantly lower maternal-fetal RRI coupling (CC1, CLF, CHF) compared to saline controls, indicating disrupted maternal-fetal autonomic communication in the autism mouse model.

At embryonic day 18.5, VPA-exposed fetuses showed generally lower maternal-fetal RRI coupling values than saline controls across all four coefficients, but the differences were not statistically significant.

Fetuses from the same mother could show differing (even opposite-direction) correlation trends with maternal heart rate at the same developmental time point, implying individualized mediator effects such as placental function.
Overall, the study concludes that impaired maternal-fetal heart rate/autonomic nervous system communication during the prenatal period is a feature of the valproic-acid-induced autism mouse model.

Gut microbiota maturation in children with ASD is developmentally stagnant, with unstable/immature early colonization and alterations occurring before age 3, coinciding with emergence of behavioral deficits.
Multiple bacterial genera showed higher relative abundance in the gut microbiota of children with ASD compared with neurotypical children.
Multiple bacterial genera showed lower relative abundance in the gut microbiota of children with ASD compared with neurotypical children.
At species level, Clostridium bolteae, Bacteroides vulgatus and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were more abundant in autistic children than neurotypical children.
Blood levels of GABA, serotonin, lipopolysaccharides and p-cresol are elevated in children with ASD.
Blood levels of homocysteine, methionine, glutathione, S-adenosylmethionine, arachidonic acid, docosahexaenoic acid and eicosapentaenoic acid are decreased in children with ASD.

SCFAs such as acetate, butyrate and propionate increase claudin and occludin expression, reducing blood-brain barrier permeability, and along with tryptophan metabolites block proinflammatory transcription factor activation in astrocytes and microglia to support cerebral homeostasis.
In animal ASD models, higher relative abundance of Lachnospiraceae bacterium A2 was associated with reduced repetitive behavior and increased regulatory T cells in mesenteric lymph nodes.

Lactobacillus reuteri increases oxytocin levels and acts via the vagus nerve on the oxytocin-dopamine system to restore social-induced synaptic plasticity and improve social deficits in mice, an effect abolished in oxytocin receptor-deficient mice.
Enterococcus faecalis reduces corticosterone levels in stressed mice by inhibiting HPA axis activation, influencing stress-related social behavior circuits.
Mice fed Lactobacillus rhamnosus showed less emotional stress and anxiety with elevated hippocampal GABA mRNA expression.
The microbial metabolite 4-EPS crosses into the bloodstream and brain to affect myelin formation and promote anxiety-like behavior in mice, an effect probably alleviated by Bacteroides fragilis.
In a pilot IBS study, Bifidobacterium longum NCC3001 decreased depression scores and improved quality of life, probably via upregulation of hippocampal BDNF.

EPHB6 deficiency mediates autism-like behavior in mice via induction of gut microbiota dysregulation, leading to vitamin B6 and dopamine deficiency and excitatory/inhibitory imbalance of prefrontal cortex pyramidal neurons through the dopamine D1 receptor pathway.

Loss of KDM5 function in Drosophila caused impaired intestinal barrier function, dysbiosis and abnormal social behavior, phenotypes partially rescued by antibiotic treatment or Lactobacillus plantarum feeding.
Colonization of germ-free mice with gut microbiota from ASD donors, but not from typically-developing donors, was sufficient to induce ASD-signature behaviors.

After transplanting fecal samples from ASD and control children into germ-free mice, ASD-transplanted mice showed altered amino acid and serotonin metabolic pathways, with lower colonic 5-HT reuptake transporter and serotonin 1A receptor expression and higher tryptophan hydroxylase 1 expression.

FMT from healthy human gut microbiota into ASD mice significantly improved anxiety-like and repetitive behaviors and increased serum chemokines involved in CNS neural development and synaptic transmission.
FMT from naive wild-type mice improved memory deficits and social withdrawal in Fmr1 knockout mice, normalizing A. muciniphila abundance and decreasing brain TNFα and Iba1 levels.
FMT restored fecal Clostridium balance and normalized hippocampal BDNF and GST levels, repairing social interaction deficits in a propionic-acid-induced ASD mouse model.

Transplanting fecal microbiota from normal mice into p-cresol-treated mice restored social behavior, VTA dopamine neuronal excitability, and normalized fecal p-cresol levels, whereas transplanting p-cresol-mouse microbiota into normal mice induced ASD-typical behavior and increased p-cresol production.

In a small open-label trial of 18 children with ASD, FMT after antibiotic pretreatment and bowel cleanse produced about 80% improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms (GSRS) and significant behavioral improvement that continued through 8 weeks, alongside increased total bacterial diversity and Bifidobacteria, Prevotella and Desulfovibrio abundance.

At 2-year follow-up, 8 autistic children who received FMT showed sustained improvement in gastrointestinal and ASD symptoms, with persistent increases in microbial diversity and Bifidobacteria/Prevotella abundance, supporting long-term safety and efficacy.

In a Chinese trial of 40 children with ASD (vs 16 typically-developing children), 4 weeks of FMT (oral or rectal, no significant difference between routes) improved gastrointestinal and ASD symptoms and serum neurotransmitter levels; Eubacterium coprostanoligenes abundance correlated positively with GSRS score and was reduced by FMT.
Plasma niacinamide nucleoside levels were decreased in children with ASD compared with healthy children among 619 plasma metabolites profiled.
Plasma octanoate and heptanoate levels were increased in children with ASD relative to healthy children.
Among 699 fecal metabolites compared between children with ASD and healthy children there was overall no significant difference, and p-cresol sulfate was not significantly increased in the ASD group.
After FMT, the plasma metabolic profile of children with ASD changed significantly, including nicotinate/nicotinamide and purine-related metabolites.
Following FMT, fecal p-cresol sulfate levels in children with ASD decreased to a level similar to that of healthy children.
A multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of FMT for ASD is currently ongoing in China.

In a large single-center prospective study of 609 adult patients receiving FMT for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, over 60% had short-term diarrhea lasting less than a week, while long-term risk of adverse events and infectious complications was low.

A single-center retrospective study of FMT safety in 114 children found a 26.32% incidence of short-term adverse events, most commonly abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever and vomiting, all self-limited within 48 hours.

In the same pediatric FMT safety cohort, one child with primary immunodeficiency died of sepsis and liver failure four weeks after FMT given for chronic intractable diarrhea; no other long-term adverse events occurred at 3-month follow-up.

In a Chinese cohort of 40 children with ASD and 16 typically-developing children, significant differences in behavior, gastrointestinal symptoms, and gut microbiota composition were observed between groups at baseline (week 1).
Both oral and rectal routes of FMT administration improved gastrointestinal symptoms in children with ASD, with no significant difference in efficacy between the two routes.

Abundance of Eubacterium coprostanoligenes was positively correlated with higher GSRS (gastrointestinal symptom) scores, and FMT reduced its abundance, which may be associated with improvement of ASD symptoms.
The review concludes that FMT is a novel treatment approach for children with ASD that can relieve both gastrointestinal and neurobehavioral symptoms, though long-term effect data remain limited.
Diagnosed Asperger's syndrome was found at a substantially elevated rate in the MENSA sample compared to general population prevalence, showing the largest effect size among all diagnosed conditions.
Diagnosed autism spectrum disorder was elevated in the gifted MENSA sample, with more than 5% of the sample reporting an Asperger's or autism diagnosis combined.
Diagnosed cancer prevalence was moderately elevated in the gifted sample relative to the general population.
A single case of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in the sample produced a very large risk ratio due to the extremely low population baseline prevalence.
Diagnosed chronic fatigue syndrome was one of seven conditions found to be significantly elevated in the gifted sample compared to general population prevalence.
Diagnosed depression rates were significantly elevated in the gifted MENSA sample compared to general population prevalence.
Diagnosed generalized anxiety disorder rates were significantly elevated in the gifted MENSA sample compared to general population prevalence.
Diagnosed irritable bowel syndrome rates were significantly elevated in the gifted MENSA sample, consistent with a stress-related mechanism.
Diagnosed allergy rates in the gifted sample did not significantly differ from the general population, failing to replicate Karpinski et al.'s (2018) finding of elevated allergies.
Diagnosed asthma rates in the gifted sample did not significantly differ from the general population, failing to replicate Karpinski et al.'s (2018) finding of elevated asthma.

Autoimmune disease prevalence was only slightly and non-significantly elevated in the gifted sample, undermining the proposed psychoneuroimmunological explanation for elevated cancer and other conditions.
When diagnosed and self-suspected conditions were combined, Asperger's syndrome showed an exceptionally elevated risk ratio, much larger than for diagnosed-only prevalence.
Participants in the top 1 percent of the IQ distribution did not differ from those in the top 2 percent in the number of diagnosed or combined health conditions.
Avoidant coping style showed the strongest correlation with number of diagnosed health conditions among coping strategies, followed by emotion-focused and problem-focused coping.
The correlation pattern between coping strategies and health conditions was more pronounced for combined (diagnosed plus suspected) conditions than for diagnosed conditions alone.
Lower Extraversion and Agreeableness, and higher Emotionality (HEXACO personality factors), were each significantly associated with a greater number of diagnosed health conditions.

GERD in the post-COVID-19 period was significantly enriched among PASC cases compared to matched controls.
A pre-existing diagnosis of IBS before COVID-19 infection was associated with increased risk of subsequently developing PASC.
A pre-existing diagnosis of concussion before COVID-19 infection was associated with increased risk of subsequently developing PASC.
A pre-existing history of nausea and vomiting before COVID-19 infection was associated with increased risk of subsequently developing PASC.
A pre-existing history of shortness of breath before COVID-19 infection was associated with increased risk of subsequently developing PASC.
A pre-existing history of respiratory abnormalities before COVID-19 infection was associated with increased risk of subsequently developing PASC.

A pre-existing history of allergic reaction to food before COVID-19 infection was associated with increased risk of subsequently developing PASC, although this association was not replicated in the post-COVID-19 period.
A pre-existing general circulatory disease diagnosis before COVID-19 infection was associated with increased risk of subsequently developing PASC.

Sixty-nine phenotypes occurring during the acute-COVID-19 period (days -14 to +28) were significantly enriched among PASC cases, predominantly respiratory (22 phenotypes), circulatory (13 phenotypes, including orthostatic hypotension and hypotension), neurological (7 phenotypes including migraine), digestive (6), and mental health (5) categories.
The strength of association between acute-COVID-19 shortness of breath and PASC increased significantly from patients with an index date in 2020 to those in 2021.
A phenotype risk score built from pre-COVID-19 predisposing PheCodes discriminated PASC cases from controls in the 2022 testing set, but with low accuracy.
A phenotype risk score built from acute-COVID-19 predisposing PheCodes discriminated PASC cases from controls better than PheRS1, but still with low accuracy.
Combining PheRS1 and PheRS2 modestly improved discrimination of PASC cases from controls but overall accuracy remained low.
Patients in the top 10% of the pre-COVID-19 PheRS distribution were significantly more likely to receive a subsequent PASC diagnosis compared to those in the lower 50%.
Patients in the top 10% of the acute-COVID-19 PheRS distribution were substantially more likely to receive a subsequent PASC diagnosis compared to those in the lower 50%.
Patients in the top 10-25% bin of the combined PheRS distribution had significantly increased odds of a PASC diagnosis, identifying roughly a quarter of COVID-19 patients as higher-risk.
Long COVID patients showed increased SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T-cell responses compared to those without long COVID.
Long COVID patients showed increased SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T-cell responses compared to those without long COVID.
Patients experiencing long COVID exhibited increased affinity of SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies.
Immune dysregulation observed during acute COVID-19 was found to persist into the convalescent period.
Persistent SARS-CoV-2 antigen presence is proposed to drive local and systemic inflammation underlying the heterogeneous clinical manifestations of long COVID.
SARS-CoV-2 spike protein stimulated BV-2 mouse microglial cells to release IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α along with increased TLR4 expression.
Infection of human HMC3 microglia with SARS-CoV-2 led to release of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α.
Activation of TLR4 increased expression of ACE2, potentially enhancing SARS-CoV-2 viral infectivity in an autocrine loop.

Recombinant whole-length spike protein stimulated human microglia to secrete IL-1β and CXCL8 via TLR-4 (not ACE2), whereas the receptor-binding domain of spike stimulated release of IL-18, TNF-α, and S100B via ACE2.
Increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, especially IL-6, were detected in the cerebrospinal fluid of COVID-19 patients and implicated in COVID-19-associated neurologic disease.
Perivascular inflammation with lymphocytic and microglial infiltration was noted in the brains of 52 deceased COVID-19 patients.
A cross-sectional study identified blood-brain barrier disruption along with increased microglial activation markers and increased B-cell responses against self and non-self antigens in COVID-19.
A study of 24 neuro-COVID patients reported increased intrathecal immunoglobulin, neopterin, and neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels.
The ApoE rs429358 polymorphism (ApoE4 allele) was associated with an increased risk of COVID-19 infection.
Elevated ApoE4 levels were reported to reflect blood-brain barrier disruption and predict cognitive decline.
SARS-CoV-2 envelope protein induced inflammatory cytokine production from mouse bone-marrow-derived macrophages via TLR2 activation, independent of viral entry.
Microglial activation was significantly higher in the brain stem of COVID-19 cases than in non-COVID cases, including in COVID-19 cases without dementia.

Mast cells enhance cellular entry of SARS-CoV-2 through generation of chymase-spike complexes, with chymase converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II to increase ACE2 expression in an autocrine fashion.
Two studies reported elevated serum chymase levels in patients with COVID-19.
Mast-cell-derived histamine was shown to increase SARS-CoV-2 entry into endothelial cells.
Extracellular mitochondrial DNA, which mast cells can release as an alarmin, was significantly elevated in COVID-19 patients.
The authors previously showed elevated IL-18 in the serum of patients with COVID-19, and noted IL-18 remains elevated longer than other cytokines in inflammatory and autoimmune disorders.
Calprotectin (S100A8/A9), associated with microglial activation, was elevated in the serum of patients with COVID-19.
S100β was shown to be associated with COVID-19 severity, promotes microglia activation, and has been linked to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline.
COVID-19 was associated with brain pathology in the UK Biobank and with neuroinflammation involving primarily the chemokine CCL11 in a mouse model.
Increased levels of CCL19 were associated with disease severity in COVID-19 patients.
Clinical trials using IL-6 inhibitors did not show consistent benefit in COVID-19 despite IL-6 being elevated and a possible independent risk factor.
A clinically available IL-1β antagonist significantly improved COVID-19 with secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistocytosis characterized by pancytopenia, hyper-coagulation, and acute kidney injury.
Glucocorticoid treatment reduced mechanical ventilation need and mortality by 20 percent in COVID-19 patients but was associated with longer hospital stays and longer viral clearance time.
A systematic review and meta-analysis showed only a minimal, non-significant trend toward higher hospital discharge rate with glucocorticoid treatment in COVID-19.
An analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials found systemic corticosteroids slightly reduced 30-day mortality in severe COVID-19 patients but showed no benefit up to 120 days.
A multicenter observational cohort study in 55 Spanish ICUs found that early administration of high-dose dexamethasone since symptom onset could be harmful for 90-day mortality.
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs did not improve COVID-19.
The luteolin analogue tetramethoxyluteolin inhibited secretion of IL-1β, TNF-α, CCL2, and CCL5 from human microglia and mast cells.
Two liposomal luteolin formulations (BrainGain and FibroProtek) were successfully used to treat a severe COVID-19 patient with brain fog.
A dietary supplement combining eriodictyol with oleuropein and sulforaphane was recently shown to have strong coronavirus inhibitory properties.
Prevalence estimates of long COVID vary widely across studies, ranging from 4.7% to 89% of infected patients.
Among hospitalized COVID-19 patients, the proportion experiencing long COVID declines over time: 52-89% at 1-2 months, 46-68% around 6 months, and 40-49% around 12 months post-discharge.
In the largest longitudinal cohort of hospitalized patients (Wuhan), 49% of survivors experienced at least one residual symptom at 1 year post-discharge.
Among non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients, an estimated 20-30% experience at least one persistent symptom after 1 month.
The UK ONS Coronavirus Infection Study found around 20% of COVID-19-positive individuals had at least one residual symptom after 5+ weeks, and 10% after 12+ weeks.

ONS reported that long COVID substantially affected wellbeing, exercise ability, and work capacity, with 57% reporting reduced wellbeing, 30% reduced exercise ability, and 39% reduced ability to work.
A meta-analysis of 15 studies found fatigue to be the most common long COVID symptom, with a pooled prevalence of 58%.

A meta-analysis found fatigue, dyspnoea, and anxiety were dominant symptoms 3-12 weeks post-onset, while fatigue and dyspnoea prevalence increased further in the chronic post-COVID stage beyond 12 weeks.
Post-exertional malaise (PEM) in long COVID is characterized by prolonged recovery and symptom deterioration 24-72h after physical/mental exertion, unrelieved by rest.
Multiple CPET studies consistently show reduced aerobic capacity and early attainment of anaerobic threshold in COVID-19 convalescents, regardless of acute disease severity.
Szekely et al. found 75% of non-hospitalized post-COVID patients had chronotropic incompetence at 3 months, with lower peak stroke volume, LVEF, and LV end-diastolic volume than controls.

de Boer et al. found that at peak exercise, long COVID subjects had significantly lower β-oxidation of fatty acids and higher blood lactate than controls, suggesting a premature switch to anaerobic glycolysis and loss of mitochondrial flexibility.
Raman et al. found that 60% of subjects investigated 2-3 months after hospital discharge showed abnormalities in the lungs.
A meta-analysis of studies with ≥3 months follow-up found 39% of long COVID patients had abnormal pulmonary function tests and 31% had impaired lung diffusion capacity.
A German cohort study found 78% of patients (median follow-up 71 days) had cardiovascular pathologies, and cardiac MRI revealed ongoing myocardial inflammation in 60%.
Myocarditis incidence after COVID-19 differs greatly by population studied: 26% in female healthcare workers at 10 weeks, versus only 2.3% in athletes and 0.08% in adolescents.
Montefusco et al. found significantly increased levels of G-CSF, MIP-1β, TNF, IL-1β, IL-4, IL-6, IL-7, IL-8, IL-10, and IL-13 in patients recovering from COVID-19 versus healthy controls at 2 months.
Studies characterizing the immune signature of long COVID patients found elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, CRP, TNF-α, IL-4, and IL-6 levels.
Eight months after index infection, increased concentrations of IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α were significantly correlated with persistent symptoms.
A combination of inflammatory markers including IFN-β and IL-6 had a prognostic accuracy of 79-82% for predicting long COVID.
An Italian study of 551 recovered COVID-19 patients found approximately half were hyperglycaemic at 2 months, despite no prior history of glycaemic abnormalities.
HOMA-IR was significantly higher post-COVID-19 compared with controls and correlated significantly with the inflammatory score.

PET studies detected decreased metabolism in the frontoparietal and temporal lobes of long COVID patients, correlating with cognitive impairment, fatigue and insomnia, and discriminating them from healthy controls.

Chioh et al. detected significantly elevated circulating endothelial cells (a biomarker of vascular injury) in COVID-19 convalescents compared with healthy controls, correlating positively with inflammatory cytokines.
Nandadeva et al. documented decreased brachial artery flow-mediated dilation in young adults with persistent COVID symptoms compared with healthy and asymptomatic controls at ≥4 weeks post-diagnosis.
A maladaptive arterial dilation was significantly associated with fatigue, chest pain and neuro-cognitive deficits in a study of 618 long COVID patients.
Increased peak thrombin, shorter thrombin lag times, elevated d-dimer, and fibrinolysis-resistant microclots indicate a persistent pro-thrombotic state and elevated thromboembolic risk in long COVID.
Gold et al. found that two-thirds of long COVID patients showed antibody evidence of Epstein-Barr virus reactivation.

A case report documented SARS-CoV-2 reactivation and viral persistence in an immunocompromised host readmitted with recurring symptoms after a 4-month symptom-free interval, with sequencing confirming the same evolved strain.

In an Italian cohort of 551 patients assessed two months after COVID-19 onset, roughly half were hyperglycaemic despite no prior glycaemic abnormalities, and HOMA-IR was significantly higher than in controls, correlating with the inflammatory score.
Hypometabolism mediated by mitochondrial dysfunction is described as a common feature of long COVID, potentially driven by viral mitochondrial hijacking and inflammatory diversion of cellular energy.

PET imaging studies found decreased metabolism in the frontoparietal and temporal lobes of long COVID patients, which discriminated them from healthy controls and correlated with cognitive impairment, fatigue and insomnia.

A hypometabolic syndrome with viral-induced shift toward glycolysis and impaired multi-source energy generation, previously documented in ME/CFS, is proposed as analogous to long COVID metabolic changes.

Chioh et al. found significantly elevated circulating endothelial cells (a biomarker of vascular injury) in COVID-19 convalescents compared to healthy controls, correlating with inflammatory cytokines.

A low nitrite/nitrate ratio and decreased endothelium-dependent flow-mediated dilation (FMD) have been consistently reported among COVID-19 convalescents, indicating persistent endothelial dysfunction.

A prospective observational study of occlusion-induced ischemia found long COVID patients had significantly reduced endothelium-mediated dilation of peripheral arteries compared with controls and acute-stage COVID-19 patients.
Nandadeva et al. documented decreased brachial artery FMD in young adults with persistent COVID symptoms compared with healthy and asymptomatic controls at least four weeks after diagnosis.
In a study of 618 long COVID patients, maladaptive arterial dilation was significantly associated with fatigue, chest pain and neurocognitive deficits.

Increased peak thrombin, shorter thrombin lag times, elevated d-dimer, and fibrinolysis-resistant microclots suggest a persistent pro-thrombotic state and increased thromboembolic risk in long COVID patients.
Gold et al. found that two-thirds of investigated long COVID patients showed serological signs of Epstein-Barr virus reactivation.

A case report described SARS-CoV-2 reactivation in an immunocompromised host readmitted with recurrent symptoms after a 4-month symptom-free interval; sequencing showed the same viral strain had persisted and evolved in the host.

A wide range of autoantibodies targeting G-protein coupled receptors, chemokines, cytokines, and tissue/cell structures such as vascular cells, platelets and connective tissue has been detected in acutely ill, convalescent and long COVID patients.

A case report showed that a DNA aptamer drug neutralizing GPCR-targeting autoantibodies significantly improved retinal capillary microcirculation and led to disappearance of long COVID symptoms, supporting a role for vasoactive autoantibodies in microcirculatory impairment.
Seeßle et al. found that patients with antinuclear antibody titres above 1:160 had a significantly higher frequency of long COVID symptoms one year after infection than those with lower titres.
Hyperactive neutrophils (marked by increased calprotectin), pronounced lymphocytopenia, and natural killer cell exhaustion are associated with severe acute COVID-19.
COVID-19 induces a decrease in haemoglobin levels, an increase in red blood cell distribution width, and irreversible damage to the erythrocyte membrane structure.
Real-time deformability cytometry showed decrements in erythrocyte size and deformability in COVID-19 patients that persisted at a median of 7.1 months after hospital discharge.
Significantly low haemoglobin levels have been documented in patients with long COVID.

Memory CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells in long COVID patients showed increased expression of the exhaustion markers PD-1 and TIM-3 for up to 8 months, interpreted as a sign of T-cell exhaustion from SARS-CoV-2 persistence or bystander activation.
Subjects with long COVID exhibited significantly decreased levels of naïve CD4+ T-cells compared with controls.

Acute disease severity influences long-term symptom persistence: at 6 months post-discharge, 84% of patients who required mechanical ventilation had at least one persistent symptom versus 66% (supplemental oxygen) and 69% (no supplemental oxygen); this severity gradient was less prominent at 12 months (52% vs 49% vs 47%).

A case study of an otherwise healthy man showed that cycling exercise mobilizes SARS-CoV-2-specific T-cells and raises neutralizing antibody levels in an intensity-dependent manner, suggesting exercise could enhance clearance of persistent virus.

Consensus guidance recommends that hospital-discharged patients should not resume physical activity if they have a resting heart rate above 100 bpm, blood pressure below 90/60 or above 140/90 mmHg, or blood oxygen saturation at or below 95%.

Multiple publications recommend energy conservation strategies such as pacing and working within individual limits — including dividing activities into smaller tasks and resting before symptoms arise — for managing fatigue-dominant long COVID symptomatology.
Reported prevalence of long COVID after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection ranges from 13.3% to 54% across studies.

Neurological sequelae have been identified in about one third of patients within six months of acute COVID-19 infection, manifesting as motor/sensory deficits, hyposmia, cognitive deficits, and postural tremor.
In a meta-analysis of 257,348 COVID-19 patients, fatigue (32%), dyspnea (25%), and concentration difficulty (22%) were among the most common long COVID symptoms at three to six months.

In a sample of 10,530 long COVID patients at 12-week follow-up, common neurological symptoms included fatigue (37%), brain fog (32%), memory issues (28%), attention disorder (22%), myalgia (28%), anosmia (12%), dysgeusia (10%), and headaches (15%).
About 30% of long COVID patients aged 30-59 reported their neurological symptoms made them severely unable to function at work.
A study of 8325 long COVID patients found non-Hispanic white patients were more likely and non-Hispanic black patients less likely to develop long COVID.
Increased severity of neurological long COVID symptoms is associated with a diminished CD4+ T cell response against the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.
mRNA COVID-19 vaccination elevated the CD4+ T cell response and helped diminish the severity of neurological symptoms in long COVID in the described cohort.

In a study of 117 patients who required high-flow nasal cannula, non-invasive, or invasive mechanical ventilation, 86% reported long COVID symptoms including fatigue, muscle weakness, sleep difficulties, and smell/taste disorders at six-month follow-up.

In a study of 13,638 patients, post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 was associated with increased 12-month mortality risk compared with PCR-negative suspected COVID-19 patients, and greater mortality risk with more severe initial infection.
A systematic review of 989,174 patients found vaccination before acute COVID-19 infection was associated with a reduced risk (RR=0.71) of developing non-neurological long COVID symptoms.
A study found no predisposition of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 polymorphisms (previously linked to COVID-19 severity) to long COVID symptoms in previously hospitalized patients.

There is overwhelming evidence of a lack of SARS-CoV-2 RNA and protein in the CSF of COVID-19 patients with neurological symptoms, in brain tissue at autopsy, and in the choroid plexus of severe disease cases, arguing against validated direct CNS viral invasion.
Persistent inflammation marked by elevated IL-6, type I interferon, and CXCL10 within the olfactory epithelium contributes to long-standing anosmia after SARS-CoV-2 invasion of supportive cells.

Co-expression analysis in SARS-CoV-2-infected human intestinal organoids showed ACE2 co-regulation with dopa-decarboxylase (DDC) and dopamine metabolic pathway genes, suggesting brain-gut axis dysfunction as a mechanism in neurological long COVID.
In a retrospective study, 25% of patients with severe acute COVID-19 had increased EA-IgG and VCA-IgG titers, proxy markers for EBV reactivation.
Two thirds of patients with symptoms 90 days after primary SARS-CoV-2 infection were positive for EBV reactivation, and higher long COVID symptom frequency correlated with increased EA-IgG titers.
In a longitudinal study of 309 patients, EBV viremia was one of four main risk factors for developing long COVID, alongside type II diabetes, SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia, and autoantibody formation.

In a cross-sectional study of 215 long COVID patients, elevated antibody reactivity to EBV gp23, gp42, and EA-D correlated with IL-4 and IL-6 producing CD4+ T cells, along with similar reactivity to VZV glycoprotein E.
An RCT in high-risk non-hospitalized adults with acute COVID-19 showed Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) rapidly reduced viral load by day five and reduced mortality and hospitalization.

In a preprint study, patients treated with oral nirmatrelvir within five days of a positive COVID-19 test (N=9217) had substantially lower risk of developing long COVID symptoms compared with untreated controls (N=47,123).

In a retrospective study of 88 COVID-19 patients with EBV reactivation, ganciclovir treatment was associated with significantly higher 28-day survival than matched controls, though neurological symptoms were not assessed.

Patients treated with oral nirmatrelvir within five days of a positive COVID-19 test had substantially lower risk of developing long COVID symptoms compared with untreated patients in a large preprint cohort study.

In a retrospective study of COVID-19 patients with EBV reactivation, those treated with ganciclovir had significantly higher 28-day survival than matched controls, though neurological symptoms were not assessed.

The active metabolite of cannabidiol, 7-OH-CBD, blocks SARS-CoV-2 replication and downregulates ACE2 and TMPRSS2, suggesting potential antiviral and neuroprotective utility in long COVID, currently being tested in a phase 2 trial.
In an RCT of twice-weekly intranasal protamine insulin gel foam for post-infectious hyposmia, olfaction scores at four weeks were significantly better in the insulin-treated group than placebo.

In 40 patients with post-COVID-19 anosmia randomized to intranasal insulin film vs saline, the treatment group showed significantly greater odor detection at 30 minutes post-administration compared with baseline and placebo.

An RCT of mometasone nasal spray plus olfactory training versus olfactory training alone in 100 COVID-19 patients with post-infection anosmia found no significant difference in time to complete smell recovery between groups.
Fluticasone nasal spray produced significant improvement in smell scores by day five compared with baseline, versus no intervention.

Flow cytometry of peripheral blood from long COVID patients showed elevated expansion of non-classical (CD14dimCD16+) and intermediate (CD14+CD16+) monocytes up to 15 months post-infection compared with healthy controls.
Severe long COVID patients were found to have increased levels of MSR1, indicating a high degree of peripheral macrophage activation that can disrupt the blood-brain barrier.

CD8+ memory T cells in long COVID serum showed increased number and cytolytic granule expression but limited breadth and reduced antigen-specific activation, a profile strongly associated with depression and decreased executive function.

One immunophenotyping study found that persistent T cell changes and neurological deficits were associated with age rather than ongoing illness or fatigue, contradicting the T cell exhaustion hypothesis.
Persistent ANA autoreactivity has been linked with long-term symptoms of dyspnea, fatigue, and brain fog in long COVID.

Anti-ACE2 antibodies, associated with fatigue and myelitis, can elicit an abnormal renin-angiotensin response, cause malignant hypertension-related ischemia, and upregulate thrombo-inflammatory pathways.

A cross-sectional exploratory study found total autoantibody levels were not elevated in the extracellular proteome of long COVID patients compared with convalescent controls, despite an array of autoantigen reactivities.

RSLV-132, an RNase fusion protein that digests RNA in autoantibodies/immune complexes, decreased fatigue in Sjogren's syndrome patients compared with placebo, and is being tested in a phase 2 trial for long COVID.
Low-dose naltrexone has shown promise in improving self-reported brain fog and fatigue in long COVID patients, with an RCT planned to further clarify efficacy.

Combined histamine H1/H2 receptor blockade (antihistamine treatment) was associated with significant symptomatic improvement in long COVID patients according to a recent observational study, drawing on parallels with MCAS.
Increased levels of ezrin in long COVID patients are associated with reactive astrocytes that upregulate NF-κB, contributing to endothelial cell death and increased extracellular glutamate.

Patients with neurological symptoms of long COVID have increased levels of CCL11, a chemokine that recruits eosinophils, crosses the BBB, induces microglial migration, disrupts hippocampal neurogenesis, and causes cognitive dysfunction such as brain fog.

The most severe long COVID patients exhibited increased levels of TNFRSF11B, an osteoblast-secreted decoy receptor implicated in neuroinflammatory processes and microglia overstimulation, with a symptom profile resembling cancer therapy-related cognitive impairment.

Fibrinolysis-resistant, large anomalous amyloid microclots up to 200 µm, formed via spike protein binding to fibrinogen, are present in the serum of long COVID patients and can occlude microcapillaries, reducing cerebral blood flow.
α2-antiplasmin, a potent plasmin inhibitor, was significantly elevated in microclots from long COVID patients compared with acute COVID patients, likely contributing to fibrinolysis resistance.

Prothrombotic antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin, anti-beta2 glycoprotein I, anti-phosphatidylserine/prothrombin) were found in 52% of serum samples from patients hospitalized with acute COVID-19.

Plasma markers of endotheliopathy, including VWF antigen, VWF propeptide, soluble thrombomodulin, and endothelial colony-forming cells, remained elevated in a long COVID cohort assessed at a median of 68 days post-infection.
Extracted SARS-CoV-2 spike protein increased blood-brain barrier permeability in microfluidic models, likely due to endotheliopathy from a pro-inflammatory response.
Persistent capillary rarefaction and perivascular leakage of fibrinogen were observed in autopsy and sublingual video microscopy studies of long COVID patients, indicating microvascular injury.

Prominent hypometabolism was observed in the bilateral pons, medulla, and cerebellum of long COVID patients, in regions with the most pronounced BBB dysfunction and pathological abnormalities, potentially explaining similarities to brainstem-related symptoms in ME/CFS.

Among twice-vaccinated hospital employees with a post-vaccination SARS-CoV-2 infection, 31.5% reported at least one persistent symptom eight weeks or more after the acute infection, meeting the study's definition of PASC/long COVID.
All participants with pre-existing chronic lung disorder (obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma) were in the PASC group, a significant association.
A higher proportion of participants with BMI>25 was seen in the PASC group compared to those without PASC.
Reporting more than five symptoms during acute infection was associated with a roughly four-fold increased risk of developing PASC, after adjusting for gender and vaccine type.
The mean number of symptoms during acute infection was significantly higher in participants who later reported PASC compared to those who did not.
The self-reported severity grade of symptoms during acute infection was significantly higher in participants who subsequently developed PASC.
Fatigue during the acute infection was significantly more common among participants who later reported PASC.
Shortness of breath during acute infection was significantly more frequent in participants who later reported PASC.
Headache or concentration deficit during acute infection was significantly more common among those who later reported PASC.
Dysgeusia and dysosmia during acute infection were significantly more common among those who later reported PASC.
Female gender was not significantly associated with increased risk of PASC.
No significant difference was found between BNT162b2 and ChAdOx1-S vaccine recipients in the risk or severity of PASC.
No association was found between SARS-CoV-2 genotype/variant and the risk of developing PASC, though the stratified groups were small.
Among participants with PASC, the number and subjectively estimated severity of symptoms positively correlated both at the time of acute infection and at follow-up.
Overall symptom severity score declined from the time of acute infection diagnosis to the eight-week follow-up among symptomatic participants.
The total reported number of SARS-CoV-2 infection-related symptoms declined markedly from acute infection to the eight-week follow-up.
Anti-spike antibody titers, measured on a voluntary/unsystematic basis, were comparable between participants with and without PASC.
Hair loss or exanthema was not reported at all during acute infection but appeared as a new symptom in a subset of participants at the eight-week follow-up.
The most significant differentiating cluster between PASC patients and SARS-CoV-2 positive controls was the R00-R99 category of nonspecific symptoms, signs, and abnormal clinical findings.
Within the R00-R09 branch, dyspnea, pain in throat and chest, and unspecified chest pain were the three most significant cuts associated with PASC.
Dysautonomia was identified as a significant PASC-related feature in the respiratory-adjacent portion of the tree-scan analysis comparing PASC patients to COVID-positive controls.
New-onset asthma emerged as a specific, strongly-signaled diagnosis associated with PASC rather than a cluster of nonspecific symptoms.

Generalized and diverse pain features, including myalgia, joint pain, knee/leg/hip pain, upper abdominal/epigastric pain, and generalized soft tissue pain, were key musculoskeletal findings enriched in PASC.
Neurologic diagnoses including headache and migraine were recurring, enriched signals in children with PASC.
Sleep disturbances and specifically sleep apnea were significant PASC-associated features, consistent with prior reports.
Endocrine findings enriched in PASC included nutritional deficiencies, volume depletion or fluid overload, and obesity, which the authors note have not been previously detailed as PASC features.

Gastrointestinal findings such as diseases of esophagus, stomach, and duodenum, and psychological findings such as reaction to severe stress and adjustment disorders, were enriched primarily at nonspecific hierarchy levels in PASC patients.
Psychological findings including reaction to severe stress and adjustment disorders were enriched in PASC compared to controls.
In contrast to prior work, this study did not identify new-onset diabetes as a persistent long-term complication of COVID-19 in the pediatric PASC cohort.
Cytomegaloviral disease diagnoses were significantly enriched in PASC patients compared to SARS-CoV-2 test-negative controls, possibly reflecting viral reactivation.

Diagnoses of D89 (other disorders involving the immune mechanism, not elsewhere classified) were enriched in PASC patients compared to SARS-CoV-2 negative controls, suggesting possible post-infectious autoimmunity.
Skin conditions such as dermatitis and eczema were significantly enriched in PASC patients compared to SARS-CoV-2 negative controls.

Additional cardiovascular and systemic features including acute myocarditis, hypotension, fever, nasal congestion, epistaxis, and tachycardia were enriched among PASC patients compared to SARS-CoV-2 test-negative patients, and pulmonary embolism/edema were also enriched, potentially reflecting follow-up care from acute infection.
Hematuria and nonspecific urinary system symptoms were detected as novel signals associated with PASC not previously reported.

In a sensitivity analysis stratified by pandemic era, pre-omicron PASC cases were enriched for metabolic, immunologic, and circulatory (hypotension) diagnoses and smell/taste disturbances, while the omicron era was enriched for urinary system conditions (hematuria) and migraine diagnoses.
The proportion of teenage long COVID patients who had moderate-to-severe acute COVID-19 illness was significantly lower than in adults.
Fatigue was the most frequent chief complaint in both teenagers and adults with long COVID, with no significant difference in prevalence between groups.
Headache was significantly more frequent as a chief complaint in teenage long COVID patients compared to adults.
Dysosmia and dysgeusia, which were common symptoms in teenagers during the Delta variant phase, almost disappeared during the Omicron variant phase.
Fatigue and headache became the predominant symptoms among teenage long COVID patients during the Omicron variant phase.
More than half of school-enrolled teenage long COVID patients were unable to attend school.
Among teenage long COVID patients who were absent from school, fatigue, headache, and insomnia were the most common symptoms.
The number of COVID-19 vaccinations received was not significantly associated with school absenteeism among teenage long COVID patients.
Teenagers comprised 11.9% (54/452) of all long COVID patients evaluated at the clinic, lower than the wide range of pediatric long COVID prevalence estimates reported previously.
Insomnia and low-grade fever, along with headache, were noted as characteristic symptoms distinguishing teenage long COVID patients from adults.
Fatigue/weakness was the most prevalent long COVID-19 symptom, reported by 469 of 471 (99.57%) convalescents.
Dyspnea and myalgia were nearly as prevalent as fatigue, each reported by 99.36% of patients.
Women convalescents had higher LVEF and exercise capacity, and better spirometric and chest imaging results, than men.
A greater percentage of women than men had hypertension prior to COVID-19.
Severity of fatigue on the Borg scale correlated positively with age, whereas dyspnea severity did not.
Neither fatigue nor dyspnea severity was related to left ventricular ejection fraction.
Patients with depressed mood/sleep disturbances reported significantly more long COVID-19 symptoms overall, including more concentration disorders and dizziness, than those without.

Myalgia, palpitations, unstable blood pressure, concentration disorders/memory deterioration, depressed mood/sleep disturbances, hair loss, and dizziness were all significantly more common in women than men.
Women reported a higher average number of long COVID-19 symptoms than men and rated their fatigue as more severe, despite men having worse exercise capacity and spirometry.
Cough and loss/impaired smell were significantly more common in patients with milder acute COVID-19 (Stage I) than in those with severe/critical disease.
Most long COVID-19 symptoms and overall symptom/dyspnea/fatigue severity did not differ according to acute COVID-19 severity or hospitalization status.
Dyspnea severity was inversely correlated with percent-predicted FVC and FEV1.
Fatigue severity was inversely correlated with percent-predicted FVC and FEV1.
Fatigue and dyspnea severity were both strongly and inversely correlated with 6-minute walk test distance.
Cough was more common and concentration disorders/memory deterioration were less common in patients further out (>24 weeks) from acute COVID-19 compared with those at 12-24 weeks.
One-third of long COVID-19 convalescents had exercise capacity reduced below the lower limit of normal on the 6-minute walk test.
Lung parenchymal abnormalities or interstitial fibrosis were seen on follow-up chest X-rays/CT in a majority of the study cohort.

Citing prior work (Ortelli et al.), the authors note that interleukin-6-related hyper-inflammation may downregulate GABA receptors and contribute to central neuromotor and cognitive fatigue in long COVID-19.
Hypozincemia (serum zinc <70 μg/dL) was detected in 43 of 194 (22.2%) long COVID patients.
Patients with hypozincemia were significantly older than normozincemic long COVID patients (median 50 vs 39 years).
Mean serum zinc concentrations did not differ significantly between male and female long COVID patients.
Serum zinc concentrations significantly decreased with age in male long COVID patients.
No significant correlation was found between age and serum zinc concentration in female long COVID patients.
Serum zinc levels in long COVID patients did not differ significantly according to the severity of the acute phase of COVID-19, overall or by sex.
Serum zinc level was not significantly correlated with serum C-reactive protein or erythrocyte sedimentation rate in long COVID patients.
General fatigue was the most frequent long COVID symptom among hypozincemic patients, occurring in 56.3% of male and 29.6% of female patients.
Male hypozincemic long COVID patients frequently reported dysosmia, headache, dizziness, dyspnea and dyssomnia.
Female hypozincemic long COVID patients frequently reported headache, dysosmia, dysgeusia and dyssomnia.

Prescription of the depression medications quetiapine and mirtazapine was significantly elevated in the post-acute period after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Asthma/COPD medications and cough suppressants showed significantly elevated post-acute use, consistent with elevated respiratory PASC diagnoses; fluticasone, dextromethorphan, benzonatate, and guaifenesin were also replicated in the OneFlorida+ cohort.
Anticoagulant medications and the beta-blocker metoprolol showed significantly elevated post-acute prescription, corresponding to elevated cardiovascular PASC diagnoses.
Ferric cation (iron supplement) use was elevated post-acutely, consistent with elevated anemia diagnoses after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Use of glucagon, insulin, and metformin was significantly elevated post-acutely, consistent with elevated new-onset diabetes mellitus diagnoses after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Use of magnesium hydroxide, esomeprazole, and simethicone was elevated post-acutely, consistent with elevated GI PASC diagnoses (constipation, abdominal pain).

The OneFlorida+ cohort replicated far fewer PASC diagnoses (11, including U099/B948) and medications (9) than the INSIGHT cohort (38 diagnoses, 59 medications) using identical screening criteria, revealing substantial cross-population heterogeneity of PASC.

Ten diagnostic conditions (dementia, hair loss, pressure ulcers, pulmonary fibrosis, dyspnea, pulmonary embolism, chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, malaise, fatigue) plus U099/B948 were consistently replicated as PASC conditions across both the INSIGHT and OneFlorida+ cohorts.

The excess burden of dyspnea and other respiratory/cardiovascular PASC conditions increased with acute infection severity, being substantially higher among patients who were hospitalized than those managed as outpatients.

The pattern of PASC excess burden differed by age: dyspnea, chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, malaise and fatigue dominated in patients under 65, while dyspnea, pulmonary fibrosis, dementia, pressure ulcers, pulmonary embolism, malaise and fatigue dominated in patients 65 and older, with all of these conditions showing higher burden in the older group in both cohorts.

Male patients had a higher excess burden of dyspnea, pulmonary fibrosis, chest pain, malaise and fatigue, while female patients had a higher excess burden of hair loss, consistently across both cohorts.
The excess burden of dyspnea after SARS-CoV-2 infection increased with acute illness severity, from 40.1 excess cases per 1000 in outpatients to 89.9 per 1000 in hospitalized patients.

Excess burden of pulmonary fibrosis, dementia, hair loss, pulmonary embolism, chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, and malaise/fatigue all increased with severity of acute infection from outpatient to inpatient settings, and this trend replicated in OneFlorida+.
The excess burden of the post-COVID-19 condition codes U099/B948 increased from 3.9 per 1000 in outpatients to 14.2 per 1000 in hospitalized patients.

Patients aged 65 and older had higher excess burden of dyspnea, pulmonary fibrosis, dementia, pressure ulcers, pulmonary embolism, malaise, and fatigue than younger patients in both cohorts, while dyspnea, chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, malaise, and fatigue had the highest excess burden in patients under 65.
Male patients had higher excess burden of dyspnea, pulmonary fibrosis, chest pain, malaise, and fatigue, whereas hair loss showed higher excess burden in female patients, in both cohorts.
Black patients had a higher excess burden of chest pain than White patients in the INSIGHT cohort, and a higher excess burden of pressure ulcers in the OneFlorida+ cohort.

Patients with pre-existing coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, or chronic pulmonary disease had higher excess burdens of pulmonary fibrosis, malaise, and fatigue after SARS-CoV-2 infection than those without such comorbidities.

Even patients without any documented baseline comorbidities ("healthy" patients) showed incident excess burden of dyspnea, pulmonary fibrosis, chest pain, and, in the INSIGHT cohort, diabetes after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

PASC burden varied by pandemic wave/variant, with the first two waves contributing most significantly to PASC burden in INSIGHT and all three waves contributing in OneFlorida+, while dyspnea remained consistently significant across all waves and both cohorts.

Negative outcome controls (clinical outcomes with no expected biological link to SARS-CoV-2, such as injury from external causes and neoplasm-related outcomes) showed no significant association with SARS-CoV-2 infection, supporting that residual confounding did not drive the main findings.

Using the less-stringent Benjamini-Yekutieli false discovery rate correction instead of Bonferroni, seven additional potential PASC diagnoses were identified in the INSIGHT cohort: cerebral ischemia, acute myocardial infarction, pulmonary heart disease, myocarditis, nausea, gastro-esophageal reflux disease, and genitourinary problems.
When the minimum case-count threshold (100 cases) was removed in a sensitivity analysis, foot drop emerged as an additional potential PASC condition in the INSIGHT cohort.

Adjusting for baseline SARS-CoV-2 vaccination status had little impact on adjusted hazard ratios, largely because most patients were infected before vaccines were widely available and over 90% had no recorded vaccination.

Sensitivity analyses using cubic B-spline modeling of index day, gradient boosting decision tree propensity score modeling, and downsampling of the INSIGHT cohort to match OneFlorida+ sample size all produced consistent adjusted hazard ratios and the same set of replicated PASC conditions as the primary analysis.

Compared with a prior VA veteran-population study (mostly male), this study found several new PASC conditions not previously reported, including dementia, pulmonary fibrosis, and pulmonary embolism, and generally larger excess burdens per 1000 patients (e.g., hair loss, dyspnea, chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, malaise/fatigue).

Comparison with Cohen et al.'s Medicare Advantage claims study in patients aged ≥65 showed broadly comparable excess burdens per 1000 for dementia, pulmonary embolism, abnormal heartbeat, and malaise/fatigue across the three datasets.

Hospitalized patients showed greater excess numbers of potential PASC diagnoses and medications compared to non-hospitalized patients in both cohorts, particularly for respiratory conditions, and this pattern was consistent with prior studies.
Nearly all participants (95%) described fatigue as a persistent and disabling PASC symptom in qualitative interviews.
All 19 participants (100%) reported that acute COVID-19 infection and resulting PASC disrupted their daily routines, work, or relationships.
68% of participants reported cognitive symptoms such as memory lapses, slowed thinking, and concentration problems ("brain fog") related to PASC.
79% of participants reported changes in sleep pattern following COVID-19 infection.
Participants reported high levels of depressive symptoms on the CESD, with the group mean exceeding the commonly used clinical cutoff of 16.
Participants reported low health-related quality of life on the SF-36 general health subscale, consistent with prior studies of post-COVID populations.

Interview-derived reports of cognitive difficulty were inversely correlated with SF-36 general health scores and positively correlated with Cognitive Failures Questionnaire scores and PSQI sleep quality scores.
Interview-derived reports of emotional upset correlated positively with questionnaire measures of cognitive problems (CFQ), fatigue (PROMIS Fatigue), and sleep disturbance (PSQI).
Interview-reported sleep disturbance was significantly correlated with Chalder Fatigue Scale scores, and showed moderate (non-significant) correlations with CFQ, PROMIS Sleep Disturbance, and PSQI.
Interview-reported physical symptoms (e.g., cough, shortness of breath, headache) were significantly correlated with PROMIS Sleep Disturbance and PROMIS Cognition scores.
A change in participants' sense of self was significantly correlated with depression (CESD) and fatigue (Chalder) scores.
On average, participants had experienced persistent PASC symptoms for nearly 11 months at the time of screening.

Some older participants attributed their post-COVID cognitive difficulties to normal aging rather than to PASC, which the authors note may cause older adults to under-seek treatment for treatable symptoms.
During acute infection, the most common symptoms reported were fever, fatigue, taste disorder, olfactory disturbance, headache, shortness of breath, and sore throat.
Early administration of anticoagulants significantly reduced coagulopathy-associated complications, such as ischemic stroke, in COVID-19 patients.
Neuropilin-1 was identified as an alternative SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor that is probably more relevant than ACE-2 in the CNS, given the very low ACE-2 expression in many brain regions.
The SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro/Nsp5) cleaves NEMO, disrupting NF-κB signaling, and via RIPK3-dependent necroptosis leads to depletion of endothelial cells forming 'string vessels' in the brain.

Brain autopsies from 11 COVID-19 deceased patients showed subgenomic viral RNA (indicative of replication) in cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus and dura mater, with some patients retaining detectable low-level viral RNA up to 239 days after disease onset.

SARS-CoV-2-infected choroid plexus organoids showed upregulated Type I interferon, inflammation and stress-response genes, downregulated ion-transport genes, and a threefold increase in cell death compared to uninfected controls.

Astrocytes, despite low ACE-2/TMPRSS2 expression, are permissive to SARS-CoV-2 via neuropilin-1, harbor more viral N/S protein than neuronal precursor cells or neurons, upregulate Type I interferon/ISGs and ion-transport genes, and induce non-autonomous death of neighboring neurons.
SARS-CoV-2-infected hamster astrocytes showed altered carbon/TCA-cycle protein expression with intense glutamine consumption, indicating glutamine metabolism favors viral replication.
Pharmacological blockade of glutaminolysis with L-DON significantly reduced SARS-CoV-2 viral replication in infected cells.
Plasma metabolomics demonstrated that glutamine and glutamate metabolism differentially clustered mild versus severe COVID-19 patients.

Microglia-like cells cocultured with SARS-CoV-2-infected brain organoids showed increased activation markers CD68 and TREM2 and synapse-elimination molecules C3 and C3AR1, with PSD95+ puncta engulfment indicating synaptic pruning.

Mild pulmonary-restricted SARS-CoV-2 infection in mice caused robust microglial activation and elevated CSF cytokines without brain neuroinvasion, with white-matter-predominant microglial activation, reduced OPCs correlating with higher CCL11, and impaired hippocampal neurogenesis, findings confirmed in human brain tissue.
In a hamster model and human samples, hippocampal immunofluorescence for IBA-1 and IL-1 showed significant microglial activation and reduced hippocampal neurogenesis, corroborating mouse findings.

SARS-CoV-2-infected rhesus monkeys showed pyknotic nuclei and vacuolization predominantly in cerebellar Purkinje cells, with confirmed apoptosis by cleaved caspase-3 staining, alongside intense microglial activation.

In SARS-CoV-2-infected monkeys, neurons were the most infected brain cell type followed by astrocytes and microglia, with neuroinflammation, astrogliosis and microglial activation more prominent in aged than young animals despite no difference in overall infection by age.

Around 40% of astrocytes in infected human epileptic-resection brain slices were positive for viral E and N proteins without cell death, and knockdown of the alternative entry receptor CD147 significantly reduced infection.
Serum levels of GFAP and neurofilament light (NFL), markers of astrocytic and neuronal degeneration respectively, were increased in COVID-19 patients.

A case report of a 29-year-old patient with mild COVID-19 but impaired cognition and short-term memory loss showed, via magnetic resonance spectroscopy, reduced glutamate, glutamine and N-acetylaspartate in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which normalized alongside symptom resolution three months later.

Among 51 patients who recovered from mild or severe COVID-19, severe-disease patients showed decreased cortical thickness and reduced sub-cortical (putamen, thalamus) volumes at 3 months, plus significantly decreased gray matter blood flow compared to mild patients, despite absence of neurological symptoms.
Autoantibodies against type I interferon, mainly anti-IFN-α, have been described in COVID-19 patients and correlate with increased likelihood of severe disease.
Autoantibodies including anti-NMDAR and anti-myelin antibodies were detected in the cerebrospinal fluid of COVID-19 patients presenting with acute encephalopathies.

Comparison of B cell receptor clonality between blood and CSF of COVID-19 patients revealed distinct, locally expanded intrathecal B cell clones producing antibodies reactive to murine brain tissue; a PhIP-seq screen identified two candidate CSF autoantigens, IFT88 and THAP3, though the study was limited to 5 patients.

Immune profiling of over 200 long-COVID patients with chronic fatigue, memory loss and confusion revealed increased circulating non-classical monocytes (CD14lowCD16+), increased IL-4+IL-6+ double-positive CD4/CD8 T lymphocytes, an approximately 50% reduction in circulating cortisol, and elevated antibody reactivity to Epstein-Barr virus envelope glycoproteins gp42 and gp350, without increased self-antigen autoreactivity or altered EBV serology.
Neuropilin-1 acts as an alternative SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor that is likely more relevant than ACE-2 in the CNS, where ACE-2 expression is very low.

CD4+ lymphocytes can become infected with SARS-CoV-2 during crosstalk with alveolar macrophages in an ACE-2-independent fashion, raising the possibility that infected lymphocytes could ferry virus to the brain.
