Microglia can be infected by SARS-CoV-2, and niches of highly activated microglia adjacent to CD8+ T lymphocytes are abundant in the brains of COVID-19 patients, often near sites of blood-brain-barrier disruption.

In 3D neural-perivascular assembloids, pericyte-like cells and astrocytes were productively infected by SARS-CoV-2, and organoids containing pericyte-like cells showed markedly higher infection, increased non-autonomous neuronal death, and a robust type I interferon response compared with standard organoids lacking vasculature-like structures.

In rhesus monkeys, the olfactory epithelium is the primary site of SARS-CoV-2 infection and a likely route of viral spread to the brain, accompanied by increased innate immune cytokine secretion and robust microglial activation.
Viral genome was detected in the eyes of infected mice and hamsters and was further confirmed in human cornea and conjunctiva, suggesting an additional site of viral presence/exposure.

Unlike other infected cell types that lost cellular interactions after SARS-CoV-2 infection, choroid plexus cells gained interactions related to extracellular matrix, barrier maintenance, and solute homeostasis, alongside modulation of VEGF expression important for choroid plexus and BBB integrity.

SARS-CoV-2 infected brain organoids showed rapid modulation of HIF-1α along with altered carbon metabolism, TCA cycle, and pyruvate metabolism gene expression, consistent with prior findings in human monocytes.

A PhIP-seq screen of over 730,000 peptides against CSF autoantibodies from COVID-19 patients identified two candidate brain antigen targets, IFT88 and THAP3, though only five patients were studied and the functional roles of these proteins in the brain remain poorly understood.
Aged rhesus monkeys infected with SARS-CoV-2 exhibited more prominent neuroinflammation, astrogliosis, and microglial activation compared with young infected animals.
Knockdown of CD147, an alternative SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor, significantly reduced astrocyte infection in human brain slice cultures.
Autoantibodies against interferon-alpha have been correlated with an increased likelihood of developing severe COVID-19.
Plasma metabolomics showed that glutamine and glutamate metabolism differed between mild and severe COVID-19 patients, allowing the two groups to be differentially clustered.

In SARS-CoV-2-infected rhesus monkeys, neurons were unexpectedly the most infected brain cell type in the cortex, followed by astrocytes and microglia, with no difference in infection rates between young and aged animals.
Long COVID is estimated to affect approximately 20% of people after SARS-CoV-2 infection, across all age ranges and infection severities.
Fatigue, postexertional malaise, and respiratory and cardiac symptoms are commonly described features of long COVID.
Neurological symptoms including cognitive changes, sensory disturbances, headaches, and dysautonomia are commonly reported in long COVID.
Proposed underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of long COVID include immune dysregulation, autoimmunity, persistent viral reservoirs, and microvascular dysfunction.
There are currently no diagnostic tests for long COVID, so evaluation should focus on identifying reversible or treatable causes of symptoms.
No specific treatments for long COVID currently exist; management relies on a multimodal, symptom-directed approach, and many patients improve over time.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom among long COVID outpatients at initial visit, occurring in 59.8% of patients.
Anxiety was the second most common symptom reported at initial visit, occurring in 42.3% of long COVID patients.
Smell disorders were reported by 41.9% of patients overall, and were the defining symptom of cluster 5 as a strong/major symptom in 26.6% of all patients.

Cluster analysis of 23 symptom variables classified long COVID outpatients into five distinct symptom clusters: fatigue alone, fatigue with respiratory/cardiac symptoms, fatigue with psychological symptoms, hair loss only, and taste/smell disorders only.

11-12.2% of patients in fatigue-predominant clusters 1-3 met criteria for POTS or clinical POTS on Schellong testing, with cluster 2 (fatigue with strong physical symptoms) showing the highest proportion (33%) of clinical POTS.
Cases in cluster 2 (fatigue with dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, forgetfulness) were more frequently complicated with clinical POTS than other clusters, based on chi-square/residual analysis.

Cluster 3, characterized by fatigue plus psychological symptoms (headache, insomnia, anxiety, loss of motivation, depressed mood, forgetfulness), had the highest percentage of patients taking leaves of absence from work or school among all clusters.

Employment status differed by cluster: patients in clusters 2 and 3 (fatigue-predominant with physical or psychological symptoms) were more likely to take leaves of absence, whereas patients in clusters 4 and 5 (hair loss; taste/smell disorders) were more likely to continue working.

In cluster 4 (hair loss predominant), performance status (fatigue severity) was high (median 6) in the acute phase but resolved to a median of 0 by the initial hospital visit, while hair loss persisted, consistent with telogen effluvium occurring roughly 2 months after infection onset.
The median age in cluster 4 (hair loss) was higher than in other clusters, and clusters 2 and 4 had a higher proportion of female patients, while BMI did not differ significantly between clusters.

Cluster 5 patients (taste and smell disorders only) had lower rates of acute-phase pneumonia complications and comorbidities, a longer time from symptom onset to hospital visit, and low fatigue severity (PS 2 at onset, 0 at visit), suggesting a distinct pathogenic mechanism from other symptom clusters.
Overall, 23.7% of the 497 long COVID outpatients had pneumonia complications during the acute phase of COVID-19 infection.
Pneumonia complications in the acute phase were more common among patients in cluster 2 and less common among those in cluster 5; comorbidities were also less common in cluster 5.

Post-hospitalization Neuro-PASC (PNP) patients were on average a decade older, more ethnically diverse, and had higher rates of hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, lung disease, and cardiovascular disease than non-hospitalized Neuro-PASC (NNP) patients.
Non-hospitalized Neuro-PASC (NNP) patients had a higher prevalence of pre-existing depression/anxiety than post-hospitalization patients.
Brain fog was the most common neurologic symptom overall, followed by headache, anosmia, dysgeusia, and dizziness among all Neuro-PASC patients.
Non-hospitalized Neuro-PASC patients more frequently reported anosmia, dysgeusia, and myalgia than post-hospitalization patients.
Shortness of breath and chest pain were significantly more common non-neurologic symptoms in post-hospitalization Neuro-PASC patients than in non-hospitalized patients.
Self-reported dysautonomia (variation of heart rate and blood pressure) was reported in about a third of Neuro-PASC patients overall.

Post-hospitalization Neuro-PASC patients had a higher prevalence of an abnormal neurologic examination, including memory, attention, sensory, gait, and motor dysfunction, than non-hospitalized patients.
Markers of inflammation (ESR, CRP, D-dimer, and ferritin) were more frequently abnormal in post-hospitalization Neuro-PASC patients than in non-hospitalized patients.

There were no significant differences between PNP and NNP groups in the frequency of abnormalities found on brain CT, brain/spinal MRI, MR vessel wall imaging, EMG, EEG, CSF analysis, and tilt table testing.

Both PNP and NNP patients showed significantly worse quality of life scores (cognition, fatigue, sleep, anxiety, depression) than the US normative population, with no significant difference between the two groups.

PNP patients performed significantly worse than NNP patients and a US normative population on NIH Toolbox tests of processing speed, attention, and working memory, whereas NNP patients only performed worse on attention compared to normative expectations.
Principal component analysis of PROMIS quality-of-life domains showed largely overlapping phenotypes between PNP and NNP, though NNP had a somewhat broader distribution.
Principal component analysis of NIH Toolbox cognitive tests showed substantial overlap between PNP and NNP groups but suggested NNP was skewed toward less severe cognitive phenotypes than PNP.
Time from symptom onset was not associated with subjective impression of recovery in either the PNP or NNP group.

In the NNP group, subjective impressions of recovery, cognitive function, and fatigue were significantly correlated with objective cognitive test results, but this correlation was not seen in the PNP group, suggesting reduced insight into cognitive deficits among post-hospitalization patients.
Fibromyalgia patients showed significantly higher trapezius intramuscular pressure than rheumatic disease controls, suggesting pressure abnormality contributes to diffuse muscle pain.
A study found elevated muscle damping (reflecting increased muscle tension) in all 14 sampled fibromyalgia patients, with mean values more than double and maxima more than triple those of controls.
A biopsy study found significantly higher peripheral fibroblast TGF-β gene expression in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.
Skin biopsies from fibromyalgia patients showed elevated IL-1β in 38% of patients, undetectable in healthy controls.
Skin biopsies from fibromyalgia patients showed elevated IL-6 in 27% of patients, undetectable in healthy controls.
Skin biopsies from fibromyalgia patients showed elevated TNF-α in 32% of patients, undetectable in healthy controls.
A microdialysis study found significantly higher interstitial lactate, glutamate, and pyruvate concentrations in fibromyalgia patients.
Dialysate lactate increased in response to acetylcholine stimulation in fibromyalgia patients.
Fibromyalgia patients had significantly lower intramuscular collagen, which may lower the threshold for muscle micro-injury.
Fibromyalgia patients have decreased peripheral blood flow, suggesting cardiovascular functional disturbance.
SARS-CoV-2 induces adipocyte-to-myofibroblast trans-differentiation.
SARS-CoV-2 infection increases mRNA levels of ACE2, TGF-β1, CTGF, and fibronectin-1, key drivers of lung fibrosis.

An autopsy series found inflammatory myositis features more pronounced in skeletal muscle than cardiac muscle after COVID-19, with low/undetectable viral load suggesting an immune-mediated rather than direct viral myopathy.
An autopsy study found muscle atrophy, necrotizing myopathy, and myositis in psoas muscle of COVID-19 deaths with no evidence of direct viral invasion, implicating cytokine-mediated damage.

A case report of a long COVID patient meeting fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria (Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire score 88) had good short-term relief with wet/dry needling; pain migrated to extremities during repeated sessions but went into remission after further needling at 12 months.
In an online survey of 100 long COVID-19 patients (82% women), 75% self-reported generalized pain and 39 met 2016 fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria, including 23 who were healthy before COVID-19.
Higher incidence of GERD/acid reflux is observed following COVID-19 as a manifestation of long COVID-19.
In a survey of 616 individuals, new-onset fibromyalgia symptoms after COVID-19 occurred significantly more often in males.
In the same survey, obesity was strongly associated with new-onset fibromyalgia symptoms after COVID-19.
Patients with hypermobility syndrome show widespread ECM disarray and increased myofibroblasts, which the model suggests predisposes to more severe fascial armoring.
Estrogen inhibits myofibroblast differentiation and is associated with lower fascial stiffness.
Hormonal contraceptive use is associated with reduced risk of fibromyalgia in women.
In convalescent non-severe COVID-19 patients followed nearly 1 year, 24% had pulmonary diffusion impairment and 56.7% had abnormal CT findings including ground-glass opacities and fibrosis.
At nearly 1-year follow-up of hospitalized COVID-19 survivors, the most frequent symptoms were sleep difficulties (43.3%), shortness of breath (40.8%), fatigue (35.8%), and joint pain (32.5%).

A cross-sectional study found only 4% of COVID-19 patients had persistently abnormal chest X-rays, yet over 60% did not feel back to full health more than 6 weeks after acute recovery, indicating symptom burden is disproportionate to radiographic findings.
In a cohort assessed near 1 year after non-severe COVID-19, pulmonary diffusion impairment was found in about a quarter of patients despite non-severe initial disease.
The majority of a convalescent non-severe COVID-19 cohort had abnormal CT findings including ground-glass opacities, fibrosis, bronchiectasis, lines/bands, and nodules at nearly 1-year follow-up.
A Chinese cohort of hospitalized COVID-19 survivors reported sleep difficulties, shortness of breath, fatigue, and joint pain as the most frequent symptoms at nearly 1-year follow-up.
More than one third of patients who had non-severe COVID-19 reported anxiety and depression at approximately 1-year follow-up.
Roughly half to two-thirds of adults reported decreased quality of life when measured 14-21 days after their initial COVID-19 test.

An international online survey found long COVID-19 relapses were mostly triggered by exercise, physical or mental activity, and stress, with participants experiencing many symptoms across multiple organ systems.
SARS-CoV-2 infection increases mRNA levels of ACE2, TGF-β1, connective tissue growth factor, and fibronectin-1, which drive lung fibrosis.

An autopsy series found inflammatory myositis features more pronounced in skeletal than cardiac muscle in COVID-19 decedents, with low or undetectable viral load, suggesting a post-infectious immune-mediated myopathy rather than direct viral invasion.

A separate autopsy study of COVID-19 deaths found muscle atrophy, necrotizing myopathy, and myositis in psoas muscle samples with no evidence of direct viral invasion, attributed to cytokine-related immune damage.
Peripheral vascular alterations in long COVID-19 include decreased flow-mediated dilation and increased arterial stiffness, suggested to reflect an inflammatory vasculopathy.
Vascular structural modification after SARS-CoV-2 infection may result from endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, potentially increasing blood vessel wall stiffness and pre-stress.
An in-vitro study showed that cyclical mechanical stress reduces myofibroblast differentiation of primary lung fibroblasts, supporting a rationale for movement-based interventions.
In an online survey of 616 individuals, male sex was strongly associated with new-onset fibromyalgia symptoms following COVID-19 infection.
In the same survey, obesity was very strongly associated with new-onset fibromyalgia symptoms following COVID-19 infection.

In the same survey, pre-existing depression was not significantly associated with new-onset fibromyalgia after COVID-19, and pre-existing anxiety showed only a weak, non-significant association, in contrast to the much larger obesity and male-sex associations, questioning a purely psychological explanation.
Hormonal contraceptives are associated with reduced risk of fibromyalgia in women, hypothesized to relate to estrogen's inhibitory effect on myofibroblast differentiation and fascial stiffness.
Low vitamin D is proposed as a predisposing factor for fascial armoring/long COVID-19 because vitamin D is involved in myofibroblast de-differentiation.

Mechanical tension applied to skin, and splint-based mechanical stimuli, have each been shown to induce myofibroblast formation, supporting the proposed risk of tight clothing/accessories for fascial armoring.

Patients with hypermobility syndrome show widespread ECM disarray and increased myofibroblasts, predicted to confer higher risk for long COVID-19 and fibromyalgia due to a more collapsible tensegrity structure.

A case report of a patient with post-COVID exertional dyspnea, brain fog, and myalgia meeting fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria (FIQ score 88/100) achieved temporary relief with dry/wet needling, experienced symptom migration to the extremities after repeated sessions, and ultimately entered remission at 12 months after further needling.
Higher incidence of gastroesophageal reflux disease/acid reflux is noted as a manifestation of long COVID-19.
Epigenetic changes are observed in long COVID-19 and may contribute to biological age acceleration.

In a 100-participant online questionnaire study of adult long COVID-19 patients, most were women, three-quarters self-reported generalized pain, and 39% met 2016 fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria, nearly two-thirds of whom had been completely healthy prior to COVID-19.
In the primary cohort, 11.1% of COVID-19 survivors met criteria for postacute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) beyond 28 days.
Breakthrough (vaccinated) COVID-19 cases had significantly lower adjusted odds of developing PASC compared with unvaccinated cases.
Patients treated with anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibodies had significantly lower adjusted odds of developing PASC compared with untreated patients.
Female COVID-19 survivors were significantly more likely to develop PASC than males.
Middle-aged COVID-19 survivors (40-64 years) were more likely to develop PASC than those aged 65 years or older.
COVID-19 survivors with a Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) of 2-4 had over double the odds of developing PASC compared with those with CCI 0-1.
COVID-19 survivors with a Charlson Comorbidity Index of 5+ had more than triple the odds of developing PASC compared with those with CCI 0-1.
Individuals with higher area deprivation index (ADI, indicating greater socioeconomic disadvantage) had lower odds of PASC than those with the lowest ADI.
Patients hospitalised with moderate acute COVID-19 disease had lower odds of PASC than patients with mild ambulatory disease.
Shortness of breath was the most common PASC symptom, occurring in 43.5% of PASC patients in the primary cohort.
COVID-19 vaccination was associated with decreased odds of developing all constitutional and systemic PASC symptoms except changes in taste and smell.
Monoclonal antibody treatment was associated with decreased likelihood of persistent shortness of breath and new-onset mood/anxiety disorders, a narrower symptom benefit than vaccination.
In the replication cohort using the TriNetX global research network, 11.2% of COVID-19 survivors met PASC criteria, closely corroborating the primary cohort estimate.
In the replication cohort, vaccination was associated with a markedly reduced odds of PASC, an even larger protective effect than seen in the primary cohort.
In the replication cohort, mAb treatment was associated with reduced odds of PASC, though a smaller effect than vaccination.
In the replication cohort, female sex was again associated with higher likelihood of PASC, confirming the primary cohort finding.
In the replication cohort, higher comorbidity burden (CCI 2-4 and 5+ vs 0-1) was again associated with higher PASC risk.
In the replication cohort, mood/anxiety disorders were the most frequently reported PASC symptom, followed by shortness of breath and malaise/fatigue.
Higher pre-pandemic plasma IL-6 levels were associated with increased risk of chronic fatigue in COVID-19-negative TwinsUK participants.
In COVID-19-positive participants, pre-pandemic plasma IL-6 levels did not predict subsequent long-COVID chronic fatigue.
Long-term fatigue prevalence was significantly higher among COVID-19-positive participants than COVID-19-negative participants.
Higher BMI was associated with increased risk of chronic fatigue among COVID-19-positive participants.
Among COVID-19-negative participants, fatigue prevalence was significantly higher in those with high pre-pandemic IL-6 levels compared to those with low levels.
Among COVID-19-positive participants, fatigue prevalence did not differ between those with high versus low pre-pandemic IL-6 levels.

Among COVID-19-positive participants, those with chronic fatigue showed a different distribution of BMI categories, with lower prevalence of healthy weight and higher prevalence of obesity compared to those without fatigue.

The qualitative pattern of fatigue symptoms on the Chalder Fatigue Scale was similar between COVID-19-positive and COVID-19-negative participants with chronic fatigue, with no significant differences across the 11 individual questions.

Sensitivity analyses restricting to samples collected within two years pre-pandemic, analyzing IL-6 without age/BMI adjustment, and excluding participants with major inflammatory disease all produced results similar to the main analysis, supporting robustness of the IL-6/COVID-status-dependent findings.
About 87% of hospitalized COVID-19 survivors have at least one Long COVID symptom by 60 days post-discharge, with 55% reporting three or more symptoms.
The most common Long COVID symptoms reported are fatigue, shortness of breath, joint pain, and chest pain.
About half of people with Long COVID meet diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS.

In a large multinational survey, roughly half of Long COVID patients were unable to work full-time six months after infection, mainly due to fatigue, postexertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction.
Experiencing more than five symptoms in the first week of COVID-19 infection predicts development of Long COVID regardless of age or sex.
Age 50 years or older confers a 47% risk of developing Long COVID.

Women show greater Long COVID prevalence, lower mortality, lower inflammation, higher lymphocyte counts, and faster antibody responses than men, suggesting male sex is a risk factor for severe acute COVID but not necessarily for Long COVID itself.
A systematic review found that COVID-19 vaccination is overall associated with reduced risk of developing Long COVID, with two doses more protective than one.
Double-vaccinated individuals infected with Omicron BA.1 were half as likely to develop Long COVID compared with double-vaccinated individuals infected with Delta.
Antiphospholipid autoantibodies were detected in 52% of serum samples from hospitalized COVID-19 patients and correlated with neutrophil hyperactivity and more severe clinical outcomes.
A pilot study showed that neutralizing GPCR-autoantibodies improved capillary impairment and fatigue in patients after COVID-19 infection.
Higher melatonin levels in acute COVID-19 were associated with lower mortality, suggesting melatonin deficiency could be a risk factor for Long COVID.
Cardiac abnormalities and myocardial inflammation, indicating cardiac injury, were observed in 78% of participants discharged from hospital after COVID-19.
The degree of pulmonary vascular shunting in COVID-19 patients strongly correlates with poor blood oxygenation.
Neutrophil degranulation is upregulated in Long COVID, indicating continued inflammatory activity and immune dysregulation after acute infection.
Patients with Long COVID show lower heart rate variability, a marker of parasympathetic function, compared with matched controls.

In a case series of nine Long COVID patients, orthostatic intolerance, cerebral hypoperfusion, and dysautonomia were present in all patients regardless of whether they met formal criteria for POTS or orthostatic hypotension.
Amyloid fibrin(ogen) aggregates ('fibrinaloid microclots') resistant to fibrinolysis have been reported in T2DM, ME/CFS, acute COVID-19, and Long COVID plasma.
Von Willebrand factor is significantly elevated in patients recovering from COVID-19, indicating endothelial cell activation.
Factor VIII is significantly elevated in patients recovering from COVID-19, indicating endothelial cell activation.
Eight months after mild-to-moderate COVID-19, endothelial markers ET-1 and angiopoietin-2 remain dysregulated in Long COVID patients.
Extracellular vesicle-tissue factor (EV-TF) activity is significantly upregulated in patients hospitalized with COVID-19 and may contribute to thrombosis.
Phosphatidylserine externalization in COVID-19 patients is strongly associated with increased D-dimer levels, and is significantly higher in patients with thrombosis than those without.

An analysis of electronic health records from 48 million adults in England and Wales found that risk of first arterial and venous thrombosis in the week following acute COVID-19 was approximately 28.7 and 33.2 times higher, respectively, than in those without COVID-19, remaining elevated for up to 49 weeks.

Analysis of 11.7 million US Veterans' health records (>153,000 with acute COVID-19) showed significantly increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes including myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, and stroke at 1 year, with elevated risk persisting even in mild cases and younger patients.
Pilot data suggest sulodexide improves symptoms and endothelial function in Long COVID.
Initial observational experience with triple anticoagulant therapy to address anomalous clotting in Long COVID has been encouraging.
A pilot study of Pycnogenol demonstrated improvements in endothelial function, microcirculation, inflammatory molecules, oxidative stress, and symptoms in Long COVID.
Graded exercise therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy have been shown to be harmful and/or ineffective in Long COVID, and several guidelines advise against their use.
Proinflammatory cytokines upregulate tissue factor expression, activating the extrinsic coagulation pathway and driving thrombin generation in Long COVID.
Chronic inflammation raises PAI-1 levels, suppressing fibrinolytic activity and contributing to a prothrombotic state in Long COVID.
Chronic systemic inflammation suppresses anticoagulant mechanisms including the antithrombin and protein C pathways, favoring a prothrombotic hemostatic balance.
Amyloid-form fibrin(ogen) aggregates ('fibrinaloid microclots') that resist fibrinolysis have been reported in the plasma of patients with T2DM, ME/CFS, acute COVID-19, and Long COVID.
The isolated SARS-CoV-2 S1 spike subunit acts as a proinflammatory inflammagen and directly interacts with platelets and fibrin(ogen) to induce hypercoagulability, independent of cellular uptake.
Long COVID microclots are highly resistant to standard proteolytic digestion protocols, unlike the microclots found in T2DM or healthy plasma, which degrade normally.

Proteomic analysis of Long COVID microclots identified trapped inflammatory molecules including alpha 2-antiplasmin, von Willebrand factor, platelet factor 4, serum amyloid A, fibrinogen chains, and various antibodies.
Endothelial cell biomarkers VWF and Factor VIII are significantly elevated in patients recovering from COVID-19.
Eight months after mild-to-moderate COVID-19 infection, endothelial markers ET-1 and angiopoietin-2 remain dysregulated in patients with Long COVID.
Elevated inflammatory mediators in Long COVID may cause shedding of the protective endothelial glycocalyx, altering microvascular resistance and capillary hemodynamics.
Activated endothelium in Long COVID upregulates cell adhesion molecules ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin, and P-selectin along with procoagulant factors, while anticoagulant factor expression is weakened.
Cytokines directly stimulate tissue factor and the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), promoting thrombosis in Long COVID.
SARS-CoV-2 can directly bind platelets via ACE2 and TMPRSS2 receptors, promoting platelet activation, adhesion, and aggregation and thereby increasing coagulation.
Antithrombin III, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and activated protein C are significantly decreased in the context of endothelial damage, promoting coagulation.
Extracellular vesicle-tissue factor (EV-TF) activity is significantly upregulated in patients hospitalized with COVID-19, and TF-positive EVs released into circulation may promote thrombosis.

Phosphatidylserine externalization in COVID-19 patients is strongly associated with increased D-dimer levels, and patients with thrombosis show significantly higher PS externalization than those without.

Antiphospholipid antibodies bind endothelial receptors and inhibit nitric oxide synthase, reducing nitric oxide production and contributing to endothelial damage, impaired vascular integrity, and platelet aggregation.
Von Willebrand factor, as a marker of endothelial activation/damage, correlates with disease severity in Long COVID.
Chronic tissue hypoxia may trigger transcription factor early growth response-1, upregulating TF expression and PAI-1, thereby increasing coagulation and promoting endothelial cell apoptosis.

In an electronic health record analysis of 48 million adults in England and Wales, the adjusted hazard ratio for first arterial thrombosis in the week following acute COVID-19 was 28.7 compared with those without a COVID-19 diagnosis, remaining elevated up to 49 weeks.
The same EHR analysis found the adjusted hazard ratio for first venous thrombosis in the week following acute COVID-19 was 33.2 compared with those without a COVID-19 diagnosis.

An analysis of 11.7 million US Veterans' health records, including over 153,000 with acute COVID-19, showed significantly increased 1-year risk of thrombosis-related cardiovascular outcomes including myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, and stroke, with elevated risk persisting even in mild cases and younger patients without underlying health issues.
Pilot data suggest sulodexide improves symptoms and endothelial function in Long COVID, though replication in randomized trials is needed.
Initial observational experience with triple anticoagulant therapy to address anomalous clotting in Long COVID has been encouraging.
A pilot study of Pycnogenol demonstrated improvements in endothelial function, microcirculation, inflammatory molecules, oxidative stress, and symptoms in Long COVID.

HELP apheresis reduces hypercoagulability and inflammatory molecules in cardiovascular disease and has potential for Long COVID, but is expensive, not widely accessible, and lacks objective efficacy data in Long COVID.
Graded exercise therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy are considered harmful and/or ineffective for patients with 'Syndromic' Long COVID and are advised against by several guidelines.
Symptomatic treatment recommendations for Long COVID include antihistamines for MCAS and cardiac rate-limiting medication for dysautonomia, titrated according to individual presentation.
At 90 days after COVID-19 diagnosis, 41.6% of the cohort met criteria for long-COVID symptoms.
Dyspnea prevalence declined progressively from day 10 to day 90 but remained the most common persistent symptom.
Fatigue prevalence rose from day 10 to day 30, then declined through day 90 but remained a common persistent symptom.
Female sex was independently associated with higher odds of developing long-COVID symptoms.
Patients aged 50 and older were nearly five times more likely to develop long-COVID symptoms than those aged 18–29.
Patients aged 40–49 had roughly five-fold higher adjusted odds of long-COVID compared to the 18–29 reference group.
Patients aged 30–39 had more than double the adjusted odds of long-COVID compared to the 18–29 reference group.
Hospitalization for acute COVID-19 was associated with a five-fold increased risk of long-COVID symptoms.
Presence of dyspnea at day 10 predicted subsequent development of long-COVID symptoms.
Presence of fatigue at day 60 predicted subsequent long-COVID symptom classification.
COVID-19 vaccination prior to infection was protective, with unvaccinated patients almost seven times more likely to develop long-COVID symptoms than vaccinated patients.
Although comorbidities were significantly associated with long-COVID in bivariate analysis, this association did not remain significant after multivariable adjustment.
A prior COVID-19 infection was not associated with long-COVID symptom occurrence.
Smoking status was not associated with development of long-COVID symptoms.
Employment status showed no significant bivariate association with long-COVID symptom occurrence.
Fatigue at day 30, though significant in bivariate analysis, was not an independent predictor of long-COVID after adjustment.
Patients with long COVID symptoms had significantly higher Fatigue Severity Scale scores than asymptomatic post-COVID patients.
Patients with long COVID symptoms had significantly higher Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores, though still within the normal range, compared to asymptomatic post-COVID patients.
Patients with long COVID symptoms had significantly higher (worse) Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores than asymptomatic post-COVID patients.
71.3% of long COVID patients had problematic fatigue (FSS ≥ 4) compared with 26.3% of asymptomatic post-COVID patients.
24.5% of long COVID patients had increased daytime sleepiness (ESS > 10) compared with 7.4% of asymptomatic post-COVID patients.
62.8% of long COVID patients had poor sleep quality (PSQI > 5) compared with 23.1% of asymptomatic post-COVID patients.

Fatigue severity (FSS) in long COVID patients did not differ significantly between those infected during the Alpha, Delta or Omicron dominated waves, indicating variant-independence of fatigue burden.

Sleep quality (PSQI) scores in long COVID patients did not differ significantly between those infected during the Alpha, Delta or Omicron dominated waves, indicating variant-independence of sleep quality impairment.

In the Omicron (5th) wave, PSQI component scores between LC and NS groups differed significantly only for subjective sleep quality, sleep onset latency and daytime dysfunction, unlike the Alpha and Delta waves where all components differed significantly.
Hypertension was the most common comorbidity among the study population (46.3%), followed by chronic respiratory diseases, other cardiovascular diseases and diabetes.
The male:female ratio was approximately 1:1 in long COVID groups but close to 3:1 (male-predominant) in asymptomatic groups across all three epidemic waves.
Patients diagnosed with COVID-19 had a substantially higher incidence of at least one long COVID symptom 12-20 weeks postindex compared with matched patients without documented COVID-19.
Joint stiffness was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom, occurring in 4.5% of COVID-19 patients postindex.
Cough was among the most commonly reported long COVID symptoms, occurring in 3.0% of COVID-19 patients postindex.
Fatigue was among the most commonly reported long COVID symptoms, occurring in 2.7% of COVID-19 patients postindex.
Among COVID-19 patients, having a baseline comorbid condition was associated with significantly higher adjusted odds of developing long COVID symptoms.
Prior diagnosis of a cognitive disorder was associated with higher odds of long COVID symptoms.
A prior diagnosis of cognitive disorder in the baseline period was associated with higher odds of long COVID symptoms among COVID-19 patients.
A prior diagnosis of transient ischemic attack in the baseline period was associated with higher odds of long COVID symptoms among COVID-19 patients.
A prior diagnosis of hypertension in the baseline period was associated with higher odds of long COVID symptoms among COVID-19 patients.
A prior diagnosis of obesity in the baseline period was associated with higher odds of long COVID symptoms among COVID-19 patients.
Mean oxygen pulse peak percent predicted was reduced across the long COVID cohort, indicating impaired oxygen extraction and stroke volume during exercise.
41% of long COVID participants (24/59) had reduced exercise capacity, defined as VO2 peak ≤84% predicted.
Among 19 non-ICU participants who completed a maximal CPET, mean HRpeak was 69% predicted, indicating chronotropic intolerance consistent with autonomic dysfunction.
30.5% of participants (18/59) showed a high VE/VCO2 slope (≥34), indicating breathing/ventilatory inefficiency.

Among women, those with reduced exercise capacity had a significantly higher VE/VCO2 slope at the anaerobic threshold than women with normal exercise capacity, suggesting hyperventilation and ventilatory inefficiency.
Women with reduced exercise capacity had a lower peak respiratory exchange ratio than women with normal exercise capacity, indicating submaximal effort and exertion intolerance.
In men, reduced exercise capacity was associated with worse pulmonary function values (FVC%, FEV1%, PEF% predicted), suggesting more severe COVID-19 disease and/or premorbid comorbidity in men.
Participants with normal exercise capacity (VO2 peak >84% predicted) showed a circulatory limitation indicated by a mean heart rate reserve below 15 beats/min.
Heart rate reserve was significantly higher in the reduced exercise capacity subgroup, possibly indicating deconditioning.

Mean VE reserve was 10.5% (range 4-26) in patients with reduced exercise capacity during maximal CPET, below the normal threshold of ≥15%, suggesting a ventilatory limitation contributing to exercise intolerance.
The majority of subjects (57.6%) did not meet the RERpeak >1.05 criterion for a maximal test, supporting suboptimal effort or exertion intolerance in this long COVID cohort.
Mean FVC was reduced to 74% predicted (range 64-90%) while other spirometry values were normal in the overall sample, suggesting a mild restrictive pattern in some long COVID patients.
Race was significantly associated with ICU admission among long COVID patients, indicating a racial disparity in illness severity/social determinants.

Inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation utilization differed markedly by ICU status, with 82.6% of ICU-admitted patients receiving pulmonary rehabilitation compared to only 6.2% of non-ICU hospitalized patients.
At 6 months, persons testing positive for SARS-CoV-2 had a 64 per 10,000 higher prevalence of pulmonary complaints (shortness of breath/cough) than persons testing negative.
At 6 months, persons testing positive had a 181 per 10,000 higher prevalence of general complaints (fatigue) than persons testing negative.

At 6 months, persons testing positive had only a 5 per 10,000 higher prevalence of neurological complaints (impaired concentration/memory/brain fog) than persons testing negative, a smaller increase than for pulmonary or general complaints.
At 6 months, an estimated additional 10-20 persons per 10,000 with COVID-19 sought primary care for combined pulmonary and general complaints compared to those without COVID-19.
Fatigue, pulmonary, and neurocognitive long COVID complaints usually occurred singly rather than in combination, in all three exposure groups.

Prevalence of single pulmonary, general, and neurological complaints increased from baseline to 2 months in all three groups, then declined from 2 to 6 months for pulmonary and general complaints, while neurological complaints showed lower prevalence and a smaller increase over time.
Persons testing positive for SARS-CoV-2 were younger, had fewer comorbidities, and were less often vaccinated than persons testing negative or untested.

Persons testing positive for SARS-CoV-2 had a higher pre-existing (2017-19) prevalence of seeking medical care for general complaints than the comparison groups, though not for all three complaint types combined.

There was no increasing overlap of complaint categories over time; the largest overlap between pulmonary and general complaints among test-positive persons occurred at 2 months and was visually lower by 6 months.

The combined prevalence of neurological plus general complaints was stable or slightly increasing from 2 to 6 months, in contrast to the declining trend seen for combined pulmonary and general complaints.
Increasing age was associated with higher odds of hospital admission for COVID-19, reaching an odds ratio of 3.3 in patients over 50 and 19 in patients over 80.
Charlson Comorbidity Index score and smoking habits were also associated with an increased risk of hospital admission for COVID-19.
Higher age was significantly associated with worsening NYHA respiratory functional score at 1 year post-COVID-19.
Being female was significantly associated with worse respiratory (NYHA) outcome at 1 year after COVID-19.
Requiring ventilatory support during acute COVID-19 was significantly associated with worse respiratory (NYHA) outcome at 1 year.
Pulmonary embolism during acute COVID-19 was significantly associated with a much higher risk of recurrent pulmonary embolism at 1-year follow-up.
A history of thromboembolic events prior to COVID-19 was significantly associated with higher recurrence of thrombosis/embolism at 1 year.
Six neurological/systemic symptoms (headache, smell disturbance, taste disturbance, feeling slowed down, fatigue, and sleepiness) significantly improved between acute COVID-19 and 1-year follow-up.
For five of the six improving symptoms, ambulatory patients showed greater improvement at 1 year than hospitalized patients.
Age over 65 was rarely associated with improvement in any of the six key neurological/symptom variables, indicating persistence of symptoms in older patients.
Higher age and comorbidity burden (CCI score) were associated with persistent headache at 1 year post-COVID.
Smell and taste disturbance were more likely to persist at 1 year in patients who were older or hospitalized.
Persistence of 'feeling slowed down' and fatigue at 1 year was only associated with increasing age.
Women aged 18-49 with prior COVID-19 scored significantly higher on the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory than age/sex-matched general-population participants, regardless of hospitalization status.
Men aged 50 and older with prior COVID-19 scored significantly higher on all four psychological questionnaires (CES-D, STAI, PSQI, MVEQ) than general-population comparators.
Women aged 50 and older with prior COVID-19 also scored significantly higher on all four psychological questionnaires than general-population comparators.

Cluster analysis of 1-year functional and neurological scores identified a distinct 'Long COVID' cluster (n=124) versus an 'Others' cluster (n=350), with good cluster separation (silhouette width 0.41, Dunn index 0.11).

Prior chronic comorbidities—especially history of atrial fibrillation or stroke—and higher CCS angina score at baseline were significantly associated with membership in the 'Long COVID' cluster, whereas male sex was protective.

During acute COVID-19 infection, the neurological symptoms of paresthesia, feeling slowed down, confusion, and insomnia were significantly associated with subsequent membership in the 'Long COVID' cluster at 1 year.
Patients who required mechanical ventilation during acute COVID-19 were significantly more likely to belong to the 'Long COVID' cluster at 1 year.
Principal component analysis of neurological items identified seven key items describing most variability, with smell and taste disturbance alone driving more than half of the cumulative variance.
Proteobacteria abundance is increased in the gut of autistic patients and is linked to host inflammation and LPS-driven reduction of brain glutathione.
Bacteroides is the main propionate-producing gut microbe and its fecal abundance correlates strongly with propionate levels in autistic patients.
Increased Clostridium levels produce endotoxins and propionate that may be associated with severity of ASD symptoms.
Faecalibacterium prausnitzii is increased in autistic children and produces anti-inflammatory butyrate, considered beneficial in ASD.
Candida albicans was found roughly twice as abundant in individuals with ASD compared to healthy controls and is hypothesized to raise GABA via an ammonia/beta-alanine mechanism.
Bifidobacterium, a GABA-synthesizing gut bacterium, is decreased in autism, correlating with low GABA levels in children with autism.
Blautia, involved in tryptophan and bile acid synthesis (serotonin precursors), is decreased in autism, potentially leading to reduced brain serotonin.
Prevotella, involved in saccharide metabolism, is decreased in autism and thought to contribute to impaired carbohydrate metabolism.

Fiorentino et al. found impaired gut and blood-brain barrier integrity in autism, with increased brain claudin-5/12, decreased barrier-forming intestinal claudin-1, occludin, and TRIC, and increased pore-forming claudins-2/10/15.
Ashwood et al. found significantly increased plasma levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 in children with ASD aged 2-5 years compared with typically developing controls.
Alzghoul et al. reported elevated plasma IL-8 and TNF-α in autistic Jordanian children compared with their unaffected siblings and unrelated healthy controls.

Oral vancomycin treatment, which suppresses Clostridia, produced short-term behavioral and GI improvement in children with autism, but effects reversed once treatment stopped due to persistence of Clostridium spores.
Lower abundance of the mucin-degrading bacterium Akkermansia in children with ASD indicates a thinner GI mucus barrier and impaired gut permeability.
Wang et al. detected higher amounts of fecal SCFAs (acetic, butyric, isobutyric, valeric, isovaleric acids) in children with ASD compared to controls.

Propionic acid, produced by Clostridia and Bacteroidetes, can cross the blood-brain barrier and induce autism-like behaviors by modulating brain serotonin and dopamine, and by generating pro-inflammatory cytokines and reducing antioxidants.

Xiong et al. analyzed urine from 62 autistic and 62 non-autistic children and found higher levels of 3-(3-hydroxyphenyl)-3-hydroxypropionic acid, 3-hydroxyphenylacetic acid, and 3-hydroxyhippuric acid in the autistic group, with the first compound linked to decreased brain catecholamine levels.
Autistic children show hyperserotonemia in blood (likely from gastrointestinal enterochromaffin cell hypersecretion) alongside reported hyposerotonemia in the brain.
GABA synthesis and activity are altered in autistic patients, hypothesized to relate to dysbiosis of GABA-producing bacteria such as Lactobacillus brevis and Bifidobacterium dentium.

Kang et al.'s open-label trial of microbiota transfer therapy (MTT) in 18 children with ASD found an 80% reduction in gastrointestinal symptoms and significant behavioral improvement that persisted 8 weeks post-treatment.
A case study using the VSL#3 probiotic mixture showed marked improvement in core autistic and GI symptoms, minimizing the ADOS social affect domain score, sustained at 10-month follow-up.

Probiotic supplementation with L. plantarum WCSF1 increased enterococci and lactobacilli and lowered Clostridium cluster XIVa in autistic patients, with improved behavior profile versus placebo on the Development Behavior Checklist.
A 6-week B-GOS prebiotic intervention combined with exclusion diet in 30 autistic children reduced abdominal pain scores and improved social behavioral scores.

In a 12-week controlled trial in children aged 2-11 with ASD and GI symptoms, the group receiving Bovine Colostrum Product alone (vs BCP+B. infantis) showed significant decreases in irritability, hyperactivity, lethargy, and stereotypical behavior.

Knivensberg et al.'s single-blind study of 20 children with autism and urinary peptide abnormalities found significant improvement in communication, language, and motor skills after one year on a GFCF diet.
Cheng et al.'s preliminary meta-analysis suggested omega-3 fatty acid supplementation may improve hyperactivity, lethargy, and stereotypy in ASD patients.
In 60 children with ASD versus 45 controls, higher Childhood Autism Rating Scale scores were positively linked to low serum vitamin D, B6, B12, and folate and high homocysteine levels.
In BTBR mice (an ASD model), a ketogenic diet altered gut microbiota, exerted antimicrobial-like effects, reversed elevated fecal Akkermansia muciniphila, and improved sociability.

Bioinformatics analysis showed increased Proteobacteria and decreased Blautia/Coprococcus in autistic children's gut microbiome, and treatment with the traditional Chinese medicine Buyang Huanwu Tang normalized this imbalance, attributed to its active ingredient calycosin-7-O-b-D-glucoside from Astragalus membranaceus.
A case study of a 12-year-old boy with ASD treated with the herbal remedy Ukgansan showed marked improvement in irritability that had not responded to antipsychotic drugs.

A 6-week prebiotic intervention with Bimuno-galactooligosaccharide combined with dietary exclusion reduced GI discomfort and abdominal pain scores and improved social behavior scores in 30 autistic children.
In healthy volunteers, B-GOS-containing prebiotic formulation reduced salivary cortisol secretion and improved attention duration compared to fructo-oligosaccharide.

In a 12-week controlled trial in ASD children with GI symptoms, the group receiving only Bovine Colostrum Product (without B. infantis) showed significant decreases in irritability, hyperactivity, lethargy and stereotypical behavior.
A one-year gluten-free casein-free diet in 20 children with autism and urinary peptide abnormalities significantly improved communication, language and motor skills.
In a BTBR mouse model of autism, a ketogenic diet altered cecal/fecal gut microbiota composition and reversed the elevated Akkermansia muciniphila content seen in these mice.
Ketogenic diet fed BTBR mice showed increased sociability, indicating improvement in autism-like behavior.
A preliminary meta-analysis by Cheng et al. suggested omega-3 fatty acid supplementation may improve hyperactivity, lethargy and stereotypy in ASD patients.

Long-term EPA/DHA supplementation restored altered gut microbiota and produced anti-inflammatory effects in maternally separated rats, with increased Bacteroidetes and altered Firmicutes levels relative to non-separated rats.
Vitamin A deficiency was found to exacerbate core ASD symptoms in children with autism.
Vitamin C, which plays a role in brain development and has antioxidant action, was noted such that its deficiency can lead to aggravation of ASD symptoms.
In 60 children with ASD compared to 45 controls, higher Childhood Autism Rating Scale scores were positively linked to low serum vitamin D, B6, B12, folate and high homocysteine levels.

Autistic children were found to have D-lactic acidosis, a by-product of bacterial fermentation of undigested carbohydrates, associated with bizarre behavioral symptoms such as disorientation, blurred vision, and confusion.
A case study implementing the Specific Carbohydrate Diet in a child with ASD found the diet well tolerated with improvement in GI and behavioral symptoms.

In children with autism, Proteobacteria was notably increased while Blautia and Coprococcus were significantly decreased, an imbalance that was normalized after treatment with the traditional Chinese medicine Buyang Huanwu Tang.
In a 12-year-old boy with ASD, the herbal remedy Ukgansan improved irritability that had not responded successfully to antipsychotic drug treatment.
Ginkgo biloba extract was found to normalize gut flora, thereby combating ASD symptoms through the gut-brain axis.

Dietary phytochemicals such as curcumin, resveratrol, naringenin, and sulforaphane enhance activation of the Nrf2/ARE antioxidant pathway by interacting with Keap1, reducing reactive oxygen species generation and potentially restraining autistic symptoms.

In a 21-day noncontrolled trial of 33 children with ASD, Delpro probiotic capsules produced a significant decrease across all Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist domain scores including speech, sociability, and behavior.

A randomized placebo-controlled trial in 100 children found Vivomix probiotic supplementation for 5 months changed ASD severity, cognitive behavior, language development, and GI symptoms, along with increased Bifidobacterium levels improving gut permeability.

In hamsters with clindamycin/propionic-acid-induced autistic-like behavior, the Protein R Bifidobacteria/Lactobacilli mixture reduced excitation, inhibition and imbalance symptoms and restored altered GABA levels.

In a 3-month Egyptian trial of 60 children given a 3-strain probiotic (L. acidophilus, L. rhamnosus, B. longum), Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus counts increased, IL-10 release was stimulated (anti-inflammatory effect), and GI and behavioral symptoms improved.

A 19-week randomized crossover trial in 13 children found VISBIOME probiotic improved gastrointestinal symptoms and, via L. plantarum, improved anti-social behavior, anxiety, and communication problems.

In a Polish trial of 22 children with ASD, L. acidophilus probiotic supplementation decreased the urinary D-arabinitol-to-L-arabinitol ratio (a candidiasis marker) from a mean of 3.14±0.14 to 2.77±0.28 after treatment.

A Finnish randomized placebo-controlled trial giving L. rhamnosus for the first 6 months of life to 15 infants, followed for 13 years, found early probiotic supplementation reduced the risk of later neuropsychiatric disorder development and changed gut microbiota composition.
A 10-day course of Amoxicillin was reported by parents to improve autism symptoms in a child.

In a rodent model, maternal use of oral non-absorbable antibiotics (sulfonamide, neomycin, bacitracin) produced offspring with impaired social interactions and fecal samples showing 50% reduction in Lactobacillus abundance with increased Clostridium.

Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam antibiotic, enhances expression of glutamate transporter 1, limiting extracellular glutamate levels and potentially improving autism symptoms via astrocyte glutamate transporter modulation.
A one-year gluten-free casein-free diet intervention in 20 children with autism and urinary peptide abnormalities produced significant improvement in communication, language and motor skills.
Levels of the intracellular antioxidant glutathione (GSH) and the methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) are significantly lower in individuals with autism.

In BTBR mice (ASD model), ketogenic diet altered gut microbiota composition, exerted an antimicrobial-like effect reducing bacterial abundance, and reversed elevated Akkermansia muciniphila levels compared to control diet.
In the BTBR mouse ASD model, ketogenic diet improved autistic behaviors and increased sociability compared to standard diet.
A preliminary meta-analysis by Cheng et al. found that omega-3 fatty acid supplementation may improve hyperactivity, lethargy and stereotypy in patients with ASD.

Long-term EPA/DHA supplementation in maternally separated rats produced an anti-inflammatory effect associated with restoration of altered gut microbiota, including increased butyrate-producing bacteria and decreased pro-inflammatory genera such as Akkermansia and Flexibacter.
Vitamin A deficiency was found to exacerbate core ASD symptoms in children with autism.
In a study of 60 children with ASD versus 45 controls, higher Childhood Autism Rating Scale scores were associated with lower serum vitamin D, B6, B12 and folate and higher homocysteine levels.

Coleman and Blass first reported that D-lactic acidosis, a bacterial fermentation byproduct arising from impaired carbohydrate digestion, was seen in autistic children and associated with disorientation, blurred vision and confusion.
A case study of the Specific Carbohydrate Diet in a child with ASD showed the diet was well tolerated and led to improvement in gastrointestinal and behavioral symptoms.

Bioinformatics analysis showed Proteobacteria abundance increased while Blautia and Coprococcus decreased in children with autism relative to healthy controls, and treatment with the traditional Chinese medicine Buyang Huanwu Tang normalized this gut microbiome imbalance.

The traditional formula 'Decoction of Four Nobles' (Radix Ginseng, Rhizoma Atractylodis Macrocephalae, Poria, Radix glycyrrhizae praeparatae), traditionally used for constipation and diarrhea, has been proposed for curbing ASD via interaction with gut microflora.
Extract from Ginkgo biloba (EGB) was shown to normalize gut flora and thereby combat ASD symptoms through the gut-brain axis.

Propionic acid crossing the blood-brain barrier can damage the electron transport chain causing mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species generation, which the Nrf2/ARE antioxidant pathway counteracts by dissociating Nrf2 from Keap1 and inducing antioxidant gene transcription.

Dietary phytochemicals such as curcumin, resveratrol, naringenin, and sulforaphane enhance Nrf2/ARE pathway activation by interacting with Keap1, decreasing pro-inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species, thereby potentially restraining autism.

The herbal remedy Ukgansan repressed hypersensitivity and hyperactivity in ASD through anti-inflammatory effects, helped control serotonin and glutamate upregulation, and prevented behavioral anomalies while enhancing neuroplasticity signaling in a social isolation mouse model.
In a case study of a 12-year-old boy with ASD, Ukgansan improved irritability that had not been successfully treated even with antipsychotic drugs.

L-Theanine, the active constituent of Camellia sinensis (green tea), is structurally similar to L-glutamic acid and binds ionotropic glutamate receptor protein kainate1, exerting a neuroprotective effect that may subdue autism symptoms.

Piperine, the active constituent of black pepper (Piper nigrum), showed a positive effect on behavioral alterations and oxidative stress in autism and demonstrated a neuroprotective effect on glutamate at 20 mg/kg.

Curcumin was found to target several cell signaling pathways, increasing intracellular glutathione and reducing inflammatory components, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative/nitrosative stress and protein aggregation, suggesting a positive effect on autism.

6-gingerol, from Zingiber officinale (ginger), showed antioxidant effects and protective action against cerebral cortical damage, counteracting reduced brain GSH and reducing elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in autism.
Vitamin C from Emblica officinalis (Amla) exerted neuroprotective and antioxidant effects by improving levels of GSH and TNF-α in the brain in autism models.

Vitamin E from Prunus amygdalus (almond/Badam) extract possesses neuroprotective and antioxidant properties, and pretreatment prevented neurochemical, histopathological and behavioral changes in an autism model.

In a 4-month uncontrolled probiotic trial of 29 children (10 ASD, 9 non-ASD siblings, 10 ASD controls) in Slovakia, supplementation with a Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium/Streptococcus blend decreased Clostridium levels, reduced TNF-α (which correlated with GI symptoms), and produced non-significant reduction in ASD symptom severity.

A 21-day, non-controlled trial of Delpro capsule probiotic (with Del-immune V powder) in 33 children with ASD in the USA produced a significant decrease across all ATEC domain scores including speech, communication, sociability, sensory/cognitive awareness and health/physical/behavior.

A randomized placebo-controlled trial of Vivomix probiotic (S. thermophilus, B. breve, B. longum) in 100 children over 5 months improved cognitive behavior, language development, GI symptoms and behavioral profiles, and increased Bifidobacterium levels which improved gut permeability.

In 50 hamsters with autistic-like behaviors induced by clindamycin and propionic acid, the Protein R probiotic mixture reduced excitation, inhibition and imbalance symptoms and restored altered GABA levels over 27 days.

In a 3-month trial of 60 children (aged 5-9) in Egypt, a 3-strain probiotic supplement significantly increased colony counts of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, stimulated anti-inflammatory IL-10 release, improved GI symptoms and improved autistic behavioral symptoms as measured by the Childhood Autism Rating Scale.

A randomized crossover trial of VISBIOME probiotic in 13 children over 19 weeks improved GI symptoms safely; L. plantarum specifically improved anti-social behavior, anxiety and communication problems, increased Lactobacilli/enterococci and decreased Clostridium, while B. infantis elevated previously reduced tryptophan levels.

In a non-controlled trial of 22 Polish children with ASD given L. acidophilus for 2 months, the urinary D-arabinitol-to-L-arabinitol ratio (a candidiasis marker) decreased from a mean of 3.14±0.14 before treatment to 2.77±0.28 after treatment, alongside improvement in concentration and ability to follow orders.
Removing modeled lower-limb compensation shifted the pelvis from a posterior position to an anterior position relative to the ankle.
Removal of compensation was associated with a significant decrease in pelvic retroversion (pelvic tilt).
Modeled removal of compensation decreased hip extension as measured by the sacrofemoral angle.
Modeled removal of compensation decreased knee flexion angle.
Modeled removal of compensation decreased ankle dorsiflexion angle.
Removal of lower-limb compensation significantly increased anterior trunk malalignment as measured by sagittal vertical axis.
Removal of lower-limb compensation significantly increased global sagittal malalignment measured from C7 to ankle.
Serum urea concentration was significantly elevated in FD patients compared to healthy relative controls in both unpaired and paired analyses.
Serum xanthine was significantly decreased in FD patients relative to healthy controls, suggesting increased purine salvaging.
Serum inosine trended toward lower concentrations in FD patients compared to controls, consistent with enhanced purine salvage.
Serum 1,7-dimethylxanthine (paraxanthine) was decreased in FD patients and was among the top ≥40% mean-difference discriminators, also significant in unpaired volcano analysis.
Serum π-methylhistidine was decreased in FD patients and was among the top ≥40% mean-difference discriminators, also significant in unpaired volcano analysis.
Serum dimethyl sulfone was one of six significant serum metabolites lower in FD patients versus controls in unpaired volcano plot analysis.
Serum methanol was one of six significant serum metabolites lower in FD patients versus controls in unpaired volcano plot analysis.
Serum levels of the branched chain amino acids valine, leucine, and isoleucine were lower in FD patients, suggesting increased amino acid catabolism consistent with energy deficit and muscle wasting.
Serum alanine was lower in FD patients, consistent with increased amino acid catabolism and energy deficit.
Serum taurine trended lower in FD patients, contrasting with elevated fecal taurine, suggesting a systemic taurine deficit linked to diet or gut absorption capacity.
Fecal taurine was significantly elevated in FD patients compared to healthy relative controls, in both unpaired and paired analyses.

Fecal choline was significantly elevated in FD patients versus healthy relative controls, identified as significant in both unpaired and paired volcano analyses, suggesting altered host/gut microbial choline metabolism or absorption.
Fecal malonate was significantly elevated in FD patients versus controls, identified in both unpaired and paired volcano analyses.
Fecal tyramine was elevated in FD patients, a gut-microbial metabolite implicated in hypertensive crises via monoamine oxidase deficiency in FD.

Fecal p-cresol was elevated in FD patients, a Clostridium-associated microbial metabolite also elevated in Autism Spectrum Disorder stool, suggesting it may serve as a shared disease marker linked to gut dysbiosis and C. difficile susceptibility.

Fecal beta-alanine was significantly elevated in FD patients, positively correlated with Clostridium abundance in prior literature, and implicated in GABA/taurine transport modulation and muscle carnosine synthesis.
Fecal valerate, a gut-protective short-chain fatty acid that inhibits C. difficile growth, trended lower in FD patients, consistent with their known susceptibility to C. difficile infection.
Fecal fumarate trended lower in FD patients, potentially reflecting limited TCA cycle activity and altered gut microbial bacterial fermentation.
The gamma-aminobutyric acid-A (GABAa) receptor gene is downregulated in stem cells derived from FD patients, and GABAa receptor agonists are used clinically to treat FD crises.

An FD patient muscle biopsy revealed functional impairment of mitochondrial electron transport chain complexes I, III, and IV, supporting a mitochondrial dysfunction mechanism underlying metabolic deficits.
Serum metabolomic profiling by 3D-PCA showed small but noticeable clustering separating FD patients from healthy relative controls, further supported by supervised PLS-DA analysis.
Fecal metabolome PCA showed little separation between FD patients and controls, but supervised PLS-DA analysis revealed a clearer separation between the two groups.

Fundoplication surgery status correlated with stool choline levels, but because a majority of stool-donating patients (28 of 41) had received fundoplication, this association was judged unlikely to have skewed the choline findings.
Adults with ASD preferred a significantly greater interpersonal distance than neurotypical control participants during the stop-distance paradigm.
Eye contact showed only a nonsignificant trend toward increasing preferred interpersonal distance, with no significant modulation by ASD group.
Attribution of the comfortable distance to self versus to the experimenter had no significant main effect on interpersonal distance, and did not differ by ASD status.
Heart rate was numerically higher in ASD participants at both baseline and during the interpersonal task, but the group difference was not statistically significant.
In both ASD and control groups, heart rate increased significantly from baseline to the interpersonal distance task.
Baseline and interpersonal-task heart rate variability were numerically lower in ASD participants compared to controls, showing a trend-level group effect.
HRV decreased significantly from baseline to the interpersonal task in controls but not in ASD participants, indicated by a significant Group x Time interaction consistent with a floor effect in ASD.

Standardized HRV measured during the interpersonal distance task at the point of reported comfortable distance did not differ significantly between ASD and control groups, and was not modulated by eye contact or attribution.

Standardized HRV during the interpersonal task did not significantly predict preferred interpersonal distance, and autism status did not moderate this relationship, although group remained a significant predictor of distance.

In ASD participants, higher trait anxiety, poorer mentalization, and attachment scores were weakly associated with greater preferred interpersonal distance, but none of these correlations survived FDR correction for multiple comparisons.
The FMR1 gene undergoes expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats beyond 200, leading to methylation and transcriptional silencing of the gene and loss of FMRP.
Loss of FMRP due to FMR1 silencing results in impaired synaptic growth and plasticity, including formation of long, thin, juvenile dendritic spines that may impair cognition and learning.
Males with FXS are more severely affected than females due to compensatory expression from a normal second X chromosome in females, who typically show a less severe phenotype.
Approximately 50-60% of males diagnosed with FXS are also diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder.
Seizures occur in 15-20% of FXS patients, and are notably more common among those who also have ASD.
ADHD is a common comorbidity in FXS, affecting over 50% of male FXS patients at some point, with symptom occurrence ranging 54-59%.

Joint hypermobility, primarily affecting small joints such as metacarpophalangeal joints, occurs in nearly half of FXS patients, alongside soft skin and skeletal features resembling connective tissue disorders.
Aortic root dilatation occurs in about one-fourth of FXS patients, consistent with connective tissue fragility affecting the heart.
Mitral valve prolapse affects between 3% and 50% of FXS patients.
FXS patients show reduced parasympathetic vagal tone together with hyperarousal, manifesting as an elevated heart rate.
Adult FXS patients over 40 years frequently experience cardiac rhythm difficulties and hypertension, each affecting 24.2% of this population.
About 30.6% of FXS individuals aged 40-71 report digestive issues such as gastro-oesophageal reflux, loose stools, and constipation, possibly related to hypotonia and connective tissue anomalies.
Ocular abnormalities are reported in at least 25% of children with FXS and a higher proportion of adults, including strabismus (8-40%), refractive errors (17-59%), and rare nystagmus (5-13%).

Sleep disturbances, including difficulty falling asleep and frequent nighttime/early morning awakenings, affect about 30% of FXS children of both sexes, with prevalence estimates ranging 27-77% across the literature.

Melatonin is regarded as the most effective treatment for sleep difficulties in FXS, promoting sleep onset and duration and exhibiting neuroplastic and antioxidative properties, though daytime sleepiness and nausea have been reported as side effects.
Sertraline, an SSRI, is an efficacious treatment for anxiety in FXS, working by increasing synaptic serotonin levels.
Risperidone and aripiprazole, atypical antipsychotics acting via serotonergic and dopaminergic receptors, can effectively address aggression and meltdowns in FXS.

Stimulant medication is first-line treatment for ADHD in FXS children aged six and above, enhancing norepinephrine and dopamine levels in the prefrontal cortex to improve attention and impulse control.
Clonidine and guanfacine, alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonists, may help manage ADHD symptoms and hyperarousal in FXS individuals who cannot tolerate or do not respond to stimulants.

Levetiracetam and oxcarbazepine are commonly used first-choice anticonvulsants for seizure management in FXS due to more controllable side effects, while phenytoin, phenobarbital, and gabapentin are avoided due to severe side effects.

Excessive mGluR-triggered protein translation, occurring in the absence of FMRP, is hypothesized to underlie the cognitive and behavioral manifestations of FXS and provides potential targets for therapy such as mGluR5 inhibition.
Parent-implemented language intervention (PILI) effectively improves language skills in children with FXS by teaching parents to use responsive communication strategies in daily activities.

Applied Behavior Analysis, including the Early Start Denver Model for children aged one to three, is used to improve language skills and social interaction in FXS children, notably those with comorbid ASD.

Physical activity is linked to enhanced attention and cognitive control in developing children, possibly mediated by exercise-induced increases in brain-derived neurotrophic factor important for neuroplasticity.

FXS is often underdiagnosed in females, with only 25-30% of affected females having intellectual disability, and about 30% presenting with borderline IQ; those with normal IQ may still experience emotional imbalance or learning disorders.
Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) using fluorescently labelled DNA probes was developed as an alternative cytogenetic method to increase detection of the fragile X site.
The combination of PCR with Southern blot analysis is the current gold-standard molecular test for FXS, identifying normal, premutation, and full-mutation FMR1 alleles and methylation status.
Testing based solely on CGG repeat number fails to detect fewer than 1% of FXS cases that are caused by deletions or missense mutations in FMR1.
Triplet primed PCR (TP-PCR), which uses three primers to amplify the full FMR1 allele and CGG repeats simultaneously, is regarded as the most accurate and reliable current diagnostic method for FXS.
Methylation-sensitive long-range PCR (MS-LR-PCR) can be used as a follow-up diagnostic test to assess FMR1 CGG methylation and FMRP silencing.

ACMGG/ACOG guidelines recommend offering prenatal FMR1 testing to couples with a personal or family history of unexplained intellectual disability, FXS-related disorders, isolated cognitive impairment, cerebellar ataxia with tremor, primary ovarian insufficiency/elevated FSH before age 40, or autism.
Sotos syndrome is listed as a differential diagnosis for FXS because it shares phenotypic overlap including ASD, ADHD, phobias, obsessive-compulsive behaviours, impulsivity, and tantrums.
Klinefelter syndrome, caused by an extra X chromosome in males, presents overlapping cognitive and behavioural features (including learning disabilities) that must be distinguished from FXS.
Rett syndrome and Angelman syndrome are differential diagnoses for FXS, sharing common features of intellectual disability, language impairment, and autistic behaviour.
Speech-language therapy (SLT) and occupational therapy (OT) are the two most preferred non-pharmacological interventions for children with FXS.
Parent-implemented language intervention (PILI), which trains parents in responsive interaction skills, effectively improves language skills in children with FXS.
The Early Start Denver Model (ESDM), an ABA-based approach, is used to refine language skills and social interaction in FXS children aged one to three in home settings.

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is useful for regulating emotions and treating elevated anxiety in children with FXS, and can help women and high-functioning males with anxiety, ADHD, social challenges, and depression.
Music therapy has increased self-expression and communication abilities in children with FXS.
Sertraline, an SSRI that increases synaptic serotonin, is described as an efficacious treatment for anxiety in FXS.
Bupropion, which elevates noradrenergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission via reuptake blockade, is used as an antidepressant in FXS.
Risperidone and aripiprazole, atypical antipsychotics acting on serotonergic and dopaminergic receptors, effectively address aggression and meltdowns accompanying anxiety in FXS.
Stimulant medication, which raises prefrontal cortex norepinephrine and dopamine, is the first-line treatment for ADHD in FXS children aged six and above.

Clonidine and guanfacine, alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonists, improve attention and reduce hyperarousal by enhancing prefrontal norepinephrine and are alternatives for young children who cannot tolerate stimulants.

Melatonin is regarded as the most effective treatment for sleep difficulties in FXS, accelerating sleep onset and increasing nighttime sleep duration, though daytime sleepiness and nausea are reported side effects.

Levetiracetam and oxcarbazepine are used as first-choice anticonvulsants for seizures in FXS due to more controllable side effects, whereas phenytoin, phenobarbital, and gabapentin are avoided due to severe side effects.

In the absence of FMRP, excessive protein translation triggered by stimulation of mGluR5 or another Gq-coupled receptor is proposed to drive the cognitive and behavioural manifestations of FXS, providing multiple candidate targets for therapy.

Physical exercise raises brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels, which are important for brain development and neuroplasticity and may explain exercise-linked improvements in attention and cognitive control.
Overall heart rate during social and non-social video conditions did not differ significantly between preschoolers with ASD and typically developing preschoolers.
Overall high-frequency heart rate variability did not differ significantly between preschoolers with ASD and typically developing preschoolers.
Older children showed lower heart rate while watching the video stimuli, across the full sample.
Older children showed higher heart rate variability while watching the video stimuli, across the full sample.
Across the whole sample, HRV was higher during the non-social Toy and social Man videos than during the incomprehensible Hungarian video, indicating condition-dependent modulation of HRV.
The typically developing group showed a significant HR increase only from the Man (social, Block 1) video to the Hungarian (unfamiliar language) video.

The ASD group showed a broader HR increase than TD, rising from both the non-social Toy and social Man videos to both the Hungarian and English videos, indicating a larger and less selective arousal response to later social/language content.

Latent profile analysis of cognitive/language/adaptive/symptom scores identified three phenotypic ASD subgroups: ASD-C1 (near-TD cognitive/language/adaptive scores but high ASD symptom severity), ASD-C2 (intermediate cognitive/language/adaptive scores with the lowest symptom severity of the three classes), and ASD-C3 (most impaired across non-verbal, language and social domains, younger age).

Only the ASD-C2 phenotypic subgroup (intermediate cognitive/language ability, lowest ASD symptom severity) showed a significant HR-by-condition interaction relative to TD, with HR increases from Toy to Hungarian and from Man to English videos, suggesting reduced re-engagement with comprehensible social content as attention waned.

Contrary to expectation, the most clinically impaired ASD phenotypic subgroup (ASD-C3) did not show the highest physiological arousal; comparing ASD-C2 to the other two ASD classes revealed no significant group or interaction effect.

A data-driven latent profile analysis of mean-centred HR and HRV across all four video conditions (total sample, both sessions) identified three physiological classes: Phys-C1 showed only small changes in HR/HRV between conditions; Phys-C2 showed higher HR and lower HRV during Block 2 (Hungarian/English) compared to Block 1 (Toy/Man); Phys-C3 showed a condition-specific pattern with a decrease to the Man video and increase to the Hungarian video.

Children who fell reliably into the physiological class showing higher HR during Block 2 (Phys-C2stable) had lower non-verbal ability, language, and adaptive communication scores than the stable low-reactivity class (Phys-C1stable), and were disproportionately from the ASD group.
The ASD group scored significantly lower than the TD group on non-verbal visual reception, expressive/receptive language, and adaptive communication and socialisation skills.
Thirty days after bilateral subdiaphragmatic vagotomy, striatal dopaminergic neurochemistry was altered relative to sham-operated rats, both at baseline and after LPS challenge.
Striatal serotoninergic neurochemistry was similarly altered 30 days after vagotomy under both physiological and inflammatory conditions.
Striatal met-enkephalin (enkephalinergic) levels were altered 30 days after vagotomy under both physiological and inflammatory conditions.
Vagotomized rats failed to show the normal inflammation-induced rise in plasma met-enkephalin seen after LPS challenge, indicating vagotomy blunts this peripheral opioid analgesic response.

The study was motivated by the observation that low vagal activity is seen in major depression and autism spectrum disorder, and found that long-term subdiaphragmatic vagotomy may increase sensitivity to pain and social stimuli during peripheral inflammation, suggesting a vagal role in sickness behavior relevant to well-being and social responsiveness.

A 2-year-old boy initially diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder due to poor social interaction, lack of eye contact, and speech delay was later found to have severe myopia and bilateral ectopia lentis leading to a diagnosis of Marfan syndrome.
