Correction of the child's refractive error (severe myopia) led to significant improvement in his social skills, eye contact, and speech, which resolved to a normal level for his age.
The authors emphasize that comprehensive evaluation of children with developmental delays should include ocular assessments before an autism spectrum disorder diagnosis is made.
Up to one-fifth of individuals who have had COVID-19 report long COVID symptoms, and 44% of those with long COVID in one survey were unable to return to work.
In a Toronto cohort, 51% of SARS-CoV survivors experienced persistent fatigue, diffuse myalgias, weakness and depression 1 year after acute illness and could not return to work.
Among 233 SARS survivors in Hong Kong, over 40% reported ongoing fatigue at 40 months after infection.
In individuals affected by MERS-CoV in Korea, prolonged symptoms and fatigue were reported up to 18 months after acute infection.

A case-control study using Veterans Affairs data found increased risks of ischaemic heart disease, pericarditis, myocarditis, arrhythmias and heart failure in the 30 days to 12 months following COVID-19 compared to matched controls.
Individuals recovering from COVID-19 showed relative tachycardia for a median of 79 days post symptom onset.
Female sex and corticosteroid use during acute COVID-19 illness were associated with muscle weakness persisting up to 1 year after infection.
Liver enzymes were elevated in 25% of people hospitalised with COVID-19 at 1 month follow-up, usually transiently.
There is an excess risk of incident diabetes and hyperglycemia in the 12 months after COVID-19, correlating with acute illness severity and higher than following other upper respiratory infections.
Hair loss was reported in 22% of hospitalised individuals at follow-up, regardless of acute oxygen requirement.
Objective cognitive impairment has been demonstrated in long COVID patients even among those without subjective cognitive complaints.
Longitudinal follow-up showed increased incidence of anxiety and depression at 12 months compared to 6 months after initial COVID-19 diagnosis.
A prolonged period of T cell activation, with increased expression of the exhaustion markers PD-L1 and TIGIT, is seen after resolution of SARS-CoV-2 infection, more marked in older individuals.
Convalescent long COVID patients show reduced naive B cell numbers compared to recovered individuals or healthy controls.
Increased innate immune activation, marked by HLADR+CD38+ myeloid cells and type I/III interferon production, is most pronounced in patients with long COVID.
Cytokines including IL-6, TNF-alpha, and IP-10 are elevated in long COVID.

Individuals with brain fog as a feature of long COVID show distinct circulating markers of blood-brain barrier disruption, including elevated TGF-beta and IL-8, compared to those fully recovered from SARS-CoV-2.
SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein was detected in intestinal biopsies 4 months after initial infection, even in mild cases, supporting the gut as a potential reservoir for viral persistence.
EBV RNAemia during acute COVID-19 illness is associated with subsequent development of long COVID fatigue, cough, and memory complaints.
Higher levels of anti-EBV antibodies associated with lytic infection have been demonstrated in individuals with long COVID compared to those without.
The gut microbiome in acute SARS-CoV-2 infection shows depletion of immunomodulatory species such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Eubacterium rectale compared with uninfected controls.
Gut microbial diversity remains depleted 6 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection, with those who had more severe initial infection showing the most marked differences.
In hospitalised patients, both microbiome composition at admission and lack of recovery of microbiome composition were associated with development of long COVID.

Zonulin, a physiologic driver of intestinal permeability, is elevated in individuals with long COVID and positively correlates with IL-6, TNFα, and IP-10, while negatively correlating with quality of life scores.
Beta-D-glucan, a marker of fungal translocation, is elevated in individuals with long COVID.
Tilt-table testing has demonstrated orthostatic intolerance in a small number of individuals with long COVID.
Post-COVID-19 fatigue has not been shown to be associated with autonomic dysfunction.
Findings of dysautonomia post-COVID-19 correlate poorly with symptoms but are associated with an objective reduction in functional capacity on cardiopulmonary exercise testing.

Invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing in individuals with persistent dyspnoea more than 1 year post acute COVID-19 and normal imaging showed exercise limitation due to impaired peripheral systemic oxygen extraction rather than deconditioning or cardiopulmonary limitation.
Lower cortisol was found in individuals with long COVID compared to recovered controls, suggesting hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysfunction.
Up to a quarter of post-COVID patients assessed had an elevated D-dimer 4 months after initial infection, reflecting sustained coagulation pathway disturbances.
Those hospitalised with acute COVID-19 have been shown to have reduced fibrinolytic potential and increased thrombin generation at a similar post-acute timepoint.

Sustained endothelial cell activation has been shown up to 10 weeks after initial acute infection in both hospitalised and non-hospitalised individuals, with increased factor VIII and soluble thrombomodulin levels.
Von Willebrand Factor, a marker of endothelial cell activation, remains elevated in individuals after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
The SARS-CoV-2 spike protein has been shown to impair blood-brain barrier function in mechanistic studies.
Alterations in cerebral bloodflow are seen after SARS-CoV-2 infection, with changes persisting up to 10 months after infection.
Increasing evidence shows structural brain changes following SARS-CoV-2 infection, associated with cognitive decline.
Physical and cognitive pacing for chronic fatigue and cognitive dysfunction have shown some improvement in functional outcomes in long COVID.
Use of the factor Xa inhibitor rivaroxaban in patients at high risk of thrombotic complications post COVID-19 has been shown to reduce the risk of venous thromboembolism 1 month after discharge.
Famotidine, a histamine 2 receptor antagonist, was associated with earlier resolution of serum type-I interferon levels and shorter time to symptom resolution in acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.

In a small case series, a combination of guanfacine (an α2 adrenoceptor agonist) and n-acetylcysteine (an anti-oxidant) was assessed in twelve individuals with long COVID brain fog, with eight reporting symptomatic improvement.
Vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 and certain modifiable lifestyle factors are associated with lower risk of long COVID.
Acute treatment with metformin during COVID-19 infection may be of benefit in reducing the risk of subsequent long COVID.

PSRT produced a statistically significant reduction in somatic symptom burden (SSS-8) from baseline at 4, 8, and 13 weeks, with the greatest reduction observed at 13 weeks, the study's primary endpoint.
The GI symptom subcomponent of the SSS-8 also showed a statistically significant reduction after PSRT at all three follow-up timepoints.
PSRT led to a statistically significant reduction in fatigue as measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale-9 across all three follow-up timepoints.
The belief that exercise worsens symptoms (measured by an FSS-9 item) dropped sharply after PSRT, from 57% of participants strongly agreeing at baseline to only 4% by weeks 8 and 13.
PSRT was associated with a statistically significant reduction in dyspnea as measured by the Multidimensional Dyspnea Profile across all three follow-up timepoints.
PSRT was associated with a statistically significant reduction in pain intensity as measured by the Brief Pain Inventory across all three follow-up timepoints.
PSRT was associated with a statistically significant reduction in anxiety related to pain, as measured by the Pain Anxiety Symptom Scale-20.
PSRT was associated with a statistically significant improvement in physical functioning as measured by PROMIS-29.

PSRT was associated with a statistically significant reduction in self-reported brain fog (difficulty thinking or concentrating), measured by a non-validated additional SSS-8-format item, across all three follow-up timepoints.

When participants were asked to visualize activities that typically triggered their symptoms, most were able to reproduce their PASC symptoms through imagination alone, supporting a centrally-mediated (predictive coding) mechanism.

Two participants with severe unexplained weight loss (20-30 lbs) and food intolerances, including one requiring a nasogastric feeding tube, had resolution of food intolerance and regained weight by the end of PSRT.
Two participants developed acute COVID-19 reinfection during the PSRT program, yet both still showed numerical improvement in their PASC symptoms by week 13 rather than worsening.
Gut microbial diversity and richness were significantly lower and beta diversity distinctly separated, persisting for six months to one year in long COVID patients.

Beneficial commensal bacteria including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, and several Bifidobacterium species with immunomodulatory properties were depleted in people infected with SARS-CoV-2, persisting through a 6-month recovery period.
Commensal bacterial families Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae, which help strengthen the gut barrier, were down-regulated in acute COVID-19 patients.
Opportunistic fungal pathogens including Candida albicans, Candida auris, and Aspergillus flavus increased in the gut mycobiome after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Patients with persisting COVID-19 symptoms had significantly higher abundance of inflammation-inducing oral microbiota genera Prevotella and Veillonella on tongue swabs.

SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in gut mucosa around seven months after acute COVID-19 in 32 of 46 IBD patients, and viral nucleocapsid protein persisted in the gut epithelium of 24 of 46 patients, with long COVID reported mostly in those with viral antigen persistence.

Among 53 IBD patients infected with SARS-CoV-2, 21 developed long COVID, asthenia was the most frequent symptom (occurring in nearly two-thirds of patients), and IBD relapse frequency did not differ between those with and without long COVID.

In a case report, high intake of dietary fibers with diverse physicochemical structures alleviated GI symptoms in a long COVID patient by shifting gut microbiota toward enrichment of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria and reducing small-intestinal bacterial fermentation and gas production.
Probiotic supplementation significantly reduced symptom duration, viral load, and lung infiltration in acute COVID-19 patients through interaction with the host immune system.

A randomized controlled trial (NCT04251767) testing washed microbiota transplantation for acute COVID-19 disease severity was withdrawn following changed government guidance, and no completed trial exists on FMT safety/efficacy in COVID-19 or long COVID.

Severe COVID-19 was associated with high levels of the tight junction permeability marker zonulin and monocyte activation marker sCD14, along with translocation of bacterial and fungal products into the blood.
Plasma levels of the fungal cell wall polysaccharide β-glucan, a marker of fungal translocation, were higher in long COVID patients compared with controls.
87.4% of patients who had recovered from COVID-19 showed persistence of at least one symptom, including GI symptoms.
Diarrhea was the most commonly reported GI symptom across long COVID studies, with prevalence ranging from 0% to 58.7% depending largely on cohort size.

GI symptoms in long COVID uniquely correlated with expanded cytotoxic CD8+ and CD4+ T cell populations, including SARS-CoV-2-specific clonotypes, that became activated during convalescence rather than during acute disease.
ACE2 receptor expression was reported to be significantly higher in human and mouse small intestines than in all other organs, including the lungs.
TMPRSS2 and TMPRSS4 transmembrane serine proteases promote SARS-CoV-2 infection of human small intestinal enterocytes and colon cells.
Liver transplant recipients showed lower long-term persistence of anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies compared with non-transplanted COVID-19 patients.
Liver MRI performed 2-3 months after COVID-19 onset showed signs of fibro-inflammation in 5 of 52 patients.
Metabolic-associated fatty liver disease was reported as highly prevalent after hospital discharge in patients with long COVID.
Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a butyrate-producing anaerobe typically associated with good health, was inversely correlated with disease severity in acute COVID-19.
People with SARS-CoV-2 infection are at increased risk of developing gastrointestinal disorders in the post-acute phase of COVID-19.

Severe COVID-19 patients showed depletion of oral Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Solobacterium and nasopharyngeal Paracoccus, alongside enrichment of nasopharyngeal Proteus, Cupravidus, and Lactobacillus.

Critically ill COVID-19 patients' lower respiratory tract microbiome was characterized by Pseudomonas alcaligenes, Clostridium hiranonis, Acinetobacter schindleri, Sphingobacterium spp., Acinetobacter spp., and Enterobacteriaceae, whereas controls were characterized by lung commensals such as Haemophilus influenzae and Veillonella dispar.
ACE2, the receptor SARS-CoV-2 uses for cell entry, is highly expressed in esophageal and intestinal epithelial cells and shows higher expression in the small intestine than in the lungs.
TMPRSS2 and TMPRSS4 transmembrane serine proteases promote SARS-CoV-2 infection of human small intestinal enterocytes and colon.
Severe COVID-19 patients had higher human-origin proteins in blood and fecal samples and elevated circulating lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, indicating gut barrier dysfunction.
Severe COVID-19 was associated with elevated tight junction permeability markers zonulin and sCD14, alongside translocation of bacterial and fungal products into the blood.
Plasma levels of the fungal cell wall polysaccharide β-glucan, a marker of fungal translocation, were higher in long COVID patients compared with controls.
People with SARS-CoV-2 infection are at increased risk of developing gastrointestinal disorders during the post-acute phase of COVID-19.
COVID-19-associated upregulation of angiotensin II disrupts efferocytosis, inducing endothelial cell senescence and vascular barrier dysfunction via angiotensin II type 1 receptors.
Probiotic supplementation significantly reduced symptom duration, viral load, and lung infiltration in acute COVID-19 patients, likely via interaction with the host immune system.
Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a butyrate-producing anaerobe associated with health, showed abundance inversely correlated with COVID-19 disease severity.

A randomized-controlled trial (NCT04251767) testing washed microbiota transplantation for acute COVID-19 severity was withdrawn following new government guidance, and no completed trials on FMT safety/efficacy in COVID-19 or long COVID exist.
An estimated 65 million people worldwide have long COVID, based on a conservative 10% incidence estimate applied to over 651 million documented COVID-19 cases.
Nearly all symptoms reported in children and adolescents with long COVID occur at similar frequencies in those without evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection, complicating diagnosis.
Using GAD-7 clinical cutoff scoring, 31% of the cohort met criteria for clinically significant anxiety approximately 6-8 months after acute COVID-19.
Using PCL-5 criterion-based scoring, 29% of the cohort met provisional criteria for PTSD after acute COVID-19.
Female sex was significantly associated with clinically significant anxiety but not with PTSD, and no other sociodemographic differences were found between groups.

Among individual GAD-7 symptoms, excessive worry, nervousness, and inability to stop worrying showed the largest effect-size differences between the Anxiety and No Anxiety groups, followed by inability to relax, irritability, fear, and restlessness.

Among the four PCL-5 PTSD symptom domains, alterations in mood and cognition and avoidance showed the greatest effect-size differences between PTSD and No PTSD groups, followed by re-experiencing and hyper-arousal.

Anxiety, PTSD, depression, and clinically significant fatigue were highly comorbid, with nearly two-thirds of those meeting anxiety criteria also meeting PTSD criteria and up to three-quarters meeting depression criteria.

Participants meeting criteria for clinically significant anxiety had higher COVID-19 symptom severity scores both during acute infection and at the study appointment, as well as higher Chalder Fatigue Scale scores, compared to those without anxiety.

Participants meeting criteria for PTSD had higher COVID-19 symptom severity scores both during acute infection and at the study appointment, as well as higher Chalder Fatigue Scale scores, compared to those without PTSD.
Clinically significant fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale score >21) was present in more than 90% of those meeting criteria for anxiety and/or PTSD.
Participants with clinically significant anxiety had significantly lower quality of life (Q-LES-Q) and lower IADL functional scores than those without anxiety.
Participants meeting PTSD criteria reported more limitations in instrumental activities of daily living and were more likely to be seeking clinical care for PASC than those without PTSD.

Participants with anxiety and/or PTSD reported significantly greater subjective difficulties with memory, language/communication, and cognitive/intellectual functioning (PAOF), but did not differ from those without anxiety/PTSD on objective neuropsychological testing (RBANS or MoCA), indicating perceived but not actual cognitive deficits.

Logistic regression identified acute COVID-19 symptom severity, prior psychiatric history, and subjective memory complaints (PAOF) as independent predictors of combined clinically significant anxiety and/or PTSD, correctly classifying 80% of affected and 87% of unaffected cases.
A prior history of psychiatric treatment was a strong independent correlate of anxiety and/or PTSD after COVID-19, suggesting a vulnerability to worsened post-COVID neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Molnupiravir use within five days of a positive SARS-CoV-2 test was associated with a 14% relative reduction in risk of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with a 38% relative reduction in post-acute death compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with a 14% relative reduction in post-acute hospital admission compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with reduced risk of the composite outcome of post-acute death or hospital admission compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with reduced risk of post-acute dysrhythmia compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with reduced risk of post-acute pulmonary embolism compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with reduced risk of post-acute deep vein thrombosis compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with reduced risk of post-acute fatigue and malaise compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with reduced risk of post-acute liver disease compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with reduced risk of post-acute acute kidney injury compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with reduced risk of post-acute muscle pain compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was associated with reduced risk of post-acute neurocognitive impairment compared with no treatment.
Molnupiravir use was not significantly associated with risk of post-acute ischemic heart disease.
Molnupiravir use was not significantly associated with risk of post-acute diabetes.
Molnupiravir use was not significantly associated with risk of post-acute dysautonomia.
Molnupiravir use was not significantly associated with risk of post-acute shortness of breath.
Molnupiravir use was not significantly associated with risk of post-acute cough.
The protective association between molnupiravir and PASC was consistent regardless of vaccination status, observed in those unvaccinated, those with one or two doses, and those with a booster dose.
The protective association between molnupiravir and PASC was consistent in people with primary SARS-CoV-2 infection and in those with reinfection.

The protective association between molnupiravir and PASC was consistent across subgroups defined by age, race, sex, smoking status, and comorbidities (cancer, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, chronic lung disease, diabetes, immune dysfunction), with no significant interaction detected.

A composite PASC symptom score/definition was developed from participant-reported symptoms including postexertional malaise, fatigue, brain fog, dizziness, GI symptoms, palpitations, changes in sexual desire, smell/taste changes, thirst, chronic cough, chest pain, and abnormal movements.
Compared with uninfected participants, SARS-CoV-2-infected participants had adjusted odds ratios of 1.5 or greater for 37 distinct symptoms.
Among participants first infected on or after December 1, 2021 and enrolled within 30 days of infection, 10% were classified as PASC positive at 6 months.
TMS-measured intracortical facilitation was significantly reduced in pCF compared with controls, indicating reduced cortical excitability.
Other TMS measures related to cortical excitability (recruitment curve asymptote, slope, I50, active and resting motor thresholds) showed no significant difference between pCF and controls.
Measures of intracortical inhibition (short-interval intracortical inhibition and cortical silent period metrics) showed no significant difference between pCF and controls.
pCF participants showed a trend towards slower visual reaction times in both biceps and first dorsal interosseous muscles, though this did not survive multiple-comparison correction.

Sensory attenuation during movement, short-latency afferent inhibition, and cutaneomuscular reflex components showed no significant differences between pCF and controls, arguing against sensory feedback disturbance as a contributor to fatigue.
Maximal grip strength was not significantly reduced in pCF, suggesting no deficit in force production for brief contractions.

Neuromuscular junction transmission efficacy (repetitive nerve stimulation) and intrinsic motoneuron excitability (peak firing rate, after-hyperpolarization) were not significantly different between pCF and controls.

Following a sustained maximal contraction, pCF subjects showed a greater reduction in electrically-evoked muscle twitch force than controls, indicating increased peripheral (muscle) fatigue, likely reflecting altered muscle energy metabolism.
Measures of motoneuron recruitment/de-recruitment (deltaF), reflecting descending neuromodulatory (serotonergic/noradrenergic) drive, showed no difference between pCF and controls.
Resting heart rate was significantly elevated in pCF subjects compared with controls, consistent with reduced vagal relative to sympathetic tone.
Tympanic temperature was modestly elevated in pCF compared with controls, though this did not survive multiple-comparison correction.
Heart rate variability (pNN50) was reduced in pCF subjects, consistent with reduced parasympathetic tone, though this did not survive multiple-comparison correction.
Habituation of the galvanic skin response to a loud sound was increased in pCF subjects, suggesting excessive sympathetic output, though this did not survive multiple-comparison correction.
Behavioural measures of subcortical inhibitory circuit function (temporal difference threshold and stop signal reaction time) showed no differences between pCF and controls.
Central activation, measuring the CNS's ability to voluntarily activate muscle maximally, was not different between pCF and controls at baseline or after fatiguing contraction.

The StartReact effect (speeding of reaction time by a startling sound) showed a trend to increase in the biceps of pCF subjects, likely driven by the baseline slowing of visual reaction time, but did not survive multiple-comparison correction and was absent in the FDI muscle.
The level of common cortical input to a motoneuron pool was not different between pCF and controls.
Blood oxygen saturation was significantly reduced in pCF subjects compared with controls, the most significant difference detected, though the absolute magnitude was small.

K-means clustering with gap analysis on the multivariate pCF measurements identified a single optimal cluster, suggesting dysregulations vary independently across individuals rather than forming discrete pCF subtypes.
A machine-learning classifier using an optimal set of six neurophysiological/behavioural features distinguished pCF from control participants with a mean accuracy of 70%.
pCF participants reported a moderate functional impact of fatigue on daily life, with a mean Fatigue Impact Scale score of 83 out of a maximum 160.
Fatigue severity (FIS score) did not correlate with time elapsed since SARS-CoV-2 infection.
One month after moderate-to-critical COVID-19 infection, peak VO2 was reduced in 100% of patients tested by CPET.
In 200 patients at 3 months post-COVID-19, only 62% had a normal first ventilatory threshold, half had VO2 peak below 85% predicted, and about a third had a peripheral limitation to exercise.

VO2 peak correlated with lower-limb muscle strength (measured by maximal leg extension test), and this association persisted after accounting for bed rest and weight loss, suggesting possible direct muscle toxicity from corticosteroids or the virus.

In a 35-patient study by Jahn et al., deconditioning was the retained mechanism of exercise limitation in 50% of patients, though a third were obese and all had received rehabilitation during hospitalization.

Combining CPET with exercise echocardiography using the Fick equation, COVID-19 patients showed lower arterial O2 content and arteriovenous O2 difference than controls, without a significant difference in absolute cardiac output, pointing to peripheral muscle impairment as the cause of reduced VO2.
In a Dutch retrospective study of 23 patients who required orotracheal intubation, mean VO2 peak reached only 57% of predicted value, and 70% had a peripheral muscular limitation.
The proportion of patients with reduced VO2 peak declined over time after COVID-19: 100% at 1 month, 56% at 6 months, 31% at 9 months, and 18% at 1 year for those with critical initial infection.
In 10 patients with persistent dyspnea and normal initial workup, CPET performed at ~3 months showed reduced VO2 peak in 80%, mainly attributed to exercise deconditioning.

In 41 symptomatic patients at 9 months, 58.5% had VO2 peak below 80% predicted despite normal PFTs, echocardiography, and chest CT, attributed mainly to muscular extraction or cardiovascular distribution defects.

In 114 patients with persistent dyspnea at 3 months (>90% previously intubated), hyperventilation syndrome, defined by elevated VE/VCO2 slope and elevated ventilatory equivalents at SV1, was diagnosed in 16% of patients, the second most common cause of limitation after deconditioning.
In a study of 10 mostly mild COVID-19 patients, hyperventilation syndrome was diagnosed in 6 based on Nijmegen score >23 and/or erratic ventilatory patterns during CPET.

In a Swiss study of 51 long COVID patients with persistent dyspnea, dysfunctional breathing was identified in 29.4%; these patients were significantly younger and had less severe initial infections than those with ventilatory limitation.
Using invasive Swan-Ganz catheterization during CPET, 2 of 7 patients showed mean pulmonary artery pressure above 30 mmHg on exercise, suggesting exercise-induced pulmonary hypertension.

In a 70-patient study, the persistent-dyspnea group had significantly higher blood ferritin, along with reduced VO2 peak, elevated VE/VCO2 slope, and reduced PetCO2 and O2 pulse, suggesting exercise-related vascular sequelae; D-dimer levels did not differ between groups.

A prospective study comparing CPET and echocardiography in COVID-19 patients versus controls found chronotropic incompetence during exercise in 75% of patients versus 8% of controls, along with a lower cardiac output and higher arteriovenous O2 difference at peak effort, suggesting cardiac dysautonomia with compensatory mechanisms.

Dorelli et al. reported ventilatory inefficiency (VE/VCO2 slope ≥32), suggestive of cardiac dysautonomia, in about 25% of a young cohort (patients >65 years were excluded), with a lower recovery heart rate in the ventilatory-inefficiency group but no difference in resting DLCO or peak VD/Vt.

The review notes that among suspected etiologies of post-COVID cardiac dysautonomia (hypovolemia, brainstem dysfunction, mast cell activation, autoimmunity), the autoimmune hypothesis may explain the female predominance reported in studies of this condition.

In 140 post-COVID-19 patients (median hospitalization 48 days, 40% intubated) undergoing ~3 weeks of rehabilitation, Barthel index improved from 55 to 95, SPPB from 4.2% to 66.7% predicted, and 6-minute walk distance from 47.7% to 68.1% predicted, all statistically significant.

In 28 previously hospitalized patients, 6-minute walk distance improved by +130 m after approximately 20 days of rehabilitation, with greater improvement in those who had required mechanical ventilation.

Comparing ICU survivors rehabilitated after COVID-19 versus non-COVID causes, both groups improved 6-minute walk distance after rehabilitation, but the gain was greater in the post-COVID-19 group (205±121 m vs 93±66 m), and greater improvement correlated with earlier initiation of rehabilitation after ICU discharge.

In Liu et al.'s study of 72 patients, those in the rehabilitation group (daily home exercises plus twice-weekly chest physiotherapy for 6 weeks) had significantly greater improvement in FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC, and DLCO than controls.

In 42 previously intubated patients, two weeks of inspiratory muscle training (threshold valve set at 50% of maximal inspiratory pressure) significantly improved dyspnea and pulmonary function test parameters compared to no training.
Several studies found no improvement in anxiety or depression (measured by HADS) after rehabilitation, despite significant gains in exercise and pulmonary function.

In 94 ICU-treated patients, health-related quality of life improved at 2 months after multidisciplinary rehabilitation but showed no further change between 2 and 12 months and remained impaired at 12 months, with new symptoms emerging that were absent at ICU discharge; obesity, active smoking, tracheostomy, and long ICU stay were associated with worse HRQoL.

Among 39 patients rehabilitated for persistent dyspnea after mild-to-moderate COVID-19, those needing rehabilitation beyond 3 months ('prolonged sequelae' group) had hyperventilation syndrome in 41% versus 0% in the comparison group, with a positive hyperventilation provocation test in 72% of the prolonged-sequelae group; this group also had more impaired quality of life despite normal 6-minute walk and PFTs.

In a historical precedent, Ong et al. (2004) found peak VO2 was impaired in 41% of ARDS survivors from the 2002-2004 SARS-CoV-1 epidemic at 3 months, with evidence suggesting muscle involvement from prolonged bed rest or corticosteroid-induced myopathy.
Gao et al. found VO2 peak was impaired in 100% of patients one month after moderate-to-critical COVID-19.

In a 200-patient cohort at 3 months post-COVID-19, only 62% had a normal first ventilatory threshold, VO2 peak was impaired (<85% predicted) in 50%, peripheral limitation was retained in about a third, and VO2 peak correlated with lower-limb muscle strength.

A study combining CPET with exercise echocardiography using the Fick equation found COVID-19 patients had lower arterial O2 content and reduced arteriovenous O2 difference versus controls, with no significant difference in absolute cardiac output, indicating peripheral muscular impairment as the driver of reduced VO2.
A Dutch retrospective study of 23 mechanically-ventilated COVID-19 survivors in rehabilitation found mean VO2 peak of only 57% predicted and peripheral muscular limitation in 70% of patients.
The proportion of long COVID patients with impaired VO2 peak declined over time: 100% at 1 month, 56% at 6 months, 31% at 9 months, and 18% at 1 year after infection.

Among 41 patients still symptomatic 9 months after infection with normal initial workup (PFTs, echocardiography, chest CT), 58.5% had a reduced VO2 peak (<80% predicted), attributed mainly to muscular deconditioning or cardiovascular distribution deficits.

It is hypothesized that SARS-CoV-2 causes inflammatory and micro-angiopathic lesions of the brainstem pre-Botzinger complex during acute infection, contributing to ventilatory instability underlying dysfunctional breathing.

In a study of 114 patients with persistent dyspnea at 3 months (>90% previously intubated), hyperventilation syndrome, defined by VE/VCO2 slope >40 and elevated ventilatory equivalents, was identified in 16% of patients, the second most common cause after deconditioning.
In a smaller study of 10 mostly mildly-affected COVID-19 patients, hyperventilation syndrome was diagnosed in 6, based on a Nijmegen score >23 and/or erratic ventilatory patterns on CPET.

A Swiss study of 51 long COVID patients with persistent dyspnea found dysfunctional breathing in 29.4% of patients, who were significantly younger and had less severe initial infections than those with ventilatory limitation; more than half (53%) of patients with mild-to-moderate initial infection had dysfunctional breathing.

Invasive Swan-Ganz catheter measurements during exercise in 7 long COVID patients revealed exercise-induced pulmonary hypertension (mean pulmonary artery pressure >30 mmHg) in 2 patients, one of whom had a low pulmonary capillary wedge pressure suggestive of thromboembolic disease.

In a study of 70 patients, those with persistent dyspnea after COVID-19 showed CPET signs of pulmonary vascular impairment (reduced VO2 peak, elevated VE/VCO2 slope, reduced PetCO2 at SV1, reduced O2 pulse) along with significantly higher serum ferritin than those without dyspnea, while D-dimer levels did not differ between groups.
D-dimer levels did not differ significantly between long COVID patients with versus without persistent dyspnea in this cohort.

A prospective study comparing CPET and echocardiography of COVID-19 patients versus controls found chronotropic incompetence during exercise in 75% of patients versus 8% of controls (p<0.001), associated with lower cardiac output and a greater arteriovenous O2 difference at peak exercise, suggesting a compensatory mechanism for cardiac dysautonomia.

Dorelli et al. found ventilatory inefficiency (VE/VCO2 slope ≥32), suggestive of cardiac dysautonomia, in about 25% of a young post-COVID-19 cohort (age >65 excluded), with lower heart-rate recovery in the affected group but no difference in resting DLCO or peak VD/Vt.

A multicenter study of 140 COVID-19 patients (median initial hospitalization 48 days, 40% intubated) showed significant improvement after ~3 weeks of rehabilitation on all three outcome measures: Barthel Index median rose from 55 to 95 (p=0.001), SPPB median from 4.2% to 66.7% predicted (p=0.001), and 6-minute walk distance from 47.7±18.9% to 68.1±15.3% predicted.

A comparative rehabilitation study of ICU survivors found significantly greater 6-minute walk distance gains in the post-COVID-19 group than in non-COVID-19 ICU patients (205±121 m vs 93±66 m, p<0.05), with improvement positively correlated with time from ICU discharge to rehabilitation start (r=-0.59, p=0.01), suggesting earlier rehabilitation yields greater benefit.

In Liu et al.'s controlled study of 72 patients, a 6-week home rehabilitation plus twice-weekly respiratory physiotherapy program produced significantly greater gains in FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC ratio, and DLCO compared to a control group (p<0.05).

In 42 previously intubated COVID-19 patients, two weeks of inspiratory muscle training (threshold valve set to 50% of maximal inspiratory pressure) significantly improved dyspnea and pulmonary function parameters compared to no training.

Several studies assessing rehabilitation impact on anxiety and depression via the HADS found no improvement in these psychological symptoms despite significant gains in exercise capacity and pulmonary function.

In 94 ICU-treated COVID-19 patients, HRQoL improved by 2 months post-rehabilitation but showed no further improvement between 2 and 12 months and remained impaired at 12 months, with new symptoms emerging; factors associated with worse HRQoL included obesity, active smoking, tracheostomy, and longer ICU stay.

In a targeted rehabilitation study of 39 patients with persistent dyspnea after mild-to-moderate infection, hyperventilation syndrome was diagnosed in 41% of those needing rehabilitation beyond 3 months versus 0% of those without prolonged functional sequelae, and ventilatory control retraining reduced the SHV rate and improved dyspnea and quality of life.

In a multicenter trial of 120 patients hospitalized for moderate-to-severe COVID-19 with persistent mMRC 2-3 dyspnea, 6 weeks of smartphone-based telerehabilitation produced greater 6-minute walk distance (MCID 50m), improved functional (but not mental) quality of life, better maximal voluntary ventilation, and reduced dyspnea versus no rehabilitation, with gains maintained at 7 months.
CSF effector memory CD4+ T cells (CD45RA−CD27−) were significantly lower in neuro-PASC patients compared with healthy volunteers.
CSF effector memory CD8+ T cells were significantly lower in neuro-PASC patients compared with healthy volunteers.
CSF B cell frequency (CD3−CD19+) was significantly increased in neuro-PASC patients versus healthy volunteers.
CSF antibody-secreting B cells (IgD−CD27high) were increased in neuro-PASC compared with healthy volunteers.
CSF NK cell frequency (CD3−CD56+) was increased in neuro-PASC compared with healthy volunteers.
The CD56 bright-dim ratio among NK cells was increased in neuro-PASC CSF compared with healthy volunteers, suggesting a shift toward more activated/regulatory NK subsets.
TIGIT expression on CSF CD8+ T cells was increased in neuro-PASC patients compared with healthy volunteers, suggesting T-cell exhaustion.
PD-L1 expression on monocytes was increased in both CSF and peripheral blood of neuro-PASC patients compared with healthy volunteers.

Plasma DHPG, a norepinephrine metabolite reflecting neuronal catecholamine turnover, was lower in neuro-PASC patients than healthy volunteers, and remained significant after excluding participants on drugs affecting catecholamine uptake.
Plasma DOPAC, a dopamine metabolite, was lower in neuro-PASC patients compared with healthy volunteers.
Baroreflex-cardiovagal gain was lower in neuro-PASC patients than in healthy volunteers, indicating impaired parasympathetic baroreflex function.
Time-domain (SDNN, CVNN) and high-frequency power heart rate variability measures were lower in neuro-PASC patients compared with healthy volunteers at supine rest.
During supine rest, neuro-PASC patients had higher mean heart rate and systolic blood pressure than healthy volunteers.
During head-up tilt, TPR increased more in neuro-PASC patients than in healthy volunteers, indicating enhanced vasoconstriction that was independent of augmented norepinephrine release.
Mean skin temperature was lower in neuro-PASC patients than healthy volunteers, both during supine rest and throughout head-up tilting.
Despite autonomic abnormalities, plasma norepinephrine and epinephrine levels rose progressively with tilting but did not differ between neuro-PASC and healthy volunteers at baseline or during tilt.
CSF levels of catechols did not differ between neuro-PASC patients and healthy volunteers.
Increased frequencies of PD-1-expressing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in CSF correlated with worse (lower) self-reported cognitive function scores in neuro-PASC patients.
Effector-memory CD4+ T cell frequency correlated with worse cognitive function scores and higher fatigue scores within the neuro-PASC cohort.

The most common persistent symptoms in the neuro-PASC cohort were fatigue and cognitive difficulties, with half of participants showing mild cognitive impairment (MoCA <26) and short-term memory affected in all participants.
Microsmia (reduced smell) was detected by UPSIT in two-thirds of neuro-PASC participants, ranging from mild to severe, though no patient had complete anosmia.

PROMIS questionnaires showed markedly elevated fatigue scores and reduced cognitive function ability scores as the most prominent abnormalities, whereas pain intensity scores were not elevated in the group.
Unique intrathecal oligoclonal bands were detected in the CSF of 3 of 12 (25%) neuro-PASC patients, none of whom had a prior history of disabling systemic infection.

Serum antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid, spike, and RBD proteins were detectable in most neuro-PASC participants months after infection, but CSF antibody responses were inconsistent and did not correlate with any clinical measures.

Brain MRI did not reveal structural brainstem or olfactory pathway abnormalities attributable to COVID-19 in the neuro-PASC cohort; one case of bilateral olfactory bulb hypoplasia was judged to be congenital rather than acquired.
Long COVID patients had a lower percent predicted peak VO2 than non-COVID controls with undifferentiated dyspnea on exertion.
Only a small minority of long COVID patients reached normal predicted aerobic capacity on exercise testing.
Chronotropic incompetence during exercise testing was more frequent in long COVID patients than in controls, suggesting autonomic impairment.
Low peak systolic blood pressure during exercise was more common in long COVID patients than controls, consistent with autonomic impairment.
Long COVID patients had a slightly lower peak heart rate and a borderline lower heart rate reserve than controls.
Peak minute ventilation was lower in long COVID patients than controls, likely reflecting the higher proportion of females in the long COVID group rather than a specific pulmonary abnormality.

Breathing reserve, minimum oxygen saturation, and ventilatory efficiency (V̇E/V̇CO2 nadir) were similar between long COVID patients and controls, indicating mild and non-distinctive pulmonary abnormalities.
Exercise-induced ST-T wave abnormalities were rare and did not differ between long COVID patients and controls.

The frequency of premature ventricular contractions during exercise testing was similar between long COVID patients and controls, with all ventricular tachycardia episodes limited to short 3-5 beat runs in both groups.
Dizziness, lightheadedness, and presyncope during exercise testing were significantly more common in long COVID patients than in controls, consistent with autonomic involvement.
Lower extremity neuromuscular or orthopedic complaints during exercise testing were reported more frequently by long COVID patients than by controls.
General fatigue as a limiting symptom during the CPET was reported more often by controls than by long COVID patients.
There was a non-significant trend towards more frequent reporting of exertional dyspnea during CPET among long COVID patients compared to controls.
Long COVID patients with autonomic abnormalities had lower percent predicted peak VO2 than those without autonomic abnormalities.
In the non-COVID dyspnea control group, patients with autonomic abnormalities also had lower percent predicted peak VO2 than those without, indicating this association is not specific to long COVID.

Echocardiography in a majority of long COVID patients showed normal left ventricular ejection fraction and only minor valve abnormalities, arguing against a cardiac cause for reduced exercise capacity.
Fatigue and dyspnea in general daily activity were the most frequently reported long COVID symptoms in this cohort.

Mean Chalder Fatigue Scale (CFQ-11) score decreased significantly by 4.5 points at 7 days and 5.5 points at 3 months after a 3-day concentrated rehabilitation program, exceeding the minimal clinically important difference.
The proportion of patients meeting criteria for severe fatigue decreased from 61% at baseline to 26% at 7 days and 18% at 3 months post-intervention.
The proportion of employed participants on sick leave decreased from 63% at baseline to 43% at 3-month follow-up.
Self-reported functional level (VAS, relative to pre-COVID function) increased from 53% at baseline to 63% at 7 days and 69% at 3 months.
WSAS score decreased from a mean of 21.9 at baseline by 6.9 points at 3 months, a reduction larger than the minimal clinically important difference.
Submaximal exercise capacity and lower extremity strength, measured by the 30-second sit-to-stand test and stair climbing test, improved significantly from baseline to 3-month follow-up.

Peak oxygen uptake per kilogram body weight increased significantly from baseline to 3-month follow-up, with patients who had severe fatigue at baseline showing significantly larger improvement than others.
Dyspnea-12 total score decreased significantly by 3.3 points from baseline to 3-month follow-up, within the range of the minimal clinically important difference.
The proportion of patients scoring ≥1 on the mMRC dyspnea scale decreased from 69.7% at baseline to 57.7% at 3-month follow-up.
Lung function parameters (FEV1% predicted, FVC% predicted, FEV1/FVC, DLCO% predicted) showed no significant change from baseline to 3-month follow-up and remained within normal limits.

None of the investigated baseline factors (gender, age, time since infection, psychiatric illness, functional level, V̇O2peak/kg) significantly modified the reduction in fatigue over time, suggesting the intervention benefits patients broadly.
The 3-day concentrated micro-choice based rehabilitation program showed no adverse events, including no indications of post-exertional malaise, with a 97.4% completion rate among 78 participants.

The results of this rehabilitation program contrast with a previous cross-sectional study reporting that under 1% of long COVID patients benefited from increased physical activity while 75% experienced symptom worsening; here, fatigue, functioning, and exercise capacity improved with no harmful effects.

At baseline, fatigue was reported by 99% and dyspnea by 63% of participants, with a mean symptom duration of 10.2 months before rehabilitation; 21% were obese, 18% had been hospitalized during acute infection, and 4% required intensive care.

Compared with a cohort of home-isolated COVID-19 patients from the same region, participants referred for rehabilitation had markedly higher fatigue prevalence (96% vs 30%) and severe fatigue prevalence (61% vs 7%), indicating greater baseline severity and making spontaneous recovery before enrollment unlikely.
60% (53/89) of hospitalized COVID-19 survivors reported persistent neurocognitive symptoms meeting the study's WHO-based neuro-PASC criteria at 6-month follow-up.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom both initially and at 6 months, with 45% of participants reporting fatigue at both timepoints.
Confusion emerged as a new symptom at 6 months in 22% of patients despite being absent at 1 month.
A longer hospital stay was significantly more common among patients who developed persistent neurocognitive symptoms.
Need for intubation during index hospitalization was associated with over five-fold increased odds of persistent neurocognitive symptoms at 6 months in univariate analysis.
In-hospital delirium during index hospitalization was associated with over five-fold increased odds of persistent neurocognitive symptoms at 6 months in univariate analysis.
Patients with persistent neurological symptoms had significantly worse PROMIS Cognitive Function scores at both 1- and 6-months compared to those without persistent symptoms.
Patients with persistent neurological symptoms had significantly worse PROMIS Cognitive Function Abilities scores at both 1- and 6-months compared to those without persistent symptoms.
Baseline PROMIS fatigue scores and HADS anxiety/depression subscale scores did not significantly differ between patients with and without persistent neurological symptoms.
Female sex was associated with substantially increased odds of persistent cognitive function disturbance, both in univariate (OR 7.11) and multivariate-adjusted (OR 5.4) analyses.
Higher baseline HADS-Anxiety subscale scores were associated with increased odds of persistent cognitive function disturbance in univariate analysis.
In multivariate analysis, higher baseline HADS-Anxiety subscale score was an independent predictor of persistent neurocognitive symptoms (neuro-PASC).

Each additional year of age was associated with decreased odds of persistent neurocognitive symptoms, persistent cognitive function disturbance, and persistent cognitive ability disturbance at 6 months.
Female sex was associated with increased odds of persistent cognitive ability disturbance in univariate analysis.
Hispanic ethnicity was associated with markedly increased odds of persistent cognitive ability disturbance in both univariate and multivariate analyses.
Higher baseline HADS-Depression subscale score was associated with increased odds of persistent cognitive ability disturbance.
Perceived socioeconomic status of 'not enough' resources was associated with a markedly increased risk of neuro-PASC in multivariate analysis compared to 'comfortable' status.
History of renal disease was unexpectedly associated with decreased odds of developing persistent neurocognitive symptoms in multivariate analysis.
No significant differences in the proportion of pre-existing comorbidities were observed between patients with and without persistent neurocognitive symptoms.

None of the COVID-19 treatments administered during hospitalization (remdesivir, convalescent plasma, therapeutic anticoagulation, dexamethasone, monoclonal antibodies, ivermectin, tocilizumab, or others) were associated with neuro-PASC.
Vaccination status at admission and rate of ICU admission were similar between patients with and without persistent neurocognitive symptoms.
The number of acute-phase COVID-19 symptoms was not significantly different between patients who did and did not later develop persistent neurocognitive symptoms.

The authors developed Fading Fatigue, a client-server self-management app offering a daily energy planner, well-being documentation aid, and progress view to support Long-COVID patients with fatigue in energy management after professional-guided therapy.
Fatigue was identified as the most prevalent symptom among individuals with Long-COVID.
AXA1125 treatment significantly reduced total fatigue scores (CFQ-11, Likert) compared to placebo after 4 weeks of treatment.
AXA1125 significantly reduced physical fatigue scores compared to placebo at Day 28.
AXA1125 significantly reduced mental fatigue scores compared to placebo at Day 28.

AXA1125 did not significantly improve post-exercise phosphocreatine recovery rate time constant (τPCr), the primary study endpoint reflecting mitochondrial oxidative capacity, compared to placebo after 4 weeks.

Baseline post-exertional τPCr was markedly elevated and highly variable across the Long COVID cohort compared with previously reported healthy reference values, indicating impaired mitochondrial oxidative capacity.
In the AXA1125 group, improvement in pre-exertional physical fatigue score correlated positively with improvement in τPCr, an association not observed in the placebo group.
AXA1125 showed a non-significant trend toward reduced post-exertional peak serum lactate compared with placebo.

Within the AXA1125 arm, patients who achieved improvement in physical fatigue severity category ('responders') showed significantly greater reduction in post-exertional τPCr than non-responders; this difference was not seen in the placebo arm.
Within the AXA1125 arm, fatigue 'responders' showed a significant increase in 6-minute walk test distance at Day 28 compared with non-responders; no such difference was seen in the placebo arm.
Physical and mental fatigue severity category improved between baseline and Day 28 in 71% and 33% of AXA1125-treated patients, respectively, compared with 20% and 5% in the placebo arm.
No significant correlation was found between change in pre-exertional total fatigue score and change in post-exertional peak lactate level in either the AXA1125 or placebo group.

More patients on AXA1125 reported treatment-emergent adverse events than on placebo, but events were predominantly mild and gastrointestinal, with one unrelated severe syncope event and no discontinuations or deaths.

AXA1125, composed of five amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine, arginine, glutamine) and N-acetylcysteine, is reported to increase β-oxidation, improve mitochondrial function, and decrease oxidative stress in a preclinical NASH model, providing rationale for its use in fatigue-predominant Long COVID.
Just over half of nonhospitalized subjects infected during the Omicron wave reported at least one long COVID symptom 6-12 months after infection.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom among the cohort.
Female gender was identified as a risk factor for long COVID.
Middle age was identified as a risk factor for long COVID.
Obesity was identified as a risk factor for long COVID.
Presence of comorbidities was identified as a risk factor for long COVID.
Receiving COVID-19 vaccination after infection was associated with increased risk of long COVID.
Having a greater number of acute-phase symptoms was associated with increased risk of developing long COVID.
Presenting with fatigue, chest tightness, headache, or diarrhea during the acute stage of infection was associated with increased risk of long COVID.
Receiving three or more vaccine doses was not associated with a lower risk of long COVID.
Among patients with at least three vaccine doses, there was no significant difference in long COVID risk between those who received CoronaVac versus BNT162b2 vaccines.

Latent class analysis of patient-reported outcome measures identified three distinct long COVID phenotypes: Class 1 (fatigue and dyspnea), Class 2 (anxiety and depression), and Class 3 (fatigue, dyspnea, anxiety, and depression).

Compared to the other classes, patients in Class 3 (fatigue, dyspnea, anxiety, depression) were more likely to be female, treated as outpatients during acute illness, and have pre-existing asthma, COPD, and depression.
At 3 months after symptom onset, Class 3 had a significantly lower EQ5D VAS (quality of life) score than Class 1 and Class 2.
At 6 months after symptom onset, Class 3 continued to have a lower EQ5D VAS compared to Classes 1 and 2.
There was no significant difference in EQ5D VAS between Class 1 (fatigue/dyspnea) and Class 2 (anxiety/depression) at either 3 or 6 months.
EQ5D VAS improved significantly over time (3 to 6 months) for Class 1 (fatigue/dyspnea) and Class 3 (fatigue, dyspnea, anxiety, depression), but not for Class 2.

Although fatigue and dyspnea scores improved over time in Classes 1 and 3, the correlation between these symptom changes and the change in EQ5D VAS was weak, suggesting other factors drive QoL improvement.
None of the long COVID phenotypic classes were associated with DLCO in either unadjusted or adjusted (age, sex, smoking history) analyses.
The overall long COVID cohort had a markedly reduced baseline quality of life compared to age-matched population norms.
Over half of the long COVID cohort experienced a clinically meaningful change in quality of life between 3 and 6 months, with more patients improving than declining.
Fatigue and dyspnea were the most commonly reported abnormal patient-reported outcome measures in the long COVID cohort at baseline.
Acute SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with increased postoperative mortality and pulmonary complications that persist for around 7 weeks after infection.
Patients with COVID-19 symptoms persisting beyond 7 weeks have a significantly higher postoperative mortality rate than those whose symptoms resolved.
Approximately 1 in 33 people in the UK report persistent symptoms following COVID-19 infection, termed long COVID.
NICE no longer recommends graded exercise therapy for ME/CFS patients due to minimal evidence of symptom improvement, and many patients report it worsens their condition.
Elevated interleukin-1β levels correlate positively with long COVID symptoms measured 8 months after initial infection.
Elevated interleukin-6 levels correlate positively with long COVID symptoms measured 8 months after initial infection.
Elevated tumour necrosis factor α levels correlate positively with long COVID symptoms measured 8 months after initial infection.
Elevated interferon levels correlate positively with long COVID symptoms measured 8 months after initial infection.
Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 proteins has been noted in long COVID sufferers, suggested to potentially drive an ongoing chronic proinflammatory process.
Immune dysregulation in long COVID may lead to reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus, a mechanism also implicated in ME/CFS.
A persistently altered gut microbiome has been noted in long COVID patients, mirroring gut dysbiosis described in ME/CFS.
Endothelial dysfunction with microcirculatory changes has been reported in both long COVID and ME/CFS, potentially causing hypoperfusion and contributing to exercise intolerance.

Long COVID patients with ongoing dyspnoea up to 3 months after non-critical COVID-19 had lower forced vital capacity, forced expiratory volume in 1 second, and diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide compared to those without dyspnoea.
Long COVID patients with dyspnoea had reduced functional capacity compared to non-breathless counterparts, as measured by the 6-minute walk test.
25% of 150 long COVID patients with no prior hospitalisation or pre-existing cardiovascular disease had echocardiographic abnormalities at 4-12 weeks post-infection.
There was a statistically significant correlation between echocardiographic abnormalities, the number of long COVID symptoms reported, and worse self-reported functional status.

Long COVID patients with dyspnoea and fatigue can have normal pulmonary function tests and echocardiography, yet cardiopulmonary exercise testing reveals reduced peak aerobic capacity and impaired oxygen extraction almost a year after infection.
Postoperative venous thromboembolism is more common in patients with recent COVID-19, with an even greater risk in those with ongoing COVID symptoms, even beyond 7 weeks post-infection.
Previous COVID-19 infection increases the risk of pulmonary embolism for up to 110 days post-infection.
Expert consensus suggests patients up to 6 months post-COVID-19 infection should receive pharmacological thromboprophylaxis postoperatively, though the appropriate duration is unspecified.

Preoperative exercise programmes before major surgery can reduce postoperative morbidity in general surgical populations, contrasting with the lack of benefit (and possible harm) of graded exercise therapy in ME/CFS.
Long COVID patients with headache were significantly younger (median 37 years) than those without headache (median 42 years).
Female proportion did not significantly differ between the Headache group (56%) and Headache-free group (54%).

Persistent fatigue, neurological complications, and cough after COVID-19 infection were of shorter duration in participants who were physically active during the pandemic compared with inactive participants.
General and symptom-specific long COVID were less likely in participants who remained physically active during the pandemic.
