Social determinants of health and distrust rooted in systemic racism were reported to complicate long COVID symptom management among Black American participants.
Long COVID was reported to affect participants' interpersonal relationships.

The authors recommend that clinicians prioritize eliminating patient exposure to discrimination, implicit bias, and microaggressions when caring for long COVID patients, particularly given the difficulty of objectively quantifying symptoms like pain and fatigue.

Among mental health-related diseases analyzed in Korea's national relevance index study, autism had a relatively low five-year weighted average relevance index of 57.1%, indicating that a substantial proportion of patients with autism sought care in medical institutions outside their home region.
Whole exome sequencing identified disease-causing variants in 66 of 209 patients referred for neurological disorders, an overall diagnostic yield of 32%.
Diagnostic yield of WES varied substantially by neurological disease subtype, ranging from 65% in spastic paraplegia to 15% in dystonia.

Eight patients with autism spectrum disorder were included in the neurodevelopmental disorder cohort undergoing WES, alongside 20 patients with intellectual disability and 23 with seizures, after FMR1 expansion and CNVs had been excluded; diagnostic rates in this NDD cohort were similar to those of the movement disorder cohort.
A custom WES gene panel comprising 1002 genes associated with autism spectrum disorder was used to prioritize candidate variants when analyzing exome data from ASD patients.

A de novo NIPBL variant (rs141976717), which appeared to be a likely benign VUS based on gnomAD frequency and in silico predictors, was reclassified as probably pathogenic after being identified de novo in a patient with growth retardation, intellectual disability, and clinical features of Cornelia de Lange syndrome.
The proportion of variants of unknown significance (VUS) was similar across most clinical groups in the cohort, differing only in patients with epilepsy.

A copy-number deletion involving the PMP22 gene was detected by WES-based analysis in a patient with clinical suspicion of hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies, illustrating improving CNV detection from WES data.

The COL2A1 c.3641delC frameshift mutation was associated with more severe ocular phenotypes, with the three affected monoallelic family members showing high myopia (greater than -11.00 D) and retinal findings such as tears and lattice degeneration.

The COL2A1 c.3853G>T missense mutation (p.Asp1285Tyr) was associated with mild ocular findings but notable joint abnormalities, including early-onset osteoarthritis requiring bilateral hip arthroplasty and multiple epiphyseal dysplasia.

A patient (III-7) inheriting both the maternal c.3853G>T and paternal c.3641delC COL2A1 mutations (biallelic heterozygosity) displayed severe combined ocular and systemic Stickler syndrome findings, including micrognathia, cleft palate, sensorineural hearing loss, and hip/femoral dysplasia; this is reported as the first documented biallelic COL2A1 case.

The patient with biallelic heterozygous COL2A1 mutations presented with severe non-verbal autism and global developmental delay, findings not typically seen in Stickler syndrome, and the authors note an unclear role for COL2A1 in brain development.

Both mutations in this family occurred in exon 51 near the C-terminus of the triple helical domain, a location commonly associated with milder Stickler Syndrome type I compared with mutations near the N-terminus.

A prior study (Zhang et al.) found that Stickler syndrome phenotype severity, graded as mild, severe, or lethal, was similar across nonsense, frameshift, and missense COL2A1 mutation types, without specifically distinguishing ocular versus joint manifestations.

A mouse model confirmed Col2a1 expression in the vitreous with weaker expression in the postnatal cornea, ciliary body, iris, lens, retina, choroid, and sclera, and Col2a1 was down-regulated in Col2a1+/- adult mice across all of these tissues.

In the largest reported case series of pediatric Stickler Syndrome type I patients with secondary infantile-onset glaucoma, all patients required multiple intraocular pressure-lowering surgeries and three eyes became phthisical in the presence of retinal detachment.
A previously reported case of biallelic heterozygous COL11A1 mutations (in trans) resulted in retinal atrophy and severe hearing loss.

A specific COL2A1 missense mutation (c.823C>T), located earlier in the coding region than the mutations in this family, has been reported as its own distinct entity causing isolated early-onset osteoarthritis without other Stickler features.
Additional COL2A1 mutations (c.2503C>T and c.2032G>A) have been identified in multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, with one affected family also exhibiting myopia and deafness.
The patient's CIPA was caused by an insertion mutation at exon 8 and a missense mutation at exon 10 of the NTRK1 gene.
Loss of pain sensation and protective response in CIPA leads to recurrent Charcot arthropathy affecting the spine and joints.
Posterior corpectomy of L2-L3 with mesh cage reconstruction and pedicle screw fusion from T12 to L5 initially corrected the patient's lumbar kyphosis and restored full motor strength.
Broad removal of damaged vertebrae with reconstruction using an over-height mesh cage was associated with increased risk of hardware migration in CIPA patients with Charcot spine.
The reported patient and six other CIPA patients in the literature developed adjacent segment disease proximal or distal to fusion sites after spinal stabilization.

Successive pedicle screw loosening with inward migration compressed the patient's spinal canal, causing severe incomplete paralysis, which was hypothesized to relate to osteoporosis and delayed bone reconstruction in CIPA.
A prior study showed that NTRK1 mutation can cause B-cell defects due to failure of cytoskeleton formation and MAP kinase activation, suggesting an immunodeficiency risk in CIPA patients.

Animal studies show NGF/NTRK1 signaling is critical for vascularization and endochondral bone ossification; disturbance of the pathway results in impaired bone growth, reduced bone mineral density, and reduced bone volume.

Studies in murine fracture models show conflicting results: NGF/NTRK1 inhibition increased fracture callus size without significantly altering overall bone bridging in some studies, while another study found that neutralizing NTRK1 antibodies did not interfere with bone healing.
Whole-exome sequencing identified an NTRK1 mutation associated with osteogenesis imperfecta in a human genetic study.
Ex vivo osteoblast analyses implicated NTRK1 as a player in NF-κB signaling relevant to bone metabolism and mineralization.
Bisphosphonate treatment should be used cautiously in CIPA patients because it has been shown to lower bone turnover and increase the risk of new fractures.
Teriparatide, an anabolic bone agent, might help induce bone formation in CIPA patients but carries a risk of osteosarcoma in younger patients.
The authors recommend 360° long-segment spinal fusion for CIPA patients with Charcot spine to reduce the risk of adjacent segment disease, though pedicle screw loosening may still occur.
Radiological examinations revealed severe osteoporosis in vertebral and multiple limb bones of the patient, likely a direct clinical complication of CIPA.

POU3F3 variants, mostly de novo, cause a developmental disorder characterized by developmental delay (especially speech), behavioral difficulties, psychiatric comorbidities, hypotonia and dysmorphic features.
Autism, hearing loss, ophthalmological anomalies, and dysmorphisms were more commonly observed in individuals carrying truncating POU3F3 variants compared to those with missense variants.
Epilepsy was observed exclusively in individuals with missense POU3F3 variants and not in those with truncating variants.
Joint hypermobility was reported as an additional clinical feature among individuals with POU3F3-related disorder.
Gastrointestinal comorbidities were reported as additional clinical features in the POU3F3-related disorder cohort.
Sleep disturbances were noted as an additional feature in individuals with POU3F3-related disorder.
Autism was more frequently observed in individuals carrying truncating POU3F3 variants compared to those with missense variants.
Hearing loss was more frequently observed in individuals with truncating POU3F3 variants than those with missense variants.
Ophthalmological anomalies were more common among individuals carrying truncating POU3F3 variants relative to those with missense variants.
Joint hypermobility was reported as an additional feature in some individuals with POU3F3-related disorder.
Sleep disturbances were reported as an additional clinical feature among individuals with POU3F3-related disorder.
The majority of POU3F3 variants identified in the cohort arose de novo, with only one inherited from an affected parent.
During early reward anticipation, CNV amplitude was significantly larger in the autism group than in the low-autistic-traits group.
During reward reception, pupillary constrictions were significantly larger in the autism group compared to the low-autistic-traits group.
Behavioral reward responsiveness, measured as accuracy-corrected reaction time, did not differ significantly between the autism, high-autistic-traits, and low-autistic-traits groups.

Across reaction times, ERPs, and pupil sizes, there was no significant interaction between group (ASC/HAQ/LAQ) and reward-type condition, with strong Bayesian evidence favoring models without this interaction.
Across the whole sample, P3 amplitude during reward reception was largest for social feedback, intermediate for monetary feedback, and smallest for neutral feedback.
Across the whole sample, CNV during early anticipation was larger for social and monetary cues than for neutral cues.
Across the whole sample, pupil dilation during both early and late reward anticipation was larger for social cues than for neutral cues.
Autistic trait levels (AQ score) were positively correlated with social anxiety traits across participants.
Higher autistic trait levels were associated with stronger avoidance-motivated behaviour (Behavioural Inhibition System) relative to approach-motivated behaviour (Behavioural Approach System).

In dimensional analyses across all participants, higher AQ scores linearly predicted enhanced neuronal (CNV) responses in early anticipation and enhanced pupillary responses in reception, without interacting with reward condition.

Despite equal or enhanced physiological reward responses, autistic participants gave lower self-reported ratings of the motivational and rewarding value of social and monetary stimuli than the comparison groups.

SPN amplitude (late anticipation) was positively correlated with CNV amplitude (early anticipation) and negatively correlated with P3 amplitude (reception), indicating internal consistency across ERP reward-processing phases.

Pupil size during reward reception was negatively correlated with pupil size during early anticipation, indicating that greater anticipatory dilation was associated with greater subsequent constriction upon reception.
Exploratory analyses found that older age was associated with diminished ERP responses in the late anticipation and reception phases.
Exploratory analyses found that females exhibited larger pupil dilation responses during late anticipation than males.
Groups did not differ in self-reported general motivation or sense of agency during the task, though reward type was rated as more important by participants with higher autistic traits.
In a cohort of 194 infants, those with nocturnal rhythms at 4 months of age showed disturbed establishment of sleep-wake rhythms by 10 months of age.
A survey of healthy Japanese children found that 60% experienced night-time crying, most of whom self-soothed back to sleep.
Sleep disturbances and night-time awakenings at one year of age were reported to correlate with signs of ASD at two years of age.
A population-based cohort study analysed the association between sleep disorders in infants and later ASD.
An association was found between the most common ASD symptoms and sleep disorders.
In an Indian survey, 93% of carers of ASD infants reported sleep problems and 95% reported bedtime resistance.

In the authors' retrospective study of 52 children with neurodevelopmental disorders (18 with ASD), those who distinguished day from night at 3-4 months had significantly higher rates of no night-time crying, good sleep-wake rhythm at one year, and good early sleep rhythm compared with those who did not distinguish day and night.
Very low-dose levodopa therapy (0.5 mg/kg/day) reduced night-time crying and awakenings in patients with ASD or Rett syndrome, suggested to ameliorate dopamine receptor hypersensitivity.
Using the SWRISS sleep-rhythm analysis tool, 80.3% of 66 ASD patients presented with sleep disturbances.

Among 53 ASD patients with sleep problems analysed by SWRISS, 64.1% showed irregular sleep rhythms, 3.4% showed free-running rhythms, and 18.9% showed frequent night-time waking, with decreased amplitude of the sleep-wake cycle.
Children with ASD have been reported to show a delayed melatonin phase as part of the pathophysiology of ASD-related sleep disorders.
Long-term melatonin treatment for sleep problems in neurodevelopmental disorders in Japan has been reported to improve not only sleep but also behavioural problems.

In a SWRISS analysis of 13 patients with Rett syndrome, 9 (69.2%) could not stay awake during the daytime despite sleeping enough at night, suggesting decreased brainstem aminergic neuron activity, and their caregivers noted hypotonia and poor feeding.
25-50% of children and adolescents with ADHD have trouble falling asleep, insomnia, night waking, and hypersomnia.
When children with ADHD received an extended night of sleep, inhibitory control (go/no-go task performance) improved by over 13% from baseline.
Children with ADHD were reported to predominantly exhibit more body movements during sleep than comparators.
25% of patients with hypersomnia have ADHD, and 22% of patients with ADHD have hypersomnia.
A small dose of aripiprazole has been reported to be effective against shortened sleep duration in hypersomnia and also exerts antidepressant effects.
Children with Down syndrome showed a high rate of daytime sleepiness combined with sleep-disordered breathing.
Sleep and behaviour problems improved after tonsillectomy in a child with ADHD.

Iron and dopamine metabolism have been implicated in restless legs syndrome, with treatment targeting a serum ferritin level of at least 50 µg/mL, and a single nightly dose of iron may dramatically improve the condition.
Iron has also been reported to be effective for neurodevelopmental disorders such as ASD, ADHD, and associated sleep problems.
Preschool children with irregular sleep rhythms showed problematic behaviours such as poor attention, impulsiveness, and anxiety.
Sleep time at four months of age was later than at one-and-a-half and three years of age, an effect attributed to the mother's sleep behaviour.
The sleep rhythm at four months affects establishment of the later sleep-wake rhythm and can be improved through intervention.
Irregular sleep rhythms in one-year-olds significantly correlated with poor finger-pointing, apathy, and emotional and behavioural problems.
Late sleep time and inability to draw triangles in five-year-old children had a significantly higher odds ratio, linking sleep deprivation to disintegration of higher cognitive function.

A case report of a nine-month-old boy with moodiness and developmental delay showed improvements in sleep rhythm, mood swings, and developmental delay after two weeks of a sleep-hygiene intervention (reduced night feedings, earlier morning waking, increased daytime social interaction).
Restless legs syndrome in children has been linked to iron and dopamine metabolism, with treatment aimed at raising serum ferritin to at least 50 µg/mL.

A single nightly dose of iron may dramatically improve restless legs syndrome, and iron has also been reported effective for neurodevelopmental disorders such as ASD and ADHD as well as sleep problems.

Konofal reported that children with ADHD show bedtime resistance, difficulty falling asleep, sleep apnoea, and restless legs syndrome, with sleep quality closely related to daytime sleepiness and concentration.

In experimental studies of adolescents with ADHD, extending night sleep improved inhibitory control on a go/no-go task by over 13% from baseline, while shorter sleep duration decreased continuous performance test scores.
Nakatani reported that children with ADHD predominantly exhibit more body movements during sleep than others, offering insight into ADHD sleep pathophysiology.
Hypersomnia and ADHD frequently co-occur, with 25% of hypersomnia patients also having ADHD and 22% of ADHD patients also having hypersomnia.
A small dose of aripiprazole was reported effective against shortened sleep duration in hypersomnia and also exerted antidepressant effects.
Carter reported a high rate of daytime sleepiness combined with sleep-disordered breathing in children with Down syndrome.
Sleep and behaviour problems improved after tonsillectomy in a child with ADHD.
Suzuki reported that irregular sleep rhythms in one-year-olds significantly correlated with poor finger-pointing, apathy, and emotional and behavioural problems.
In five-year-old children, late sleep time and inability to draw triangles had a significantly higher odds ratio, linking sleep deprivation to disintegration of higher cognitive function.
A five-year-old girl's auditory hypersensitivity completely improved after her bedtime was moved earlier from 11 p.m. to 9 p.m., illustrating the impact of sleep on sensory symptoms.
Shinkoda found that infants' sleep time at four months of age was later than at one-and-a-half and three years, an effect attributed to the mother's own sleep behaviour.
Adachi found that the sleep rhythm at four months of age affects establishment of the later sleep-wake rhythm and that this could be improved through intervention.

A large one-year Finnish survey found that infants with slower sleep-wake rhythm development had later sleep onset, more difficulty settling to sleep, frequent night waking, shorter sleep periods, and irregular circadian rhythms.

Use of the smartphone Nenne Navi app, which supports reciprocal interaction between caregivers and paediatric sleep experts, succeeded in improving night-time sleep duration and reducing night-time awakenings.
Night-time media use and light exposure decrease melatonin levels, which fails to improve sleep rhythms and contributes to abnormal sleep-wake rhythms in children.
A 32-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder developed serotonin syndrome after only four days of low-dose sertraline (50 mg) monotherapy for depression.
Physical exam revealed bilateral upper extremity tremors, ocular clonus with lateral eye movement, and inducible clonus in the right ankle, meeting Hunter's criteria for serotonin syndrome.
Elevated whole blood serotonin (hyperserotonemia) is present in more than 25% of children with autism spectrum disorder and was the first identified biomarker in ASD.
The authors hypothesize that baseline hyperserotonergic state in ASD patients could be a risk factor predisposing them to serotonin syndrome with SSRI monotherapy at therapeutic doses.
The patient's serotonin syndrome symptoms resolved after IV fluids, potassium repletion, and IV lorazepam 1 mg, with discontinuation of sertraline recommended at discharge.

Cyproheptadine, a serotonin and histamine receptor antagonist, is recommended for serotonin syndrome patients who do not improve with benzodiazepines and supportive care, though this is based on anecdote rather than clinical trials.

A Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability score of 7 (probable) and a probable/likely rating from the WHO-UMC causality assessment system both supported sertraline as the cause of the patient's serotonin syndrome.

Inflammatory joint disease was more frequently the final diagnosis in patients whose rheumatic disease onset followed SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with those whose onset followed COVID-19 vaccination.
Polymyalgia rheumatica was diagnosed more frequently in patients whose rheumatic disease onset followed COVID-19 vaccination than in those whose onset followed SARS-CoV-2 infection.
The proportion of patients diagnosed with connective tissue disease did not differ between post-COVID-19 and postvaccine cohorts.
The proportion of patients diagnosed with vasculitis did not differ between post-COVID-19 and postvaccine cohorts.
Within the inflammatory joint disease subgroup, psoriatic arthritis was diagnosed more frequently in postvaccine than post-COVID-19 patients.

New-onset acrosyndrome (e.g., Raynaud's-type or chilblain-like microvascular skin changes) within the connective tissue disease subgroup was more prevalent after SARS-CoV-2 infection than after vaccination.

Patients with post-infectious or post-vaccine inflammatory joint disease showed a favorable response to first-line treatment, with both cohorts achieving roughly a 30% reduction in disease activity from baseline.
Patients with post-infectious or post-vaccine PMR showed marked improvement in disease activity after first-line therapy, with PMR-AS decreasing about 70-74% from baseline.
Follow-up duration was significantly shorter in post-COVID-19 PMR patients than postvaccine PMR patients, with no other significant differences between the groups.
The mean delay between exposure (COVID-19 diagnosis or vaccine administration) and onset of rheumatic manifestations did not differ between the two cohorts.

A subset of patients under age 50 (six postvaccine, one post-COVID-19) presented with a PMR-like clinical picture with elevated inflammatory markers and steroid responsiveness and were classified as PMR despite atypical age.
Peripheral spondyloarthritis was the single most frequent specific diagnosis within the inflammatory joint disease category in both post-COVID-19 and postvaccine cohorts.
Mice with homozygous deletion of oxytocin or its receptor develop late-onset obesity but remain normophagic (not overeating).
Oxtr-knockout mice have lower body temperature than wild-type mice, providing initial evidence that oxytocin regulates thermogenesis.
Cold exposure in wild-type mice increases Oxtr mRNA in hypothalamus, white adipose tissue, and brown adipose tissue, while decreasing circulating oxytocin via negative feedback in the brain.
Cold stress increases oxytocin levels in skeletal muscle.
Infusion of oxytocin increases body temperature.

Post-mortem studies of Prader-Willi Syndrome individuals show a reduction in paraventricular nucleus (PVN) volume and a strong decrease in the number of Oxtr-expressing neurons compared to healthy controls.
The thermosensory system is atypical in Autism Spectrum Disorder, with cold stimuli sometimes perceived as hot or burning and reduced sensitivity to ambient temperature.
The abnormal thermal sensory perception in ASD may be due to impairment of small-fiber sensory nerves.
PWS individuals show decreased perception of cold and increased sensitivity to hot temperatures, along with altered pain perception related to thermal stimuli.
Children and adolescents with PWS have been reported with episodes of high fever resembling septic shock without infection, as well as severe hypothermia.
In the Magel2 mouse model of Schaaf-Yang Syndrome, high cold sensitivity is observed, which can be corrected by intranasal administration of an oxytocin receptor agonist.
MAGEL2 mutations have been identified in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder, intellectual disability, and Prader-Willi Syndrome.
Magel2-deficient mice display impaired suckling at birth (which can be fatal) and reduced hypothalamic oxytocin expression; feeding problems are rescued by a single oxytocin dose shortly after birth.
In children with PWS aged 5-11 years, plasma oxytocin levels are reported higher than in healthy siblings.
PWS individuals have lower insulin levels and less insulin resistance than BMI-matched controls, suggesting a protected glucose metabolism phenotype.
Oxt- and Oxtr-knockout mice have lower adrenalin levels than control mice, suggesting altered autonomic nervous system activity.
An fMRI study found that PWS individuals show a delayed brain satiety response to glucose ingestion in regions associated with food intake and reward, attributed to hypothalamic dysfunction.

In a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial of 24 children aged 5-11 with PWS given 5 days of intranasal oxytocin versus placebo, outcome parameters improved from day 3-6 favoring oxytocin but never reached statistical significance from day 6-14; the treatment was safe with no lab abnormalities.

In a 3-month intranasal oxytocin RCT in 26 children aged 3-11 with PWS, there was no overall significant effect on hyperphagia or social behavior, but boys showed significant positive effects on hyperphagia and social/eating behavior while girls did not, and patients with the deletion subtype benefited while those with maternal uniparental disomy did not.
The ratio of acylated to unacylated ghrelin was lower after oxytocin treatment than placebo, indicating decreased orexigenic drive in oxytocin-treated PWS patients.

In an 8-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial of intranasal oxytocin in 23 children aged 5-18 with PWS, placebo was associated with modest improvement in hyperphagia and repetitive behavior, whereas oxytocin showed no improvement.
An increase in salivary oxytocin at week 4 of treatment was positively correlated with an increase in hyperphagia drive but negatively correlated with ritualistic behavior.

A randomized placebo-controlled trial of carbetocin (an oxytocin analogue with improved receptor selectivity) in PWS patients aged 10-18 showed significant improvement in hyperphagia and behavioral symptoms after 14 days, reducing compulsiveness and improving overall functioning.
Liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, did not significantly reduce BMI in children with PWS compared with placebo/no treatment, though an apparent improvement in hyperphagia was seen.

In infants under 6 months with PWS, escalating doses of oxytocin over 7 days normalized suckling and improved swallowing regardless of dose, with 88% of subjects showing normalized suckling and improved swallowing immediately after treatment, plus increased alertness and less social withdrawal.

Long-term observational follow-up showed improved muscle tone and motor coordination in oxytocin-treated PWS infants, who were able to crawl as toddlers compared to untreated age-matched PWS controls.

Altered pain and thermal perception in PWS may be related to a reduction in sensory neurons in dorsal root ganglia due to absence of necdin expression, rather than to peripheral nerve damage from metabolic factors or obesity.

Cold stress down-regulates fast-twitch glycolytic myosin heavy chain 2b while increasing the myosin heavy chain 1 (slow-oxidative)/myosin heavy chain 2b ratio in soleus but not tibialis anterior muscle, consistent with a shift toward slow-twitch oxidative muscle for shivering thermogenesis.

PWS-derived induced pluripotent stem cell neurons show decreased prohormone convertase 1, the enzyme that cleaves inactive oxytocin into its active form, potentially explaining excess inactive oxytocin in PWS.
OXTR gene expression may be suppressed in the PVN of PWS individuals due to a genetic defect or DNA methylation.
Growth hormone treatment in PWS patients improves body composition with increased muscle size and decreased fat mass.

Absence of necdin expression is linked to reduced sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia, which may explain altered pain and thermal perception in PWS rather than peripheral nerve damage from obesity.
Magel2-deficient mice show a PWS-like phenotype with impaired suckling, reduced hypothalamic oxytocin, and feeding problems that are rescued by a single dose of oxytocin given shortly after birth.
PWS individuals have lower insulin levels and less insulin resistance than BMI-matched obese controls, suggesting a relatively protected glucose metabolism.

An fMRI study of the satiety response found a delayed brain activation response to glucose ingestion in PWS individuals in regions associated with food intake and reward, attributed to hypothalamic dysfunction.

In a randomized placebo-controlled trial, carbetocin (an oxytocin analogue with improved receptor selectivity) given for 14 days significantly improved hyperphagia and behavioral symptoms, reducing compulsiveness, in PWS patients aged 10-18.
Liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, did not significantly reduce BMI in children with PWS compared with placebo/no treatment, although an apparent improvement in hyperphagia was observed.

In infants under 6 months with PWS, escalating doses of intranasal oxytocin over 7 days normalized suckling and improved swallowing regardless of dose, with 88% of subjects showing normalized suckling and swallowing immediately after treatment.
Infants with PWS treated with oxytocin showed increased connectivity of the right superior orbitofrontal network, proposed to mediate long-term behavioral benefits.
In mice, cold stress for 6 hours induced cardiac histopathological changes including necrosis and fibrosis, which decreased after 5 days of cold stress when circulating oxytocin had declined.
Cold stress induces expression of TRPV1 and Oxtr in skeletal muscle (soleus and tibialis anterior), with higher induction in slow-twitch muscle.
Cold stress decreases oxytocin in brown adipose tissue after 6 hours but increases oxytocin levels in bone, consistent with oxytocin's role in modulating both energy metabolism and bone.

In a clinical trial, intranasal oxytocin improved hyperphagia and social/eating behavior significantly in boys but not girls with PWS, and in patients with the deletion subtype but not maternal uniparental disomy.
The ratio of acylated to unacylated ghrelin after oxytocin treatment was lower than after placebo, indicating a decreased orexigenic drive in oxytocin-treated PWS patients.

In an 8-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial, placebo was associated with modest improvement in hyperphagia and repetitive behavior in PWS children, while intranasal oxytocin showed no improvement.
An increase in salivary oxytocin at week 4 of treatment was positively correlated with increased hyperphagia drive but negatively correlated with ritualistic behavior in PWS children.

In individuals with autism spectrum disorder, the thermosensory system is atypical, such that a cold stimulus can be perceived as hot or burning, along with reported insensitivity to outside temperature.

Neonatal Magel2 mutant mice show cold hypo-reactivity that is mimicked in control pups by pharmacogenetic inactivation of hypothalamic oxytocin neurons, indicating the thermosensory deficit is caused by loss of the oxytocin system.

The patient's Lyme disease antibody panel showed two positive bands (41 KD IgG and 23 KD IgM), below the five-band minimum typically required for diagnosis, yet clinicians proceeded with empiric treatment.
A two-week course of doxycycline for presumed early-disseminated Lyme disease produced no improvement in long COVID symptoms and coincided with worsening of several symptoms.

A new-onset right bundle branch block with occasional premature ventricular contractions was found on multiple ECGs during long COVID evaluation, though echocardiography and stress testing were negative.
The patient was diagnosed with new-onset PCOS after long COVID onset, based on an elevated LH:FSH ratio, oligomenorrhea, and nocturnal hypoglycemia on continuous glucose monitoring.
Metformin escalation with diet modification led to moderate reduction in menstrual cycle length and morning hypoglycemic symptoms.
A self-designed graded horizontal exercise program (reclined bicycle, rowing) modeled on POTS rehabilitation, with extensive rest periods, contributed to symptom improvement.
Traditional vertical exercise (treadmill, elliptical, or strenuous strength training) reliably exacerbated the patient's fatigue and was ultimately abandoned.
Graded compression stockings provided only temporary benefit for palpitations/tachycardia and over time became overly compressive, contributing to symptom re-exacerbations.
Multiple sessions of osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) reduced myalgias, headaches, and scalp allodynia and provided at-home pain-reduction strategies.
A CGRP antagonist used for migraine-like post-COVID headaches was ineffective and caused a moderate increase in fatigue and brain fog during treatment.

Completion of the two-dose Moderna mRNA COVID-19 vaccine course was associated with moderate improvement in fatigue and brain fog within 24 hours of the first dose, with headaches/scalp allodynia resolving months later.
Self-administered N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation led to a subjective increase in headache frequency and duration, with no other discernible benefit.
Self-treatment with vitamin C, vitamin D, vitamin B12, B-complex vitamins, and turmeric extract provided no discernible benefit for long COVID symptoms.
Antiviral treatment with molnupiravir during a SARS-CoV-2 reinfection was associated with spontaneous recovery without relapse of any long COVID symptoms, as was a second untreated reinfection.

Self-guided smell re-training and a digital therapeutic gaming clinical trial for cognitive impairment (NCT04843930) each provided moderate symptom alleviation for phantosmia and brain fog respectively.
Cognitive behavioral therapy, peer support networks, and sleep hygiene improvements made small but recognizable improvements in fatigue and cognition.

The paper notes that persistent SARS-CoV-2 PCR-positivity (post-viral shedding) occurs more commonly in the long COVID population and may correlate with symptom onset, with potential predictive/diagnostic value.

The authors suggest that co-infections such as Lyme disease (as in this case) or Epstein-Barr virus/other herpesvirus infection or reactivation warrant further consideration in long COVID pathogenesis and management.

Based on this case, the authors propose a phasic model of long COVID progression: an initial infection phase (Phase 0), an acute hyperinflammatory 'hyperactive' symptom phase (Phase 1), a 'hypoactive' symptom phase as inflammation subsides (Phase 2), and a final phase with recession of some symptoms alongside emergence of possibly permanent deficits (Phase 3).

SARS-CoV-2 spike RBD-specific IgG titers declined non-significantly over time in both PCS+ and PCS− and showed no significant difference between the two groups at either timepoint, indicating antibody titer is not a marker for PCS.
IL-4 levels were significantly increased in PCS+ compared to PCS− and to healthy controls, showing the most significant increase of all cytokines/chemokines tested.
Plasma CD40 ligand (CD40L) levels were significantly higher in PCS+ compared to healthy controls at both timepoints.
Frequencies of total CD4+ T-cells were significantly increased in PCS+ compared to both controls and PCS− at the 6-week timepoint.
Transitional memory CD4+ T-cells (TTM) were significantly higher in PCS+ compared to controls at both timepoints and constituted the largest CD4+ memory subpopulation in PCS+.
Central memory CD4+ T-cells (TCM) were significantly reduced in PCS+ compared to healthy controls at both timepoints, consistent with prior data on severe acute COVID-19.
PD-1 and CXCR3 expression on CD4+ T-cells was highest in healthy controls (CTRL > PCS+ = PCS−), suggesting CD4+ subpopulations in convalescents were neither exhausted nor activated.
Plasmacytoid dendritic cell (pDC) frequencies were almost equally distributed between PCS+, PCS−, and control groups.

Type 1 regulatory T-cells (TR1) were significantly increased in PCS+ versus controls (2.7-3.9 fold higher) and showed a similar but non-significant trend versus PCS-, likely due to limited case numbers.
PD-1 expression on TR1 cells was significantly reduced in both PCS+ and PCS− compared to controls, with no relevant difference between PCS+ and PCS−.
HLA-DR expression on plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC) was increased in PCS+ compared to both PCS− and controls, indicating a more activated pDC phenotype in PCS.

In unstimulated PBMC assay controls, SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T-cells secreting IFNγ, TNF, and expressing CD40L were 5-12 times more frequent in PCS+ than PCS−, indicating elevated baseline inflammation in PCS.

After protein-S1 stimulation, frequencies of SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells secreting IFNγ, TNF, and expressing CD40L were significantly highest in PCS+ versus PCS− and controls, being 2-13-fold more frequent than in PCS− at both timepoints.
Patients with PCS had a higher proportion of pre-existing conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, or other metabolic diseases (44%) compared to convalescents without PCS (19%) and controls.
The incidence of concomitant symptoms in PCS+ decreased over time from 93.75% at 6 weeks to 37.5% at 7 months after symptom onset.

SARS-CoV-2 Nsp15 interacts with pRB, inducing its nuclear export and ubiquitination for proteasomal degradation, and cells expressing Nsp15 lose contact inhibition and show increased proliferative potential.

The papain-like protease domain of SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 interacts with and stabilizes the E3 ubiquitin ligase RCHY1, promoting RCHY1-mediated degradation of p53, analogous to a mechanism previously shown for SARS-CoV-1.
SARS-CoV-2 Nsp2 interacts with mitochondrial chaperones PHB1 and PHB2, and their depletion triggers ROS leakage to the nucleus and oxidative damage, impairing transactivation of p53-dependent genes.

SARS-CoV-2 ORF8 interacts with the autophagy receptor p62, forming ORF8/p62 liquid droplets that sequester ER-phagy receptors FAM134B and ATL3, inhibiting ER-phagy and promoting formation of viral double-membrane replication vesicles and ER stress.

AHR was localized in the nucleus of IDO2-expressing PBMC and brain cells from PASC patients, indicative of transcriptional activity driving IDO2 expression.
In cultured PBMC from PASC patients, an AHR antagonist dose-dependently inhibited IDO2 expression, autophagy, and apoptosis, nearly eradicating IDO2 expression at 5 μM.
All PASC patients showed increased plasma xanthurenic acid levels compared to reference values, which were higher than in other SARS-CoV-2 patient groups.

Median plasma 3OH-anthranilic acid levels were highest in PASC patients (up to 106-fold above reference), though not statistically significant, and were also elevated in recovered and non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
In PBMC metabolomics, kynurenine was enhanced and tryptophan reduced in PASC patients compared to fully recovered SARS-CoV-2 patients, confirming metabolically active IDO2.
Besides tryptophan, 14 other amino acids were present at reduced levels in PBMC from PASC patients compared to recovered patients.
PBMC from PASC patients showed reduced levels of pyruvate, acetyl-CoA, citric acid and nicotinamide riboside, suggesting altered Krebs cycle and mitochondrial activity.

Basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates in PBMC from PASC patients were reduced compared to both recovered patients and healthy uninfected controls, with no difference between recovered and healthy.
Spare respiratory capacity of PBMC was reduced in both PASC and recovered patients compared to healthy controls, with no difference between PASC and recovered.

In an exploratory sPLS-DA restricted to the most extreme quartiles, citric acid, glutamine, cysteine, arginine and cystine were the top discriminators between high and low mitochondrial respiration (OCR/SRC) in PBMC.

Autopsy brain tissue from two PASC patients showed abundant IDO2 expression spatially associated with 3OH-anthranilic acid, quinolinic acid, and nuclear AHR, with predominant autophagy and limited apoptosis, and no detectable SARS-CoV-2 N-protein.
IDO2-expressing cells in PASC and recovered patients were identified as monocytes (CD14+) and lymphocytes (CD3+), predominantly CD4+ T cells and CD20+ B cells.

Patients with fatal/severe COVID-19 had the highest plasma levels of kynurenine metabolites (3OH-kynurenine, quinolinic acid, kynurenic acid) and the lowest tryptophan and 3OH-anthranilic acid levels compared to PASC, recovered, and non-hospitalized groups.

Although plasma/serum kynurenine was elevated versus reference values across all SARS-CoV-2-infected groups, kynurenine levels did not significantly differentiate between PASC, recovered, hospitalized, and fatal/severe COVID-19 groups.

All groups of SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals (PASC, recovered, hospitalized, fatal/severe) had systemically elevated kynurenine pathway metabolites compared to reference values, persisting even when sampled a median of 294 days post-infection.
National survey data show 7.5% (about 1 in 13) of people diagnosed with COVID-19 reported long-term symptoms, and these individuals were more likely to be younger than 59, female, and Hispanic.
After controlling for medical and psychiatric causes, clinically significant post-COVID fatigue occurs in an estimated 10% to 35% of patients at 6 months.
In a case-control study, ME/CFS patients had significantly higher anti-hypothalamic antibody (56%) and anti-pituitary antibody (33%) positivity than healthy controls.
Markers of the stress response—ACTH, cortisol, and IGF-1—were lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
In a prospective case-control study of acute COVID-19 patients, AHA was detected in 31% and APA in 51%, with adrenal insufficiency present in 8.1% of cases.
SARS-CoV-2 binds preferentially to ACE2, which is expressed on adrenal glands, and the virus may replicate within adrenal cells.
Autopsy studies of severe COVID-19 patients found adrenal hemorrhage, infarct, fibrin deposition, and microthrombi in the adrenal vasculature.
Acute COVID-19 can trigger a cytokine storm involving pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1, IL-6, and TNF, with the magnitude of this response correlated with disease severity.
Expression of Th1 and Th17 cell-mediated immunity factors has been reported to be downregulated in ME/CFS patients.
Following Epstein-Barr virus and West Nile virus infection, patients who developed post-viral fatigue had higher IL-2 and IL-6 expression than those who recovered without fatigue.
Patients experiencing PASC have shown increased levels of pro-inflammatory biomarkers including IL-6, C-reactive protein, and D-dimer.
Imaging studies of patients with COVID-19 symptoms lasting more than 30 days showed increased FDG uptake in bone marrow and blood vessels, indicating increased inflammation.
Elevated GDF-15, an indirect marker of mitochondrial stress, has been found in a significant proportion of patients hospitalized with COVID-19.
A cohort study of 100 COVID-19-recovered individuals found cardiac involvement including fibrosis in 78% and ongoing myocardial inflammation in 60%, independent of preexisting cardiovascular disease.
A subsequent similar analysis by Malek found the prevalence of cardiac pathology in COVID-19 recovered patients to be roughly twofold lower than the original Puntmann estimate.
Among 20 COVID-19-recovered patients with persistent neuromuscular symptoms, EMG showed myopathic changes in 55%, while nerve conduction studies were normal in all patients.
A systematic review found depressive symptoms present in 11%-28% of patients more than 12 weeks after COVID-19 infection, regardless of initial infection severity.

Neuropsychological assessment of recovered COVID-19 patients found higher perceived exertion/fatigue, apathy, executive deficits, and impaired cognition compared with controls, with physiologic testing suggesting a possible link to GABA dysfunction.
An estimated 50% to 75% of all patients with COVID-19 infection experience sleep disturbance.

A multicenter cohort study found sleep disturbance in 33.2% of patients at 6-10 months post-COVID, decreasing to 27.7% at 11-15 months, with a slower rate of decline than seen after other major medical events.

Data from the International Committee on Fatigue Following Infection suggest that clinically significant post-COVID fatigue occurs in 10% to 35% of patients at 6 months after controlling for medical and psychiatric causes.

Illness severity predicts risk of long-term sequelae: about two-thirds of outpatients with COVID-19 return to full health by week four, whereas 50.9% of emergency-department-evaluated patients (two-thirds eventually hospitalized) developed chronic symptoms.
Acute mental health disorders, anxiety, depression, and PTSD are common after COVID-19, with PTSD reported in 23.5% of ward survivors and 46.9% of ICU survivors.

Vulnerable populations including pregnant women, minority racial and ethnic groups, and individuals of low socioeconomic status are considered at higher risk for post-COVID-related illness according to the PASC Collaborative review.

The PASC Collaborative recommends a graded, individualized return-to-activity program guided by the Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion scale, using a 'rule of 10s' (10% increase in duration, frequency, intensity every 10 days) tailored to mild, moderate, or severe fatigue severity.

Energy conservation strategies summarized as the '4 Ps' (Pacing, Prioritizing, Positioning, Planning) are recommended patient education tools to reduce overexertion and aid recovery from PASC-related fatigue.

A diet high in whole grains, polyphenol-rich vegetables, and omega-3 fatty acid-rich foods has been suggested to potentially improve disease-related fatigue symptoms linked to pro-inflammatory states, although evidence specific to PASC is limited.
There is currently no evidence to support supplementation with B vitamins, omega-3 fatty acids, or coenzyme Q10 for improving PASC-related fatigue.

Patients with COVID-19 have shown radiological lung abnormalities including fibrosis and impaired pulmonary function, including diffusion capacity, months after initial infection, which may contribute to fatigue.
Hypercoagulable sequelae such as fibrin deposition and microthrombi in adrenal vasculature have been observed and may persist following initial COVID-19 infection even in mild cases.

A systematic review by Soares and colleagues found some similarities between skeletal muscle changes seen in PASC and those seen in chronic fatigue syndrome, though this overlap has not been fully investigated.
A study of a nonhospitalized PASC cohort identified 33 distinct clinical phenotypes, illustrating substantial phenotypic heterogeneity in PASC.

Retrospective studies suggest risk factors for developing PASC include female sex, age over 50, severe acute COVID-19, obesity, smoking, immunocompromised status, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic conditions.
Persistent SARS-CoV-2 virions and/or viral antigens have been detected in body fluids and tissues of both asymptomatic and PASC patients, at a higher frequency than in fully recovered COVID patients.

Sequence comparison of SARS-CoV-2 proteins against over 20,000 human proteins found 3781 human proteins sharing at least six amino acid sequences with CoV-2 proteins, of which 17 were molecular chaperones consistent with heat shock proteins, supporting molecular mimicry as a plausible autoimmune mechanism in PASC.

PASC patients have been reported to develop new-onset autoimmune disorders including systemic lupus erythematosus, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, autoimmune thyroid disease (Graves' and Hashimoto's), and Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Some PASC patients present with clinical manifestations of excessive mast cell activity (pruritus/urticaria, GI symptoms), consistent with an MCAS-like picture, hypothesized to result from COVID exacerbating undiagnosed MCAS or sustained mast cell activation via persistent viral particles and complement activation from immune complexes.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of over 250,000 patients found vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 significantly reduced the odds of developing PASC, with no significant adverse effects when patients with pre-existing PASC were subsequently vaccinated.

Elevated production of inflammatory mediators including IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, and TGF-β is proposed to contribute to persistent innate and adaptive immune dysregulation and organ inflammatory damage in PASC.
PASC is commonly associated with dysautonomia, manifesting as postural orthostatic hypotension, cardiac dysrhythmias, and gastrointestinal motility disorders.

An ongoing phase 2 trial is evaluating RSLV-132, an IV ribonuclease designed to digest RNA within autoantibodies/immune complexes, for effects on fatigue in PASC patients measured by the PROMIS Fatigue 7a questionnaire after 71 days.

An ongoing 8-week placebo-controlled multicenter trial is testing Immulina, a Spirulina-derived immunomodulatory dietary supplement, for effects on inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, D-dimer, IL-6) and symptoms (fatigue, neurocognitive impairment, dyspnea) in PASC patients.

An active trial from Cleveland Hospital is evaluating anti-inflammatory effects of vitamin K2 (MK-7) and vitamin D3 supplementation in PASC patients with elevated inflammatory mediators, assessing correlations between biomarkers and clinical symptoms.
A Stanford-led study is investigating whether a 15-day course of nirmatrelvir + ritonavir (Paxlovid), compared to the standard 5-day acute course, has positive effects on symptoms in PASC patients.
A Yale-led trial is comparing 15 days of nirmatrelvir + ritonavir to ritonavir placebo on PROMIS-29 questionnaire scores reflecting overall clinical condition in PASC patients.

The PLEXCOVIL trial is studying effects of plasmapheresis on constitutional PASC symptoms including fatigue, postexertional malaise, dyspnea, headache, myalgia, neurocognitive impairment, anosmia/ageusia, and anxiety/depression at 3 and 6 months.
53 EDS patients carried collagen type V gene (COL5A1/COL5A2) changes previously linked to classical EDS, supporting the validity of the DNA testing approach.
EDS patients had significantly more history and physical findings on the systematic checklist than patients evaluated but not meeting EDS criteria.
EDS females had higher joint hypermobility (Beighton) scores than EDS males, and both exceeded general-population averages.
Brain fog and chronic fatigue, attributed to an adrenergic response from lower-body blood pooling (POTS mechanism), were highly frequent among EDS females.
Bowel irregularity and bloating/reflux, features of irritable bowel syndrome attributed to cholinergic suppression, were common among EDS females.
Rashes and asthma/dyspnea, features of mast cell activation syndrome, occurred frequently in EDS females.
Migraines and poor balance were common neuromuscular findings in EDS females, and nearly all patients had at least one of twelve neuromuscular findings.

Most of the 37 mitochondrial genome genes assessed were altered in EDS patients, and nuclear POLG variants in 17 patients are proposed to deplete mitochondrial number/energy supply to nerve and muscle.

SARS-CoV-2 entry depends on spike protein binding to the ACE2 receptor followed by endocytosis and cleavage by TMPRSS2 (or cathepsin L), and variants in both host genes are among those associated with COVID-19 severity.
NLRP3 is a gene relevant to both EDS and COVID-19 severity, with its associated disease presenting joint pain, muscle aches, and mast cell activation symptoms.
Altered ratios of ADAMTS13 and von Willebrand factor (VWF) proteins are linked to thrombosis and COVID-19 mortality, paralleling clotting-related gene variants (including VWF) found in EDS patients.

A chemokine receptor gene cluster (CCR1/CCR5-CXCR6) mediating macrophage activation is uniquely clustered among COVID-19 severity genes and is also linked to susceptibility to HIV, hepatitis, and West Nile virus.

Genes regulating interferon action (IFNAR1/2, STAT2) and T-cell signaling (TNFRSF13B) are classified as autonomic-immune response genes modifying COVID-19 severity, all associated with immunodeficiency disorders.

An estimated 6.2% of people with documented COVID-19 infection develop one of three persisting symptom clusters (fatigue with pain/mood, cognitive problems, or respiratory problems), defining long COVID-19.
Long COVID-19 cohorts had a more balanced male-to-female ratio (about 1.2:1) than the strongly female-predominant EDS cohort (85% female).
COVID-19 hospitalization and mortality rates were not increased in patients with fibromyalgia, although this diagnosis omits many EDS-dysautonomia features and has limited biomarker association.

An FLG termination variant was qualified as acting synergistically with a COL3A1 variant in an example EDS patient, reflecting skin inflammation with decreased tissue constraint rather than the single symptom (ichthyosis) used in commercial reporting.

In an illustrative patient, the common MTHFR 677C>T variant was judged of uncertain significance for clotting diathesis given its high population frequency and multifactorial disease association, and no EDS-relevant variant was found in this patient.

An illustrative patient's homozygous HBB variant, though a well-established molecular change, was noted as not necessarily diagnosing sickle cell anemia without clinical correlation, paralleling reports of mild symptoms in some homozygous Jamaican patients.

POLG variants are proposed to relate to developmental disability in one context but to dysautonomia symptoms (encephalopathic-gastrointestinal dysmotility) in 17 EDS patients, illustrating that the same gene can map to different mechanisms depending on associated disease.
Genes related to immune/inflammatory response to viral infection made up a much larger share of COVID-19 severity genes than of EDS-relevant genes.
Of 104 genes linked to COVID-19 severity and 317 linked to EDS, 18 were similar and 6 were identical between the two gene sets.
Autonomic imbalance symptoms including brain fog, chronic fatigue, asthma/dyspnea, sleep difficulties, and tachycardia are common to both EDS and long COVID-19.
Small-fiber neuropathy and thyroid dysfunction occur in both EDS and COVID-19, supporting overlapping gene network involvement alongside shared joint, muscle, and dysautonomia symptoms.

An estimated 6.2% of people develop one of three long COVID-19 symptom clusters (persistent fatigue with bodily pain/mood swings, cognitive problems, or ongoing respiratory problems) after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A systematic review by Deer et al. included 59 of 303 screened studies covering 81 heterogeneous long COVID-19 cohorts with an overall male-to-female ratio of about 1.2 to 1.
COVID-19 hospitalization and mortality rates were not increased in patients with fibromyalgia, although fibromyalgia is a heterogeneous diagnosis with limited biomarker association.

POLG gene variants are linked to developmental disability in patients via an encephalopathy-associated disease, but relate to dysautonomia symptoms in 17 EDS patients via a distinct POLG-associated disease with encephalopathic-gastrointestinal dysmotility features, illustrating disease-specific mechanistic interpretation of the same gene.

The FLG (profilaggrin) gene, with 40 variants found among EDS patients, was qualified as having synergistic diagnostic action for EDS-related skin/tissue laxity rather than being attributed only to ichthyosis vulgaris as a commercial lab might report.

The common MTHFR 677C>T variant, present at about 30% frequency in normal population databases, was judged of uncertain significance for a multifactorial clotting diathesis and not diagnostic for EDS.

Patient 4 carried a homozygous HBB beta-globin variant assigned evident diagnostic utility for sickle cell carrier status, illustrating that even a well-established molecular change requires clinical correlation before being treated as a diagnosis.

Comparison of the 317 EDS-relevant genes to the 104 COVID-19 severity genes identified 18 genes with molecular/symptom similarity and 6 identical genes shared between the two disorders, spanning clotting, immune/inflammatory, transport, and DNA polymerase/regulatory functions.

Ten EDS-related genes (including NDUFA11, NDUFS3, OPA1, TYMP) and three COVID-19-related genes (STAT2, TLR3, NDUFAF7) impact mitochondrial function, suggesting a shared mitochondrial mechanism between the two disorders.
184 (62%) of the 298 disorders associated with EDS-relevant genes present with at least three tissue dysplasia symptoms, supporting a model of modular pleiotropy among connective tissue genes.
Small-fiber neuropathy and thyroid dysfunction occur in both EDS and COVID-19 patients, consistent with overlapping gene network involvement between the two disorders.

EDS-relevant genes are more often structural (76 genes, 25%) than COVID-19 severity genes (6 genes, 7.2%), while COVID-19 severity genes are more often signaling genes (20 genes, 35%) than EDS genes (39 genes, 12%).
Genes related to immune/inflammatory processes comprised 31% (26 of 82) of genes influencing COVID-19 severity versus 8.8% of the 317 genes contributing to EDS.

EDS and COVID-19 gene sets differed significantly in proportions of genes affecting autonomic function (14% vs 2.4%), muscle (11% vs 3.2%), bone (22% vs 1.2%), joints (6.3% vs 2.4%), and renal function (0.95% vs 4.8%), while cardiovascular, neural, clotting, and skin proportions were similar between groups.
The DPP7 and DPP9 peptidases, which cleave proline residues abundant in collagens, are COVID-19 severity-associated genes with molecular similarity to EDS-relevant collagen pathways.
The DDR1 receptor, which binds fibrillar collagens, is a COVID-19 severity-associated gene with molecular similarity to EDS-relevant collagen-binding mechanisms.

Renal-disease-associated COVID-19 severity genes include ACE1, AGT, and AGTR1, which affect angiotensinogen-angiotensin conversion, and ADAMTS13, whose product is similar to the EDS-related ADAMTS2 metalloprotease and is associated with a clotting diathesis and renal disease reminiscent of COVID-19 thrombotic complications.
An estimated at least 10% of people who had COVID-19 globally go on to develop long COVID.
Radiological abnormalities have been observed in the olfactory bulb, brain, heart, lung and other sites in individuals with long COVID.
Microclots and other blood markers of hypercoagulation have been found in some body sites in long COVID, implicating endothelial activation and clotting abnormalities.
Diverse auto-antibody specificities have been found in long COVID patients, without clear consensus or correlation with symptom clusters.
There is support for a role of persistent SARS-CoV-2 viral reservoirs in the pathogenesis of long COVID.
Epstein-Barr virus reactivation may contribute to long COVID pathogenesis.
Broad immune perturbation is evidenced by changes in immune cell subsets in long COVID patients.
VO2 peak improved significantly more in long COVID patients than in coronary artery disease patients following the 4-week exercise rehabilitation program.
VO2 at the first ventilatory threshold significantly increased after exercise rehabilitation in all three patient groups with no difference between groups.
Maximal aerobic power significantly increased after exercise rehabilitation in all three groups with no differential effect between groups.
Handgrip (muscular) strength significantly increased after exercise rehabilitation in all three groups, with a borderline non-significant group interaction.

No significant improvement was observed in resting heart rate, baroreflex sensitivity, or HRV indices (RMSSD, LF, HF, LF/HF) after the 4-week exercise rehabilitation program in any of the three groups.
At baseline, long COVID patients showed higher aerobic capacity than coronary artery disease and fibromyalgia patients.
At baseline, fibromyalgia patients showed lower anaerobic (muscular) capacity compared to long COVID and coronary artery disease patients.
Long COVID patients most frequently reported asthenia, exertional dyspnea, sleep disorder, cognitive impairment, diffuse pain, anxiety syndrome and chest pain as persistent symptoms.
Cited prior work found that exercise capacity was reduced in long COVID patients compared to individuals without persistent symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Cited prior work found that long COVID patients had reduced global HRV, increased sympathetic modulation and decreased parasympathetic modulation compared to healthy controls.

Post-exertional symptom exacerbation (PESE) prevalence in long COVID varies widely across the literature, and a cross-sectional study found that 75% of participants reported worsening symptoms with physical activity.
Overall, exercise rehabilitation was as effective for long COVID patients without PESE as for coronary artery disease and fibromyalgia patients in improving main physical performance parameters.
Ten sessions of TMS produced a statistically significant reduction in QIDS depression scores from before to after treatment in both Long-COVID and Post-Vaccine patient groups.
PHQ9 scores significantly improved after 10 TMS sessions in both Long-COVID and Post-Vaccine groups.
GAD7 anxiety scores significantly improved after 10 TMS sessions in both Long-COVID and Post-Vaccine groups.
Performance Status (PS), used as a fatigue indicator, significantly improved after 10 TMS sessions, but the authors caution this may not be attributable to TMS itself.
There were no significant differences in initial QIDS, PHQ9, GAD7, or PS scores at first visit between Long-COVID and Post-Vaccine patients.

In univariate analysis, the QIDS improvement rate (ΔQIDS) differed significantly between Long-COVID and Post-Vaccine patients, with Long-COVID patients appearing to have a better improvement rate, but this difference was not detected after MANCOVA adjustment.

Higher fatigue severity (Performance Status) at the initial visit was significantly associated with a worse (poorer) improvement rate in QIDS depression scores after TMS, confirmed across three MANCOVA models including propensity-score adjustment.
Both Long-COVID and Post-Vaccine patients showed a consistent pattern at first visit with significantly higher PHQ9 than GAD7, and higher PS (fatigue) than QIDS scores.
QIDS and PS scores were correlated both at the initial visit and after TMS treatment, suggesting a link between fatigue and depression severity.
PHQ9 and PS scores were significantly correlated after TMS treatment.

Patients with ME/CFS reportedly show higher oxidative stress and more widespread brain microglial activation than healthy subjects, with microglial activation correlating with cognitive impairment, depression severity, and pain.
Autopsy reports of patients who died from COVID-19 showed brain microglial activation even when SARS-CoV-2 infection of the brain itself was not confirmed.
In mouse experiments, SARS-CoV-2 infection confined to the lungs still induced microglial activation in brain white matter.
A recent cited study found that Long-COVID patients had higher oxidative stress than healthy subjects.

The authors propose that anti-idiotype antibodies (Ab2) generated after SARS-CoV-2 infection or COVID-19 vaccination may bind and regulate ACE2 receptor function, potentially driving widespread inflammation common to both Long-COVID and post-vaccine syndrome.

US CDC surveillance through March 2023 recorded 9,445 MIS-C cases and 78 deaths, with a mean age of 9 years, 98% testing positive for SARS-CoV-2, disproportionate representation among Hispanic/Latino and Black children, and 60% male predominance.

Immunoprofiling of antibody binding kinetics against 24 SARS-CoV-2 proteins revealed distinct IgM/IgG/IgA epitope diversity and avidity signatures that differentiate children with mild/moderate COVID-19, severe COVID-19, and MIS-C.

Children with MIS-C produced higher titers of IgA antibodies and highly functional IgG antibodies, suggesting local GI mucosal inflammation potentially driven by unremitting intestinal SARS-CoV-2 infection with continued antigen release.

A case series of five Swedish children with long COVID reported persistent fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations/chest pain, headache, and cognitive difficulties beginning about 2 months after COVID-19, with chronic fatigue and inability to return to full-time school persisting at 6-8 months follow-up.

In a cohort of 129 children diagnosed with COVID-19, persistent symptoms beyond 60 days included insomnia, respiratory symptoms, nasal congestion, fatigue, muscle/joint pain, and difficulty concentrating, occurring even in children with asymptomatic or mild acute infection.

In a retrospective cohort of 92 pediatric patients with post-acute COVID-19 symptoms, 51% reported persistent symptoms—particularly fatigue, loss of taste/smell, and headache—appearing 1 to 3 months after disease onset.

In an ambidirectional cohort comparing 236 children with confirmed COVID-19 to 142 children with other infections, persistent symptoms including fatigue, cognitive sequelae, headache, and taste/smell disturbance were significantly more common after COVID-19 than after other infections.

In a large mobile-app cohort of 258,790 children (1734 SARS-CoV-2 positive), headache (62.2%) and fatigue (55%) were the most frequent symptoms in the first 4 weeks, but only 1.8% had symptoms persisting at least 56 days.

Among 21,663 Italian children across 8 regions, cumulative incidence of long COVID symptoms was 24.3% in primary care patients versus 58% in hospitalized patients, and prevalence was 46.5% in children symptomatic during acute infection versus 11.5% in those asymptomatic.

In the VirusWatch England/Wales cohort, 9.9% of 5032 children reported at least one long-term condition, and the prevalence of persistent symptoms was only 2.6% among children with a documented history of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

A Danish national cohort of 37,522 PCR-confirmed children versus 78,037 test-negative controls found symptoms lasting >4 weeks were more frequent in infected children, but overall long COVID was rare and mainly short-lived, resolving within 1-5 months.

The Danish LongCOVIDKidsDK survey found long COVID (symptoms >8 weeks) prevalence of 31.2% in 0-3 year-olds, 26.5% in 4-11 year-olds, and 32.5% in 12-14 year-olds among SARS-CoV-2-positive children, all higher than matched test-negative controls.

In a prospective Italian cohort, 67% of adults versus 32% of children with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection reported at least one persistent symptom; females had higher risk of persistent symptoms in adults but not in children, and pediatric symptom differences resolved by 6-9 months.

In a cohort of 679 children with RT-PCR-confirmed infection, the most frequent persistent symptoms were fatigue (19%), headache (12%), insomnia (7.5%), muscle pain (6.9%), and difficulty concentrating (6.8%), with the proportion remaining symptomatic declining from 4% at 1-5 months to 0.7% at 12 months across viral variants.

In a household cohort study, persistent symptoms one year after SARS-CoV-2 infection were significantly more numerous in women, with adolescent girls at particular risk of prolonged symptoms, and long-lasting symptoms tended to cluster within families.

In a case-control study of 251 children with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 versus 251 healthy controls, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, and elevated D-dimer levels were predictive laboratory findings for long COVID, alongside persistent headache and joint/back pain lasting an average of 5 months.

In a national cohort of 23,048 SARS-CoV-2-positive adolescents versus 27,798 negative controls, fatigue (39%), headache (23.2%), and shortness of breath (23.4%) were more common in positive adolescents than in negative controls (24.4%, 14.2%, 15.8% respectively), with multiple symptoms more frequent in females.
Transcriptomic data indicate that children express lower levels of ACE2 protein than adults, which may partly explain milder SARS-CoV-2 infection in children.

Children express much higher levels of angiotensin II receptor type 2 (ATR2), which competitively blocks the inflammatory ATR1 receptor and may counterbalance low ACE2 levels, contributing to milder COVID-19 in children.

In mouse models and postmortem human tissue, SARS-CoV-2 spike protein accumulated in the skull marrow and meninges and penetrated brain structures long after acute infection, potentially driving the neurological manifestations of long COVID.

Postmortem examination of patients who died of COVID-19 revealed activation of microglia and pronounced infiltration of the brainstem, cerebellum, and meninges with cytotoxic T lymphocytes, alongside detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA/proteins in cranial nerves and brainstem cells.

Children with PASC had higher concentrations of plasmablasts and IgD-CD27+ memory/switched B cells than recovered children, while recovered controls had significantly higher naïve and unswitched B cell subsets.
Serum IL-6 and IL-1β concentrations were increased in both PASC and recovered children but were markedly higher in children with PASC, suggesting innate immune system involvement.

Long-term autoantibodies targeting endothelial adhesion molecule PLVAP, angiogenesis regulator RSPO3, the metabotropic glutamate receptor, hypocretin (orexin) receptor 2, and matrix metalloproteinases MMP7 and MMP9 have been detected in patients with persistent post-COVID symptoms.

Patients with symptoms lasting more than 3 months after acute illness more commonly showed increased proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α), chemokines (MCP-1, IP-10), and vascular damage markers (ICAM-1, VCAM-1).

Patterson et al. found significantly increased intermediate and nonclassical monocytes in patients with PASC symptoms persisting up to 15 months after acute infection, with a significant proportion of nonclassical monocytes harboring SARS-CoV-2 S1 protein, indicating a reservoir function.

EBV reactivation after or concurrent with SARS-CoV-2 infection is hypothesized to contribute to pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS) and chronic post-acute COVID manifestations via immune-mediated chronic neuroinflammation.

A sharp increase in new cases of juvenile dermatomyositis in older female children was observed during the COVID-19 pandemic, with dysregulation of the type I interferon signaling pathway and deposition of myxovirus-resistance protein A in capillaries and muscle fibers proposed as a pathogenic mechanism.

Musculoskeletal manifestations including myalgia, protracted myositis, rhabdomyolysis, and autoimmune necrotizing myositis occur in approximately 10-25% of COVID-19 patients, thought to arise via proinflammatory cytokine release, immune complex deposition, and molecular mimicry between viral antigens and muscle cells.
Adults with long-COVID-associated gut dysbiosis showed elevated Ruminococcus gnavus and Bacteroides vulgatus alongside reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii.

Stool analysis of asymptomatic infants with COVID-19 revealed decreased Bifidobacterium bifidum, Akkermansia muciniphila, Eubacterium limosum, Enterocloster clostridioformis, Blautia hominis, Veillonella dispar, and Enterobacter cloacae, with the anti-inflammatory taxa Bifidobacterium bifidum and Akkermansia muciniphila considered of particular importance.

SARS-CoV-2 infection of the GI tract triggers release of zonulin, a coordinator of intercellular tight junctions, increasing intestinal permeability ('leaky gut') and facilitating translocation of viral antigens into blood/lymph, leading to hyperinflammation and autoimmune phenomena.

In patients with chronic COVID-19, commensal immunomodulatory bacteria (F. prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, Bifidobacteria) were reduced while proinflammatory oral taxa such as Prevotella and Veillonella were significantly increased.

Recent publications highlight a particularly elevated risk of developing autoimmune diseases (systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease, Behçet's disease, polymyalgic vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, type 1 diabetes) within months after COVID-19.

Anti-IFN autoantibodies correlate with age and increase COVID-19 severity by delaying the immune system's prompt reaction against the virus; severe COVID-19 patients show high rates of autoantibodies against IFN, complement, interleukins, and chemokines.

Among 171 persons with self-reported arthritis who had confirmed COVID-19, 53.5% (n=91) reported being troubled by persistent symptoms (long COVID) at least 12 weeks post-infection.
The most frequently reported long COVID symptoms among persons with arthritis were fatigue, myalgia, weakness, breathlessness, low mood, anxiety, and sleep disturbance.
Female sex was significantly associated with higher likelihood of long COVID among persons with arthritis in multivariable analysis.
Having been hospitalized for COVID-19 was associated with increased likelihood of long COVID among persons with arthritis.
Having at least one other chronic disease in addition to arthritis was associated with increased likelihood of long COVID.
Persons with arthritis and long COVID showed substantial declines in global health status, usual activities, mobility, personal care, and employment status compared to their pre-COVID status.
Among those with long COVID, 37% reported a moderate to severe increase in pain compared to their pre-COVID baseline.
Patients with long COVID walked significantly more meters in the 6-minute walk test after completing the rehabilitation program than before.
No significant differences were found in Borg dyspnea scale or Fatigue Impact Scale scores before versus after the rehabilitation program.
Systolic blood pressure was significantly lower after the rehabilitation intervention compared to baseline.
Patients who responded to rehabilitation treatment had significantly higher serum creatinine levels than nonresponders.
Responders had a lower protein/creatinine ratio than nonresponders, and a ratio greater than 10 predicted treatment response with 78% accuracy, 75% sensitivity, and 80% specificity.
Patients with obesity had a significantly higher frequency of severe acute COVID-19 requiring hospital admission compared to non-obese patients.
Patients with obesity walked significantly fewer meters in the 6-minute walk test prior to rehabilitation than non-obese patients.

Patients with obesity had significantly higher alanine aminotransferase levels than non-obese patients.
Patients with obesity had significantly higher gamma-glutamyl transferase levels than non-obese patients.

The change in Fatigue Impact Scale score with rehabilitation negatively correlated with antinuclear antibody titers, whereas no correlation was found with classical inflammatory parameters.
The improvement in percentage of meters walked after rehabilitation correlated positively with baseline creatinine levels.
Platelet count and fibrinogen levels were increased in nonresponding patients compared to responders.
The long COVID cohort showed abnormally elevated mean fibrinogen and erythrocyte sedimentation rate at baseline evaluation relative to reference values.
Patients hospitalized for acute COVID-19 preceding long COVID had mean interleukin-6 levels above the reference range at admission.
Patients hospitalized for acute COVID-19 preceding long COVID had mean D-dimer levels above the reference range at admission.
16.7% of long COVID patients had positive autoimmunity markers, including two ANA-positive patients (titers 1/320 and 1/640) and one lupus anticoagulant-positive patient.
In neuropsychological screening, 57.1% of long COVID patients had anxiety and 14.3% had depression.
The most frequent symptoms among long COVID patients were fatigue, headache, dyspnea, and amnesia, with a mean of 4.07 symptoms per patient.

NMNAT1 expression was upregulated in lungs of K18-hACE2 mice 6 days after SARS-CoV-2 challenge.

Arthralgia has consistently been associated with Long COVID throughout the literature examined, unlike other symptoms whose prevalence changed over time.
The authors argue that Long COVID's interconnected symptom profile requires interdisciplinary, dynamically updated rehabilitative management rather than static, single-discipline care.
Among 492 infected volunteers, 26.7% developed long COVID-19 while 20.7% did not.
Fatigue was the most common long COVID-19 manifestation, reported by 57% of affected individuals.
Hair loss was reported by 39% of individuals with long COVID-19.
Loss or change in the sense of smell or taste was reported by 35% of individuals with long COVID-19.
Gender was significantly correlated with development of long COVID-19.
Presence of comorbidities was significantly correlated with development of long COVID-19.
Age was significantly correlated with development of long COVID-19.
Duration of acute infection was significantly correlated with development of long COVID-19.

At 12 months after acute COVID-19, 53.0% of respondents reported at least one long COVID symptom, most commonly cognitive dysfunction, concentration difficulties, amnesia, fatigue, and anxiety.
