The prevalence of fatigue increased over the 24-month follow-up period as cognitive impairment improved.
The incidence of amnesia increased over time, reaching 30.3% at 24 months, higher than at any earlier time point.
Moderate or severe disease activity during acute COVID-19 was a statistically significant risk factor for long-term fatigue at 24 months.
The risk of amnesia tended to be higher in people older than 50 years, but this association did not reach statistical significance.
Anxiety, depression, insomnia, concentration difficulty, and cognitive dysfunction at 24 months were not significantly associated with acute disease severity, age ≥50, or sex.
Respondents with long COVID symptoms at 24 months more often reported increased consumption of healthy foods compared to those without symptoms.
Respondents with long COVID symptoms tended to report more physical activity than those without symptoms, but the difference was not statistically significant.
The occurrence of long COVID at 24 months was not significantly affected by COVID-19 vaccination status or the number of vaccinations received.
The proportion of respondents reporting reduced quality of life due to anxiety and depressive symptoms did not significantly change between 12 and 24 months after COVID-19.
After 20 days of combined H1/H2 antihistamine treatment, fatigue completely resolved in 43% of treated long-COVID patients.
Brain fog fully disappeared in 43% of treated patients after 20 days of antihistamine therapy.
Increased heart rate resolved in 57% of treated patients after 20 days of H1/H2 antihistamine therapy.
Abdominal/gastrointestinal disorders resolved in 57% of treated patients after 20 days of antihistamine therapy.

Nearly one-third of treated patients (29%) had complete disappearance of all long-COVID symptoms after 20 days of antihistamine therapy, versus none of the untreated controls, though the between-group difference in complete resolution did not reach statistical significance.
Untreated long-COVID patients showed no significant improvement or disappearance of any of the four target symptoms over the same 20-day period.
No adverse effects or symptom worsening were reported in either treated or untreated patients during the 20-day study period.

The authors note that beta-blockers, commonly used for tachycardia, do not address the underlying mast-cell-activation mechanism and may paradoxically worsen heart rate by lowering blood pressure and triggering baroreflex-mediated tachycardia, as observed in many of their patients.
Combined blockade of histamine H1 and H2 receptors was associated with reduced heart rate and increased blood pressure in these long-COVID patients, contrasting with the effect of beta-blockers.

A prior study by Weinstock et al. found that MCAS symptom burden was increased in long-COVID patients and closely mimicked the symptom profile and severity seen in patients with mast cell activation syndrome itself.
A separate retrospective study of 26 long-COVID patients treated with combined H1/H2 antihistamines showed significantly better clinical response than 23 untreated patients.
At the 20-day follow-up, the prevalence of fatigue, increased heart rate, and abdominal disorders was significantly lower in the antihistamine-treated group compared with the untreated group.
Mild (non-hospitalized) acute COVID-19 severity was associated with higher adjusted odds of fatigue in the PASC cohort compared with severe acute COVID-19.
Mild acute COVID-19 severity was associated with higher adjusted odds of subjective cognitive impairment in the PASC cohort.
Mild acute COVID-19 severity was associated with higher adjusted odds of post-acute headaches.
Mild acute COVID-19 severity was associated with higher adjusted odds of dizziness in the post-acute period.
Mild acute COVID-19 severity was associated with markedly lower odds of severe dyspnea compared with severe acute infection.
Longer PASC duration was positively correlated with higher odds of fatigue, subjective cognitive impairment, headaches, severe fatigue, and severe cognitive impairment.
Female PASC patients reported more fatigue, headaches, and cognitive impairment than male patients, with perceived cognitive impairment nearly five-fold more severe in women.
Advanced age (≥65 years) was modestly associated with higher odds of fatigue in the PASC cohort.
Private insurance coverage and self-reported white race were associated with severe anxiety but not with other PASC symptoms.
Participants reporting persistent cough were more likely to have received corticosteroids during acute COVID-19 infection.

Antecedent Alpha-strain infection (versus Delta) was associated with lower rates of anxiety, while critical COVID-19 was associated with more dyspnea but less cognitive impairment, joint pain, anosmia, and fatigue/depression severity.
Acute-phase treatment with remdesivir was associated with lower prevalence of post-acute fatigue and fewer patients reporting severe fatigue and severe cognitive impairment on PROMIS scales.
Fatigue prevalence increased and persisted beyond 3 months from acute COVID-19 onset, defining an apparent temporal breakpoint.
Subjective cognitive impairment prevalence was significantly higher after 3 months from acute COVID-19 and continued to rise with longer PASC duration.

Severe fatigue (PROMIS >1.5 SD) prevalence was highest beyond 9 months from onset and continued to rise, while severe cognitive impairment rose significantly at 6–9 months and remained highest beyond 6 months.
Headache prevalence spiked at 9–12 months post-infection before declining, representing a distinct temporal pattern from fatigue and cognitive impairment.
Among PASC clinic patients, the most prevalent post-acute symptoms were dyspnea, fatigue, subjective cognitive impairment, cough, dizziness, and headache.
Severe fatigue and severe cognitive impairment (scoring >1.5 SD on PROMIS scales) were common, whereas severe dyspnea was infrequent.
New or worsening moderate-to-severe depression and anxiety were reported by 26% and 16% of PASC patients, respectively.

In a small ICU cohort of 17 COVID-19 patients, a reduction in heart rate variability (SDNN) predicted a subsequent rise in CRP of more than 50% within 72 hours, suggesting HRV as a marker of worsening inflammation, though it did not correlate with clinical outcomes.
In a case-control study of 63 COVID-19 patients versus 43 matched healthy controls, a much higher proportion of COVID-19 patients showed elevated parasympathetic tone (RMSSD ≥40ms).
In contrast to the time-domain RMSSD results, frequency-domain analysis in the same case-control study showed reduced parasympathetic activity in COVID-19 patients.

In an ICU study of 16 COVID-19 patients, higher mean ANI (indicating increased parasympathetic tone) was observed in patients who died compared to survivors, and an ANIm threshold of 80 predicted mortality with high accuracy.
SDNN correlated inversely with the SOFA severity score but did not correlate with mortality or inflammatory markers (IL-6, CRP, procalcitonin) in the same ICU cohort.

A retrospective Mayo Clinic study identified 27 patients with para-/post-infectious autonomic dysfunction after SARS-CoV-2 infection, of whom 17 had peripheral autonomic abnormalities consistent with autonomic neuropathy.
An observational study in an Indian population found sudomotor dysfunction in 13 of 50 patients with unspecific long-lasting symptoms after COVID-19.

A report of two pediatric German patients described one case of autonomic dysfunction with elevated vagal activity during acute COVID-19 and another case of orthostatic hypotension occurring two weeks after resolution of acute infection.

A case series of six patients reported dysautonomia with autonomic symptoms emerging after remission of acute COVID-19, ranging from orthostatic hypotension and postural tachycardia to cardiovagal impairment.
A retrospective analysis in Chile identified 20 patients with signs of orthostatic dysautonomia detected via tilt table or 10-minute standing test following COVID-19.

A case report described dysautonomic signs (sinus arrhythmia, postural hypotension, profuse sweating, constipation, erectile dysfunction, chest squeezing sensation) during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection preceding development of acute axonal motor neuropathy.

Immunohistochemical mapping of the murine brain showed ACE2 expression is highest in brainstem autonomic centers including the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, area postrema, and nucleus tractus solitarius, supporting a potential route for SARS-CoV-2 neuroinvasion into autonomic control centers.
A meta-analysis identified more than 50 long-term symptoms associated with prior COVID-19 infection, the majority of which relate to dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system.
A meta-analysis estimated the pooled prevalence of long COVID at 43% among individuals with prior COVID-19 infection.

A systematic review and meta-analysis found that postural orthostatic tachycardia occurs in up to 62% of patients with long COVID, more frequently than in acute COVID-19, while acute COVID-19 more often presents with reflex syncope and blood pressure instability.

Cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction shows higher recovery rates in acute COVID-19 than in long COVID, and affected acute-phase patients tend to be younger and more often female than those with long COVID-related autonomic dysfunction, suggesting differing underlying pathophysiology.

A prospective study of 40 individuals discharged after COVID-19 for six months found that HRV differed between those with and without persistent diffusion dysfunction, showing a tight association with pulmonary fibrosis.

An observational study found that SDNN and HF components of HRV were decreased in long COVID patients compared to controls, while RMSSD and LF showed no between-group difference, alongside an increased LF/HF ratio, consistent with attenuated parasympathetic activity.

In contrast, another study found that long COVID patients symptomatic beyond 3 months had increased SDNN and decreased RMSSD compared to non-infected controls, while LF, HF, and LF/HF ratio remained unaltered, a pattern that contradicts the previous study's findings.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia occurs in up to 62% of patients with long COVID, more frequently than in acute COVID-19.

A prospective study of 40 patients six months after COVID-19 discharge found HRV differed between those with and without persistent diffusion dysfunction and was closely associated with pulmonary fibrosis.

An observational study found SDNN and high-frequency HRV power were decreased and the LF/HF ratio increased in long COVID patients compared to controls, while RMSSD and LF power showed no between-group difference, suggesting attenuated parasympathetic activity.

In another study, a subgroup with long COVID symptoms persisting beyond 3 months showed increased SDNN and decreased RMSSD compared to SARS-CoV-2-uninfected patients, while LF, HF, and LF/HF ratio were unaltered.

In a randomized trial, six weeks of HRV biofeedback training significantly increased SDNN in coronary artery disease patients compared to conventional-therapy controls, with the effect sustained at 18 weeks.
HRV biofeedback was shown to lower blood pressure in prehypertensive subjects by modulating autonomic cardiovascular function, indicating clinical benefit beyond HRV changes alone.
A randomized controlled trial of a portable, self-guided HRV biofeedback device in prior myocardial infarction patients demonstrated feasibility of self-administration and an increase in HRV.
A randomized trial of 6-week HRV biofeedback in heart failure patients (NYHA I-III) showed improved exercise tolerance on the 6-minute walk test.
A sham-controlled randomized trial in acute multidisciplinary stroke unit patients in Germany showed elevated HRV and alleviated autonomic symptoms three months after biofeedback intervention.
In a Taiwanese cohort of stroke survivors, HRV biofeedback improved HRV and alleviated symptoms of anxiety and depression.
A small wait-list-controlled randomized trial found HRV biofeedback reduced autonomic reactivity during anger events and enhanced autonomic recovery afterward in coronary artery disease patients.

A randomized study of 210 coronary artery disease patients found HRV biofeedback improved cardiovascular prognosis and neurocardiac autonomic homeostasis at one year, with fewer all-cause readmissions and emergency visits; mortality could not be assessed due to absence of deaths.

A systematic review of 12 studies concluded that HRV biofeedback may have positive therapeutic effects on clinical outcomes across several cardiovascular diseases but could not determine its effect on cardiovascular mortality.

A position paper proposed that COVID-19 survivors display cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction that may worsen clinical outcomes together with psychological sequelae, and speculated that HRV biofeedback training could counteract this cycle.
The ongoing HEARTLOC trial (planned n=30) is testing whether HRV biofeedback can modulate autonomic function and alleviate dysautonomia-related symptoms in long COVID patients.
Another ongoing trial (planned n=20) is assessing feasibility of HRV biofeedback in long COVID patients and its effects on cognition, pain, fatigue, anxiety, depression, and quality of life.
Serum neurofilament light chain (sNfL) did not change following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Serum glial fibrillary acidic protein (sGFAP) did not change following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
sNfL was not significantly associated with headache, fatigue, anosmia, or ageusia after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
sGFAP was not significantly associated with headache, fatigue, anosmia, or ageusia after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

sNfL did not significantly increase in individuals with Long-COVID.
Individuals reported neurological associated symptoms such as headache, fatigue, anosmia and ageusia following mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Nearly half of the 24 lognormal model parameters describing the ECG PQRST complex showed a statistically significant relationship with infant age after correction for multiple comparisons.
Certain lognormal parameters, such as the time-offset (t0) of the S component and the mu (scale) parameter of the T- component, showed particularly clear and strong correlations with infant age.

None of the parameters modeling the Q wave component reached statistical significance in their relationship with infant age, possibly due to superposition with the much larger neighboring R component.

A mixed-effects model using age as a fixed effect and subject as a random effect produced a predicted PQRST waveform trajectory across age that was easier to interpret than direct averaging of raw ECG time series across subjects.

The reinforcement-learning-based lognormal fit of ECG PQRST complexes achieved lower average fitting SNR than a comparable prototype-based lognormal model previously applied to human movement (speed) data, likely due to systematic resting-potential offsets in ECG not present in movement signals.

The paper cites prior literature indicating that absence of the Q wave has been considered a marker suggestive of abnormal left ventricular diastolic function, which under the proposed model would correspond to a near-zero D parameter for the Q component.

The authors propose that future extension of this ECG lognormal/reinforcement-learning model to the full heartbeat sequence (rather than isolated PQRST complexes) could provide insight into autonomic nervous system control and enable clinical applications in conditions where autonomic control is atypical, citing autism spectrum disorder as an example.
Children with autism show reduced microbial biodiversity with characteristic increases in Clostridium genera, Bacteroidota, Bacillota, Bifidobacterium, and Lactobacillaceae.

Children with autism have elevated short-chain fatty acids such as propionic acid in the gastrointestinal tract, a marker of intestinal dysbiosis potentially affecting genes associated with CNS development.

Elevated plasma serotonin has been observed in children with autism, and an inverse link between high plasma serotonin and low serotonergic neurotransmission has been demonstrated in young adult males with autism spectrum disorder.

The relationship between gut microbiota composition and autism spectrum disorder remains one of the most controversial and unresolved associations, with causality not yet established given the wide clinical and microbial heterogeneity.
A few studies indicate a possible beneficial effect of probiotics in restoring intestinal dysbiosis and ameliorating autism symptoms.
Adults with ASD showed reduced parasympathetic activity, as measured by ECG-derived HRV parameters, compared to patients with no diagnosis.
Adults with ASD showed increased sympathetic activity, as measured by ECG-derived HRV parameters, compared to patients with no diagnosis.
Heart rate variability-derived biological parameters discriminated ASD from pooled other-diagnosis/no-diagnosis groups with an AUC of 0.736.
The extensive standardised clinical assessment discriminated ASD from pooled other-diagnosis/no-diagnosis groups with a higher AUC (0.856) than the biological HRV parameters.
Among 65 patients who underwent surgery for adult spinal deformity with fusion of more than five levels, 6 patients (9%) developed persistent orthostatic hypotension (POH) postoperatively.
Patients with POH were significantly more likely to have diabetes mellitus than those without POH.

Neurodegenerative disease (Parkinson's disease or multiple system atrophy) was found to be an independent predictor of postoperative POH after multivariate adjustment, with nearly a 4-fold increase in odds.
Patients requiring walking aids preoperatively were significantly more likely to develop postoperative POH than those without walking aids.
Patients with a preoperative ASIA grade D (impaired neurological function) were significantly more likely to develop POH than those with ASIA grade E (normal function).
Patients with POH had a significantly longer mean hospital stay than those without POH.
The preoperative minor axis of the inferior vena cava was significantly larger in patients who subsequently developed postoperative POH than in those who did not.
The postoperative minor axis of the inferior vena cava was significantly smaller in patients with POH compared to those without, suggesting IVC collapse contributed to reduced cardiac output and POH.
Preoperative brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) concentrations did not significantly differ between patients with and without postoperative POH, arguing against heart failure as an underlying cause.
There was no significant difference in perioperative IVC dimensions between patients who underwent a posterior-only surgical approach versus a combined lateral and posterior approach.
Patients with postoperative POH were treated with amezinium metilsulfate and midodrine hydrochloride to raise blood pressure, and sodium chloride to promote fluid retention.
Patients with POH developed secondary problems that required more invasive procedures and may have contributed to their extended hospital stay.
Children with ASD showed significant deficits in manual coordination, strength and agility, and total motor composite scores compared to typically developing peers.
Children with ASD exhibited significantly reduced time-domain heart rate variability measures compared to typically developing children.
Children with ASD exhibited significantly reduced frequency-domain heart rate variability measures compared to typically developing children.
No statistically significant differences in arterial stiffness were found between children with ASD and typically developing children.

Stretch marks in the two children with ASD showed higher frequency and wider distribution across the abdomen than in the non-ASD obese control, suggesting greater severity of underlying connective tissue alteration.

Ultrasound and elastosonography of the control subject's stretch marks revealed increased echogenicity and altered collagen fiber organization forming rigid/semi-rigid columns extending from the dermis into the deep hypodermis, consistent with connective tissue atrophy.
A scratch/excoriation lesion was observed overlapping the abdominal stretch marks of the ASD boy, suggesting that the stretch marks caused itching or discomfort leading to self-scratching.

Tactile sensitivity did not differ between children with and without ASD, but the stimulus detection threshold for tactile stimuli was higher in ASD children across various ages, indicating altered tactile perception.
The authors hypothesize that a generalized connective tissue disorder, previously described in individuals with ASD, may exacerbate the severity and distribution of stretch marks.
Children with autism spectrum disorder have a higher risk of obesity than typically developing children, attributed mainly to sedentary lifestyle and poor eating habits.
In non-ASD subjects, substantial weight gain leads to stretch marks in more than 50% of subjects.
Some studies report a correlation between stretch mark severity and pelvic organ prolapse, as well as obstetric anal sphincter injuries.

The authors hypothesize that stretch marks, by further weakening already compromised connective tissue, may worsen motor symptoms and postural instability already documented in ASD, especially in combination with obesity-related core instability.
A therapy combining magnetic fields and vacuum applied simultaneously (V-EMF) appears promising for treating 'albae' stretch marks, though its applicability to ASD subjects is uncertain.
No apparent differences in distribution pattern or thickness of stretch marks were observed between the girl and boy with ASD, excluding sexual dimorphism in this small sample.
Across participants, saccadic reaction times were slower during overlap trials compared to baseline trials.
Faces elicited faster saccadic orienting responses than non-face stimuli across participants.
The advantage of multi-modal over uni-modal stimuli for faster attention orienting was more evident in children without ADHD and/or autism than in those with these diagnoses.
In autistic participants without ADHD, smaller pre-saccadic pupil size was linearly associated with faster saccadic reaction times.
In children with ADHD without autism, saccadic reaction times were slower when intra-individual pre-saccadic pupil size was either smallest or largest, indicating a quadratic (U-shaped) relationship.
The authors conclude that dysregulated autonomic arousal likely affects oculomotor attention-orienting mechanisms differently in autism and ADHD.
A K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier trained on ECG-derived HRV features distinguished infants at elevated vs. typical familial likelihood for ASD with above-chance accuracy and AUC-ROC.
Infants at elevated familial likelihood for ASD (EL) showed higher Cardiac Sympathetic Index (CSI) values than typical-likelihood (TL) infants.
Infants at elevated familial likelihood for ASD (EL) showed lower Cardiovagal Index (CVI) values than typical-likelihood (TL) infants, suggesting reduced parasympathetic activation.
EL infants showed lower median NN (normal beat interval) values than TL infants, consistent with altered heart rate variability.
EL infants exhibited lower pNN20 (percentage of successive NN intervals differing by more than 20 ms) values than TL infants, indicating reduced short-term HRV.
EL infants showed lower HTI (HRV triangular index) values than TL infants.
EL infants showed lower CVNN (coefficient of variation of NN intervals) values than TL infants.
Among the seven HRV features used, MedianNN was identified as the single most important feature for the KNN classifier's discrimination between EL and TL infants via permutation feature importance.

Wearable ECG sensors were well tolerated by all infants during naturalistic object- and caregiver-interaction sessions, with only 12% of recordings (9 participants) rejected due to signal quality issues.
In wild-type mouse ileum, 94% of submucosal neurons express Nlgn3 mRNA in the cell soma as detected by RNAScope.
Cholinergic (ChAT+) submucosal neurons showed Nlgn3 mRNA expression (92%) with a distribution and copy number similar to total submucosal neurons.

Non-cholinergic VIP-expressing submucosal neurons show a significantly right-skewed distribution of Nlgn3 mRNA expression compared to total submucosal neurons, though average copy number per neuron was not significantly different.
Most myenteric neurons (87%) express Nlgn3 mRNA in the cell soma, averaging 16.1 copies per neuron.
Calretinin-immunoreactive myenteric neurons showed Nlgn3 mRNA expression (86%) with distribution and copy number similar to the total myenteric neuron population.
nNOS-immunoreactive myenteric neurons showed Nlgn3 mRNA expression (87%) with distribution and copy number similar to total myenteric neurons.
Nlgn3 mRNA is expressed in a subset (31%) of submucosal glial cells in the wild-type mouse ileum, the first report of Nlgn3 expression in enteric glia.
In the myenteric plexus, 55% of glial cells express Nlgn3 mRNA, a higher proportion than in submucosal glia.

scRNAseq analysis of enteric neuron classes (ENC1-12) shows Nlgn3 expression across all classes, with the highest expression level and proportion of expressing cells (~50%) in ENC6, corresponding to intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs).
Unlike in the brain where NLGN3 predominantly heterodimerises with NLGN1, in the enteric nervous system Nlgn2 and Nlgn3 have largely overlapping expression profiles across neuronal classes.

Neurexin binding partners of Nlgn3 show class-specific enrichment in enteric neurons: Nrxn1 is highest in interneuron class ENC11, Nrxn2 is highest in IPAN class ENC6, and Nrxn3 is highest in ENC6/7/10.
scRNAseq of myenteric glia shows Nlgn3 is strongly expressed across glial clusters (38% of 10,535 cells) compared to negligible Nlgn1 and sub-50% Nlgn2, with neurexins minimally expressed in glia.
The autism-associated Nlgn3 R451C mutation significantly reduces overall Nlgn3 mRNA expression in submucosal neurons compared to wild-type.
In Nlgn3R451C mice, cholinergic (ChAT+) submucosal neurons show markedly reduced Nlgn3 mRNA copy number and a smaller proportion of expressing cells compared to wild-type.

In VIP-expressing submucosal neurons, the R451C mutation reduced the proportion of Nlgn3-expressing neurons and altered the mRNA distribution, but average copy number per neuron showed only a borderline trend toward increase compared to wild-type.
The R451C mutation significantly reduces Nlgn3 mRNA copy number in myenteric neurons overall compared to wild-type.
Calretinin-immunoreactive myenteric neurons show significantly reduced Nlgn3 mRNA expression and lower proportion expressing Nlgn3 in Nlgn3R451C mice compared to wild-type.

nNOS-immunoreactive myenteric neurons show markedly reduced Nlgn3 mRNA copy number and reduced proportion expressing Nlgn3 in Nlgn3R451C mice compared to wild-type, potentially contributing to altered nitrergic signalling.
Submucosal glia showed similar Nlgn3 mRNA distribution between WT and Nlgn3R451C mice, with only a borderline trend toward increased copy number per glial cell in mutants.
Myenteric glia show a dramatic reduction in Nlgn3 mRNA copy number and proportion of expressing cells in Nlgn3R451C mice compared to wild-type, unlike submucosal glia which were unaffected.

Human carriers of the NLGN3 R451C mutation exhibit GI dysfunction including diarrhoea, faecal incontinence, post-meal regurgitation, oesophageal inflammation, chronic intestinal pain, and delayed bladder and bowel control.
Nlgn3 knockout mice exhibit distended colons and more rapidly propagating colonic muscle contractions, indicating a role for NLGN3 in gut motor function.
Nlgn3R451C mice display faster intestinal transit, increased numbers of myenteric neurons in the small intestine, and GABAA receptor-mediated colonic dysmotility.
In mouse whole-brain samples, the R451C mutation does not change Nlgn3 mRNA levels but reduces NLGN3 protein levels, indicating a post-transcriptional effect of the mutation in brain tissue.
Nlgn3 knockout mice show distended colons and more rapidly propagating colonic muscle contractions, indicating a role for NLGN3 in gut motility.
Nlgn3R451C mice display faster intestinal transit, increased numbers of myenteric neurons in the small intestine, and GABAA receptor-mediated colonic dysmotility.

Patients carrying the NLGN3 R451C mutation show gastrointestinal dysfunction including diarrhoea, faecal incontinence, post-meal regurgitation, oesophageal inflammation, chronic intestinal pain, and delayed bladder and bowel control.
In mouse whole-brain samples, the R451C mutation does not change Nlgn3 mRNA expression levels but reduces NLGN3 protein levels.
In addition to somatic expression, Nlgn3 mRNA was also detected in neuronal and glial fibres of the submucosal plexus.
A prior study by the same group reported an increased proportion of nNOS-expressing myenteric neurons in the jejunum and caecum of Nlgn3R451C mice.
scRNAseq detected Nlgn3 mRNA in only 38% of myenteric glial cells compared to 65% detected by RNAScope, likely reflecting lower sensitivity of the scRNAseq approach.
Prior studies show that Nlgn3 is also expressed in non-neuronal enteroendocrine cells of the intestine.
PSD93 interacts with nNOS via a PDZ-PDZ domain interaction, and some nNOS-expressing myenteric neurons express PSD93, suggesting a postsynaptic scaffolding link relevant to NLGN3 function.
Plasma choline concentration is decreased in ASD patients, and reduced hippocampal cytosolic choline has been correlated with autism severity.

The largest population-based study to date found that prenatal maternal stress from the death of a first-degree relative during the third trimester increased risk of both ADHD and ASD in offspring, while bereavement during the second postnatal year increased risk of ASD only.
Two large population-based prospective studies found no association between early-life stress exposure before, during, or in the three years after pregnancy and increased risk of ASD.
Maternal history of childhood abuse or exposure to natural disasters (hurricanes, storms) has been associated with increased prevalence of ASD risk in offspring.

Adverse perinatal conditions including prior abortion, partner abuse, depression, alcohol use, smoking, gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, preterm birth (<37 weeks), and low birth weight contribute to increased ASD risk.
Children whose mothers experienced intimate partner violence in the 2 years before the child's birth had increased ASD risk, independent of other confounding factors.
Prenatal stress exposure at 21-32 weeks gestation, peaking at 25-28 weeks, was associated with a higher incidence of ASD in offspring, suggesting a critical developmental window.
Depressed mood and/or anhedonia during pregnancy are associated with increased ADHD and ASD risk in offspring.
The association between adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and ASD may be moderated by family income and mental health conditions.
Children with ASD and a history of high exposure to adverse childhood experiences are at increased risk for mental health problems, with diagnosis and treatment initiation often delayed.

Children with neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism and ADHD often show atypical HPA axis and locus coeruleus-norepinephrine/autonomic nervous system function, both at rest and during social or environmental stressors.

In a rodent model, low maternal licking/grooming (an early-life stress paradigm) increased DNA methylation of cytosines within exon 17 of the NR3C1 gene, blocking NGFI-A transcription factor binding and reducing hippocampal glucocorticoid receptor expression, whereas high maternal licking/grooming reduced this methylation and increased hippocampal GR expression.
Children who later developed and maintained a PTSD diagnosis after motor vehicle accidents had higher serum IL-6 and evening salivary cortisol concentrations than those who did not develop PTSD.

In children with chronic PTSD after motor vehicle accidents, plasma noradrenaline progressively increased over months 1 and 6 while evening salivary cortisol gradually normalized, contrasting with non-PTSD and control groups.
Sexually abused girls with depressive symptomatology showed elevated 24-hour urine catecholamine concentrations compared to matched controls.

Morning salivary cortisol was significantly elevated in maltreated children with a history of physical and sexual abuse or neglect/emotional abuse, whereas children with isolated physical abuse exhibited lower morning cortisol.

An asymmetry was found between salivary alpha-amylase (sympathetic marker) and cortisol responses to a social stressor in maltreated adolescents, suggesting decoupling between the two stress-response systems.

Maltreated adolescent girls showed an attenuated HPA axis (cortisol) response to the Trier Social Stress Test compared to controls, who showed a normal rise and gradual decrease in cortisol after the test.

A longitudinal study following girls with chronic familial maltreatment from age 6 to 30 found a significantly less steep (attenuated) non-stress cortisol trajectory over time compared to expected, supporting the 'attenuation hypothesis' of cortisol secretion following chronic early trauma.
The association between prenatal maternal stress and ADHD symptoms appears sex-specific, being stronger in boys than in girls, independent of sociodemographic factors or smoking.

Children with ADHD aged 4-17 years had higher exposure to adverse childhood experiences compared to controls, and the ACE score was associated with ADHD symptom severity; cumulative ACE exposure had a stronger association with ADHD than a single ACE.

The COVID-19 pandemic and associated lockdown-related physical and social isolation acted as a severe, long-acting stressor for pregnant women, children and adolescents, precipitating PTSD, depression, anxiety disorders and psychosis, particularly in adolescents.
In adults who died weeks to months after acute COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2 RNA persisted across multiple tissue groups including several brain regions despite being undetectable in plasma.
Subgenomic RNA, indicative of ongoing viral replication, was detected in at least one non-respiratory tissue in over half of patients examined beyond day 14 post-infection.
Two adults with clinically diagnosed long COVID who underwent unrelated surgery 175 and 426 days after infection had SARS-CoV-2 RNA detected in breast, appendix, and skin tissue.

Plasma profiling of 181 individuals showed persistence of viral protein in people with long COVID alongside proinflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokine perturbations, compared with those without long COVID and uninfected controls.
In a 14-month-old girl who died of COVID-19 pneumonitis, SARS-CoV-2 RNA-positive cells were identified by RT-qPCR in the choroid plexus, lateral ventricle, and cortex.
A 5-year-old girl had SARS-CoV-2 RNA (along with Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex DNA) detected in a cerebellar biopsy 35 days after infection.

A pediatric patient developed cerebral vasculitis secondary to SARS-CoV-2 infection, with high SARS-CoV-2 IgM levels detected in the CSF 15 days after infection along with parenchymal infarct and perivascular inflammatory infiltrates.
In a girl who died of acute fulminant cerebral oedema during SARS-CoV-2 infection, no viral RNA was detected in CSF, blood, brain tissue, or lung samples.

In asymptomatic/mildly infected children, SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detectable months later in a substantial minority of tonsil and adenoid samples, with CD123+ dendritic cells identified as the most commonly infected cell type.

In 110 convalescent children with negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR, pharyngeal tissue showed persistent expansion of germinal-centre CXCR5+ CD8+ T cells and CD57+ T-cell populations along with viral RNA, resembling progenitor cells that sustain antiviral responses in chronic infection.

A girl with persistent gastrointestinal symptoms 3 months after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection had nucleocapsid protein detected in the intestinal lamina propria with an associated lymphocytic infiltrate.

SARS-CoV-2 was identified by immunofluorescence in the mesenteric lymph node and ileum of two children who underwent surgery for intussusception, suggesting a possible link between viral persistence and this complication.
In a multinational retrospective study, SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA was present in the organs of 4 of 6 autopsied stillborn babies following maternal COVID-19 infection during pregnancy.

A fetal death at 24 weeks gestation 7 days after maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection showed viral RNA in lung, liver, spleen and trachea, and spike protein by immunohistochemistry in stomach, liver, lymph node, and heart.
In an extremely premature neonate who died 4 days after birth, subgenomic RT-PCR positivity suggested active SARS-CoV-2 replication in lung, heart, and liver tissue.

Children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome had neutrophils with a distinct granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cell signature, altered metabolism, and extensive spontaneous neutrophil extracellular trap formation triggered by SARS-CoV-2 immune complexes.

Observational studies have reported an increase in newly onset immune-mediated diseases, such as type 1 diabetes, in children previously infected with SARS-CoV-2, though a causal link has not been clearly established.

In a large retrospective cohort of high-risk patients, nirmatrelvir treatment during acute infection was associated with reduced risk of long COVID overall and of 10 of 12 prespecified long COVID outcomes compared with untreated patients.

A case series reported symptom improvement with nirmatrelvir in four patients with established long COVID, though this is regarded as preliminary given uncertainty about whether persisting viral RNA reflects actively replicating virus.

A 2023 systematic review found that COVID-19 vaccines might have therapeutic effects on long COVID by boosting and rebalancing the immune system, though this was based on low-quality studies and no pediatric data exist.

A pilot study by the authors found that a subgroup of children with long COVID had a compromised innate-to-adaptive immune switch, shown by contraction of naive and switched B-cell compartments and an unstable regulatory T-lymphocyte balance, with no significant difference in pro-inflammatory cytokine expression versus recovered children.
Circulating microclots entrapped with pro-inflammatory molecules have been shown in patients with long COVID and may play a key role in the more severe spectrum of the condition.
A predictive signature of long COVID chronicity included elevated plasma concentrations of type II interferon and interleukin-2.
Studies have documented highly activated innate immune signatures with higher type I and type III interferon expression, as well as CXCL9 and CXCL10, 8 months after non-severe SARS-CoV-2 infection.

In two children with long COVID and chronic gastrointestinal symptoms and evidence of persistent viral shedding, a gastrointestinal anti-inflammatory and immune-stimulating agent successfully eliminated the virus from stool and resolved symptoms.
Children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome, expected to have been infected 1-3 months earlier, have been found to have persistent fecal SARS-CoV-2 positivity.

In seven pediatric patients with COVID-19-associated chilblains, immunohistochemistry detected SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in dermal capillary endothelial cells and eccrine gland epithelial cells 4-30 days after infection.
Immunofluorescence identified SARS-CoV-2 in the mesenteric lymph node and ileum of two children who underwent surgery for intussusception, five days after detection.
SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid and spike antigens were detected in plasma of 3 of 53 (5.7%) paediatric multisystem inflammatory syndrome samples more than 2 weeks after acute infection.
Immunofluorescence identified SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in intestinal cecum cells of a 12-year-old boy with multisystem inflammatory syndrome, 6 weeks after acute infection.

In 110 SARS-CoV-2 PCR-negative convalescent children, tonsil and adenoid germinal centres showed expanded populations of CXCR5-expressing lymphocytes including CXCR5+ CD8+ T cells resembling progenitor cells that sustain antiviral responses in chronic infection.
Various CD57+ T-cell populations, which typically develop after repeated antigen exposure in chronic infections, were enriched in tonsil/adenoid tissue of convalescent children.

SARS-CoV-2 can infect monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages without producing infectious virus while preserving infectivity, suggesting these cells could harbor and spread virus or drive inflammation.

Children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome show neutrophils with a distinct granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cell signature, altered metabolism, and extensive spontaneous neutrophil extracellular trap formation triggered by SARS-CoV-2 immune complexes.
Observational studies have found an increase in newly onset immune-mediated diseases, such as type 1 diabetes, in children previously infected with SARS-CoV-2, though causality is not established.

Patients surviving long COVID report a higher number and similar range of chronic symptoms compared with controls, resembling those reported after other infections including Lyme disease, Ebola, influenza, and chikungunya.

A strong link between Epstein-Barr virus and multiple sclerosis has been established, likely via reprogramming of latently infected B lymphocytes and chronic presentation of viral antigens, offered as a model for SARS-CoV-2 persistence research.

Measles RNA has been detected in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, urine, and respiratory secretions for months after natural infection, and anomalous persistent measles particles are found in patients who later develop subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, offered as a model for understanding SARS-CoV-2 persistence.

In two children with long COVID and persistent gastrointestinal viral shedding, treatment with a gastrointestinal anti-inflammatory and immune-stimulating agent eliminated SARS-CoV-2 from stool and resolved symptoms.
Children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome, expected to have been infected 1-3 months earlier, have been found to have persistent fecal SARS-CoV-2 positivity.

Highly activated innate immune signatures with higher expression of type I and type III interferons, as well as CXCL9 and CXCL10, were documented 8 months after non-severe SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A predictive signature for chronicity of long COVID included elevated plasma concentrations of type II interferon and IL-2.
Self-reactive immune responses have been documented in association with long COVID, along with clonal and mutational maturation of memory B cells.

Plasma profiling of 181 individuals with and without long COVID and uninfected controls showed persistence of viral protein in long COVID cases along with proinflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokine perturbations.
Two adults with a clinical diagnosis of long COVID who underwent surgery 175 and 426 days after initial infection had evidence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in breast, appendix, and skin tissue.
In immunocompromised patients, persistent SARS-CoV-2 has been shown to replicate, evolve, and generate new variants.
Non-human primates infected with SARS-CoV-2 have shown similar viral RNA persistence findings, reinforcing evidence for persistence seen in humans.

A 2023 systematic review found that COVID-19 vaccines might have therapeutic effects on long COVID by boosting and rebalancing the immune system, though based on low-quality evidence and not studied in children.

In a pilot study, a subgroup of children with long COVID showed a compromised innate-to-adaptive immune switch, with contraction of naive and switched B-cell compartments and an unstable regulatory T lymphocyte balance, while pro-inflammatory cytokine expression did not significantly differ from recovered children.
A systematic review of over 250,000 COVID-19 survivors found that 54% experienced at least one long COVID symptom at 6 months or more after infection.
A meta-analysis found a significant increase in the number of COVID-19 patients experiencing fatigue and/or cognitive impairment after resolution of acute infection.
A large meta-analysis of over 1.28 million COVID-19 survivors across 32 countries reported that approximately half had persistent symptoms 12 months after hospital discharge.
Autopsy studies detected SARS-CoV-2 viral copies in the brain of patients who died from COVID-19, at lower levels than in the lung, indicating broad organotropism including neuroinvasion.
Song et al. detected specific spike protein staining in the brains of three patients who died from severe COVID-19, with associated pathological changes but minimal immune cell infiltration.
An in vitro blood-brain barrier cell culture assay showed that the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein S1 subunit can cross the human brain endothelial cell barrier.
Intranasal or intravenous administration of radioiodinated SARS-CoV-2 S1 protein crossed the blood-brain barrier in mice via adsorptive transcytosis.
SARS-CoV-2 crosses the blood-brain barrier via a transcellular pathway involving basement membrane disruption without alteration of tight junctions.

SARS-CoV-2 caused significant neuronal death in human brain organoids, and in hACE2-overexpressing mice, brain infection (via intraventricular administration) was lethal, whereas lung infection alone caused pathology without death.
UK Biobank brain imaging in n=785 showed long-lasting structural effects linked to the olfactory cortex after SARS-CoV-2 infection, associated with loss of taste and smell.
A retrospective study found that subjects co-infected with SARS-CoV-2 and EBV had approximately a three-fold increased risk of severe COVID-19 symptoms compared with SARS-CoV-2 infection alone.
Gold et al. reported that many long COVID symptoms including fatigue, insomnia, headaches, myalgia, and confusion may be due to EBV reactivation triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A longitudinal study of 309 COVID-19 patients found that EBV viremia was associated with long COVID symptoms such as fatigue and sputum production.

In a cohort of 280 individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection, Peluso et al. found that long COVID symptoms such as fatigue and cognitive impairment at 4 months were independently associated with recent EBV reactivation.
X-box-binding protein 1 (XBP-1) in the endoplasmic reticulum, in combination with protein kinase D, can activate EBV gene expression, suggesting a role for XBP-1 in EBV reactivation.
A population-based retrospective study found that use of SSRIs with sigma-1 receptor agonism at or prior to COVID-19 infection was associated with a reduced risk of developing long COVID.

A randomized placebo-controlled double-blind trial found that fluvoxamine 100 mg daily for 10 days during active COVID-19 significantly reduced the incidence of fatigue at 12 weeks compared with placebo, though other symptom differences did not reach significance likely due to low dose.

Yeoh et al. found that gut microbiome composition was significantly altered in COVID-19 patients compared with non-COVID-19 controls, correlated with disease severity and blood inflammatory markers, with alterations persisting in recovered patients.

A meta-analysis of 16 studies showed that gut microbiome diversity was lower in COVID-19 patients (both acute and recovery phase) than non-COVID-19 subjects, with reduced anti-inflammatory butyrate-producing microbes and enrichment of pro-inflammatory taxa.
Fecal metabolites in Chinese COVID-19 patients were altered compared with age- and sex-matched healthy controls, and were associated with clinical features and gut microbiome composition.

A prospective study found neuropsychiatric symptoms and fatigue in long COVID correlated with nosocomial gut pathogens such as Clostridium innocuum and Actinomyces naeslundii, while butyrate-producing bacteria showed a significant inverse correlation with post-acute COVID-19 syndrome.
High levels of fungal translocation from the gut and/or lung epithelium were detected in the plasma of patients with long COVID compared with patients without long COVID.
Reduced abundance of Corynebacterium in the nasal microbiome was associated with loss of olfactory function in COVID-19 patients.

Haran et al. found that COVID-19 patients with prolonged symptoms had higher abundance of inflammation-causing oral microbes, and the oral microbiome of long COVID patients resembled that of chronic fatigue syndrome patients.
SARS-CoV-2 was detected in fecal samples of COVID-19 patients and remained detectable in feces up to four months after infection.

Gut microbiome composition was significantly altered in COVID-19 patients compared with non-COVID-19 controls, correlated with disease severity and blood inflammatory markers, and alterations persisted in recovered patients.

A meta-analysis of 16 studies found lower gut microbiome diversity in both acute and recovery phases of COVID-19 relative to non-COVID subjects, with reduced anti-inflammatory butyrate-producing microbes and enrichment of pro-inflammatory taxa during the acute phase.
Fecal metabolites in Chinese COVID-19 patients were altered compared with age- and sex-matched healthy controls, correlating with clinical features and gut microbiome composition.

Neuropsychiatric symptoms and fatigue in long COVID patients correlated with nosocomial gut pathogens such as Clostridium innocuum and Actinomyces naeslundii, while butyrate-producing bacteria showed a significant inverse correlation with post-acute COVID-19 syndrome.
Host phenotype combined with multi-kingdom microbiome profiling was suggested as a potentially useful prognostic tool for COVID-19 patients.
Serum IgG responses against EBV dUTPase were heightened in both ME/CFS and long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
IgG response against HSV-1 dUTPase was strikingly higher in both mild and severe long COVID patients compared to controls.
A modest but significant increase in IgG response against HHV-6 dUTPase was observed specifically in ME/CFS patients.
IgG response against HHV-6 dUTPase was decreased in SARS-CoV-2 infected (long COVID cohort) patients compared to healthy controls, in contrast to the ME/CFS pattern.
Transient expression of HSV-1, HHV-6, or EBV dUTPase in cultured human cells induced a hyperpolarized, hyperfused mitochondrial phenotype with increased mitochondrial surface area.
Mitochondrial fusion protein Mfn1 was upregulated by transient expression of all three herpesvirus dUTPases (EBV, HSV-1, HHV-6), regardless of subcellular localization.
All three viral dUTPases inhibited mitophagy to varying degrees, with EBV dUTPase most efficiently decreasing LC3β protein expression.

TMRE staining showed EBV dUTPase-expressing cells had decreased mitochondrial membrane potential in the presence of oligomycin, indicating poor mitochondrial health, whereas HSV-1 and HHV-6 dUTPase showed no significant effect.
Exposure of cultured cells to recombinant EBV dUTPase induced dose-dependent Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fragmentation with increased Drp1 protein levels.

Mass spectrometry of proteins co-immunoprecipitated with herpesvirus dUTPases showed enrichment of cytoskeletal proteins including neurofilament medium chain (NEFM), epiplakin 1 (EPPK1), and plectin (PLEC), indicating strong dUTPase-cytoskeleton association.

Purified immunoglobulins from severe ME/CFS patients (as little as 1 μg) induced mitochondrial fragmentation within 12 hours when applied to primary HUVEC cells, an effect that was cell-type dependent and pronounced compared to mild/moderate ME/CFS or healthy control immunoglobulins.
The fragmented mitochondrial phenotype induced by immunoglobulins from severe ME/CFS patients was associated with decreased Mfn1 and PLD6 protein levels.

Mass spectrometry of purified IgG-bound circulating immune complexes revealed decreased amounts of fibronectin (FN1), alpha-2-macroglobulin (A2M), and serotransferrin (TF) in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.

Antibody microarray profiling of 120 autoantigens found IgM against fibronectin was among the antibodies selectively decreased in severe ME/CFS patients, contributing to clustering that separated healthy, mild/moderate, and severe patients.

Circulating serum fibronectin levels were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls and positively correlated with disease severity, achieving an AUROC of 79.8% for identifying severe ME/CFS.
Only long COVID patients (mild and severe) showed significantly higher circulating fibronectin levels compared to healthy controls and SARS-CoV-2 positive individuals without long COVID.

Analysis of circulating fibronectin composition showed increases in both EDA-negative plasma fibronectin (plFN1) and EDA/CBD-positive cellular fibronectin (clFN1) in ME/CFS patients relative to healthy controls.
Circulating fibronectin levels were significantly higher in females than males among healthy controls, SARS-CoV-2 positive patients without long COVID, and severe long COVID patients.

Serum IgM against fibronectin (IgM-FN1) was significantly decreased in all SARS-CoV-2 positive patient groups (no LC, mild LC, severe LC) compared to both healthy controls and ME/CFS patients, with the strongest decrease in severe long COVID.
IgG against fibronectin was significantly decreased in all three groups of SARS-CoV-2 positive patients compared to healthy controls, with severe long COVID patients showing a trend toward recovery.
Natural IgM levels against fibronectin, phosphorylcholine and MDA tended to be more abundant in healthy females than in healthy males.
Female ME/CFS patients showed a significant decrease in IgM-FN1 compared to male ME/CFS patients, a difference not seen in other patient groups.

All natural IgM levels tested (against FN1, PC and MDA) were significantly lower in all three long COVID patient groups compared to healthy controls, with no clear association with gender in this cohort.
ME/CFS patients showed an overall increase in both EDA-negative plasma fibronectin and EDA/CBD-positive cellular fibronectin compared to healthy controls.
Severe long COVID patients showed a trend towards recovery of IgG-FN1 levels relative to milder groups, despite overall depletion compared to healthy controls.

A combined panel of circulating fibronectin and IgM-FN1 levels distinguished severe ME/CFS patients from healthy controls with 83.7% accuracy and severe long COVID with 85.3% accuracy in multivariate ROC analysis.
Multiple logistic regression using FN1 and IgM-FN1 levels separated healthy controls from severe ME/CFS patients with 83.7% accuracy and from mild/severe long COVID patients with 83.3% accuracy.
Severe ME/CFS and severe long COVID patients closely resembled each other in terms of circulating FN1 and IgM-FN1 amounts, supporting shared pathophysiology between the two conditions.

The authors' prior work showed presence of EBV dUTPase protein within brain biopsies of ME/CFS patients, supporting a role for tissue-localized herpesvirus reactivation in the neurological symptoms of ME/CFS.

Circulating fibronectin is proposed to bind TLR4 and induce an inflammatory cytokine response, and specific fibronectin domains activate platelets and mast cells, providing a mechanistic link between elevated FN1 and disease pathology.

The authors propose that alterations in CD4+ T cells, including T cell exhaustion and changes in CXCR4+ regulatory T cell numbers previously documented in ME/CFS, could impair B1 B cell function within primary hematopoietic tissues and drive natural IgM depletion.
In the first 4 weeks after a positive COVID-19 test, individuals had significantly higher risk of fatigue compared to propensity-matched controls.
In the first 4 weeks after a positive COVID-19 test, individuals had significantly higher risk of embolism compared to propensity-matched controls.
In the first 4 weeks after a positive COVID-19 test, individuals had a reduced likelihood of new anxiety and depression diagnoses compared to controls.
Beyond 4 weeks after a positive COVID-19 test, individuals continued to have a significantly higher risk of fatigue compared to controls.
Beyond 4 weeks after a positive COVID-19 test, individuals continued to have a significantly higher risk of embolism compared to controls.
All individuals with a positive COVID-19 test were found to be at substantially greater risk of post-viral illness compared to matched controls.
Community-acquired COVID-19 was associated with increased risk of respiratory conditions relative to matched controls.

Despite statistically significant elevated hazard ratios for several conditions after COVID-19, life table (absolute risk) analysis showed that only a small minority of the overall study population were actually affected.

Post-viral SARS-CoV-2 patients can develop a sympathetic-parasympathetic imbalance favoring sympathetic activity, manifesting as inner restlessness, reduced sleep quality, sweating, nausea, and heart racing/irregular heart rate.
Postural changes in post-viral SARS-CoV-2 patients can trigger severe dizziness, tachycardia, and concurrent blood pressure drop, consistent with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS).

Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is identified as a key phenomenon in post-viral SARS-CoV-2 sequelae, where exertion beyond current capacity triggers symptom worsening ("crashes"), and pacing is recommended as an evidence-based strategy to avoid this.

Traditional standardized cognitive training (as commonly used in neurological rehabilitation) was found in practice to consume more energy than benefit for patients with grade 2-4 KLOK-scale impairment, whereas everyday-life-oriented, KRAH-based occupational therapy approaches showed better effect.

Nerve stretching during everyday activities (e.g., tying shoes) was observed to provoke PEM/crashes in post-viral SARS-CoV-2 patients, leading to avoidance of neurodynamic exercises in practice pending further research.

Monitoring heart rate and oxygen saturation during daily activities was recommended to help patients recognize symptom-worsening thresholds, since performing activities with too high heart rate or too low oxygen saturation can worsen symptoms and desaturation can go unnoticed by patients.

Hyperventilation syndrome (HVS) has been described in association with post-viral SARS-CoV-2 sequelae, with warning signs including shortness of breath, chest pressure/pain, dizziness, and anxiety, addressed via breathing techniques such as pursed-lip breathing.

Post-viral SARS-CoV-2 patients frequently exhibit altered (typically lowered) sensory thresholds affecting olfactory, gustatory, visual, auditory, tactile, vestibular, and temperature perception, often transient.
Flexible, graduated 'return to work' plans were reported to support people with post-viral SARS-CoV-2 sequelae in returning to the workplace.
Infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus is identified as a risk factor for chronic fatigue syndrome.
Profound fatigue is a feature of infectious mononucleosis but typically resolves within three months.
The overall plasma proteome of Neuro-PASC patients differed more substantially from COVID-19 convalescents and healthy controls than post-COVID-19 groups differed from healthy controls.
Neuro-PASC patients 3-9 months after acute COVID-19 showed alterations in inflammatory proteins and pathways relative to COVID convalescents and healthy controls.
Proteomic markers associated with Neuro-PASC symptoms of brain fog and fatigue included changes in markers of DNA repair, oxidative stress, and neutrophil degranulation.

An increase in plasma concentration of the oxidative phosphorylation protein COX7A1 correlated with Neuro-PASC patients' lower subjective impression of recovery to pre-COVID-19 baseline, and was also associated with neurologic symptoms, fatigue, impaired quality of life, and cognitive dysfunction.
Other oxidative phosphorylation-associated proteins were found to correlate with central nervous system symptoms in Neuro-PASC patients.
About one in five COVID-19 cases reported at least one persistent symptom at a median of 8.3 months follow-up, most commonly shortness of breath, fatigue, and loss of smell/taste.
Among cases who were asymptomatic during acute infection, a substantial proportion developed new fatigue and other symptoms months later.
New fatigue and new loss of taste/smell at follow-up were significantly more common among COVID-19 cases than controls.
Cases had a significantly higher prevalence of likely depression than controls at follow-up as measured by PHQ-2.
There was no significant difference in likely anxiety between cases and controls at follow-up as measured by GAD-2.
Both cases and controls reported minimal cognitive dysfunction at follow-up, with no clinically meaningful difference between groups on the Cognitive Function Instrument.
Functional activity status did not differ between cases and controls at follow-up as measured by the Duke Activity Status Index.

Neuropsychiatric PASC symptoms such as brain fog, slowed thinking, and insomnia were more common in COVID-19 cases and in controls with subsequent infection than in controls without subsequent infection.
At baseline, anti-nucleocapsid antibody levels were markedly higher in COVID-19 cases than in seronegative controls, regardless of vaccination status.

A large majority of COVID-19 cases underwent sero-reversion of anti-nucleocapsid antibodies below the assay's positive threshold by a median of 8 months after infection, most of whom had mild or asymptomatic disease.
In adjusted linear mixed effects models, anti-nucleocapsid antibody levels significantly decreased over time among cases but not among controls.
Anti-spike antibody levels declined substantially with time since vaccination in both cases and controls.
Cases with prior infection plus vaccination had persistently higher anti-spike antibody levels than vaccinated controls without prior infection, consistent with hybrid immunity.
Among controls, anti-nucleocapsid antibody levels remained stable at near-zero unless a subsequent COVID-19 infection occurred, after which levels increased.
Long COVID (PASC) is estimated to occur in 10 to 20% of patients who have recovered from acute COVID-19 infection.
Circulating microclots are proposed as one possible cause of the persistent symptoms of PASC.
Thromboinflammation, a hallmark of acute COVID-19 hypercoagulability, continues in some patients even after the virus has been cleared.
Viral spike proteins and RNA can be detected in patients months after recovery, which may drive persistent thromboinflammation and microclot formation.
Long-term anticoagulation, antiplatelet therapy, and vascular endothelial protection have shown inconsistent results and do not always provide beneficial treatment effects for long COVID.
PASC is a heterogeneous condition, and microclots cannot account for all presenting symptoms, suggesting a need for symptom- or biomarker-based stratified approaches in future research.

Of 1,050 hospitalized COVID-19 patients successfully interviewed by phone, 256 (24.3%) reported at least one symptom persisting for eight weeks or more after discharge, defining the study's long COVID prevalence.
Dyspnea was the most common post-acute sequela, reported by 42.40% of the 256 patients and lasting from 7 to 300 days.
Fatigue was the second most common PASC, reported by 28.29% of patients and lasting from 10 to 300 days.
Arthralgia-myalgia was reported by 16.33% of patients, lasting from 2 to 270 days.
Post-discharge cough was reported by 13.15% of patients, lasting from 10 to 360 days.
Back pain was reported by 7.17% of patients, lasting from 15 to 180 days.
Patients with pre-existing lung disease were more likely to report persistent dyspnea (60%) than those without lung disease (40.6%).
Patients with a history of ICU admission during acute COVID-19 had higher rates of persistent dyspnea (66.67%) than those not admitted to ICU (39.7%).
Patients discharged with oxygen therapy had higher rates of persistent dyspnea (63.64%) than those who did not require it (40.5%).
Patients who experienced a cytokine storm during acute infection had higher rates of persistent dyspnea (63.9%) than those without (36.11%).
In multivariate logistic regression, having lung disease was an independent risk factor for persistent dyspnea, though the model showed poor discrimination (AUC 0.622).
Post-discharge cough was more frequent in patients with pulmonary involvement >50% during acute infection (25.64%) than in those with <50% involvement (12.41%).
In multivariate logistic regression, pulmonary involvement >50% during acute COVID-19 was an independent risk factor for persistent cough, with poor model discrimination (AUC 0.608).
A significant correlation was found between loss of smell as a persistent symptom and length of hospital stay during acute COVID-19 infection.
Dizziness as a persistent symptom was more common among patients with >50% lung involvement (10.3%) than those with <50% involvement (2.1%).
In multivariate logistic regression, longer hospital stay during acute infection was an independent risk factor for persistent myalgia, though model discrimination was poor (AUC 0.578).
No statistically significant relationship was found between any of the long COVID symptoms and either age or gender.
No correlation was found between chest pain, backache, headache, myalgia, malaise, or loss of taste and patients' demographic characteristics and clinical findings.
Persistent loss of smell in this cohort had a longer median duration (35 days, range 10-120) than reported in a prior olfactory dysfunction study.
Chronic pulmonary disease was present in 16.28% of the 256 patients with persistent PASC symptoms.
A composite symptom-survey-based long COVID propensity score (LCPS) discriminated LC participants from others with high diagnostic accuracy.
POTS was a prevalent comorbidity among LC participants, with over a third having formal diagnostic testing and clinical evaluation for it.
Fatigue, brain fog, memory difficulty and confusion were the most commonly self-reported symptoms among LC participants.
Circulating non-conventional (CD14lowCD16high) monocytes were significantly higher in LC participants compared with convalescent controls, remaining significant after adjustment for age, sex and BMI.
Expression of MHC class II (HLA-DR) was significantly elevated in LC participants relative to convalescent controls.
Circulating conventional type 1 dendritic (cDC1) cells were significantly lower in LC participants, an association retained after adjusting for age.
Activated (CD86highHLA-DRhigh) B lymphocytes were significantly more prevalent among LC participants than among convalescent or healthy controls.
Double-negative (IgD-CD27-CD24-CD38-) B cells were elevated in both relative percentage and absolute count in LC participants compared with controls.
The relative percentage of circulating CD4+ central memory T cells was significantly lower in LC participants, although absolute counts did not differ.
Absolute counts of exhausted (PD-1+TIM3+) CD4+ T cells were significantly elevated in LC participants, though relative percentages of exhausted CD4+ and CD8+ subsets did not differ.
After ex vivo stimulation, both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from LC participants produced significantly more intracellular IL-2 than cells from controls.
Stimulated CD4+ T cells from LC participants produced significantly higher intracellular IL-4 than controls.
Stimulated CD8+ T cells from LC participants produced significantly higher intracellular IL-6 than controls.
LC participants uniquely showed elevated levels of polyfunctional IL-4/IL-6 double-positive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells compared with controls.

Vaccinated LC participants had significantly higher anti-S1 IgG levels than convalescent controls, and LC status remained a significant positive predictor of anti-spike humoral response after adjusting for demographic differences.

Consistently inactive individuals have greater risk of hospitalization, ICU admission, and death due to COVID-19 compared with those who engage in some physical activity or meet physical activity guidelines.

A systematic review found that rehabilitation interventions improved dyspnea, anxiety, kinesiophobia, muscle strength, walking capacity, sit-to-stand performance, and quality of life in individuals with long COVID.
In an observational study of 213 participants with persistent post-COVID symptoms, 58.7% met the threshold for post-exertional malaise, and exercise is not recommended for these individuals.
SARS-CoV-2 infection results in reduced ACE2 during the recovery period, potentially producing a mild hypercoagulable state that may contribute to chronic pulmonary vessel remodeling in long COVID.

Endothelial dysfunction is described as a critical component of acute pulmonary pathogenesis in COVID-19, contributing to progressive hypoxic respiratory failure and ARDS, and may also underlie ongoing long COVID symptoms.
A meta-analysis found that 24% of individuals who survived acute COVID-19 continued to experience unresolved dyspnea.
Prevalence of persistent dyspnea correlates with the severity of the initial COVID-19 infection, with outpatients showing the least and critically ill patients showing the most persistent dyspnea.
Impaired diffusing capacity (DLCO) is reported as the most common pulmonary function test abnormality in long COVID patients.

Kersten et al. found that individuals with highly symptomatic long COVID had impaired diffusion capacity and reduced 6-minute walk test distance despite average or only mildly affected mechanical lung function.
Early data on hospital-discharged COVID-19 patients indicated that anemia and deconditioning were significant factors contributing to cardiopulmonary limitations.

A meta-analysis of CPET studies reported that mechanisms beyond anemia or deconditioning—including decreased peripheral oxygen extraction, preload failure, and chronotropic incompetence—may contribute to exercise limitations in long COVID.
SARS-CoV-2 infection results in reduced ACE2 levels during the recovery period, which may contribute to a mild hypercoagulable state.
Persistent SARS-CoV-2 spike protein has been reported in long COVID patients and may promote a prolonged inflammatory response.

More than 20% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients develop acute kidney injury (AKI), with rates approaching 50% among ICU patients, and nearly 10% of hospitalized patients require kidney replacement therapy.

In a retrospective cohort of 12,891 hospitalized adults with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection, an episode of COVID-19-associated AKI was associated with decreased survival, and AKI severity correlated with worse recovery of kidney function and increased mortality.

Analysis of Veterans Health Administration electronic health records found that SARS-CoV-2 infection increased the long-term risk of developing chronic kidney disease, with the highest risk in those with the most severe infections.

A study from China found that 35% of patients had an eGFR below 90 mL/min/1.73m2 six months after COVID-19 hospitalization, and 13% of those with initially normal kidney function developed a decline in eGFR at follow-up.
In a small cohort of pre-diabetic post-COVID patients, podocyte-specific proteins remained elevated in urine for up to 1 year post-infection, suggesting persistent podocyte injury.

Following SARS-CoV-2 infection, patients show variable kidney function trajectories including rapid decline, complete recovery, recurrent AKI, incomplete recovery without further GFR decline, and incomplete recovery with progressive CKD.
The authors note that interaction between SARS-CoV-2 infection and genetic risk factors such as APOL1 gene mutations for progressive CKD warrants further investigation.
After 8 weeks of functional exercise combined with breathing techniques, the FE group showed a significant intragroup reduction in fatigue scores.
The FE group showed a significant intragroup improvement in functional performance measured by repetitions on the 30 Seconds Standing Test.

Among 79 hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed for a median of 648 days, 41.8% developed long COVID.

Residence in Scotland was associated with a lower likelihood of a recorded WHO-defined Long Covid symptom compared with other UK nations.
