Among 2,190,579 COVID-19 patients from 39 N3C data partner sites, 17,036 (0.78%) were diagnosed with the U09.9 ICD-10-CM long COVID code.

Logistic regression and random forest models predicted long COVID occurrence using acute-phase EHR features with median AUROC between 0.74 and 0.77 across all-patient, inpatient, and outpatient cohorts.

AUPRC scores of both models were low (0.02-0.08 median), reflecting the low prevalence of long COVID diagnoses; the random forest model outperformed a random predictor by roughly 3-5 fold depending on cohort.

In an ablation study, models including drug-ordering features achieved significantly higher AUROC than those without, with drug feature exclusion causing an average 5.06% decrease in median AUROC for the all-patient cohort.

Models trained on data from a single N3C site and tested on other sites showed comparable AUROC to models trained on all sites for the all-patient and outpatient cohorts, but a notable 18.92% decrease for inpatients, suggesting limited single-site generalizability for inpatient predictions.
Higher age at COVID-19 diagnosis was among the top SHAP-ranked predictive features favoring long COVID prediction, consistent with age being a known risk factor for long COVID.
Female sex was the top-ranked SHAP feature in the logistic regression model favoring long COVID prediction, consistent with known female predominance in long COVID risk.
Greater severity of acute COVID-19 infection and longer hospital length of stay were important predictive features associated with increased long COVID risk.
Chest pain during the acute infection was an important predictive feature, consistent with existing literature that chest pain persists in some long COVID patients.

Pre-existing comorbidities including obesity, anxiety/depression, dementia, diabetes, kidney disease, and chronic lung disease were among the top predictive features associated with increased long COVID risk.
Melatonin and polyethylene glycol 3350 use during/after acute infection were identified as predictive drug features indicative of long COVID.

Respiratory symptom-relief drugs including benzonatate, guaifenesin, and albuterol ordered during acute infection were important predictive features for long COVID, reflecting respiratory symptom burden.

Corticosteroid medications dexamethasone and prednisone, used to decrease immune response during acute COVID-19, were important predictive drug features; corticosteroids have been proposed to reduce long COVID symptoms and associated immunological alterations, though their role in long COVID treatment remains under investigation.
Remdesivir administration during COVID-19 hospitalisation was among the top predictive features for long COVID.

Enoxaparin, an anticoagulant used prophylactically for deep vein thrombosis, was identified as a predictive drug feature for long COVID; prophylactic enoxaparin use has separately been associated with reduced COVID-19 mortality.

Antihistamines and azithromycin, proposed for early COVID-19 treatment to reduce severity and long COVID risk, were identified as predictive features; antihistamines are hypothesized to inhibit the proinflammatory cytokine storm and viral binding.
Presence of cough and fatigue during the acute COVID-19 infection influenced the logistic regression model toward predicting long COVID occurrence.

Among patients incorrectly predicted as long COVID (false positives), 8.78% had been diagnosed with the older, less specific B94.8 sequelae code, suggesting some may represent under-coded long COVID cases rather than true model errors.
Both LR and RF models yielded their lowest AUROC and AUPRC scores in the outpatient cohort compared to inpatient and all-patient cohorts.
Participants with longstanding type 2 diabetes had a significantly higher total COMPASS 31 score than both the early diabetes group and healthy controls.
Among the COMPASS 31 domains, the secretomotor and gastrointestinal domains contributed most to the higher total score seen in longstanding diabetes.
In the longstanding diabetes group, use of DPP-4 inhibitors (mostly sitagliptin) was associated with a higher total COMPASS 31 score and higher secretomotor and gastrointestinal domain scores.
Women scored higher than men on the total COMPASS 31 score and in all domains except bladder function, with the largest sex differences in the secretomotor and gastrointestinal domains.

The prevalence of definite or borderline cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (CAN) by cardiovascular reflex tests did not differ significantly between longstanding diabetes, early diabetes, and controls.
Monofilament testing showed a significantly higher prevalence of possible/likely peripheral neuropathy in longstanding diabetes compared to controls.

Across all groups combined, COMPASS 31 scores correlated with the presence of definite or borderline cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy, although no within-group associations with CARTs or heart rate variability were found.
COMPASS 31 total and domain scores showed no significant association with objective sudomotor function testing, monofilament testing, or sural nerve conduction testing.
No significant associations were detected between COMPASS 31 scores and rectal sensitivity or rectally evoked brain potentials.

Using the recommended COMPASS 31 threshold of 16 points, sensitivity for detecting CAN was poor (0.33) but specificity was 0.68; lowering the cut-off to 10 points markedly improved sensitivity to 0.83 with only a modest reduction in specificity to 0.55 and a high negative predictive value.
Increasing adrenergic spatial density (ASD) progressively shortened atrial action potential duration, with APD20 shortening by 42% and APD50 by 22% between 0% and 5% ASD.

Spatial heterogeneity of action potential duration (coefficient of spatial variation, CoSV) increased with ASD and reached its maximum at 15% ASD for all APD types, with APD20 showing the largest CoSV (31%) compared to APD50 (16%).

Low adrenergic spatial densities (5-10% ASD) lowered the atrial excitation threshold, allowing conduction at currents at or below baseline (18 μA/cm2, probability ~0.60), whereas ASD greater than 10% raised the threshold, requiring 20 μA/cm2 or more for reliable conduction (probability ≥0.92).

During rapid activation (≥10 Hz), atrial sheets with high ASD showed markedly prolonged APD50 and APD20 compared to baseline, with APD50 increasing from 30 ms to 71 ms at 17 Hz and APD20 from 4 ms to 24 ms at 20 Hz in sheets with 20% ASD.
Temporal heterogeneity of repolarization (coefficient of temporal variation) increased with activation rate and ASD, reaching up to 45% for APD50 at 13 Hz and up to 100% for APD20 at 23 Hz.

Increasing ASD altered the activation cycle length of captured beats during rapid pacing, with absolute changes of 50 ms at 13 Hz and up to 120 ms at 23 Hz relative to the baseline 300 ms cycle length.

The probability of a uniform wavefront fragmenting into curvilinear wavefronts during rapid activation was highest at 10% ASD (0.7±0.06) and decreased at higher ASDs, with fragmentation probability strongly correlated with spatial heterogeneity of APD20.

The proportion of successfully captured beats during rapid pacing decreased with higher activation rates (from one-to-one capture at 3 Hz down to 18-36% at ≥10 Hz) but this decrease depended only on activation rate, not on ASD.

Citing prior clinical work, the authors note that patients with a history of persistent atrial fibrillation have a higher density of adrenergic nerve fibers in their myocardium than patients with only paroxysmal or post-operative atrial fibrillation.

Prior clinical reports cited in this paper indicate that young patients with PTSD but without underlying cardiac substrate remodeling developed atrial fibrillation earlier than those without PTSD, suggesting psychological/autonomic factors can alter atrial electrophysiology independent of structural remodeling.

The computational model simulated beta-adrenergic stimulation by altering conductance/kinetics of slow delayed rectifier and ultra-rapid K+ channels, L-type Ca2+ channels, SERCA, ryanodine receptors, troponin I, and the Na+ pump, mimicking isoproterenol-like effects without alpha-adrenergic contribution.

Combination probiotic and oxytocin treatment significantly improved SDNN, a time-domain HRV metric, compared to placebo in individuals with ASD.

Mean heart rate was positively correlated with baseline oxytocin levels among individuals showing significant HRV improvements with combination therapy.
Baseline oxytocin levels correlated positively with mean heart rate changes observed after combination probiotic and oxytocin therapy.
Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS) raw total scores correlated with mean heart rate, linking autonomic function to autism symptom severity.
Aberrant Behavior Checklist (ABC) raw total scores correlated strongly with mean heart rate, suggesting a link between behavioral symptoms and autonomic regulation.
Lamb-Shaffer syndrome is caused by variants in SOX5 leading to haploinsufficiency of this HMG-domain transcription factor important for brain development.
Autism spectrum disorder is reported as one of the neurodevelopmental features of Lamb-Shaffer syndrome, alongside intellectual disability, speech delay, attention deficits and hyperactivity.
Patients with Lamb-Shaffer syndrome may present distinct facial dysmorphism including a wide mouth with full lips, small chin, broad nasal bridge, and deep-set eyes.
Some patients with Lamb-Shaffer syndrome present short stature, scoliosis, and joint hypermobility as additional physical features.
In the Spanish cohort, pain insensitivity and hypermetropia appeared to occur more frequently among Lamb-Shaffer syndrome patients than previously reported in the literature.
Pain insensitivity appears to be more frequent among Lamb-Shaffer syndrome patients than previously reported in the literature, based on findings in the Spanish cohort.
Hypermetropia (farsightedness) appears more frequent in Lamb-Shaffer syndrome patients than previously reported, based on the Spanish cohort.
Patients with Lamb-Shaffer syndrome commonly present distinct craniofacial dysmorphic features including a wide mouth with full lips, small chin, broad nasal bridge, and deep-set eyes.
Additional physical features reported in some Lamb-Shaffer syndrome patients include short stature and scoliosis.
Autism spectrum disorder is described as one of the neurodevelopmental clinical features seen in patients with Lamb-Shaffer syndrome.
Attention deficits and hyperactivity are reported clinical features among patients with Lamb-Shaffer syndrome.
Seizures are reported as a clinical feature in some patients with Lamb-Shaffer syndrome.
New SOX5 variants identified in the Spanish cohort affect functional domains of the protein other than the HMG DNA-binding domain, expanding the known mutational spectrum.

Autistic participants had higher rates of chronic physical health conditions across every organ system studied compared to non-autistic participants, even after adjustment for demographics, lifestyle factors, and family history.
Autistic people were two to three times more likely to have gastrointestinal, rheumatological, neurological, and renal/hepatic conditions compared to non-autistic people.
Irritable bowel syndrome was significantly more prevalent among autistic participants (25.00%) than non-autistic participants (11.75%), remaining significant across all adjustment models.

Coeliac disease risk was significantly higher in autistic participants when adjusting for demographics, alcohol, smoking and BMI, but this became non-significant after accounting for family history of the condition.
Rheumatological conditions overall were substantially more common among autistic participants, consistent with prior literature.
Fibromyalgia was reported far more frequently in autistic than non-autistic participants and remained significant across all adjustment levels.
Joint hypermobility was markedly more common in autistic women than non-autistic women, with a very large effect size retained after adjustment.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was reported at a substantially higher rate in autistic women than non-autistic women, and the association remained significant even after controlling for family history.

The authors note that a prior genetic analysis has implicated genes such as matrix metalloproteinase 9 as co-implicated in both autism and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, suggesting a possible shared biological mechanism.
Neurological conditions overall were about twice as common among autistic participants relative to non-autistic participants.
Migraine was significantly more prevalent in autistic than non-autistic participants and remained significant across all adjustment models, at higher rates than typically reported in other studies.
Chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) was reported roughly three times more often in autistic than non-autistic participants, remaining significant across all models.
Syncope was reported roughly four times more often among autistic than non-autistic participants across all adjustment models.
Vertigo was reported roughly three to four times more often among autistic than non-autistic participants across adjustment models.

Unlike epilepsy in autistic females (which showed a large elevated risk), epilepsy/seizure rates did not significantly differ between autistic and non-autistic males, contrary to prior literature showing elevated epilepsy risk in autism, likely due to under-sampling of autistic males and those with co-occurring intellectual disability.
Renal/hepatic conditions overall, and urinary incontinence specifically, were significantly more common among autistic participants.
Reproductive endocrine conditions - polycystic ovarian syndrome, premenstrual tension, and endometriosis - were significantly more common in autistic women than non-autistic women.

In an age-stratified analysis, endocrine disorder prevalence was similar between autistic and non-autistic participants aged 41 and over, despite endocrine disorders being significantly elevated in autistic participants under 41.

Network analysis showed a more densely connected network of co-occurring physical health conditions among autistic participants than non-autistic participants, with a significant difference in overall global network strength.

Central sensitivity syndromes, including TMJ syndrome, IBS, ME/CFS, and fibromyalgia, were found at elevated rates among autistic compared to non-autistic participants, extending prior uncontrolled findings on CSS prevalence in autism.
Tinnitus was reported nearly four times more often in autistic than non-autistic participants across all adjustment models.
Dermatological conditions overall, including eczema, psoriasis, and acne, were significantly more common in autistic participants than non-autistic participants.

Psychomotor training significantly reduced mediolateral CoP displacement (CoPLx) in the trained group compared to pre-training.

In a cohort of 390 children with neurodevelopmental disorders (developmental delay/intellectual disability and/or autism spectrum disorder) screened via dried-blood-spot 3-OMD testing, none exceeded the diagnostic cutoff for AADC deficiency.

During assay validation, all 80 genetically confirmed AADC deficiency cases showed blood 3-OMD levels above the cutoff while all 110 control cases were below it, yielding 100% sensitivity and specificity.
Among the screened neurodevelopmental disorder cohort, classic AADC deficiency signs were present only in a minority: hypotonia in 14%, movement disorder in 9%, and dysautonomia in 2% of patients.
Epilepsy/EEG abnormalities were present in 27% of the screened neurodevelopmental disorder patients, a higher rate than typically reported in AADC deficiency.

A prior systematic review by the same group found that behavioral problems, including autistic features, are more frequently represented in AADC deficiency patients than classic cardinal signs such as ptosis or dystonia, though not pathognomonic, increasing underdiagnosis risk.

Population genetic analyses using gnomAD exome data found the worldwide heterozygous carrier frequency for pathogenic/likely pathogenic DDC variants to be 0.17%, with the highest frequency in East Asians (0.78%) and the lowest in South Americans (0.07%).
The estimated frequency of AADC deficiency in the European Union is 1 in 116,000, corresponding to about 45 new cases per year and an estimated 853 living patients.
A Taiwanese newborn screening program using 3-OMD testing on dried blood spots found an AADC deficiency prevalence of about 1 in 32,000, higher than a prior estimate of 1 in 42,000.
A separate genetic epidemiology study estimated the worldwide incidence of AADC deficiency at 1 in 1,374,129, and 1 in 65,266 among East Asians.

Gene therapy with eladocagene exuparvovec, an AAV2 vector delivering the DDC transgene administered intraputaminally, alleviates disease-related signs and symptoms and improves motor and cognitive performance in AADC deficiency, and is generally well tolerated.

A recent study found that approximately half of AADC deficiency patients were misdiagnosed before reaching the correct diagnosis, and about 80% of healthcare professionals took 12 months or more to refer patients to an experienced specialist.
Approximately 80% of previously described AADC deficiency patients present with a severe phenotype, characterized by little or no developmental milestones and full dependence on caregivers.

Patients with mild-to-moderate AADC deficiency phenotypes respond better to both pharmacological treatment (dopamine agonists, MAO inhibitors, vitamin B6) and gene therapy than those with severe phenotypes.

Individualized rehabilitative treatments such as CBT and graded exercise therapy, delivered by trained therapists within a supportive relationship, can help patients with CFS/ME gain control of their illness and achieve improvement or recovery.
After 40 years of research into CFS/ME, no specific biological defect, pathology, or biomarker has been identified for the condition.
Post-exertional malaise, though often considered specific to CFS/ME, is also observed in patients with other diagnoses.
Persistent fatigue occurs across many different illnesses, making it unlikely to indicate a single distinct disease with specific pathology.
Diagnoses such as CFS/ME, post-covid-19 condition, and burnout have questionable validity and reliability and show substantial overlap with one another despite implying different treatments.
Pathophysiological abnormalities reported in CFS/ME are non-specific and have also been found in patients with chronic pain, fibromyalgia, and conditions conventionally regarded as psychological.
The public narrative recommending inactivity, isolation, and sensory deprivation risks worsening symptoms and increasing associated disability.
A gradual, controlled increase in activity, deliverable in primary care, can reduce symptoms by allowing the affected stress-response systems to readapt to activity.
Patients with these fatigue-related conditions do recover and return to work, and receiving appropriate help improves their chances of recovery.
Among metabolites depleted in both acute and post-acute COVID-19, serotonin was the most significantly altered in the Penn Medicine PASC cohort.
Post-acute serotonin levels predicted whether a COVID-19 patient would fully recover or develop long-term sequelae.
In an independent Cork, Ireland cohort, serotonin was again one of the metabolites most strongly depleted in Long COVID patients versus healthy controls.
In contrast to other cohorts, no serotonin reduction was observed in participants of the longitudinally enrolled UNCOVR cohort, possibly reflecting lower overall PASC severity in that cohort.
In the UCSF LIINC cohort, plasma serotonin levels negatively correlated with the number of symptoms reported 3-4 months after acute COVID-19.
Serotonin levels measured during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection did not predict subsequent development of PASC.
Serotonin levels were strongly decreased in patients with non-SARS-CoV-2 systemic viral infections compared to healthy controls, suggesting a general feature of viral infection.
SARS-CoV-2 infection of K18-hACE2 and wild-type (beta variant) mice reduced circulating serotonin, mirroring findings in human cohorts.

Chronic (but not acute, cleared) viral infection sustains serotonin reduction: LCMV clone 13 (persistent) maintained low serotonin while LCMV Armstrong (acute, cleared) returned to baseline; VSV infection similarly decreased serotonin.

Repeated poly(I:C) injection (mimicking viral RNA) was sufficient to reduce plasma and platelet serotonin, an effect that was fully reversible within a week of stopping treatment, and was dependent on TLR3, IFNAR, and STAT1 signaling.

Pharmacological inhibition of the serotonin-synthesizing enzyme TPH1 enhanced viral loads and pathogenesis during VSV infection but had no effect on SARS-CoV-2 replication, indicating serotonin depletion is not a host-defense mechanism.
Plasma tryptophan was reduced in acute COVID-19 and remained decreased in Long COVID patients, and this was replicated in the UCSF LIINC and Rush University cohorts.

Plasma tryptophan was reduced during chronic LCMV infection and poly(I:C) treatment in mice, and feeding a tryptophan-deficient diet phenocopied poly(I:C)-induced serotonin reduction, supporting substrate limitation as a mechanism.

Although kynurenine was elevated during acute COVID-19, it was not persistently elevated in PASC, and neither IDO1 deficiency nor TDO2 inhibition prevented serotonin depletion, ruling out kynurenine production as the major driver of serotonin loss.

Poly(I:C)-induced viral inflammation strongly downregulated intestinal amino acid transporter genes including ACE2 (B0AT1 chaperone), Slc6a19 (B0AT1), Slc6a14 (ATB0,+), and Slc7a8 (LAT2), impairing tryptophan absorption.
In intestinal organoids, TLR3, NF-κB, and STAT1 were each required for poly(I:C)- and type I interferon-induced downregulation of Ace2 and Slc6a19, acting in an epithelial-intrinsic manner.
SARS-CoV-2-infected human small intestinal organoids showed strong transcriptional inhibition of ACE2 and SLC6A19, corroborating the mouse mechanism in a human system.

Autopsy tissue showed the gastrointestinal tract remained SARS-CoV-2 RNA-positive during the post-acute phase (>2 weeks) while other organs cleared virus, and viral RNA was also detected in the stool of a subset of PASC patients but not in symptom-free recovered controls.

Ace2-deficient mice showed a stepwise, gene-dose-dependent reduction in tryptophan levels and were unable to absorb an oral bolus of tryptophan, confirming ACE2's role in intestinal tryptophan uptake.

Supplementing poly(I:C)-treated mice with a glycine-tryptophan dipeptide diet (bypassing B0AT1) or with the serotonin precursor 5-HTP (bypassing tryptophan requirement) restored circulating tryptophan and/or serotonin levels.

Platelet counts were strongly decreased following acute VSV infection, chronic LCMV infection, and poly(I:C) injection, and poly(I:C)-induced thrombocytopenia was dependent on TLR3-IFN-STAT1 signaling.

Viral RNA sensing via poly(I:C) caused strong transcriptional downregulation of the intestinal amino acid transporters Slc6a14 (ATB0,+), Slc6a19 (B0AT1), Slc7a8 (LAT2), and their chaperone ACE2 in mouse ileum.

TLR3 deletion prevented poly(I:C)-induced downregulation of Ace2 and Slc6a19 in both mice and intestinal organoids, implicating TLR3-mediated viral RNA sensing as the trigger for loss of amino acid transporters.
Pharmacological inhibition of NF-κB (IKK-16) blunted the interferon response and prevented downregulation of Ace2 and Slc6a19 in poly(I:C)-treated intestinal organoids.
Direct exposure of small intestinal organoids to interferon-α or interferon-β was sufficient to reduce expression of tryptophan absorption genes, independent of viral RNA presence.

STAT1 was required in an epithelial cell-intrinsic manner for poly(I:C)-induced transcriptional inhibition of Ace2 and Slc6a19, demonstrated using STAT1-/- mice and intestinal epithelium-specific STAT1 deletion.

Downregulation of Ace2 and Slc6a19 in ileum occurred during both acute VSV infection and chronic LCMV clone 13 infection in mice, showing the transcriptional response generalizes to natural viral infections in vivo.
SARS-CoV-2 infection of human small intestinal organoids caused strong transcriptional inhibition of both ACE2 and SLC6A19.

In autopsy tissue from COVID-19 decedents, SARS-CoV-2 RNA remained detectable in the gastrointestinal tract during the post-acute phase (>2 weeks after infection) even as it cleared from most other organs.

SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in stool samples from a subset of individuals with PASC but not established similarly in a comparison group of individuals with prior infection but no persistent symptoms, suggesting a link between intestinal viral persistence and long-term symptoms.
Plasma tryptophan levels decreased in a stepwise, gene-dose-dependent manner from wild-type to heterozygous to homozygous Ace2-deficient mice.

Poly(I:C) treatment of heterozygous Ace2-deficient mice impaired oral tryptophan absorption comparably to homozygous Ace2 knockout, showing transcriptional Ace2 downregulation phenocopies genetic deficiency.
The number of serotonin-producing enterochromaffin cells in the intestine was unaltered by poly(I:C) treatment, ruling out loss of biosynthetic capacity as the bottleneck for serotonin depletion.
A glycine-tryptophan dipeptide diet, which bypasses the need for the B0AT1 transporter, restored both plasma tryptophan and serotonin levels in poly(I:C)-treated mice.
Supplementation with the serotonin precursor 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP), which bypasses the requirement for tryptophan uptake, rescued serotonin levels in poly(I:C)-injected mice.

Platelet counts were strongly decreased following acute VSV infection, chronic LCMV infection, and poly(I:C) injection, indicating virus-induced thrombocytopenia contributes to serotonin loss since platelets are the major reservoir of circulating serotonin.

Poly(I:C)-induced thrombocytopenia and increased mean platelet volume were dependent on TLR3, type I interferon signaling, and STAT1, indicating this signaling axis drives platelet loss during viral inflammation.

Antibody-mediated platelet depletion abolished circulating serotonin levels without affecting intestinal tryptophan uptake gene expression, demonstrating that platelet loss and reduced tryptophan uptake are independent contributors to serotonin depletion.
